# Best Postal Alternatives in 2026: Self-Hosted Mail Servers and Email Platforms Compared

Path: /blog/best-postal-alternatives
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-postal-alternatives
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-postal-alternatives.md

The best Postal alternatives for self-hosted email: Reloop, KumoMTA, Haraka, Plunk, useSend, Listmonk and mailcow, compared on what each one actually does, licenses, requirements, inbound mail and whether you still need Amazon SES.

**The short version:** if you want what Postal does (self-hosted sending with an HTTP API, SMTP and webhooks) **plus** templates, contacts, campaigns and real inboxes, pick **Reloop**. If you want a raw, high-volume MTA to build your own platform on, look at **KumoMTA** or **Haraka**. If you're happy for Amazon SES to do the actual sending, **Plunk** and **useSend** are lighter open-source platforms. **Listmonk** is the pick for newsletters only, and **mailcow** is for hosting people's mailboxes, not app email.

We build Reloop, so factor that in. Each section says plainly where another option is the better choice.

---

## Why teams look for a Postal alternative

[Postal](https://github.com/postalserver/postal) is a mature, MIT-licensed mail delivery platform with around 17k GitHub stars. It does sending well, and its IP pools with routing rules are excellent for isolating senders. Teams usually look elsewhere for one of these reasons (facts from [Postal's docs](https://docs.postalserver.io/)):

- **It's only the delivery layer.** There are no stored templates, contacts, campaigns or automations, so you still bolt those on.
- **Inbound mail is forwarded, not kept.** Postal sends incoming messages to an HTTP endpoint, an SMTP server or an address. There's no mailbox to thread, search or reply from.
- **There's no hosted option.** If you want to start hosted and self-host later, or fall back to a managed service, Postal can't do that.
- **The stack.** It's written in Ruby and requires MariaDB 10.6 or newer (MySQL isn't supported), which some teams would rather not operate.

---

## Top picks at a glance

| Category | Pick | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Best overall Postal alternative** | Reloop | Sending, templates, campaigns, automations and inboxes; hosted or self-hosted |
| **Best raw high-volume MTA** | KumoMTA | Rust MTA built for high-volume sending, scripted in Lua |
| **Best programmable SMTP server** | Haraka | Node.js SMTP server with a plugin for every stage |
| **Best open-source platform on top of SES** | Plunk | Transactional, campaigns, workflows; SES does delivery |
| **Best open-source Resend-style API on SES** | useSend | Developer API with a hosted tier; still in beta |
| **Best for newsletters only** | Listmonk | Single Go binary, very light, needs an SMTP server |
| **Best for hosting people's mailboxes** | mailcow | Full mail server and groupware suite |

---

## Three different kinds of "Postal alternative"

Search results mix up tools that solve different problems. It helps to sort them first:

1. **Email platforms** replace Postal and the tools around it: Reloop, Plunk, useSend.
2. **MTAs and SMTP servers** replace Postal's delivery engine and leave the rest to you: KumoMTA, Haraka.
3. **Adjacent tools** people consider by mistake: Listmonk (newsletters, needs an SMTP server like Postal or Reloop behind it) and mailcow (mailboxes for humans, not app email).

---

## The comparison table

| | Reloop | Postal | KumoMTA | Haraka | Plunk | useSend | Listmonk | mailcow |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **What it is** | Email platform | Mail delivery platform | MTA | SMTP server | Email platform | Email API | Newsletter manager | Mail server suite |
| **License** | Apache 2.0 | MIT | Apache 2.0 | MIT | AGPL-3.0 | AGPL-3.0 | AGPLv3 | GPL-3.0 |
| **Language** | TypeScript (Bun) | Ruby | Rust | Node.js | TypeScript | TypeScript | Go | Mixed (Postfix, Dovecot) |
| **Sends mail itself** | Yes (KumoMTA) | Yes | Yes | Yes | No (Amazon SES) | No (Amazon SES) | No (external SMTP) | Yes (Postfix) |
| **HTTP send API** | Yes | Yes | Injection API | No (plugins) | Yes | Yes | Template-based tx API | No |
| **Hosted option** | Yes | No | No | No | Yes | Yes | No | No |
| **Templates, contacts, campaigns** | Yes | No | No | No | Yes | Contacts and campaigns | Campaigns | No |
| **Automations** | Event-triggered | No | No | No | Workflows | Not listed | No | No |
| **Inbound** | Mailboxes, API, MCP, IMAP | Forward to HTTP, SMTP or address | Build it | Plugins | Routing rules | On the roadmap | No | Mailboxes (IMAP, webmail) |

Sources: [Postal](https://github.com/postalserver/postal), [KumoMTA](https://github.com/KumoCorp/kumomta), [Haraka](https://github.com/haraka/Haraka), [Plunk](https://www.useplunk.com/pricing), [useSend](https://usesend.com), [Listmonk](https://listmonk.app/), [mailcow](https://github.com/mailcow/mailcow-dockerized), [Reloop](/pricing).

---

## 1. Reloop: best overall Postal alternative

[Reloop](/self-host) is open-source email infrastructure under Apache 2.0. Like Postal it sends over an HTTP API and SMTP, signs mail with DKIM, fires signed webhooks and keeps a suppression list. On top of that it has stored templates (`{{{variables}}}`), contacts, campaigns, event-triggered automations, and inbound **mailboxes** your app, your agents or a person over IMAP can read and reply from. It delivers mail with KumoMTA, so there's no dependency on Amazon SES.

```bash
curl -fsSL https://reloop.sh/install.sh | sudo bash
```

**Pricing:** self-hosting is free, with no limits on emails, inboxes or domains. The [VPS guide](/docs/self-host/vps) lists a minimum of 2 vCPUs and 4 GB of RAM. If you'd rather not run servers, Reloop Cloud is Free (6,000 a month), Pro $10 for 50,000, and Growth $20 for 100,000 with a dedicated IP, hosted on Hetzner with EU data centers.

**Strengths**

- Replaces Postal **and** the template, contact, campaign and inbox tools you'd otherwise add.
- Real inbound mailboxes with threads, an MCP server and IMAP, not just forwarding.
- Same API hosted or self-hosted, so you can start on Reloop Cloud and move later by changing the SDK's `baseUrl`.
- PostgreSQL instead of MariaDB.
- Webhooks signed with HMAC-SHA256 in the `Reloop-Signature` header.

**Weaknesses**

- Postal's IP pools with per-sender routing rules are more flexible than Reloop's dedicated IPs, which matters if you run mail for many separate clients.
- Reloop runs more services (API services, dashboard, KumoMTA, PostgreSQL, Redis, NATS), so it's heavier than Postal.
- Self-hosting either one means owning IP reputation, warm-up and uptime.

**Best for:** teams that want Postal's self-hosted sending plus everything they'd otherwise build around it. Full breakdown: [Reloop vs Postal](/blog/reloop-vs-postal).

---

## 2. KumoMTA: best raw high-volume MTA

[KumoMTA](https://github.com/KumoCorp/kumomta) describes itself as "the first Open-Source high-performance MTA developed from the ground-up for high-volume email sending environments". It's written in Rust, licensed Apache 2.0, configured with Lua policy scripts, and accepts mail over SMTP or an HTTP injection API. It's also the MTA Reloop uses for delivery.

**Strengths**

- Built for very high volume, with fine-grained traffic shaping per destination.
- Policy as code in Lua.
- Apache 2.0.

**Weaknesses**

- It's only an MTA. No dashboard, no templates, no contacts, no inbound mailboxes, no suppression UI.
- You write the policy and the tooling around it.

**Best for:** email service providers and high-volume senders building their own platform. If you want KumoMTA with a product around it, that's what Reloop is.

---

## 3. Haraka: best programmable SMTP server

[Haraka](https://github.com/haraka/Haraka) is "a fast, highly extensible, and event driven SMTP server" written in Node.js and licensed MIT. Every stage of an SMTP transaction (connect, helo, mail, rcpt, data) is a hook you can extend with a JavaScript plugin, and it works as both an inbound filter and an outbound delivery engine.

**Strengths**

- Extremely flexible: write a plugin for any routing, filtering or logging rule.
- Lightweight, with a large plugin ecosystem.
- MIT license.

**Weaknesses**

- No built-in web interface or HTTP send API.
- Everything Postal gives you out of the box (credentials, webhooks, a dashboard) is yours to build.

**Best for:** teams that need custom SMTP behavior, such as an inbound gateway or a filtering relay, and are comfortable writing Node.js plugins.

---

## 4. Plunk: best open-source platform on top of SES

[Plunk](https://www.useplunk.com/) is an AGPL-3.0 email platform with a transactional API, SMTP, contacts, segments, campaigns, workflows and inbound routing rules. Self-hosted, it runs with Docker and sends through **your Amazon SES account**, so SES owns deliverability.

**Pricing:** hosted, a free tier of 1,000 emails a month with Plunk branding, then $0.001 per email with no base fee. Self-hosting is free, but you pay AWS for SES sending.

**Strengths**

- Full platform: transactional, campaigns and workflows.
- No IP warm-up when self-hosting, because SES does the sending.

**Weaknesses**

- Requires an AWS account, the SES sandbox review and SNS wiring.
- Mail passes through SES even when the app is on your server.
- AGPL-3.0.

**Best for:** teams that want a self-hosted platform without running their own MTA. Full breakdown: [Reloop vs Plunk](/blog/reloop-vs-plunk).

More options: [Plunk alternatives](/blog/best-plunk-alternatives)

---

## 5. useSend: best open-source Resend-style API on SES

[useSend](https://usesend.com) (formerly Unsend) is an AGPL-3.0 Resend alternative with a developer-friendly API, SMTP, signed webhooks, contacts and campaigns. Like Plunk, it sends through Amazon SES.

**Pricing:** hosted free tier of 3,000 a month (100 a day), then $0.40 per 1,000 transactional and $1.00 per 1,000 marketing emails, with a $10 monthly minimum.

**Strengths**

- Clean API in the style of Resend.
- Hosted tier if you don't want to run it.

**Weaknesses**

- Still in beta, per its README.
- Self-hosting needs AWS SES and SNS.
- Inbound email is on the roadmap, not shipped.

**Best for:** developers who want a lightweight open-source sending API and are fine with SES. Full breakdown: [Reloop vs useSend](/blog/reloop-vs-usesend).

More options: [useSend alternatives](/blog/best-usesend-alternatives)

---

## 6. Listmonk: best for newsletters only

[Listmonk](https://listmonk.app/) is a self-hosted newsletter and mailing list manager: a single Go binary plus PostgreSQL, licensed AGPLv3. Its homepage cites a 7+ million email campaign with a peak RAM use of 57 MB. It doesn't send mail itself; it delivers over SMTP to a server you configure, which can be Postal or Reloop.

**Strengths**

- Very light and fast.
- Mature campaign UI with SQL-based segmentation.

**Weaknesses**

- Not a Postal replacement on its own: it needs an SMTP server behind it.
- No drip sequences or inbound mail.

**Best for:** teams that only need newsletters. Pair it with Reloop's SMTP relay if you want a sender behind it. Full breakdown: [Reloop vs Listmonk](/blog/reloop-vs-listmonk).

More options: [Listmonk alternatives](/blog/best-listmonk-alternatives)

---

## 7. mailcow: best for hosting people's mailboxes

[mailcow: dockerized](https://github.com/mailcow/mailcow-dockerized) is a GPL-3.0 mail server and groupware suite that bundles Postfix, Dovecot, Rspamd, SOGo webmail and ClamAV in Docker.

**Strengths**

- Complete mail hosting for a team or organization: mailboxes, webmail, calendars and spam filtering.
- Large community.

**Weaknesses**

- Built for people's mailboxes, not app email. There's no HTTP send API, templates, webhooks or campaign tooling.

**Best for:** replacing Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 mailboxes, not replacing Postal. If you need both, run them on separate domains or subdomains.

---

## How to choose

- **"We want Postal's sending plus templates, campaigns and inboxes."** Reloop.
- **"We need per-client IP pools with routing rules."** Stay on Postal, or build on KumoMTA.
- **"We're building our own ESP and need a raw MTA."** KumoMTA or Haraka.
- **"We don't want to warm IPs or run an MTA."** Plunk or useSend on SES, or Reloop Cloud.
- **"We only send newsletters."** Listmonk with an SMTP server behind it.
- **"We need mailboxes for our staff."** mailcow.

---

## Switching from Postal

1. **Stand up the new system** on a fresh server, or sign up for the hosted option.
2. **Verify your sending domains.** Publish the new DKIM key and merge the new SPF include into your existing record (never publish a second SPF record).
3. **Swap the client.** Postal's `POST /api/v1/messages/message` with the `X-Server-API-Key` header becomes the new provider's send call. On Reloop, that's `reloop.mail.send`. SMTP users only change host and credentials.
4. **Move webhooks** to the new event names and verify signatures.
5. **Import your suppression list** so you don't email addresses that bounced or complained.
6. **Ramp traffic** over one to two weeks while watching bounce and complaint rates, then retire Postal.

---

## FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="What is the best open-source Postal alternative?">
    For most teams, Reloop: it's Apache 2.0, sends with its own MTA like
    Postal does, and adds templates, contacts, campaigns, automations and
    inbound mailboxes. For a raw MTA, KumoMTA.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Is there a hosted version of Postal?">
    No. Postal is self-host only. Reloop, Plunk and useSend each offer both a
    hosted service and a self-hosted edition.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Do I need Amazon SES to self-host?">
    Not with Reloop, Postal, KumoMTA or Haraka, which deliver mail
    themselves. Plunk and useSend send through SES, so you need an AWS
    account and production SES access.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Is mailcow a Postal alternative?">
    Not really. mailcow hosts mailboxes for people (IMAP, webmail,
    calendars). Postal and Reloop send email from applications.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="How much server do I need?">
    Postal's docs list 2 CPU cores, 4 GB of RAM and 25 GB of disk. Reloop's
    docs list a minimum of 2 vCPUs and 4 GB of RAM. Listmonk is far lighter,
    but it needs an SMTP server behind it.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# Self-Host Your Email Infrastructure for $5/Month

Path: /blog/self-host-email-5-dollars
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/self-host-email-5-dollars
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/self-host-email-5-dollars.md

A complete guide to running your own transactional email stack with Reloop on a cheap VPS (SMTP, REST API, analytics dashboard, and bounce handling) for less than a cup of coffee a month.

## The math on managed email providers

At 10,000 emails/month: SendGrid charges $19.95. Resend charges $20. Mailgun charges $15. Postmark charges $15.

Scale to 50,000/month and you're looking at $19.95 (SendGrid Essentials), $20 (Resend), or $35 (Mailgun). Per month. Every month. With per-email overages if you spike.

A Hetzner CAX11 ARM VPS costs **€3.29/month** (~$3.50). With a custom domain and proper DNS, running Reloop on that server gives you everything those managed providers offer (the REST API, the analytics dashboard, SMTP relay, bounce handling, webhook events, template management) for a fixed cost that doesn't scale with volume.

This guide walks you through the full setup, from provisioning the server to sending your first production email.

---

## What you get with a self-hosted Reloop stack

| Feature | Managed providers | Self-hosted Reloop |
|---------|-------------------|-------------------|
| REST API | ✅ | ✅ |
| SMTP relay | ✅ | ✅ |
| Analytics (opens, clicks, bounces) | ✅ | ✅ |
| Webhook events | ✅ | ✅ |
| Template management | ✅ | ✅ |
| Multi-tenancy | Paid plan | ✅ |
| Data ownership | ❌ | ✅ |
| Source code access | ❌ | ✅ |
| Monthly cost at 50k emails | $75–$90 | ~$4 |

## Prerequisites

Before starting, you need:

- A **VPS provider account** (we'll use Hetzner, but DigitalOcean, Linode, OVH, or Vultr all work)
- A **domain name** with DNS access (Cloudflare DNS is free and recommended)
- Basic comfort with **SSH and the Linux command line**
- About **45 minutes**

---

## Step 1: Choose and provision your server

### Minimum specs

| Resource | Minimum | Recommended |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| CPU | 1 vCPU | 2 vCPU |
| RAM | 1 GB | 4 GB |
| Disk | 20 GB | 40 GB |
| OS | Ubuntu 22.04 | Ubuntu 22.04 LTS |

For Hetzner specifically: the **CAX11** (ARM, 2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM, 40 GB SSD) at €3.29/month is the sweet spot. ARM instances have excellent price/performance for this workload.

### Provision on Hetzner

1. Go to [hetzner.com/cloud](https://hetzner.com/cloud) and create an account
2. Create a new project
3. Click **Add Server**
4. Select location closest to your users (Nuremberg/Helsinki for EU, Ashburn for US East)
5. Image: **Ubuntu 22.04**
6. Type: **CAX11** (ARM)
7. Add your SSH public key (or create one: `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your-email"`)
8. Click **Create & Buy Now**

Note your server's public IP address. You'll need it shortly.

### Important: check port 25

Many VPS providers block outbound SMTP (port 25) by default to prevent spam abuse. Hetzner blocks it initially. Before setting up email, **request port 25 to be opened** through Hetzner's support panel. They typically approve within a few hours for legitimate use cases. For what each port is for, see [SMTP ports explained](/blog/smtp-ports-explained).

While you wait, continue with DNS setup.

---

## Step 2: Configure DNS

Good DNS setup is what separates a self-hosted email stack that lands in the inbox from one that [goes straight to spam](/blog/why-emails-land-in-spam-fix). Do this before installing anything.

### A record: point your domain to the server

```
Type: A
Name: mail (or reloop, or whatever subdomain you prefer)
Value: YOUR_SERVER_IP
TTL: 300
```

This creates `mail.yourdomain.com` pointing to your server.

### PTR record (reverse DNS)

This is critical and often overlooked. A PTR record is the reverse of an A record: it maps an IP address back to a hostname. ISPs check PTR records to verify that the IP sending email is who it claims to be.

In Hetzner's console, go to your server → **Networking** → **Set rDNS** and set it to `mail.yourdomain.com` (matching your A record).

Most spam issues from fresh self-hosted setups come from missing PTR records. Don't skip this.

### MX record: for receiving email (optional but recommended)

If you want to receive email (not just send), add an MX record:

```
Type: MX
Name: @ (root domain)
Value: mail.yourdomain.com
Priority: 10
TTL: 3600
```

### SPF, DKIM, DMARC

You'll add these after Reloop is running. The dashboard gives you the exact records to add. If you want to know what each record does first, read our [SPF, DKIM and DMARC setup guide](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide). For now, add a placeholder SPF:

```
Type: TXT
Name: @ (root domain)
Value: v=spf1 ~all
TTL: 300
```

You'll update this once Reloop is running.

---

## Step 3: Install Docker and Docker Compose

SSH into your server:

```bash
ssh root@YOUR_SERVER_IP
```

Install Docker:

```bash
# Update package index
apt update && apt upgrade -y

# Install Docker
curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sh

# Install Docker Compose plugin
apt install docker-compose-plugin -y

# Verify
docker --version
docker compose version
```

---

## Step 4: Deploy Reloop

### Clone the repository

```bash
git clone https://github.com/reloop-labs/reloop /opt/reloop
cd /opt/reloop
```

### Configure environment variables

```bash
cp .env.example .env
nano .env
```

The critical variables to set:

```bash
# Your sending domain
MAIL_DOMAIN=mail.yourdomain.com

# A secure random string for API auth
RELOOP_API_SECRET=your-very-secure-random-string-here

# Database (Reloop includes Postgres in the compose file)
DATABASE_URL=postgresql://reloop:reloop@postgres:5432/reloop

# Your server's public IP or domain
PUBLIC_URL=https://mail.yourdomain.com

# SMTP settings (Reloop IS the SMTP server, but it needs your hostname)
SMTP_HOSTNAME=mail.yourdomain.com
```

Generate a secure API secret:
```bash
openssl rand -base64 32
```

### Start the stack

```bash
docker compose up -d
```

This pulls all images and starts:
- Reloop API server (port 3000)
- Reloop dashboard (port 3001)
- Reloop SMTP server (port 25, 587)
- PostgreSQL database
- Redis (for the job queue)

Check all services are healthy:

```bash
docker compose ps
docker compose logs --tail=50
```

---

## Step 5: Set up SSL with Caddy

You need HTTPS for the dashboard and API. Caddy is the easiest way to add automatic SSL:

```bash
apt install caddy -y
```

Create the Caddyfile:

```bash
nano /etc/caddy/Caddyfile
```

```
mail.yourdomain.com {
  reverse_proxy localhost:3000
}

dashboard.yourdomain.com {
  reverse_proxy localhost:3001
}
```

Start Caddy:

```bash
systemctl enable caddy
systemctl start caddy
```

Caddy automatically obtains Let's Encrypt certificates and handles renewal. Your API is now available at `https://mail.yourdomain.com/v1` and your dashboard at `https://dashboard.yourdomain.com`.

---

## Step 6: Configure authentication records

Open your dashboard at `https://dashboard.yourdomain.com`. On first login:

1. Add your sending domain (`mail.yourdomain.com`)
2. The dashboard shows you the exact DNS records to add:
   - **SPF**: the `include:` directive for your server
   - **DKIM**: two CNAME records with your public key
   - **DMARC**: a starter `p=none` record

Add them all to your DNS. Then click **Verify** in the dashboard. It will confirm each record is in place.

---

## Step 7: Send your first email

Create an API key in the dashboard under **Settings → API Keys**.

Test with curl:

```bash
curl -X POST https://mail.yourdomain.com/v1/emails \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "from": "hello@yourdomain.com",
    "to": "your-personal-email@gmail.com",
    "subject": "Hello from my self-hosted Reloop!",
    "html": "<p>It works. 🎉</p>",
    "text": "It works."
  }'
```

Check your inbox. If it's not there, check:
1. `docker compose logs reloop-api`: any errors?
2. `docker compose logs reloop-smtp`: SMTP handshake issues?
3. DNS is propagated: `dig TXT yourdomain.com` shows your SPF record?

A fresh server IP has no sending reputation yet. Ramp volume up over a few weeks with an [IP warming schedule](/blog/ip-warming-guide) instead of sending your whole list on day one.

---

## Step 8: Integrate with your application

The Reloop API is compatible with the Resend API shape. If you're [migrating from Resend](/blog/reloop-vs-resend), it's usually a one-line change:

```typescript
// Before (Resend)
const client = new Resend(process.env.RESEND_API_KEY);

// After (Reloop, self-hosted)
const client = new Reloop(process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY, {
  baseUrl: "https://mail.yourdomain.com/v1",
});

// The send call is identical
await client.emails.send({
  from: "hello@yourdomain.com",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Welcome",
  html: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
});
```

```bash

docker compose pull
docker compose up -d
```

Rolling restart with zero downtime for the API. SMTP connections in flight will complete before the old container stops.

### Monitoring disk usage

Email logs can grow fast. Set up a log rotation policy:

```bash
# Check current disk usage
df -h
docker system df

# Clean up old logs
docker system prune --volumes
```

Consider adding a monitoring alert when disk usage exceeds 80%.

## Is self-hosting right for you?

**Self-hosting is the right choice if:**
- You send predictable, moderate volume (< 500k/month)
- You care about data sovereignty or have GDPR/compliance requirements
- You want to eliminate per-email pricing as you scale
- You have basic DevOps comfort (or someone on your team does)

**A managed provider is better if:**
- You need zero operational overhead
- You're sending at very high volume (millions/month) where infrastructure complexity is real
- You need guaranteed SLAs with financial backing
- Your team has no one comfortable maintaining a Linux server

For most early-stage and growing startups, self-hosting Reloop on a $4–6/month VPS is the highest-leverage infrastructure decision you can make. The cost savings compound and the control you gain is permanent.

# Reloop vs Mandrill (2026): A Mailchimp Transactional Alternative

Path: /blog/reloop-vs-mandrill
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-mandrill
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-mandrill.md

Reloop vs Mandrill (Mailchimp Transactional) for developers: block pricing and the required Mailchimp plan, API and templates, webhooks, inbound, dedicated IPs, and how to migrate.

**Mandrill, now sold as Mailchimp Transactional, is a solid sending API with one big catch: you can't buy it on its own.** It's an add-on to a paid Mailchimp Standard or Premium plan, billed in blocks of 25,000 emails. **Reloop is a standalone email API with a free tier, $10 for 50,000 emails, inboxes for replies, and open-source code you can self-host.**

This post is for developers sending password resets, receipts and notifications from code. If you're comparing Mailchimp's marketing product, read [Reloop vs Mailchimp](/blog/reloop-vs-mailchimp) instead. We build Reloop, so weigh this accordingly. Mandrill's numbers below come from [Mailchimp's transactional pricing page](https://mailchimp.com/pricing/transactional-email/) and the [Mailchimp Transactional docs](https://mailchimp.com/developer/transactional/).

---

## The 30-second comparison

| | **Reloop** | **Mandrill (Mailchimp Transactional)** |
|---|---|---|
| Buy on its own | Yes | No: add-on to Mailchimp Standard or Premium |
| Free tier | 6,000 / mo, 200 / day | Up to 500 trial sends to a verified domain |
| Billing unit | Monthly plan + $0.50 per 1,000 over | Blocks of 25,000 emails |
| 50,000 emails / mo | **$10** | $40 in blocks + Mailchimp plan |
| 100,000 emails / mo | **$20** | $80 in blocks + Mailchimp plan |
| Dedicated IP | Included on Growth ($20) | $29.95 / mo add-on |
| Templates | `{{{variables}}}`, visual editor | Merge tags `*\|VAR\|*` or Handlebars |
| Webhook signing | HMAC-SHA256, `Reloop-Signature` | HMAC-SHA1, `X-Mandrill-Signature` |
| Inbound email | Mailboxes with threads, API, MCP, IMAP | Routes posted to your webhook |
| SMTP relay | Yes | Yes |
| Open source / self-host | Yes (Apache 2.0) | No |

---

## Pricing: blocks plus a Mailchimp plan

Mandrill's pricing has two parts.

**1. Blocks of 25,000 emails.** From Mailchimp's pricing page:

| Blocks per month | Emails | Price per block |
|---|---|---|
| 1–20 | Up to 500k | $20 |
| 21–40 | 500k–1M | $18 |
| 41–80 | 1M–2M | $16 |
| 81–120 | 2M–3M | $14 |
| 121–160 | 3M–4M | $12 |
| 161+ | 4M+ | $10 |

**2. A paid Mailchimp Marketing plan.** Transactional is "available as an add-on to Standard and Premium plans, or the legacy Monthly Plan". The Essentials plan isn't eligible, and there's no free entry point beyond up to 500 trial sends.

Here's what that means at common volumes, before the cost of the Mailchimp plan itself:

| Monthly volume | Reloop | Mandrill blocks only |
|---|---|---|
| 3,000 | $0 | $20 (1 block) |
| 50,000 | $10 | $40 (2 blocks) |
| 100,000 | $20 | $80 (4 blocks) |
| 250,000 | $20 + $75 overage = $95 | $200 (10 blocks) |

On top of the blocks you pay for a Mailchimp Standard or Premium plan, which is priced by your marketing contacts. If you only want to send transactional mail, you're paying for a marketing plan you may never use.

At very high volume the gap narrows. Above 4 million emails a month, a block costs $10, or $0.40 per 1,000, and Mailchimp advertises discounts through sales. If you send millions a month and already pay for Mailchimp, the math is closer than these tables suggest.

<Callout type="tip">
  Blocks are bought in whole units of 25,000. A month with 26,000 emails needs two blocks. Reloop's overage is per 1,000, so you only pay for what you send.
</Callout>

---

## Sending from code

Both APIs take a JSON payload and send one message per call.

**Mandrill**

```typescript

const client = mailchimpTx(process.env.MANDRILL_API_KEY!);

const response = await client.messages.send({
  message: {
    from_email: "hello@acme.com",
    subject: "Reset your password",
    html: "<p>Click the link to reset your password.</p>",
    to: [{ email: "user@example.com", type: "to" }],
  },
});
```

**Reloop**

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY! });

const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Reset your password",
  html: "<p>Click the link to reset your password.</p>",
});
```

A few differences in shape:

| | Reloop | Mandrill |
|---|---|---|
| Payload | Flat: `from`, `to`, `subject`, `html` | Nested under `message`, with `to` as `{ email, type }` objects |
| Errors | Returned as a value with `message`, `why` and `fix` | Thrown by the client |
| Stored templates | `template: { id, variables }` in the same call | Separate `messages/send-template` endpoint |
| SMTP host | `smtp.reloop.sh` | `smtp.mandrillapp.com` |
| SMTP password | Your API key | Your API key |

---

## Templates: merge tags and Handlebars

Mandrill supports two merge languages, chosen in your sending defaults or per message with `merge_language`:

- **Mailchimp merge tags:** `*|FNAME|*`
- **Handlebars:** `{{fname}}` (escaped) and `{{{fname}}}` (raw HTML)

Values go in `global_merge_vars` (one value for everyone) or `merge_vars` (per recipient).

Reloop templates substitute `{{{variable}}}` placeholders, with default values, a visual editor and versioning. They don't run logic. **This is a real point for Mandrill:** with Handlebars you can write conditionals and loops inside the template. With Reloop, you resolve those in your code and pass the result as a variable.

```typescript
await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
  to: user.email,
  subject: "Reset your password",
  template: {
    id: "tmpl_password_reset",
    variables: { name: user.name, reset_url: resetUrl },
  },
});
```

---

## Webhooks

Both send delivery events to your endpoint and sign them, but differently:

| | Reloop | Mandrill |
|---|---|---|
| Signature header | `Reloop-Signature` | `X-Mandrill-Signature` |
| Algorithm | HMAC-SHA256 | HMAC-SHA1, Base64 encoded |
| Signed content | Request body | Webhook URL plus sorted POST parameters |
| Payload | One JSON event per request | `mandrill_events` array, batched (up to 1,000 per request) |
| Event names | `email.delivered`, `email.bounced`, `email.complained`, ... | `send`, `hard_bounce`, `soft_bounce`, `open`, `click`, `spam`, `unsub`, ... |

Mandrill's batching is efficient at volume, but your handler must loop over the array and verify a signature built from form parameters rather than a raw JSON body.

---

## Receiving email

**Mandrill** handles inbound on a dedicated domain or subdomain. You point its MX records at Mailchimp, add routes with wildcard patterns like `*@reply.acme.com`, and Mailchimp posts each parsed message to your webhook. Storage, threading and replies are up to you.

**Reloop** receives mail into **mailboxes**. Messages are stored, threaded and spam-scored with Rspamd, and you can read them over the API, the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) or IMAP, and reply in-thread with one call. That's the difference between "here's a webhook" and "here's an inbox", and it matters if you're building a support inbox or an [AI agent that answers email](/blog/build-ai-agent-sends-emails).

---

## Deliverability and dedicated IPs

Mandrill has sent transactional mail for over a decade and handles the fundamentals well: SPF and DKIM, bounce and complaint handling, a rejection list, and open and click tracking.

The differences are cost and control:

- **Dedicated IP.** Mandrill charges $29.95 a month. Reloop includes one on Growth ($20/mo, 100k emails).
- **Sending path.** Reloop runs its own MTA (KumoMTA) with per-domain throttling and automatic pauses when bounce or complaint rates spike. See [how bounce processing works](/blog/email-bounce-processing-automation).
- **Checks before you send.** Reloop ships free [domain reputation](/tools/domain-reputation-checker), [blocklist](/tools/blocklist-checker) and [auth](/tools/auth-checker) checkers.

---

## Self-hosting and lock-in

Mandrill is hosted only, and tied to your Mailchimp account. Reloop is Apache 2.0: start on Reloop Cloud, and if you later need data residency or full control, run it on your own server with the [one-command installer](/self-host). Point the SDK's `baseUrl` at your instance and nothing else in your code changes.

---

## Where Mandrill is the better choice

- **Your marketing team already pays for Mailchimp Standard or Premium.** The plan cost is sunk, and keeping transactional mail in the same account is convenient.
- **You send millions of emails a month.** Block prices fall to $10 per 25,000, and sales discounts are available.
- **Your templates rely on Handlebars logic** and you don't want to move it into code.

Comparing more transactional providers? See the [best Mandrill alternatives](/blog/best-mandrill-alternatives).

## Where Reloop is the better choice

- **You only need transactional email** and don't want to pay for a marketing plan to get it.
- **You send under a few hundred thousand emails a month,** where Reloop costs a fraction of Mandrill's blocks.
- **You need replies as real inboxes,** for support or AI agents.
- **You want transactional mail, campaigns and automations** in one product with one suppression list.
- **You need open source or self-hosting.**

---

## Switching from Mandrill to Reloop

1. **Add your sending domain in Reloop.** Publish the DKIM record (`reloop._domainkey`) and merge `include:reloop.sh` into your existing SPF record. Don't create a second SPF record.
2. **Swap the client.** Replace `messages.send({ message })` with `reloop.mail.send`. Flatten the payload: `from_email` becomes `from`, and the `to` array of `{ email, type }` becomes a string or array of addresses (`cc` and `bcc` are separate fields).
3. **Move templates.** Map the placeholders:

   | Mandrill | Reloop |
   |---|---|
   | `*\|FNAME\|*` | `{{{fname}}}` |
   | `{{fname}}` (Handlebars) | `{{{fname}}}` |
   | `{{#if}}`, `{{#each}}` | Resolve in code, pass the result as a variable |
   | `global_merge_vars` / `merge_vars` | `template.variables`, one send per recipient |

4. **Switch SMTP** if you use it: host `smtp.reloop.sh`, port 587 with STARTTLS, API key as username and password.
5. **Import suppressions.** Export your Mandrill rejection list and import it into Reloop so you don't re-mail bounced or complaining addresses.
6. **Rewrite webhook handlers** for single JSON events signed with `Reloop-Signature`.
7. **Move inbound** if you use it: create a Reloop mailbox and point the inbound subdomain's MX records at Reloop.
8. **Ramp traffic** from 10% to 100% over a week or two, then cancel the Mandrill add-on.

Our [SendGrid migration guide](/blog/migrating-from-sendgrid) shows a traffic-split flag and a suppression import script you can reuse.

# Best Brevo Alternatives in 2026: Cheaper, Developer-Friendly and Open-Source Options

Path: /blog/best-brevo-alternatives
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-brevo-alternatives
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-brevo-alternatives.md

The best Brevo (Sendinblue) alternatives of 2026 compared: Reloop, Mailchimp, Mailjet, Loops, Customer.io, Elastic Email and Listmonk on pricing, free tiers, automations, deliverability, inbound and self-hosting.

**The short version:** if developers own your email and you send real volume, **Reloop** is the best Brevo alternative: $10 for 50,000 emails where Brevo's entry plan is $9 for 5,000, automations on every plan, a dedicated IP at $20, and open source. If you want to stay with a marketer-first suite, **Mailjet** has a 6,000-a-month free tier and a strong editor. If you only need newsletters and can host them, **Listmonk** is free.

We build Reloop, so factor that in. Every competitor fact below comes from our researched head-to-head posts, which link each provider's own pricing page, and each section says where that tool beats us.

---

## Why teams leave Brevo

Brevo (formerly Sendinblue) is a capable all-in-one marketing suite. People usually look elsewhere for one of these reasons:

1. **The price climbs with volume.** Starter begins at $9 for 5,000 emails, and larger volumes are set on a slider. Professional starts at $499 a month for 150,000 emails.
2. **Automations need a higher plan.** Automations, A/B testing and advanced stats start on Standard, from $18.
3. **Dedicated IPs sit on the higher tiers**, and Brevo's shared IPs carry a lot of marketing mail alongside your password resets.
4. **It's built for marketers, not developers.** Inbound mail arrives as a webhook, not a mailbox, and there's no self-hosted option.

If your team needs SMS, WhatsApp, live chat and a CRM in one bill, Brevo is still a good fit. We say when to stay at the end.

## 1. Reloop: best overall for developer-led teams

Reloop is open-source email infrastructure: a transactional API, SMTP relay, contacts, broadcast campaigns, event-triggered automations and inbound mailboxes in one product. Like Brevo, it charges for emails sent, not contacts stored, but each dollar goes much further.

**Pricing:** Free is 6,000 emails a month (200 a day). Pro is $10 for 50,000. Growth is $20 for 100,000 and includes a dedicated IP. Extra mail costs $0.50 per 1,000, and pay-as-you-go credits cost the same $0.50 per 1,000 and stay valid for 6 months. Self-hosting is free under Apache 2.0.

**Strengths**

- **$10 buys 50,000 emails**, where $9 buys 5,000 on Brevo's Starter.
- **Automations on every plan**, driven by events from your app:

```typescript
const { automationError } = await reloop.automations.start({
  event: "user.signed_up",
  email: user.email,
  firstName: user.name,
  properties: { plan: user.plan },
});
```

- A dedicated IP included at $20 a month, so product mail doesn't share a pool with other senders' newsletters.
- **Inbound mail as real mailboxes** with threads, readable over the API, the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) or IMAP, which suits support inboxes and AI agents.
- Errors return `message`, `why` and `fix`, and there are SDKs in nine languages.
- Reloop Cloud runs on Hetzner, a German hosting company, with EU data centers, which matters to many Brevo customers. Or [self-host](/self-host) it.

**Weaknesses**

- No SMS, WhatsApp, live chat, landing pages or sales CRM.
- Brevo's visual builder and templates are more mature for marketers.
- The free tier is smaller per day (200 vs 300).

**Best for:** product teams that send from code and want lower prices, automations without a plan upgrade, and the option to self-host.

## How to choose

1. **Do developers own your email, and do you send more than a few thousand a month?** → Reloop.
2. **Do you need SMS or push in the same journey, with deep segmentation?** → Customer.io (or stay on Brevo for SMS and WhatsApp on a smaller budget).
3. **Do you want a Brevo-style marketer suite with a bigger free tier?** → Mailjet.
4. **Is your list small and do you rely on integrations?** → Mailchimp.
5. **Do you want a focused SaaS lifecycle tool?** → Loops.
6. **Do you want cheap no-code newsletters with paid subscriptions?** → Elastic Email.
7. **Do you want free, self-hosted newsletters?** → Listmonk.

### When to stay on Brevo

- You need email, SMS, WhatsApp, live chat and a CRM in one bill.
- Your marketing team runs everything visually without engineers.
- You send a few hundred emails a day and the free plan's 300 a day covers you.

## Switching from Brevo

1. **Export contacts and suppressions**, including unsubscribed and blocklisted addresses, and import them as suppressed.
2. **Verify your domain** with the new provider. Merge its include into your existing SPF record rather than adding a second one. See our [SPF, DKIM and DMARC guide](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide).
3. **Move templates.** Brevo uses `{{ params.first_name }}`. In Reloop, placeholders use triple braces: `{{{first_name}}}`.
4. **Recreate automations**, ideally triggered by events from your app.
5. **Ramp traffic** over one to two weeks and watch bounce and complaint rates.

# SMTP Ports Explained: 25 vs 465 vs 587 vs 2525

Path: /blog/smtp-ports-explained
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/smtp-ports-explained
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/smtp-ports-explained.md

What each SMTP port is for, which one to use for sending email from your app, why port 25 is blocked on most clouds, and how to fix connection timeouts on 587 and 465.

**Use port 587 with STARTTLS to send email from an application.** Use port 465 if your client prefers implicit TLS. Use an alternate port such as 2525 or 2587 only when your network blocks 587. Do not use port 25 for sending from an app: it is for server-to-server delivery, and most cloud providers block it.

That is the short answer. The rest of this guide explains why, and how to fix the timeouts and TLS errors that come with picking the wrong port.

---

## SMTP ports at a glance

| Port | Purpose | Encryption | Use it for |
|------|---------|------------|------------|
| **25** | Relay between mail servers (MTA to MTA) | Optional STARTTLS | Receiving mail on your MX. Not for app sending. |
| **587** | Message submission (client to server) | STARTTLS, required | **Default choice** for apps and email clients |
| **465** | Message submission over implicit TLS | TLS from the first byte | Clients that prefer implicit TLS |
| **2525** | Unofficial alternate for 587 | STARTTLS | Networks that block 587 |
| **2587 / 2025** | Provider-specific alternates | STARTTLS, like 587 | Networks that block standard ports |

---

## Port 25: server to server only

Port 25 is the original SMTP port from 1982 ([RFC 821](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc821)). Today it has one job: **mail servers delivering to other mail servers.** When Reloop delivers your message to Gmail, it connects to Gmail's MX on port 25.

You should not send from your app on port 25:

- **AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, DigitalOcean, Hetzner and most residential ISPs block outbound port 25** by default to stop spam from compromised machines. Some unblock it on request, and many never do.
- Port 25 usually does not require authentication, so providers do not accept submissions there.
- Many networks allow it without TLS, so credentials and content can travel in plain text.

If you are self-hosting and need port 25 for **inbound** mail, that is fine. The [self-hosted email infrastructure guide](/blog/self-hosted-email-infrastructure) covers what to open.

---

## Port 587: the default for sending

Port 587 is the **message submission** port, defined in [RFC 6409](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6409). It exists so that mail clients and applications can hand mail to a provider with authentication, separate from server-to-server traffic.

The connection starts in plain text, then upgrades with the `STARTTLS` command before any credentials are sent:

```
S: 220 smtp.reloop.sh ESMTP
C: EHLO app.example.com
S: 250-smtp.reloop.sh
S: 250 STARTTLS
C: STARTTLS
S: 220 Ready to start TLS
   ... TLS handshake ...
C: EHLO app.example.com
S: 250 AUTH PLAIN LOGIN
C: AUTH PLAIN ...
```

A correctly configured provider refuses `AUTH` before `STARTTLS`, so your password is never sent unencrypted.

**Use 587 unless you have a reason not to.** Every SMTP library supports it, and almost no network blocks it.

---

## Port 465: implicit TLS

Port 465 has a messy history. It was registered for SMTPS in 1997, revoked a year later, and then **brought back for submission over implicit TLS** in [RFC 8314](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8314) in 2018.

With implicit TLS, the TLS handshake happens **as soon as the TCP connection opens**. There is no plain-text phase and no `STARTTLS` command. RFC 8314 actually recommends implicit TLS over STARTTLS because it removes the window for downgrade attacks.

### 465 vs 587

| | 587 | 465 |
|---|-----|-----|
| TLS starts | After `STARTTLS` command | Immediately |
| Downgrade risk | Low if the server requires STARTTLS | None |
| Library setting | `secure: false` (Nodemailer), `starttls()` (Python) | `secure: true` (Nodemailer), `SMTP_SSL` (Python) |
| Support | Universal | Universal in modern libraries |

Both are secure when configured correctly. The most common mistake is **mixing up the setting with the port**:

- `secure: true` on port 587 hangs, because the client waits for a TLS handshake the server never starts.
- `secure: false` on port 465 fails with `wrong version number` or `ECONNRESET`, because the server speaks TLS immediately.

---

## Port 2525: the fallback

Port 2525 is **not** an official SMTP port. Providers listen on it because some hosting companies and corporate firewalls block 587 and 465. It behaves like 587 (STARTTLS).

Some providers use other alternates. Reloop accepts submissions on **587**, **2587** and **2025**, all with STARTTLS. It does not offer implicit TLS on 465, so use 587 with `secure: false` (Nodemailer) or `starttls()` (Python). Check your provider's docs for the exact list.

---

## Which port should you use?

```
Sending from an app or script?
├── Yes → 587 (STARTTLS)
│         └── Blocked or timing out? → your provider's alternate (2525, 2587) or 465 if offered
└── No, I run a mail server receiving mail → 25 inbound
```

Or skip SMTP entirely. If you control the code, an **HTTP email API** avoids port blocking altogether because it runs on 443. It also gives you structured errors, idempotency and attachments without MIME encoding. See [how to send email in Node.js](/blog/send-email-nodejs) for both approaches side by side.

---

## Configuration examples

All examples use Reloop's SMTP relay. The username can be any string, and the password is your API key ([full SMTP docs](/docs/examples/smtp/introduction)).

### Nodemailer (Node.js)

```javascript

const transporter = nodemailer.createTransport({
  host: "smtp.reloop.sh",
  port: 587,
  secure: false, // STARTTLS. Reloop does not offer port 465
  auth: {
    user: "reloop",
    pass: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY,
  },
});
```

### Python smtplib

```python
from email.message import EmailMessage

msg = EmailMessage()
msg["From"] = "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>"
msg["To"] = "user@example.com"
msg["Subject"] = "Hello"
msg.set_content("Sent over port 587 with STARTTLS.")

with smtplib.SMTP("smtp.reloop.sh", 587) as server:
    server.starttls()
    server.login("reloop", os.environ["RELOOP_API_KEY"])
    server.send_message(msg)
```

For a provider that offers port 465, replace `smtplib.SMTP(...)` and `starttls()` with `smtplib.SMTP_SSL(host, 465)`. With Reloop, stay on 587 and use 2587 if 587 is blocked.

### Environment variables (most frameworks)

```env
SMTP_HOST=smtp.reloop.sh
SMTP_PORT=587
SMTP_SECURE=false
SMTP_USER=reloop
SMTP_PASSWORD=rl_your_api_key
```

Laravel, Django, Rails, Ghost, Supabase Auth and most CMSs accept these values directly.

---

## Troubleshooting SMTP connections

### Test whether a port is open

```bash
# STARTTLS ports (587, 2525, 2587)
openssl s_client -starttls smtp -connect smtp.reloop.sh:587 -crlf

# Implicit TLS (465), for providers that offer it
openssl s_client -connect smtp.example.com:465 -crlf

# Plain TCP reachability
nc -vz smtp.reloop.sh 587
```

If `nc` times out, the port is blocked between you and the server. Try the next port.

### Common errors

| Error | Likely cause | Fix |
|-------|-------------|-----|
| `ETIMEDOUT` / `Connection timed out` | Port blocked by your host or firewall | Switch to your provider's alternate port (2587 on Reloop) |
| `wrong version number` / `ECONNRESET` | `secure: false` on port 465 | Set `secure: true` or use 587 |
| Hangs on connect, no error | `secure: true` on port 587 | Set `secure: false` |
| `530 5.7.0 Must issue a STARTTLS command first` | Tried to `AUTH` before TLS | Call `starttls()` or enable `requireTLS` |
| `535 5.7.8 Authentication failed` | Wrong API key or password | Check the key and that it has sending access |
| `554 5.7.1 Relay access denied` | Not authenticated, or `From` domain not verified | Authenticate and [verify the domain](/docs/learn/domain) |
| `self signed certificate` | Connecting to a local or misconfigured server | Fix the certificate. Do not disable verification in production. |

Once mail is flowing, make sure it lands in the inbox: set up [SPF, DKIM and DMARC](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide) and check the [Gmail and Yahoo sender requirements](/blog/gmail-yahoo-bulk-sender-requirements).

---

## FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Is port 587 or 465 more secure?">
    Both encrypt the whole session when configured correctly. Port 465 starts
    TLS immediately, so there is no plain-text phase at all. RFC 8314 prefers
    implicit TLS for that reason. Port 587 is equally safe when the server
    refuses authentication before STARTTLS, which every reputable provider
    does.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Why is port 25 blocked on my server?">
    Cloud and residential providers block outbound port 25 to stop
    compromised machines from sending spam directly to mail servers. Use 587
    or 465 to send through a provider instead. If you need port 25 to deliver
    mail yourself, ask your host to unblock it, but expect a review.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="What SMTP port does Gmail use?">
    For sending through Gmail's own SMTP server (smtp.gmail.com), use 587
    with STARTTLS or 465 with implicit TLS. Gmail receives mail from other
    servers on port 25.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Is port 2525 an official SMTP port?">
    No. It is a convention some providers adopted as a fallback when 587 is
    blocked. It is not registered with IANA, so check that your provider
    actually listens on it.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Should I use SMTP or an HTTP API?">
    Use SMTP when the software only speaks SMTP, such as a CMS, Supabase Auth
    or a legacy app. Use the HTTP API when you write the code: it runs on port
    443, returns structured errors and avoids MIME encoding.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# Best Resend Alternatives in 2026: Cheaper, Open-Source and Self-Hosted Options

Path: /blog/best-resend-alternatives
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-resend-alternatives
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-resend-alternatives.md

The best Resend alternatives in 2026 compared: Reloop, useSend, Postmark, Amazon SES, SendGrid, Mailgun, MailerSend and Cloudflare Email Service on price at 50k and 100k emails, inbound, self-hosting and developer experience.

**The short version:** if you like Resend's API but want it cheaper, with real inboxes and the option to self-host, **Reloop** is the closest match: same API shape, $10 for 50k emails instead of $20, and open source. If you want open source on top of Amazon SES, look at **useSend**. If transactional deliverability is all you care about, **Postmark**. If you want the cheapest raw pipe and you're on AWS, **Amazon SES**.

Resend set the bar for a modern email API, and plenty of teams are happy on it. The reasons people look elsewhere are usually the same few:

- **Price at volume.** The free tier is generous (3,000 a month), but the next steps are $20 for 50k and $35 for 100k, with $0.90 per extra 1,000.
- **Hosted only.** There's no way to run Resend yourself, for data residency, security review or cost.
- **Inbound is a webhook.** Resend can receive mail and post each message to your webhook, but storage, threading and replies are yours to build.
- **Dedicated IPs** need the $90 Scale plan plus a $30/mo add-on.

We build Reloop, so weigh this accordingly. Every price below comes from our researched head-to-head posts and each provider's public pricing page, and each section says where that alternative beats us.

---

## Top picks at a glance

| Category | Pick | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Best overall Resend alternative** | Reloop | Same API shape, $10 for 50k, inboxes, open source |
| **Best open source on Amazon SES** | useSend | Resend-style API, AGPL, per-email pricing |
| **Best for transactional deliverability** | Postmark | A decade of transactional-only focus |
| **Cheapest raw sending pipe** | Amazon SES | $0.10 per 1,000, if you build the rest |
| **Best for enterprise procurement** | SendGrid | Twilio contracts, subusers, mature compliance |
| **Best for routing and validation** | Mailgun | Inbound routes, email validation |
| **Best no-code builder** | MailerSend | Drag-and-drop editor, SMS, split testing |
| **Best for apps on Workers** | Cloudflare Email Service | One binding, $0.35 per 1,000 |

---

## The comparison table

| | Resend | Reloop | useSend | Postmark | Amazon SES | SendGrid | Mailgun | MailerSend |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Free tier** | 3,000 / mo (100 / day) | 6,000 / mo (200 / day) | 3,000 / mo (100 / day) | 100 / mo | $200 credits, 6 months | 60-day trial, 100 / day | 100 / day, trial | 500 / mo |
| **~50,000 / mo** | $20 | **$10** | $20 | $87 | ~$5 | $19.95 | $35 | $35 |
| **~100,000 / mo** | $35 | **$20** | $40 | $177 | ~$10 | $34.95 | $90 | $68 |
| **Inbound** | Webhook | Mailboxes, API, MCP, IMAP | Roadmap | Webhook | Receipt rules | Parse webhook | Routes | Forwarding |
| **Campaigns** | Broadcasts | Yes + automations | Yes | Broadcast streams | No | Separate plans | Limited | Via MailerLite |
| **Open source** | No | Yes (Apache 2.0) | Yes (AGPL) | No | No | No | No | No |
| **Self-host** | No | Yes | Yes (needs SES) | No | No | No | No | No |

Postmark figures are Basic list price plus overage; Mailgun at 100k is its $90 Scale plan; useSend is our math from its per-email rates. Cloudflare Email Service is covered in its own section, since it bills through Workers Paid.

---

## 1. Reloop: best overall Resend alternative

[Reloop](/) is open-source email infrastructure: a transactional API, SMTP relay, inbound mailboxes, contacts, campaigns, automations and webhooks. Its API follows the same shape as Resend's on purpose, so switching is mostly a client swap.

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY! });

const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Welcome",
  html: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
});
```

**Pricing:** Free for 6,000 emails a month (200 a day), double Resend's free tier. Pro is $10 for 50,000, Growth is $20 for 100,000 with a dedicated IP, and extra mail is $0.50 per 1,000. Or skip the subscription and buy pay-as-you-go credits at $0.50 per 1,000, valid for 6 months. Self-hosting has no per-email fee.

**Strengths**

- **Half Resend's price at 50k and about 40% less at 100k.** Over a year at 100k a month, that's $180 saved, or $1,200 if you need a dedicated IP.
- **Inbound mail into real inboxes.** Messages are stored, threaded, spam-scored and readable over the API, the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) or IMAP, so AI agents and support teams can reply in-thread.
- **Transactional, campaigns and event automations** in one product with one suppression list.
- **Open source (Apache 2.0)** and self-hostable with a [one-command installer](/self-host). Reloop Cloud runs on Hetzner, a German hosting company, with EU data centers.
- **Dedicated IP on the $20 plan**, where Resend needs the $90 Scale plan plus a $30/mo add-on.
- **Errors that explain themselves**, with `why` and `fix` fields.

**Weaknesses**

- Smaller ecosystem of community examples than Resend.
- Hosted inboxes are capped by plan (3 on Free, 5 on Pro, 10 on Growth); self-hosted is unlimited.

**Best for:** teams past 50k emails a month, anyone building AI agents that handle email, and teams that want open source or self-hosting. Full comparison: [Reloop vs Resend](/blog/reloop-vs-resend). See also [Resend alternative](/alternatives/resend) and [compare Reloop and Resend](/compare/resend).

---

## 2. useSend: best open source on Amazon SES

[useSend](https://usesend.com) (formerly Unsend) is an open-source Resend alternative under AGPL-3.0. It wraps Amazon SES with a clean API, dashboard, contacts and campaigns, and offers a hosted cloud.

**Pricing:** Free for 3,000 a month (100 a day). Paid is usage-based with a $10 monthly minimum: $0.0004 per transactional email and $0.001 per marketing email.

**Strengths**

- Resend-style API and SDK, open source.
- At millions of transactional emails a month, $0.40 per 1,000 is hard to beat on a hosted plan.
- Self-hosting lets Amazon handle IP reputation.

**Weaknesses**

- Inbound email is on the roadmap, not shipped.
- Self-hosting needs an AWS account, SES sandbox approval, SNS callbacks and GitHub OAuth.
- Still marked beta.

**Best for:** teams already on AWS that want an open-source, SES-backed Resend. Full comparison: [Reloop vs useSend](/blog/reloop-vs-usesend).

More options: [useSend alternatives](/blog/best-usesend-alternatives)

---

## 3. Postmark: best for transactional deliverability

[Postmark](https://postmarkapp.com) has focused on transactional email for over a decade, with separate message streams so marketing mail never affects password resets.

**Pricing:** a developer plan with 100 emails a month. Basic is $15 for 10,000, then $1.80 per 1,000 ($87 at 50k, $177 at 100k at list price). Pro and Platform lower overage to $1.30 and $1.20.

**Strengths:** strong deliverability reputation, message streams, excellent docs and support.

**Weaknesses:** the most expensive option here per email, a tiny free tier, no contacts or automations, and hosted only.

**Best for:** teams where transactional inbox placement is the only priority and budget isn't. Full comparison: [Reloop vs Postmark](/blog/reloop-vs-postmark).

More options: [Postmark alternatives](/blog/best-postmark-alternatives)

---

## 4. Amazon SES: cheapest raw sending pipe

[Amazon SES](https://aws.amazon.com/ses/) is a sending pipe at $0.10 per 1,000 emails. Resend itself sends through SES.

**Pricing:** $200 in AWS Free Tier credits for the first 6 months, then $0.10 per 1,000 plus $0.12 per GB of outbound data. About $10 for 100k.

**Strengths:** the lowest per-email price, IAM, SNS and Lambda integration.

**Weaknesses:** you build the product around it: sandbox exit, bounce and complaint handling through SNS, suppression, templates, logs and inbound.

**Best for:** AWS-native teams with engineering time to build what Resend gave them. Full comparison: [Reloop vs Amazon SES](/blog/reloop-vs-aws-ses).

---

## 5. SendGrid: best for enterprise procurement

[SendGrid](https://sendgrid.com), part of Twilio, is the incumbent for large organizations.

**Pricing:** a 60-day trial at 100 a day. Essentials is $19.95 for 50k and $34.95 for 100k; Pro, with dedicated IPs, subusers and SSO, starts at $89.95.

**Strengths:** enterprise compliance, subuser management, full Handlebars logic in templates.

**Weaknesses:** no lasting free tier, marketing on separate plans, inbound is a parse webhook.

**Best for:** companies already inside Twilio that need procurement checkboxes. Full comparison: [Reloop vs SendGrid](/blog/reloop-vs-sendgrid).

---

## 6. Mailgun: best for routing and validation

[Mailgun](https://www.mailgun.com) is one of the original developer email APIs, with inbound routes, webhooks and email validation.

**Pricing:** a trial at 100 a day. Basic is $15 for 10,000; Foundation is $35 for 50,000, with overage from $1.30 per 1,000.

**Strengths:** regex inbound routes, detailed logs, validation built in.

**Weaknesses:** no real free tier, validation is an add-on, marketing sits in a separate product.

**Best for:** teams that need inbound routing rules and validation from one vendor. Full comparison: [Reloop vs Mailgun](/blog/reloop-vs-mailgun).

---

## 7. MailerSend: best no-code builder

[MailerSend](https://www.mailersend.com) is a developer API with the most complete no-code side here.

**Pricing:** free for 500 emails a month. Hobby is $7 for 5,000; Starter is $35 for 50k and $68 for 100k.

**Strengths:** drag-and-drop builder, SMS, email verification and split testing.

**Weaknesses:** small free tier, inbound is forwarded rather than stored, and each forward counts toward your quota.

**Best for:** teams where non-developers edit emails. Full comparison: [Reloop vs MailerSend](/blog/reloop-vs-mailersend).

---

## 8. Cloudflare Email Service: best for apps on Workers

[Cloudflare Email Service](https://developers.cloudflare.com/email-service/) adds sending to Cloudflare's Email Routing. From a Worker it's one binding and one `send()` call.

**Pricing:** sending to any recipient needs Workers Paid ($5 a month minimum), which includes 3,000 emails, then $0.35 per 1,000. About $21 at 50k and $39 at 100k.

**Strengths:** cheap at high volume, one `send()` call from a Worker, and unlimited inbound through Email Routing.

**Weaknesses:** sending is in public beta, your domain must use Cloudflare DNS, and it's transactional only with no templates, contacts or campaigns.

**Best for:** apps that live entirely on Workers and send only transactional mail. Full comparison: [Reloop vs Cloudflare Email Service](/blog/reloop-vs-cloudflare-email).

More options: [Cloudflare Email Service alternatives](/blog/best-cloudflare-email-alternatives)

---

## How to choose

- **"We like Resend's API but the bill is growing."** Reloop. Same shape, $10 at 50k and $20 at 100k.
- **"We need open source."** Reloop (Apache 2.0, its own MTA) or useSend (AGPL, on SES).
- **"We need agents or humans to read and reply to inbound mail."** Reloop, the only option here with stored mailboxes, MCP and IMAP.
- **"Deliverability for receipts is everything."** Postmark.
- **"We're on AWS and have engineers to spare."** Amazon SES.
- **"Procurement needs a big vendor."** SendGrid.
- **"Our app runs on Cloudflare Workers."** Cloudflare Email Service.

---

## Switching from Resend

Most of the work is DNS, not code.

1. **Add your domain** in the new provider and publish its DKIM record. Merge its SPF include into your existing SPF record; never publish a second one.
2. **Swap the client.** For Reloop, replace `resend.emails.send` with `reloop.mail.send` and rename `replyTo` to `reply_to` and `scheduledAt` to `scheduled_at`.
3. **Move templates.** React Email components keep working. Stored templates in Reloop use triple braces: `{{{first_name}}}`.
4. **Import suppressions** so you don't email addresses that bounced or unsubscribed.
5. **Point webhooks** at a new handler. Reloop's events (`email.delivered`, `email.bounced` and so on) are signed with HMAC-SHA256 in the `Reloop-Signature` header.
6. **Ramp traffic** from 10% to 100% over one to two weeks, then remove Resend's DNS records.

# Introducing Reloop: Open-Source Email Infrastructure Developers Actually Want to Use

Path: /blog/introducing-reloop
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/introducing-reloop
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/introducing-reloop.md

Open-source email infrastructure for indie hackers, startups, product teams, and enterprises. Ship transactional mail, agent inboxes, and inbound on Reloop Cloud or self-host: same product, no lock-in.

Here's the one thing every developer and every company cares about with email infrastructure:

**Will the mail land, and will we still own the stack when it does?**

Pretty dashboards, fancy editors, and feature checklists are secondary. Password resets, receipts, and agent replies only matter if they reach the inbox, stay affordable as you grow, and don't trap you in a vendor you can't leave.

Today we're introducing Reloop: [open-source email infrastructure](https://github.com/reloop-labs/reloop) built around the five things people actually evaluate when they pick (or regret picking) an email provider. Prefer a side-by-side? Start with [Compare Reloop](/compare) or our [2026 provider comparison](/blog/email-provider-comparison-2026).

## The five things that matter

### 1. Deliverability

If mail lands in spam, nothing else counts. Reloop is built as real [delivery infrastructure](/features/deliverability): [SMTP](/features/smtp), [DKIM/SPF-oriented setup](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide), bounce classification, and the operational pieces that keep reputation from becoming someone else's mystery. Use Reloop Cloud when you want managed reputation and IP pools. [Self-host](/self-host) when you want the sending path on your own terms. See [self-hosted email infrastructure](/blog/self-hosted-email-infrastructure) for when that tradeoff is worth it.

### 2. Developer experience

You should ship a [transactional email](/features/transaction-emails) in minutes, not a sprint. Reloop has a clean REST API (familiar if you've used modern email APIs), [SDKs for every major language](/sdk), and [SMTP drop-in](/features/smtp) for Nodemailer, Laravel, Django, and the rest. Prefer the product tour for builders? See [Developers](/developers).

<SendEmailCodeSamples />

Local and production should feel like the same product. [Docs](/docs) should help you ship, not send you hunting.

### 3. Cost that doesn't punish growth

Email SaaS pricing often feels cheap at low volume and painful once you scale. Don't take that on faith. Check the numbers yourself:

- [Reloop pricing](/pricing) for hosted plans and what you get at each tier
- [Compare Reloop vs Resend](/compare/resend), [vs SendGrid](/compare/sendgrid), [vs Mailgun](/compare/mailgun), and [vs AWS SES](/compare/aws-ses)
- Full grid: [all provider comparisons](/compare)
- Deeper write-up: [email provider comparison 2026](/blog/email-provider-comparison-2026)

Reloop gives you two answers: a hosted path when you want zero ops, and a [full open-source path](/self-host) when you want to run the stack yourself and stop renting your outbound channel forever, including a [low-cost self-host path](/blog/self-host-email-5-dollars) if you're optimizing ops spend.

### 4. Ownership (no vendor lock-in)

This is the quiet deal-breaker. Proprietary APIs, opaque logs, and "you can't leave without a rewrite" are how email becomes a hostage situation. Reloop is [Apache 2.0](/license). The cloud product runs the same codebase you can `docker compose up` on Fly, Coolify, Kubernetes, or your own machines. See [Fly.io](/blog/reloop-flyio-deployment) and [Coolify](/blog/reloop-coolify-setup) guides, or the [self-host docs](/self-host). Audit it. Fork it. Move it. Your data and compliance boundary stay yours. More on the bet: [why we open-sourced email infrastructure](/blog/why-we-open-sourced-email-infrastructure) and [why open source](/why-open-source).

### 5. Visibility and the full loop

"Did it send?" is not enough. You need deliveries, opens, clicks, bounces, and complaints as signed [webhooks](/features/webhooks) your app can act on: retries, suppressions, support alerts, plus [email analytics](/features/email-analytics) when you need the operational view. And for modern products (especially AI agents), send-only is half a system. Reloop includes inbound parsing, [agent inboxes](/features/ai-agents), and MCP support so agents can send, receive, and inspect mail with structured tools instead of scraping a random mailbox. See [email infrastructure for AI agents](/blog/email-infrastructure-for-ai-agents) and the [AI agent inbox use case](/use-cases/ai-agent-inbox).

## Why we open-sourced it

Linux, Postgres, Redis, Nginx: the boring foundations of the internet are open. Email sits in that category. If it fails, users can't log in, can't reset passwords, and can't get receipts.

Open source is how we make the five things above credible. You can read how delivery works. You can leave without rewriting your notification stack. The roadmap gets shaped by people shipping real mail, not only by a [pricing page](/pricing). Full rationale: [why we open-sourced email infrastructure](/blog/why-we-open-sourced-email-infrastructure) and our [product beliefs](/about).

We're not open-sourcing a demo. Reloop Cloud and Reloop open source are the same product, with the same APIs whether you use [hosted](/pricing) or [self-host](/self-host).

## Who should care

Indie hackers, startups, side projects, product teams, and enterprises: if you're looking for your thing in email, Reloop is built for you.

Maybe that's cheap transactional mail that doesn't become your most expensive utility ([pricing](/pricing)). Maybe it's multi-tenant delivery without standing up an MTA team. Maybe it's self-host or cloud with real ownership and no lock-in. Maybe you're migrating off [SendGrid](/compare/sendgrid), [Resend](/compare/resend), or [Mailgun](/compare/mailgun) and want parity without a science project ([SendGrid migration guide](/blog/migrating-from-sendgrid)). Or you're building AI agents that need inbound and outbound as [real infrastructure](/features/ai-agents).

Whatever your scale or stack, if deliverability, DX, cost, ownership, and visibility are how you judge email tools, keep Reloop on your radar, and verify the claims on [compare](/compare), [pricing](/pricing), and the [docs](/docs).

## Get in

- GitHub: [github.com/reloop-labs/reloop](https://github.com/reloop-labs/reloop) (star it, watch it, contribute)
- Cloud: [reloop.sh/dashboard/signup](https://reloop.sh/dashboard/signup) (first email in a couple of minutes)
- Docs: [Docs](/docs) · [Pricing](/pricing) · [Compare](/compare) · [Self-host](/self-host)
