# How to Send Email in Java: Jakarta Mail, Spring Boot and API

Path: /blog/send-email-java
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/send-email-java
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/send-email-java.md

Send email from Java with Jakarta Mail, Spring Boot's JavaMailSender, or an email API. Copy-paste examples for HTML email, attachments, background sending and retries without duplicates.

**Java sends email over SMTP with Jakarta Mail, the library formerly known as JavaMail.** Spring Boot wraps it as `JavaMailSender`. For anything in production, send through a provider: either over SMTP with Jakarta Mail or Spring's `spring.mail.*` settings, or over HTTPS with an email API SDK.

This guide covers plain Jakarta Mail, the Reloop Java SDK and Spring Boot, then the production details: attachments, background sending and safe retries.

Working in another language? See [how to send email in Node.js](/blog/send-email-nodejs) or [in Python](/blog/send-email-python).

---

## Which approach should you use?

| | Jakarta Mail / Spring `JavaMailSender` | Email API SDK |
|---|---------------------------------------|---------------|
| **Install** | `angus-mail`, or `spring-boot-starter-mail` | `sh.reloop:reloop-java` |
| **Transport** | SMTP on port 587 (STARTTLS) | HTTPS on port 443 |
| **Building the message** | `MimeMessage`, `MimeMultipart`, `MimeMessageHelper` | A `SendMailParams` object with `html`, `text`, `attachments` |
| **Errors** | `MessagingException` or Spring's `MailException` | `ReloopApiException` with an HTTP status |
| **Safe retries** | No, a retry can send twice | Yes, with an idempotency key |
| **Works with libraries that need `JavaMailSender`** | Yes, natively | Through SMTP settings |

If a framework or library already sends mail through `JavaMailSender`, use SMTP settings. If you are writing the send call yourself, use the API.

---

## Prerequisites

1. **Java 17 or later** (Spring Boot 3 requires it)
2. A **verified sending domain** with [SPF, DKIM and DMARC](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide)
3. An **API key** from the [Reloop dashboard](https://reloop.sh/dashboard). Keys start with `rl_`, and the same key works for the API and SMTP.

```bash
```

Keep the key in the environment or a secrets manager, never in your code or git.

## Method 1: Send email with Jakarta Mail

JavaMail was renamed Jakarta Mail when it moved to the Eclipse Foundation. Version 2.0 changed the package from `javax.mail` to `jakarta.mail`, so old tutorials that import `javax.mail.*` will not compile against current libraries or Spring Boot 3. The implementation is now called Angus Mail:

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.eclipse.angus</groupId>
  <artifactId>angus-mail</artifactId>
  <version>2.0.5</version>
</dependency>
```

It pulls in the `jakarta.mail-api` package. Then build a `MimeMessage` with a plain-text part and an HTML part:

```java

public class SendWelcome {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws MessagingException {
        Properties props = new Properties();
        props.put("mail.smtp.host", "smtp.reloop.sh");
        props.put("mail.smtp.port", "587");
        props.put("mail.smtp.auth", "true");
        props.put("mail.smtp.starttls.enable", "true");
        props.put("mail.smtp.starttls.required", "true");
        props.put("mail.smtp.connectiontimeout", "10000");
        props.put("mail.smtp.timeout", "30000");
        props.put("mail.smtp.writetimeout", "30000");

        Session session = Session.getInstance(props, new Authenticator() {
            @Override
            protected PasswordAuthentication getPasswordAuthentication() {
                return new PasswordAuthentication("reloop", System.getenv("RELOOP_API_KEY"));
            }
        });

        MimeMessage message = new MimeMessage(session);
        message.setFrom(new InternetAddress("Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>"));
        message.setRecipients(Message.RecipientType.TO, InternetAddress.parse("user@example.com"));
        message.setSubject("Welcome to Acme", "UTF-8");

        // Plain-text part first, then the HTML alternative
        MimeBodyPart text = new MimeBodyPart();
        text.setText("Welcome! Thanks for signing up.", "UTF-8");

        MimeBodyPart html = new MimeBodyPart();
        html.setContent("<h1>Welcome!</h1><p>Thanks for signing up.</p>", "text/html; charset=UTF-8");

        MimeMultipart body = new MimeMultipart("alternative");
        body.addBodyPart(text);
        body.addBodyPart(html);
        message.setContent(body);

        Transport.send(message);
    }
}
```

The username can be any string. The password is your API key.

`starttls.enable` upgrades the connection to TLS, and `starttls.required` makes the send fail instead of falling back to plain text if the upgrade does not happen. Set the timeouts too: Jakarta Mail waits forever by default, which can hang a thread when the network misbehaves.

### When port 587 is blocked

Some hosts block outbound 587. Reloop also accepts STARTTLS on port **2587** (and 2025), so only the port number changes:

```java
props.put("mail.smtp.port", "2587");
```

Reloop does not offer implicit TLS on port 465, so do not set `mail.smtp.ssl.enable` or use the `smtps` protocol with it. If the connection hangs or times out, see [SMTP ports explained](/blog/smtp-ports-explained).

### Handle SMTP errors

```java
try {
    Transport.send(message);
} catch (AuthenticationFailedException e) {
    System.err.println("Wrong API key");
} catch (SendFailedException e) {
    System.err.println("Rejected recipients: " + Arrays.toString(e.getInvalidAddresses()));
} catch (MessagingException e) {
    System.err.println("Send failed: " + e.getMessage());
}
```

Both `AuthenticationFailedException` and `SendFailedException` extend `MessagingException`, so catch them first.

### Can I send with Gmail from Java?

For a personal script, yes: use `smtp.gmail.com` on port 587 with an [App Password](https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/185833). For an app, no. Gmail limits personal accounts to about 500 recipients a day, every message comes from your `@gmail.com` address, and bulk sending gets the account suspended.

## Method 2: Send email with the Java SDK

### Install

Maven:

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>sh.reloop</groupId>
  <artifactId>reloop-java</artifactId>
  <version>2.0.0</version>
</dependency>
```

Gradle:

```kotlin
implementation("sh.reloop:reloop-java:2.0.0")
```

The SDK uses the JDK's built-in `java.net.http.HttpClient` and Jackson, so it adds no HTTP library to your build.

### Send an email

```java

public class SendWelcome {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ReloopClient reloop = new ReloopClient(System.getenv("RELOOP_API_KEY"));

        SendMailParams params = new SendMailParams();
        params.from = "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>";
        params.to = "user@example.com";
        params.subject = "Welcome to Acme";
        params.html = "<h1>Welcome!</h1><p>Thanks for signing up.</p>";
        params.text = "Welcome! Thanks for signing up.";

        try {
            SendMailResponse result = reloop.mail.send(params);
            System.out.println("Sent: " + result.id);
        } catch (ReloopApiException e) {
            System.err.println("Failed: " + e.getStatus() + " " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
```

The SDK **throws** unchecked exceptions:

- `ReloopApiException` for any non-2xx response or network failure. `getStatus()` returns the HTTP status, or `0` when the request never got a response. `getBody()` holds the API's `message` and `why`.
- `ReloopValidationException` when `from`, `to` or `subject` is missing. It is thrown before any HTTP call.

Create the client **once** and reuse it. It wraps a single `HttpClient`, which is safe to share between threads, and there is nothing to close. Requests time out after 30 seconds.

### Send to several recipients

`to`, `cc`, `bcc` and `replyTo` take either one address or a list:

```java

SendMailParams params = new SendMailParams();
params.from = "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>";
params.to = List.of("ada@example.com", "grace@example.com");
params.cc = "team@acme.com";
params.replyTo = "support@acme.com";
params.subject = "Your weekly report";
params.text = "Here is your report.";
params.tags = List.of(new SendMailTag("type", "weekly_report"));

reloop.mail.send(params);
```

Every address in `to` sees the others. For personalized mail, send one message per recipient.

### Send a stored template

Keep copy out of your code so non-developers can edit it. Create the template in Reloop, then send it by ID with variables:

```java

SendMailTemplate template = new SendMailTemplate();
template.id = "tmpl_welcome";
template.variables = Map.of("first_name", "Ada", "plan", "Pro");

SendMailParams params = new SendMailParams();
params.from = "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>";
params.to = "user@example.com";
params.subject = "Welcome to Acme";
params.template = template;

reloop.mail.send(params);
```

See [templates](/docs/learn/templates) for variables and defaults.

## Spring Boot

### SMTP with `spring-boot-starter-mail`

Add the starter. It brings in Angus Mail and auto-configures a `JavaMailSender` bean from `spring.mail.*` properties:

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-mail</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

```properties
# application.properties
spring.mail.host=smtp.reloop.sh
spring.mail.port=587
spring.mail.username=reloop
spring.mail.password=${RELOOP_API_KEY}
spring.mail.properties.mail.smtp.auth=true
spring.mail.properties.mail.smtp.starttls.enable=true
spring.mail.properties.mail.smtp.starttls.required=true
spring.mail.properties.mail.smtp.connectiontimeout=10000
spring.mail.properties.mail.smtp.timeout=30000
spring.mail.properties.mail.smtp.writetimeout=30000
```

Everything under `spring.mail.properties` is passed straight to Jakarta Mail, so these are the same settings as Method 1. Keep `mail.smtp.ssl.enable` off: Reloop uses STARTTLS, not implicit TLS. If 587 is blocked, set `spring.mail.port=2587`.

Use `MimeMessageHelper` to build a message with both bodies:

```java

@Service
public class WelcomeMailer {
    private final JavaMailSender mailSender;

    public WelcomeMailer(JavaMailSender mailSender) {
        this.mailSender = mailSender;
    }

    public void sendWelcome(String to) throws MessagingException {
        MimeMessage message = mailSender.createMimeMessage();
        // true = multipart, needed for text + HTML and for attachments
        MimeMessageHelper helper = new MimeMessageHelper(message, true, "UTF-8");
        helper.setFrom("Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>");
        helper.setTo(to);
        helper.setSubject("Welcome to Acme");
        helper.setText(
                "Welcome! Thanks for signing up.",
                "<h1>Welcome!</h1><p>Thanks for signing up.</p>");
        mailSender.send(message);
    }
}
```

`setText(plain, html)` only works when the helper is in multipart mode. `mailSender.send` throws Spring's unchecked `MailException`: `MailAuthenticationException` for a wrong key and `MailSendException` for connection or recipient failures.

### The SDK as a Spring bean

Register one `ReloopClient` for the whole application:

```java

@Configuration
public class ReloopConfig {
    @Bean
    public ReloopClient reloopClient(@Value("${reloop.api-key}") String apiKey) {
        return new ReloopClient(apiKey);
    }
}
```

```properties
# application.properties
reloop.api-key=${RELOOP_API_KEY}
```

Then inject it into a `@Service`:

```java

@Service
public class ContactMailer {
    private final ReloopClient reloop;

    public ContactMailer(ReloopClient reloop) {
        this.reloop = reloop;
    }

    public String forward(String visitorEmail, String message) {
        SendMailParams params = new SendMailParams();
        params.from = "Acme Website <contact@mail.acme.com>";
        params.to = "support@acme.com";
        params.replyTo = visitorEmail;
        params.subject = "New message from " + visitorEmail;
        params.text = message;
        return reloop.mail.send(params).id;
    }
}
```

And call it from a controller:

```java

@RestController
public class ContactController {
    private final ContactMailer contactMailer;

    public ContactController(ContactMailer contactMailer) {
        this.contactMailer = contactMailer;
    }

    public record ContactRequest(@Email @NotBlank String email, @NotBlank String message) {}

    @PostMapping("/contact")
    public Map<String, String> contact(@Valid @RequestBody ContactRequest body) {
        try {
            return Map.of("id", contactMailer.forward(body.email(), body.message()));
        } catch (ReloopApiException e) {
            throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.BAD_GATEWAY, "Could not send message", e);
        }
    }
}
```

The validation annotations need `spring-boot-starter-validation`. The visitor's address goes in `replyTo`, never in `from`. You can only send from your verified domain, and putting someone else's domain in `from` fails [DMARC](/blog/gmail-yahoo-bulk-sender-requirements).

### Quarkus

Quarkus has its own mailer extension, `quarkus-mailer`, configured the same way:

```properties
quarkus.mailer.from=Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>
quarkus.mailer.host=smtp.reloop.sh
quarkus.mailer.port=587
quarkus.mailer.start-tls=REQUIRED
quarkus.mailer.username=reloop
quarkus.mailer.password=${RELOOP_API_KEY}
```

Inject `io.quarkus.mailer.Mailer` and call `mailer.send(Mail.withHtml(to, subject, html))`. In dev and test mode the mailer is mocked by default and does not send anything. The Java SDK also works in Quarkus: produce a `ReloopClient` from a CDI producer method, just like the Spring `@Bean` above.

## Attachments

With the SDK, pass base64 content:

```java

byte[] pdf = Files.readAllBytes(Path.of("invoice-1042.pdf"));

SendMailAttachment invoice = new SendMailAttachment();
invoice.filename = "invoice-1042.pdf";
invoice.content = Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(pdf);
invoice.contentType = "application/pdf";

SendMailParams params = new SendMailParams();
params.from = "Acme Billing <billing@mail.acme.com>";
params.to = "user@example.com";
params.subject = "Your invoice #1042";
params.text = "Your invoice is attached.";
params.attachments = List.of(invoice);

reloop.mail.send(params);
```

With Spring's `MimeMessageHelper` in multipart mode, call `addAttachment`:

```java
helper.addAttachment("invoice-1042.pdf", new FileSystemResource("invoice-1042.pdf"));
```

With plain Jakarta Mail, wrap the text and HTML in a `mixed` multipart next to the file:

```java
MimeBodyPart content = new MimeBodyPart();
content.setContent(body); // the "alternative" multipart from Method 1

MimeBodyPart pdf = new MimeBodyPart();
pdf.attachFile(new File("invoice-1042.pdf"), "application/pdf", null);

MimeMultipart mixed = new MimeMultipart("mixed");
mixed.addBodyPart(content);
mixed.addBodyPart(pdf);
message.setContent(mixed);
```

Keep attachments small. Many inboxes reject messages over 25 MB, and large files hurt deliverability. For big files, send a signed download link.

---

## Send in the background with @Async

Sending inside a web request adds latency and fails the request when the provider is slow. In Spring Boot, the quickest fix is `@Async`. Turn it on once:

```java

@SpringBootApplication
@EnableAsync
public class Application {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(Application.class, args);
    }
}
```

Then mark the send method `@Async` and retry only the errors that can succeed on a second try:

```java

@Service
public class SignupMailer {
    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(SignupMailer.class);
    private static final int MAX_ATTEMPTS = 5;

    private final ReloopClient reloop;

    public SignupMailer(ReloopClient reloop) {
        this.reloop = reloop;
    }

    @Async
    public void sendWelcome(String email) throws InterruptedException {
        SendMailParams params = new SendMailParams();
        params.from = "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>";
        params.to = email;
        params.subject = "Welcome to Acme";
        params.text = "Thanks for signing up.";

        for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
            try {
                reloop.mail.send(params);
                return;
            } catch (ReloopApiException e) {
                if (!isRetryable(e) || attempt == MAX_ATTEMPTS) {
                    log.error("Welcome email to {} failed: {} {}", email, e.getStatus(), e.getMessage());
                    throw e;
                }
                Thread.sleep(1000L * (1L << attempt)); // 2s, 4s, 8s, 16s
            }
        }
    }

    private static boolean isRetryable(ReloopApiException e) {
        int status = e.getStatus();
        return status == 0 || status == 429 || status >= 500;
    }
}
```

**Retry** network errors (status `0`), `429` and `5xx`. **Do not retry** other `4xx` errors: an invalid address or unverified domain fails the same way every time.

Call `sendWelcome` from another bean, such as your controller, and it returns immediately. Calling it from inside `SignupMailer` itself skips the proxy and runs synchronously.

`@Async` runs on an in-memory thread pool, so pending emails are lost if the process restarts. For emails that must arrive, write a row to an outbox table in the same transaction as the business change and have a scheduled worker send pending rows, or hand the job to a persistent queue such as RabbitMQ, SQS or a job library like JobRunr.

---

## Retries without duplicate emails

A request times out and your code retries. If the first attempt actually went through, the user gets two emails. The API prevents this with an [`Idempotency-Key` header](/docs/api/idempotency): repeat a request with the same key and Reloop returns the original result instead of sending again.

The Java SDK does not set this header yet, so call the endpoint with `java.net.http.HttpClient`. Jackson is already on your classpath through the SDK:

```java

public class ReceiptSender {
    private static final HttpClient HTTP = HttpClient.newBuilder()
            .connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(10))
            .build();
    private static final ObjectMapper JSON = new ObjectMapper();

    public static String sendReceipt(String orderId, String to)
            throws IOException, InterruptedException {
        String body = JSON.writeValueAsString(Map.of(
                "from", "Acme <orders@mail.acme.com>",
                "to", to,
                "subject", "Receipt for order " + orderId,
                "text", "Thanks for your order."));

        HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
                .uri(URI.create("https://reloop.sh/api/mail/v1/send"))
                .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(30))
                .header("x-api-key", System.getenv("RELOOP_API_KEY"))
                .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
                .header("Idempotency-Key", "receipt-" + orderId)
                .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body))
                .build();

        HttpResponse<String> response = HTTP.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
        if (response.statusCode() >= 400) {
            throw new IOException("Send failed: " + response.statusCode() + " " + response.body());
        }
        return JSON.readTree(response.body()).get("id").asText();
    }
}
```

Base the key on the business event (`receipt-` plus the order ID), not a new UUID per attempt, so retries from any thread or server are safe. A `409` means a request with that key is still running: wait a second and retry with the same key.

---

## Testing without sending real email

- **Unit tests:** put the SDK behind your own small interface (for example `Mailer`) and mock that. `ReloopClient.mail` is a final field, so mocking the client directly is awkward.
- **Integration tests:** [GreenMail](https://greenmail-mail-test.github.io/greenmail/) runs an in-memory SMTP server inside JUnit 5. Register `GreenMailExtension` with `ServerSetupTest.SMTP`, point a `JavaMailSenderImpl` at `localhost:3025`, and assert on `greenMail.getReceivedMessages()`.
- **Local SMTP:** run [Mailpit](https://mailpit.axllent.org) with `docker run -p 1025:1025 -p 8025:8025 axllent/mailpit` and point a dev profile at it. Open `http://localhost:8025` to see the messages.

```properties
# application-dev.properties
spring.mail.host=localhost
spring.mail.port=1025
spring.mail.username=
spring.mail.password=
spring.mail.properties.mail.smtp.auth=false
spring.mail.properties.mail.smtp.starttls.enable=false
spring.mail.properties.mail.smtp.starttls.required=false
```

In staging, send to [test addresses](/docs/guides/testing-email-addresses) so you do not hurt your [sender reputation](/blog/why-emails-land-in-spam-fix) with bounces.

---

## Production checklist

- [ ] API key in an environment variable or secrets manager
- [ ] Sending domain verified with SPF, DKIM and DMARC
- [ ] `from` on your verified domain; user addresses in `replyTo`
- [ ] Both HTML and plain-text bodies
- [ ] One shared `ReloopClient` bean, created at startup
- [ ] SMTP timeouts set (`connectiontimeout`, `timeout`, `writetimeout`)
- [ ] Sending off the request thread (`@Async`, an outbox or a queue)
- [ ] Retries only on network errors, `429` and `5xx`
- [ ] Idempotency keys on anything that retries
- [ ] [Webhooks](/features/webhooks) for bounces and complaints
- [ ] Disposable addresses blocked at signup ([how](/blog/block-disposable-emails-at-signup))

## FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="How do I send an HTML email in Java?">
    With Jakarta Mail, build a MimeMultipart of type alternative with a
    plain-text MimeBodyPart and an HTML MimeBodyPart set to text/html. With
    Spring, create a MimeMessageHelper in multipart mode and call setText with
    both bodies. With the Reloop SDK, set html and text on SendMailParams.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="What is the difference between javax.mail and jakarta.mail?">
    They are the same library under two names. Jakarta Mail 2.0 moved the
    package from javax.mail to jakarta.mail. Spring Boot 3 and current
    application servers use jakarta.mail, so replace the javax.mail imports
    and the old com.sun.mail dependency with Angus Mail.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Should I use port 587 or 465 with Jakarta Mail?">
    Use 587 with mail.smtp.starttls.enable and mail.smtp.starttls.required set
    to true. Port 465 expects implicit TLS through mail.smtp.ssl.enable, which
    Reloop does not offer. If 587 is blocked, use 2587 with the same STARTTLS
    settings.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Is the Reloop Java SDK thread-safe?">
    The client holds no per-request state and sends through a single
    java.net.http.HttpClient, which is safe to share between threads. Create
    one ReloopClient at startup, for example as a Spring bean, and use it
    everywhere.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Why do my Java emails go to spam?">
    Usually the sending domain is not authenticated, or the From domain does
    not match the domain that signed the message. Set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC,
    send from your own domain, and always include a plain-text body.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# Reloop vs Brevo (2026): Pricing, Features and Which to Choose

Path: /blog/reloop-vs-brevo
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-brevo
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-brevo.md

Reloop vs Brevo compared honestly: pricing by email volume, the transactional API, campaigns and automations, inbound and agent inboxes, deliverability, self-hosting, and how to switch.

**Brevo (formerly Sendinblue) is an all-in-one marketing suite; Reloop is email infrastructure built for developers.** Both send transactional mail and marketing campaigns, and both price by emails sent rather than contacts stored. Brevo adds SMS, WhatsApp, live chat, a CRM and a drag-and-drop builder that marketers love. **Reloop gives you a cleaner developer API, mailboxes your AI agents can read and reply from, a dedicated IP at $20 a month, and an Apache 2.0 codebase you can self-host.**

We build Reloop, so weigh this accordingly. Brevo's prices below come from [brevo.com/pricing](https://www.brevo.com/pricing/), and where Brevo is the better pick, we say so.

---

## The 30-second comparison

| | **Reloop** | **Brevo** |
|---|---|---|
| Free tier | 6,000 / mo, 200 / day | 300 / day |
| Entry paid plan | **$10** for 50,000 emails | Starter from $9 for 5,000 emails |
| Plan with automations | Every plan | Standard and up (from $18) |
| Priced by | Emails sent | Emails sent |
| Dedicated IP | Included on Growth ($20) | Higher tiers only |
| Open source | Yes (Apache 2.0) | No |
| Self-host | Yes | No |
| Inbound email | Mailboxes with threads, API, MCP, IMAP | Inbound parsing to a webhook |
| Agent inbox | Yes | No |
| SMS and WhatsApp | No | Yes |
| CRM and live chat | No | Yes |
| SMTP relay | Yes | Yes |

Prices change; check [Brevo's pricing page](https://www.brevo.com/pricing/) and [ours](/pricing) before you commit.

---

## Pricing

Both products charge for the mail you send, not the size of your list, which already makes them cheaper than contact-priced tools like [Mailchimp](/blog/reloop-vs-mailchimp) for large, quiet lists.

The difference is in how far each dollar goes:

| | Reloop | Brevo |
|---|---|---|
| Free | 6,000 emails / mo (200 / day) | 300 emails / day |
| Cheapest paid plan | Pro: **$10 for 50,000 emails** | Starter: from $9 for 5,000 emails |
| Automations, A/B and advanced stats | Automations on every plan | Standard: from $18 |
| Large volume | Growth: $20 for 100,000, then $0.50 per 1,000 | Professional: from $499 (starts at 150,000 emails) |

Brevo's prices rise with a volume slider, so the exact price at 50k or 100k depends on the plan builder on their pricing page. What's published is the entry point: **$9 buys 5,000 emails on Brevo, while $10 buys 50,000 on Reloop.** At 100,000 emails a month, Reloop is $20 with a dedicated IP included.

Brevo's free plan is more generous day to day for small senders (300 a day vs 200), so if you send a few hundred emails a day and never more, it's worth a look.

And if you self-host Reloop, there's no per-email fee at all. You pay for the server. See [self-hosted email infrastructure](/blog/self-hosted-email-infrastructure) for what that really involves.

<Callout type="tip">
  Price the volume you expect in a year, not today's. Moving providers later means re-verifying DNS and rebuilding reputation.
</Callout>

---

## Developer experience

Brevo's transactional API is solid and well documented. It's one endpoint among many in a large marketing API, and it shows in the naming.

**Brevo**

```typescript
const res = await fetch("https://api.brevo.com/v3/smtp/email", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    "api-key": process.env.BREVO_API_KEY!,
    "content-type": "application/json",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    sender: { name: "Acme", email: "hello@acme.com" },
    to: [{ email: "user@example.com" }],
    subject: "Welcome",
    htmlContent: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
  }),
});
```

**Reloop**

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY! });

const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Welcome",
  html: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
});
```

| | Reloop | Brevo |
|---|---|---|
| Send endpoint | `POST /api/mail/v1/send` | `POST /v3/smtp/email` |
| Auth header | `x-api-key` | `api-key` |
| Body fields | `from`, `to`, `html`, `reply_to`, `scheduled_at` | `sender`, `to[]`, `htmlContent`, `replyTo`, `scheduledAt` |
| Template variables | `{{{first_name}}}` | `{{ params.first_name }}` |
| Error format | `message`, `why` and `fix` | `code` and `message` |
| React Email | Pass a component or rendered HTML | Rendered HTML |

Reloop's error shape is our one strong opinion. When a send fails, the error tells you **why** it failed and **how to fix it**:

```json
{
  "message": "Domain not found",
  "why": "The domain mail.acme.com was not found or is not authorized for your organization",
  "fix": "Ensure the domain is registered and verified in your dashboard"
}
```

---

## Campaigns, contacts and automations

This is Brevo's home turf. It started as a marketing platform and it shows:

- **Brevo** has a drag-and-drop email editor, a large template gallery, landing pages, signup forms, A/B testing, send-time optimization, a sales CRM, live chat, and SMS and WhatsApp campaigns in the same account.
- **Reloop** has contacts with custom properties, groups, subscription channels, scheduled broadcast campaigns and **event-triggered automations** with delays, conditions and email steps.

Reloop's automations are built to be driven from code. Your app reports an event and every automation listening for it starts for that contact:

```typescript
const { automationError } = await reloop.automations.start({
  event: "user.signed_up",
  email: user.email,
  firstName: user.name,
  properties: { plan: user.plan },
});
```

If your marketing team builds journeys visually and wants SMS in the same flow, Brevo is the better fit. If your product team wants onboarding and dunning emails triggered by app events, with the same API and suppression list as your transactional mail, Reloop is. See [welcome sequences that convert](/blog/welcome-email-sequences-that-convert) for a worked example.

---

## Receiving email and agent inboxes

**Brevo** supports inbound parsing: mail sent to your domain is posted to your webhook. Storage, threading and replies are up to you.

**Reloop** receives mail into **mailboxes**. Messages are stored, threaded, spam-scored with Rspamd, and readable over the API, the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) or IMAP. You can reply in-thread with one call, and there's an `email.received` webhook for push notifications.

| | Reloop | Brevo |
|---|---|---|
| Receive on your domain | Yes | Yes (inbound parsing) |
| Stored mailboxes with threads | Yes | No |
| Reply in thread via API | Yes | Build it yourself |
| MCP access for agents | Yes | No |
| IMAP access | Yes | No |

That matters if you're building [AI agents that read and reply to email](/blog/build-ai-agent-sends-emails), support inboxes, or reply-to-comment flows.

---

## Deliverability

Both handle the fundamentals: SPF and DKIM on your domain, bounce and complaint handling, unsubscribe management and suppression of bad addresses.

- **Sending path.** Reloop runs its own MTA (KumoMTA), with per-domain throttling and automatic pauses when bounce or complaint rates spike. Read [how bounce processing works](/blog/email-bounce-processing-automation).
- **Dedicated IPs.** Reloop includes one on Growth ($20/mo). On Brevo, dedicated IPs belong to the higher tiers.
- **Shared reputation.** Brevo's shared IPs carry a lot of marketing mail. That's fine for most senders, but if your password resets share a pool with newsletters, a dedicated IP or a provider focused on product mail can help.
- **Tools.** Reloop ships free [domain reputation](/tools/domain-reputation-checker), [blocklist](/tools/blocklist-checker) and [auth](/tools/auth-checker) checkers.

---

## Self-hosting and lock-in

Brevo is hosted-only. Your contacts, templates, logs and suppression lists live in Brevo's database.

Reloop is Apache 2.0. Start on Reloop Cloud, move to your own server later with the [one-command installer](/self-host) or [Coolify](/blog/reloop-coolify-setup), and point the SDK's `baseUrl` at your instance. Nothing else in your code changes.

Self-hosting isn't free in effort. You own IP reputation, warm-up and uptime. Most teams should start hosted and keep self-hosting as an option.

---

## Where Brevo is the better choice

- **Your marketing team runs email without engineers.** The visual builder, templates, forms and landing pages are mature.
- **You need SMS, WhatsApp, chat and a CRM** in one bill.
- **You send a few hundred emails a day** and the free plan's 300 a day covers you.

Weighing more than these two? See the [best Brevo alternatives](/blog/best-brevo-alternatives) for cheaper and developer-first picks.

## Where Reloop is the better choice

- **Developers own your email.** A clean API, SDKs in nine languages, and errors that tell you how to fix them.
- **You send real volume.** $10 for 50,000 emails and $20 for 100,000 with a dedicated IP.
- **You need inbound mail as real inboxes**, especially for AI agents.
- **You want open source or self-hosting** for compliance, data residency or peace of mind.

---

## Switching from Brevo to Reloop

1. **Add your domain in Reloop** and publish the DKIM record (`reloop._domainkey`). Merge `include:reloop.sh` into your existing SPF record. Don't add a second SPF record.
2. **Swap the send call.** Replace `POST /v3/smtp/email` with `reloop.mail.send`, and map `sender` → `from`, `htmlContent` → `html`, `replyTo` → `reply_to`, `scheduledAt` → `scheduled_at`.
3. **Move templates.** Change `{{ params.first_name }}` to `{{{first_name}}}`.
4. **Export contacts** from Brevo as CSV and import them into Reloop, keeping your custom attributes as contact properties. Bring your blocklisted and unsubscribed addresses across so nobody who opted out gets mail.
5. **Rebuild automations** as Reloop automations, and replace Brevo's event tracking with `reloop.automations.start`.
6. **Point webhooks** at a new handler. Reloop events are named `email.delivered`, `email.bounced`, `email.complained` and so on, signed with HMAC-SHA256 in the `Reloop-Signature` header.
7. **Ramp traffic** from 10% to 100% over a week or two, then remove Brevo's DNS records.

Our [SendGrid migration guide](/blog/migrating-from-sendgrid) covers the same steps in more detail, including a traffic-split flag and a suppression import script.

# How to Send Email in Rust: lettre, Axum and API

Path: /blog/send-email-rust
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/send-email-rust
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/send-email-rust.md

Send email from Rust with lettre over SMTP or with an email API. Copy-paste examples for Axum and Actix Web, HTML email, attachments, background sending with tokio and retries without duplicates.

**Rust has no email client in the standard library. Use the `lettre` crate to send over SMTP, or call an email API over HTTPS.** For anything in production, send through a provider either way, from a domain you have verified.

This guide covers `lettre` with async tokio, the Reloop Rust SDK, Axum and Actix Web, then the production details: attachments, background sending and safe retries.

Working in another language? See [how to send email in Python](/blog/send-email-python) or [how to send email in Node.js](/blog/send-email-nodejs).

---

## Which approach should you use?

| | `lettre` (SMTP) | Email API SDK |
|---|-----------------|---------------|
| **Install** | `cargo add lettre` | `cargo add reloop-email` |
| **Transport** | SMTP on port 587 (STARTTLS) | HTTPS on port 443 |
| **Building the message** | `Message::builder()`, `MultiPart` | A `serde_json::json!` value with `html`, `text`, `attachments` |
| **Errors** | `smtp::Error` with `is_permanent()` and `is_transient()` | `Result` with a boxed error |
| **Safe retries** | No, a retry can send twice | Yes, with an idempotency key |
| **Async** | Yes, with the `tokio1` feature | Yes, async only |

If you already have SMTP settings or need to work with a relay you do not control, use `lettre`. If you are writing the send call yourself, use the API.

---

## Prerequisites

1. **A recent stable Rust toolchain** (`rustup update stable`) and a tokio runtime
2. A **verified sending domain** with [SPF, DKIM and DMARC](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide)
3. An **API key** from the [Reloop dashboard](https://reloop.sh/dashboard). Keys start with `rl_`, and the same key works for the API and SMTP.

```bash
```

Keep the key in the environment or a secrets manager, never in your code or git.

---

## Method 1: Send email with lettre

`lettre` is the standard SMTP crate for Rust. It builds the MIME message, handles encoding and headers, and talks to the server. Enable the async tokio transport:

```toml
# Cargo.toml
[dependencies]
lettre = { version = "0.11", features = ["tokio1", "tokio1-native-tls"] }
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }
```

Then build a message with a plain-text and an HTML body, and send it:

```rust
use std::time::Duration;

use lettre::message::MultiPart;
use lettre::transport::smtp::authentication::Credentials;
use lettre::{AsyncSmtpTransport, AsyncTransport, Message, Tokio1Executor};

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let email = Message::builder()
        .from("Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>".parse()?)
        .to("user@example.com".parse()?)
        .subject("Welcome to Acme")
        // Plain-text body first, then the HTML alternative
        .multipart(MultiPart::alternative_plain_html(
            String::from("Welcome! Thanks for signing up."),
            String::from("<h1>Welcome!</h1><p>Thanks for signing up.</p>"),
        ))?;

    let creds = Credentials::new("reloop".to_owned(), std::env::var("RELOOP_API_KEY")?);

    // starttls_relay connects on port 587 and requires STARTTLS
    let mailer = AsyncSmtpTransport::<Tokio1Executor>::starttls_relay("smtp.reloop.sh")?
        .credentials(creds)
        .timeout(Some(Duration::from_secs(30)))
        .build();

    mailer.send(email).await?;
    Ok(())
}
```

The username can be any string. The password is your API key.

Build the transport **once** and reuse it. `AsyncSmtpTransport` keeps a connection pool and is cheap to clone. Not using async? `lettre::SmtpTransport` has the same builder and a blocking `send(&email)`.

### When port 587 is blocked

Some hosts block outbound 587. Reloop also accepts STARTTLS on port **2587** (and 2025), so only the port changes:

```rust
let mailer = AsyncSmtpTransport::<Tokio1Executor>::starttls_relay("smtp.reloop.sh")?
    .port(2587)
    .credentials(creds)
    .timeout(Some(Duration::from_secs(30)))
    .build();
```

Reloop does not offer implicit TLS on port 465, so do not use `relay()` with it: in `lettre`, `relay()` means implicit TLS on 465, and `starttls_relay()` means STARTTLS on 587. If the connection hangs or times out, see [SMTP ports explained](/blog/smtp-ports-explained).

### Handle SMTP errors

```rust
match mailer.send(email).await {
    Ok(response) => println!("Accepted: {:?}", response.code()),
    // 5xx reply: bad API key, rejected sender or recipient. Do not retry.
    Err(e) if e.is_permanent() => eprintln!("Rejected: {e}"),
    // 4xx reply: temporary. Safe to retry later.
    Err(e) if e.is_transient() => eprintln!("Try again later: {e}"),
    // Timeout, TLS or connection failure
    Err(e) => eprintln!("Send failed: {e}"),
}
```

A bad address fails earlier, when `.parse()` returns an `AddressError`. Parse user input before you queue anything.

### Can I send with Gmail from Rust?

For a personal script, yes: use `starttls_relay("smtp.gmail.com")` with an [App Password](https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/185833). For an app, no. Gmail limits personal accounts to about 500 recipients a day, every message comes from your `@gmail.com` address, and bulk sending gets the account suspended.

---

## Method 2: Send email with the Rust SDK

### Install

```bash
cargo add reloop-email serde_json
cargo add tokio --features full
```

The crate is `reloop-email` and you import it as `reloop_email`.

### Send an email

```rust
use reloop_email::ReloopClient;
use serde_json::json;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let reloop = ReloopClient::new(std::env::var("RELOOP_API_KEY")?, None);

    let sent = reloop
        .mail()
        .send(json!({
            "from": "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
            "to": "user@example.com",
            "subject": "Welcome to Acme",
            "html": "<h1>Welcome!</h1><p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
            "text": "Welcome! Thanks for signing up.",
        }))
        .await?;

    println!("Sent: {} ({})", sent.id, sent.status);
    Ok(())
}
```

`send` takes a `serde_json::Value`, so the field names match the [send email API](/docs/api/mail/post-api-mail-v1send) one to one. It returns `Result<SendMailResponse, Box<dyn std::error::Error>>`. On success you get `id`, `message_id` and `status`. On a non-2xx response the error message contains the API's JSON error body (`message`, `why`, `fix`), but the status code is not exposed as a field.

```rust
match reloop.mail().send(params).await {
    Ok(sent) => println!("Sent: {}", sent.id),
    Err(e) => eprintln!("Send failed: {e}"),
}
```

The error type is not `Send`. You cannot hold it across an `.await` inside `tokio::spawn`, or return it from a spawned task. Log it or turn it into a `String` right away.

Create the client **once** at startup and share it. It wraps a `reqwest` client with a connection pool. `ReloopClient` does not implement `Clone`, so put it in an `Arc`. The second argument to `new` is the base URL: pass `None` for Reloop Cloud, or `Some("https://mail.acme.com".to_owned())` if you [self-host Reloop](/blog/self-hosted-email-infrastructure).

### Send to several recipients

```rust
reloop
    .mail()
    .send(json!({
        "from": "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
        "to": ["ada@example.com", "grace@example.com"],
        "cc": "team@acme.com",
        "reply_to": "support@acme.com",
        "subject": "Your weekly report",
        "text": "Here is your report.",
        "tags": [{ "name": "type", "value": "weekly_report" }],
    }))
    .await?;
```

Every address in `to` sees the others. For personalized mail, send one message per recipient.

### Send a stored template

Keep copy out of your code so non-developers can edit it. Create the template in Reloop, then send it by ID with variables:

```rust
reloop
    .mail()
    .send(json!({
        "from": "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
        "to": "user@example.com",
        "subject": "Welcome to Acme",
        "template": {
            "id": "tmpl_welcome",
            "variables": { "first_name": "Ada", "plan": "Pro" },
        },
    }))
    .await?;
```

See [templates](/docs/learn/templates) for variables and defaults.

---

## Axum

Put the client in your router state and extract it in handlers. Axum clones the state for every request, so wrap the client in an `Arc`:

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;

use axum::{Json, Router, extract::State, http::StatusCode, routing::post};
use reloop_email::ReloopClient;
use serde::Deserialize;
use serde_json::{Value, json};

#[derive(Clone)]
struct AppState {
    reloop: Arc<ReloopClient>,
}

#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct ContactForm {
    email: String,
    message: String,
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let api_key = std::env::var("RELOOP_API_KEY").expect("RELOOP_API_KEY is not set");
    let state = AppState {
        reloop: Arc::new(ReloopClient::new(api_key, None)),
    };

    let app = Router::new()
        .route("/contact", post(contact))
        .with_state(state);

    let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind("0.0.0.0:3000").await.unwrap();
    axum::serve(listener, app).await.unwrap();
}

async fn contact(
    State(state): State<AppState>,
    Json(form): Json<ContactForm>,
) -> Result<Json<Value>, (StatusCode, &'static str)> {
    let sent = state
        .reloop
        .mail()
        .send(json!({
            "from": "Acme Website <contact@mail.acme.com>",
            "to": "support@acme.com",
            "reply_to": &form.email,
            "subject": format!("New message from {}", form.email),
            "text": &form.message,
        }))
        .await
        .map_err(|e| {
            eprintln!("contact form send failed: {e}");
            (StatusCode::BAD_GATEWAY, "Could not send message")
        })?;

    Ok(Json(json!({ "id": sent.id })))
}
```

This uses Axum 0.8 (`axum::serve` with a `TcpListener`). The `map_err` turns the SDK error into a response before anything else is awaited, which keeps the handler future `Send`.

The visitor's address goes in `reply_to`, never in `from`. You can only send from your verified domain, and putting someone else's domain in `from` fails [DMARC](/blog/gmail-yahoo-bulk-sender-requirements). Full example: [Axum guide](/docs/examples/rust/axum).

---

## Actix Web

Actix Web runs on tokio, so the same client works. Share it with `web::Data`, which is already an `Arc` inside:

```rust
use actix_web::{App, HttpResponse, HttpServer, post, web};
use reloop_email::ReloopClient;
use serde::Deserialize;
use serde_json::json;

#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct ContactForm {
    email: String,
    message: String,
}

#[post("/contact")]
async fn contact(reloop: web::Data<ReloopClient>, form: web::Json<ContactForm>) -> HttpResponse {
    let result = reloop
        .mail()
        .send(json!({
            "from": "Acme Website <contact@mail.acme.com>",
            "to": "support@acme.com",
            "reply_to": &form.email,
            "subject": format!("New message from {}", form.email),
            "text": &form.message,
        }))
        .await;

    match result {
        Ok(sent) => HttpResponse::Ok().json(json!({ "id": sent.id })),
        Err(e) => {
            eprintln!("contact form send failed: {e}");
            HttpResponse::BadGateway().body("Could not send message")
        }
    }
}

#[actix_web::main]
async fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let api_key = std::env::var("RELOOP_API_KEY").expect("RELOOP_API_KEY is not set");
    // Create the client once, outside the factory closure
    let reloop = web::Data::new(ReloopClient::new(api_key, None));

    HttpServer::new(move || App::new().app_data(reloop.clone()).service(contact))
        .bind(("0.0.0.0", 8080))?
        .run()
        .await
}
```

The closure passed to `HttpServer::new` runs once per worker thread. Build the client outside it, or every worker gets its own client and connection pool.

---

## Attachments

With the SDK, pass base64 content. Add the `base64` crate for the encoding:

```rust
use base64::{Engine as _, engine::general_purpose::STANDARD};

let pdf = tokio::fs::read("invoice-1042.pdf").await?;

reloop
    .mail()
    .send(json!({
        "from": "Acme Billing <billing@mail.acme.com>",
        "to": "user@example.com",
        "subject": "Your invoice #1042",
        "text": "Your invoice is attached.",
        "attachments": [{
            "filename": "invoice-1042.pdf",
            "content": STANDARD.encode(&pdf),
            "content_type": "application/pdf",
        }],
    }))
    .await?;
```

With `lettre`, wrap the body and the file in a `mixed` multipart:

```rust
use lettre::message::{Attachment, MultiPart, header::ContentType};

let email = Message::builder()
    .from("Acme Billing <billing@mail.acme.com>".parse()?)
    .to("user@example.com".parse()?)
    .subject("Your invoice #1042")
    .multipart(
        MultiPart::mixed()
            .multipart(MultiPart::alternative_plain_html(
                String::from("Your invoice is attached."),
                String::from("<p>Your invoice is attached.</p>"),
            ))
            .singlepart(
                Attachment::new(String::from("invoice-1042.pdf"))
                    .body(pdf, ContentType::parse("application/pdf")?),
            ),
    )?;
```

Keep attachments small. Many inboxes reject messages over 25 MB, and large files hurt deliverability. For big files, send a signed download link.

---

## Retries without duplicate emails

A request times out and your code retries. If the first attempt actually went through, the user gets two emails. The API prevents this with an [`Idempotency-Key` header](/docs/api/idempotency): repeat a request with the same key and Reloop returns the original result instead of sending again.

The Rust SDK does not set this header, and its errors do not carry the HTTP status you need to decide whether to retry. For sends that retry, call the endpoint directly with `reqwest`:

```toml
reqwest = { version = "0.13", features = ["json"] }
```

```rust
use std::time::Duration;

use serde_json::Value;

#[derive(Debug)]
struct SendError {
    status: u16, // 0 means the request never got a response
    message: String,
}

impl SendError {
    fn is_retryable(&self) -> bool {
        self.status == 0 || self.status == 429 || self.status >= 500
    }
}

async fn send_email(
    http: &reqwest::Client,
    api_key: &str,
    idempotency_key: &str,
    body: &Value,
) -> Result<Value, SendError> {
    let res = http
        .post("https://reloop.sh/api/mail/v1/send")
        .header("x-api-key", api_key)
        .header("Idempotency-Key", idempotency_key)
        // reqwest sends no User-Agent by default, and the API rejects requests without one
        .header("User-Agent", "acme-app/1.0")
        .json(body)
        .timeout(Duration::from_secs(30))
        .send()
        .await
        .map_err(|e| SendError { status: 0, message: e.to_string() })?;

    let status = res.status();
    if status.is_success() {
        return res
            .json()
            .await
            .map_err(|e| SendError { status: 0, message: e.to_string() });
    }

    Err(SendError {
        status: status.as_u16(),
        message: res.text().await.unwrap_or_default(),
    })
}
```

Base the key on the business event (`receipt-{order_id}`, `welcome-{user_id}`), not a new UUID per attempt, so a retry from any task or process is safe. Failed requests do not store the key, so you can fix the problem and retry with the same one.

---

## Send in the background with a tokio task

Sending inside a request handler adds latency and fails the request when the provider is slow. A simple option is a channel and a worker task that owns the retries:

```rust
use tokio::sync::mpsc;

struct WelcomeEmail {
    user_id: String,
    to: String,
}

fn spawn_email_worker(api_key: String) -> mpsc::Sender<WelcomeEmail> {
    let (tx, mut rx) = mpsc::channel::<WelcomeEmail>(1_000);
    let http = reqwest::Client::new();

    tokio::spawn(async move {
        while let Some(job) = rx.recv().await {
            let body = serde_json::json!({
                "from": "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
                "to": job.to,
                "subject": "Welcome to Acme",
                "text": "Thanks for signing up.",
            });
            // Same key on every attempt, based on the event
            let key = format!("welcome-{}", job.user_id);
            let mut delay = Duration::from_secs(1);

            for attempt in 1..=5 {
                match send_email(&http, &api_key, &key, &body).await {
                    Ok(_) => break,
                    Err(e) if e.is_retryable() && attempt < 5 => {
                        eprintln!("attempt {attempt} failed ({}), retrying", e.status);
                        tokio::time::sleep(delay).await;
                        delay *= 2;
                    }
                    Err(e) => {
                        // Other 4xx, or out of attempts: log it and move on
                        eprintln!("giving up on {key}: {} {}", e.status, e.message);
                        break;
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    });

    tx
}
```

Store the `Sender` in your Axum state and enqueue from the handler with `try_send`, which fails fast instead of waiting when the channel is full:

```rust
if let Err(e) = state.emails.try_send(WelcomeEmail { user_id, to: form.email }) {
    eprintln!("email queue full or closed: {e}");
}
```

**Retry** network errors (status `0`), `429` and `5xx`. **Do not retry** other `4xx` errors: an invalid address or unverified domain fails the same way every time.

Be honest about what this queue is. The channel lives in memory, so a deploy, crash or OOM kill loses every job still in it. That is fine for a "someone commented" notification. For email that must arrive, such as receipts and password resets, write the job to your database in the same transaction as the change that caused it (an outbox table), and have the worker read from that table and mark rows as sent. The idempotency key makes it safe for the worker to pick up a row twice.

---

## Testing without sending real email

- **Unit tests:** put sending behind a small trait of your own (for example `trait Mailer { async fn send(...) }`) and use a fake that records messages in tests.
- **Staging:** send to [test addresses](/docs/guides/testing-email-addresses) so you do not hurt your [sender reputation](/blog/why-emails-land-in-spam-fix) with bounces.
- **Local SMTP:** run [Mailpit](https://mailpit.axllent.org) with `docker run -p 1025:1025 -p 8025:8025 axllent/mailpit` and point `lettre` at it without TLS or credentials. Open `http://localhost:8025` to see the messages.

```rust
let mailer: AsyncSmtpTransport<Tokio1Executor> =
    AsyncSmtpTransport::<Tokio1Executor>::builder_dangerous("localhost")
        .port(1025)
        .build();
```

`builder_dangerous` skips TLS, which is what Mailpit expects. Only use it for local testing.

---

## Production checklist

- [ ] API key in an environment variable or secrets manager
- [ ] Sending domain verified with SPF, DKIM and DMARC
- [ ] `from` on your verified domain; user addresses in `reply_to`
- [ ] Both HTML and plain-text bodies
- [ ] One shared client or transport, created at startup and held in state
- [ ] Sending in a worker task, not the request handler
- [ ] A durable queue or outbox table for email that must arrive
- [ ] Retries only on network errors, `429` and `5xx`
- [ ] Idempotency keys on anything that retries
- [ ] [Webhooks](/features/webhooks) for bounces and complaints
- [ ] Disposable addresses blocked at signup ([how](/blog/block-disposable-emails-at-signup))

---

## FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="How do I send an HTML email in Rust?">
    With lettre, give the message builder a multipart body that holds a
    plain-text part and an HTML part, as in the example above. With the Reloop
    SDK, put html and text keys in the json! value you pass to send.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="What is the difference between relay and starttls_relay in lettre?">
    relay connects with implicit TLS on port 465. starttls_relay connects on
    port 587 and upgrades the connection with STARTTLS. Reloop only offers
    STARTTLS, so use starttls_relay, and add .port(2587) if 587 is blocked.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Is there a blocking Rust SDK?">
    The Reloop Rust SDK is async and needs a tokio runtime. In synchronous code,
    use lettre's blocking SmtpTransport, or build a tokio runtime and call
    block_on around the send.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Why do I get 'future cannot be sent between threads safely'?">
    The SDK returns a boxed std::error::Error that is not Send. If you keep it
    alive across an .await inside tokio::spawn or an Axum handler, the future
    is no longer Send. Convert the error to a String or log it before the next
    await.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Why do my Rust emails go to spam?">
    Usually the sending domain is not authenticated, or the From domain does
    not match the domain that signed the message. Set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC,
    send from your own domain, and always include a plain-text body.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# Reloop vs Listmonk (2026): Self-Hosted Newsletter and Email Platforms Compared

Path: /blog/reloop-vs-listmonk
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-listmonk
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-listmonk.md

Reloop vs Listmonk compared honestly: what each one is, sending infrastructure, newsletters vs transactional mail, automations, inboxes, resource use and licensing, plus how to switch or run them together.

**Listmonk and Reloop are both open source and both self-hostable, but they sit at different layers.** Listmonk is a newsletter and mailing list manager: it stores subscribers, builds campaigns and hands each message to an SMTP server you provide. Reloop is the email infrastructure itself: **it runs its own MTA, sends transactional and campaign mail, runs event-triggered automations, and receives mail into inboxes.** That's why many teams don't pick one: they point Listmonk at Reloop's SMTP.

We build Reloop, so weigh this accordingly. Every Listmonk fact below comes from [its GitHub repository](https://github.com/knadh/listmonk) and [documentation](https://listmonk.app/docs/), and where Listmonk is the better pick, we say so.

---

## The 30-second comparison

| | **Reloop** | **Listmonk** |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | Email infrastructure: API, SMTP relay, campaigns, automations, inboxes | Newsletter and mailing list manager |
| License | Apache 2.0 | AGPLv3 |
| Hosted option | Yes (Reloop Cloud) | No, self-host only |
| Sends mail itself | Yes, own MTA (KumoMTA) | No, needs an external SMTP server |
| Stack | Bun services, Postgres, KumoMTA | Single Go binary + Postgres |
| Transactional API | Yes | Yes (`POST /api/tx`, template-based) |
| Campaigns / newsletters | Yes | Yes, its core strength |
| Event-triggered automations | Yes | No drip sequences |
| Inbound email / inboxes | Yes, with threads, API, MCP and IMAP | No |
| Bounce handling | Built into the MTA | POP3 bounce mailbox or provider webhooks |
| Segmentation | Groups, properties, channels | SQL expressions |

---

## Different layers of the stack

The most useful way to understand the comparison is to look at what happens when you hit "send".

**With Listmonk**, the app renders your campaign, queues it, and delivers every message over SMTP to a provider you configure: Amazon SES, Postmark, your own Postfix, or anything else. Listmonk's homepage lists "multi-SMTP e-mail queues" and "throughput and sliding window rate limiting", so you can spread sends across several relays and throttle them. But IP reputation, DKIM signing and the actual delivery to Gmail or Outlook belong to whoever runs that SMTP server.

**With Reloop**, the same stack does both jobs. The API, campaigns and automations sit on top of a KumoMTA delivery pipeline with per-domain throttling and automatic pauses when bounce or complaint rates spike. If you self-host Reloop, you own that MTA. If you use Reloop Cloud, we run it.

So "Reloop vs Listmonk" is partly "Reloop vs Listmonk plus SES". Keep that in mind when you compare cost and effort.

---

## Pricing and running costs

Listmonk is free software with no hosted plan. Your costs are a small server for the app and Postgres, plus whatever your SMTP provider charges per email.

Reloop is free to self-host as well, or you can use the hosted plans:

| Monthly volume | Reloop Cloud |
|---|---|
| 6,000 (200 / day) | $0 |
| 50,000 | $10 |
| 100,000 | $20, includes a dedicated IP |
| Beyond 100,000 | $0.50 per 1,000 |

See [reloop.sh/pricing](/pricing) for current plans.

On resources, Listmonk is famously light. Its homepage describes a "single binary application with nominal CPU and memory footprint" and cites a 7+ million email campaign with a peak RAM use of 57 MB. Reloop does more (an MTA, inbound mail, spam scoring, automations), so it needs more: the [self-hosting requirements](/docs/self-host/requirements) list 2 vCPUs and 4 GB of RAM as a minimum.

---

## Newsletters and campaigns

This is Listmonk's home turf, and it's very good at it.

- **Lists with single and double opt-in**, scaling to millions of subscribers.
- **SQL segmentation.** You query subscribers with SQL expressions, which is extremely flexible if your team is comfortable with SQL.
- **Editors.** A visual drag-and-drop builder, WYSIWYG, Markdown, HTML and plain text.
- **Templates in Go's templating language**, with logic and 100+ functions.
- **Built-in analytics** for campaign performance, bounces and top links.
- **Media library** with S3-compatible storage, i18n, and OIDC single sign-on with roles.

Reloop's campaigns cover the same ground in a different shape: contacts with custom properties, groups, subscription channels so people can opt out of one kind of mail without leaving everything, and scheduled broadcasts. Segmentation uses properties and groups rather than raw SQL.

If your main job is a newsletter and you love SQL, Listmonk will feel at home.

---

## Transactional email

Both can send one-off messages from your app, but they approach it differently.

**Listmonk** has a transactional endpoint that renders a stored template for a recipient:

```bash
curl -u "api_user:token" -X POST https://listmonk.example.com/api/tx \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "subscriber_email": "user@example.com",
    "template_id": 3,
    "subscriber_mode": "fallback",
    "data": { "order_id": "1234" }
  }'
```

The template reads that data with `{{ .Tx.Data.order_id }}`. By default the recipient must already exist as a subscriber; `fallback` and `external` modes let you send to addresses that aren't in the database.

**Reloop** treats transactional mail as the main path, with an SDK and raw HTML or stored templates:

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY! });

const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <orders@mail.acme.com>",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Your order #1234",
  html: "<p>Thanks for your order.</p>",
});
```

On top of that you get per-message logs, delivery and bounce events, signed webhooks (`Reloop-Signature`, HMAC-SHA256), idempotency keys and scheduled sends. Stored templates use triple braces: `{{{order_id}}}`.

---

## Automations

Listmonk is intentionally a newsletter tool and doesn't ship drip sequences or event-triggered workflows. Teams that need them usually glue Listmonk's transactional API to an external workflow tool such as n8n.

Reloop has automations built in. You track an event from your app, and every active automation listening for it starts for that contact:

```typescript
const { automationError } = await reloop.automations.start({
  event: "user.signed_up",
  email: user.email,
  firstName: user.name,
  properties: { plan: user.plan },
});
```

Automations support delays, conditions and email steps. Our [welcome sequence guide](/blog/welcome-email-sequences-that-convert) builds a four-email onboarding flow this way.

---

## Receiving email

Listmonk is one-way. It sends mail and processes bounces, but it doesn't give you inboxes.

Reloop receives mail on your domains into **mailboxes**: messages are stored, threaded, spam-scored with Rspamd, and available over the API, the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) and IMAP. You can reply in-thread with one call. That covers "reply to this email" flows, support inboxes, and [AI agents that read and answer email](/blog/build-ai-agent-sends-emails).

---

## Bounces and deliverability

**Listmonk** processes bounces in two ways: by scanning a dedicated bounce mailbox over POP3, or by accepting webhooks. It understands webhooks from Amazon SES, Azure Communication Services, SendGrid, Postmark, Forward Email and Lettermint, plus a generic `/webhooks/bounce` endpoint. You then choose what happens at each threshold (none, blocklist or delete). Deliverability itself depends on your SMTP provider.

**Reloop** handles bounces, complaints and suppression inside the MTA, so there's nothing to wire up. One suppression list covers transactional mail, campaigns and automations. Free [domain reputation](/tools/domain-reputation-checker), [blocklist](/tools/blocklist-checker) and [auth](/tools/auth-checker) checkers help before you send.

---

## Licensing

Listmonk is **AGPLv3**. You can self-host and modify it freely, but if you offer a modified version to users over a network, the AGPL requires you to share those changes.

Reloop is **Apache 2.0**, a permissive license without that requirement. For most self-hosters neither license matters. It matters if you plan to embed or resell the software.

---

## Where Listmonk is the better choice

- **You only need newsletters.** Listmonk does that one job extremely well, with a mature UI and editors.
- **You want the smallest possible footprint.** A single Go binary and Postgres, running large campaigns in tens of megabytes of RAM.
- **Your team thinks in SQL.** Segmenting with SQL expressions is hard to beat for flexibility.
- **You already have a sending provider** you're happy with, such as SES at a contracted rate.

If you want to compare more newsletter tools, hosted or self-hosted, see the [best Listmonk alternatives](/blog/best-listmonk-alternatives).

## Where Reloop is the better choice

- **You send transactional mail and campaigns from one product**, with one suppression list and one set of logs.
- **You need automations** triggered by events in your app, without an external workflow tool.
- **You need inbound mail**, reply handling or inboxes for AI agents.
- **You don't want to run a separate SMTP provider.** Reloop includes the MTA, or you can use it hosted.

---

## Using them together

You don't have to choose. Listmonk can send through Reloop like any SMTP server:

1. **Verify your sending domain in Reloop.** Publish the DKIM record (`reloop._domainkey`) and merge `include:reloop.sh` into your SPF record.
2. **Create an API key** in the Reloop dashboard (it starts with `rl_`).
3. **In Listmonk, go to Settings → SMTP** and add a server:
   - Host: `smtp.reloop.sh`
   - Port: `587` with STARTTLS
   - Username and password: your Reloop API key
4. **Send a test campaign** to yourself and check the message in Reloop's logs.
5. **Forward bounces.** Reloop isn't one of Listmonk's built-in bounce providers, so subscribe a small handler to Reloop's `email.bounced` and `email.complained` webhooks and post them to Listmonk's `/webhooks/bounce` endpoint.

Listmonk keeps the newsletter UI your team knows, and Reloop handles delivery, transactional mail and inboxes.

## Switching from Listmonk to Reloop

If you'd rather run one system:

1. **Export subscribers** from Listmonk with their attributes and list memberships.
2. **Import them as contacts** in Reloop, mapping lists to groups or subscription channels and attributes to contact properties. Keep blocklisted and unsubscribed addresses suppressed.
3. **Recreate templates.** Change Go template expressions like `{{ .Subscriber.FirstName }}` to triple-brace variables such as `{{{first_name}}}`.
4. **Swap transactional calls** from `POST /api/tx` to `reloop.mail.send`.
5. **Rebuild recurring flows** as Reloop automations triggered by events from your app.
6. **Send a small campaign first**, watch bounce and complaint rates, then move the rest.

Our [self-hosted email infrastructure guide](/blog/self-hosted-email-infrastructure) covers running Reloop on your own server.

---

# How to Block Disposable Emails at Signup (Free Temp Email Checker)

Path: /blog/block-disposable-emails-at-signup
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/block-disposable-emails-at-signup
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/block-disposable-emails-at-signup.md

Stop throwaway signups before they bounce, burn free trials, and tank sender reputation. Use Reloop's free temp email checker: ~210k disposable domains, no SMTP probing.

Temporary inboxes are useful for privacy. They are expensive for anyone who sends email for a living.

A disposable address often dies within an hour. Every message you send after that is a hard bounce. Sustained bounce rates are how mailbox providers decide your domain belongs in spam, for every recipient, not just the throwaway ones.

If you run a SaaS free tier, a newsletter, or a product waitlist, disposable signups also inflate your metrics and farm your credits. The fix is simple: check the address at signup, before it lands in your database.

This guide covers when to block temporary emails, how a [temp email checker](/tools/temp-email-checker) works, and how to wire Reloop's free public API into a registration flow.

## What a temp email checker actually checks

A temp email checker (also called a disposable email detector) answers one question: *is this address from a known throwaway provider?*

Reloop's [free Temp Email Checker](/tools/temp-email-checker) does more than a domain string match. On each request it:

1. **Parses RFC syntax**: malformed input never reaches the catalogue or DNS.
2. **Matches ~210,000 disposable providers**, including Mailinator, Yopmail, Temp-Mail, Guerrilla Mail, and 10MinuteMail, plus wildcard suffixes for providers that mint endless subdomains.
3. **Flags role prefixes**: `info@`, `billing@`, `support@` are shared inboxes, not burners. They are reported separately so you can apply your own policy.
4. **Looks up MX records**: confirms the domain publishes a mail exchanger. That is routing evidence, not proof the mailbox exists.
5. **Never opens an SMTP session**: no mailbox probe, no stored addresses, no account required.

A disposable verdict means the domain is on the catalogue. A clear verdict means "not currently known to be disposable." New temp-mail services appear constantly, so treat the check as a strong signal, not a lifetime guarantee.

For a deeper walkthrough of detection methods, see [how to check if an email is disposable](/blog/disposable-email).

## Why disposable emails damage deliverability

Mailbox providers track bounce rate as a core reputation signal. Industry guidance keeps hard bounces well under ~2%. Throwaway inboxes make that threshold easy to miss:

- The mailbox is deleted minutes or hours after signup.
- Your welcome email, password reset, or drip sequence hard-bounces.
- Those failures are scored against your sending domain and IP.
- Reputation damage spreads to legitimate recipients: password resets and receipts start landing in spam.

That is the same chain that ends with [emails in the spam folder](/blog/why-emails-land-in-spam-fix). Authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) and [IP warming](/blog/ip-warming-guide) matter, but none of them fix a list full of dead temporary addresses.

Prevention sits in front of bounce handling. Validate at signup, then suppress hard bounces immediately so dead temporary addresses never get a second send.

## Signup abuse patterns a checker stops

Deliverability is one reason to block. Product abuse is the other.

| Pattern | What happens without a check | What a temp email checker does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Free trial farming | Unlimited throwaway accounts, unlimited trials | Block at registration when `isDisposable` is true |
| Coupon / referral fraud | Same offer claimed with a new burner each time | Reject or flag before the promotion is applied |
| Waitlist inflation | Fake demand, useless launch emails | Keep the list honest before you send |
| Newsletter padding | Open rates collapse; engagement signals look terrible | Suppress burners before the first campaign |
| Multi-account bots | Shared disposable domains scale abuse cheaply | Catch the domain family, including wildcard providers |

Role addresses (`admin@`, `sales@`) are a different problem: they are real and persistent, but shared. Reloop flags them separately so you can require a personal inbox without treating Gmail or Outlook as disposable.

## When to block vs when to flag

Blocking every temporary email is not always the right product decision.

**Block at signup when:**

- You offer a free trial, freemium tier, or usage credits
- You run new-customer discounts or referral rewards
- Fake accounts distort activation or retention metrics
- You send transactional email and cannot afford bounce spikes

**Flag or allow when:**

- Privacy-sensitive audiences expect anonymous access
- The flow is feedback, bug reports, or one-off downloads
- You will suppress later rather than reject at the door

A practical middle path: block disposable domains on paid or trial signup, and on newsletter forms either soft-warn or accept then suppress before campaigns. Pair the check with email confirmation and CAPTCHA so you are not relying on a single signal.

## How to check an address with Reloop (free)

### Option 1: Use the web tool

Paste an address into the [Reloop Temp Email Checker](/tools/temp-email-checker). You get a verdict, disposable match details, role and free-provider flags, MX hosts, confidence, and risk score instantly, with no signup.

Examples:

- `alex@gmail.com`: deliverable consumer mailbox (free provider, not disposable)
- `you@mailinator.com`: disposable
- `demo@yopmail.com`: disposable

### Option 2: Call the public API at signup

The checker is a thin wrapper over one public endpoint. No API key. No account. Rate limited per IP, so keep it to signup-time checks, not bulk scrubbing.

`POST https://reloop.sh/api/tools/v1/temp-email-checker`

<TempEmailCheckerCodeSamples />

A throwaway mailbox returns `"verdict": "disposable"` and `"isDisposable": true`:

```json
{
  "input": "you@mailinator.com",
  "kind": "email",
  "domain": "mailinator.com",
  "verdict": "disposable",
  "isValidSyntax": true,
  "isDisposable": true,
  "disposableMatch": {
    "kind": "exact",
    "domain": "mailinator.com"
  },
  "isAllowlisted": false,
  "isRoleAddress": false,
  "isFreeProvider": false,
  "signals": {
    "syntax": "pass",
    "disposable": "fail",
    "role": "pass",
    "freeProvider": "pass"
  },
  "mxRecords": ["spool.mailinator.com"],
  "confidence": 0.99,
  "riskScore": 0.95,
  "flags": ["DISPOSABLE_DOMAIN", "PUBLIC_INBOX_DETECTED"]
}
```

Reject or challenge the signup when `isDisposable` is `true`. Optionally treat high `riskScore` or role addresses as soft warnings.

Need to clean an existing list rather than gate one registration? Use Reloop's free [email validator](/tools/email-validator) for syntax, disposable detection, live MX, and CSV cleaning (up to 1,000 rows) in one pass. For production volume and policy controls, see [email validation](/features/email-validation) on Reloop.

## Layer checks that protect reputation end to end

Disposable detection is one layer. Strong signup hygiene stacks several:

1. **Temp / disposable check**: [Temp Email Checker](/tools/temp-email-checker) at account creation
2. **List hygiene before campaigns**: [Email Validator](/tools/email-validator)
3. **Authentication health**: [SPF, DKIM & DMARC checker](/tools/auth-checker) and the [setup guide](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide)
4. **Inbox placement tests**: [Deliverability tester](/tools/deliverability-tester)
5. **Blocklist monitoring**: [IP & domain blocklist checker](/tools/blocklist-checker)
6. **Transactional quality**: keep password resets and receipts on a dedicated subdomain with proper auth so the mail you do send deserves the inbox

Reloop is open-source email infrastructure. You can use the hosted tools, call the public checker API, or [run Reloop yourself](/blog/why-we-open-sourced-email-infrastructure) when you want the same checks on your own servers.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is blocking disposable emails legal?

Yes. Temporary email services are legal for users. Choosing not to accept them on your product is a normal terms-of-service and fraud-prevention decision, in the same category as blocking known bot ASNs or requiring phone verification.

### Will a temp email checker catch brand-new throwaway domains?

List-based detection only knows what is on the catalogue. Reloop resyncs roughly every two hours across ~210,000 providers, which catches most new services quickly, but a brand-new domain can slip through until it is listed. Combine the check with confirmation email and rate limits.

### Does Reloop prove the mailbox exists?

No. MX lookup shows mail can be routed to the domain. Reloop never probes the mailbox over SMTP. That keeps the tool fast, privacy-friendly, and suitable for a public endpoint.

### Is Gmail or Outlook disposable?

No. Free consumer providers are persistent. Reloop may flag them as free providers so you can apply your own rules; they are not treated as throwaway.

### Temp email checker vs email validator: which should I use?

Use the [temp email checker](/tools/temp-email-checker) to block burners at signup (single address, public API). Use the [email validator](/tools/email-validator) when you need bulk CSV cleaning, fuller health scoring, and export for campaign hygiene.

## Next step

Run a known throwaway address through the [free Temp Email Checker](/tools/temp-email-checker), then wire the same check into your registration handler with the public API above.

If you are already sending through Reloop or evaluating open-source transactional email, start free at [reloop](https://reloop.sh) and keep disposable addresses out of the path that builds your sender reputation.
