# Building a Webhook Delivery System That Actually Retries

Path: /blog/building-webhook-delivery-system
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/building-webhook-delivery-system
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/building-webhook-delivery-system.md

How Reloop delivers webhooks: idempotent events, per-endpoint filters and rate limits, HMAC-SHA256 signatures, SSRF protection with DNS pinning, a 7-attempt retry schedule over 17 hours, auto-disable and manual replays.

**A webhook system is only as good as what it does when your endpoint is down.** Reloop's webhook system delivers every event at least once: it stores the event, creates one delivery per subscribed endpoint, signs the body with HMAC-SHA256, and POSTs it from a BullMQ worker. If the endpoint fails, the delivery is retried up to 7 times over about 17 hours. Endpoints that keep failing are disabled instead of hammered, and any delivery can be replayed by hand.

This post walks through how that works in the [Reloop codebase](https://github.com/reloop-labs/reloop), with the numbers taken straight from the code. (The code is public because [we open-sourced the whole stack](/blog/why-we-open-sourced-email-infrastructure).)

---

## The flow

```text
Something happens (email delivered, contact created, domain verified, …)
   │
   ▼  NATS event
workflow service — dispatcher (queue group "webhook-dispatcher")
   │  1. insert webhook_event (idempotent)
   │  2. find active endpoints subscribed to this event type
   │  3. per endpoint: filters → rate limit → insert webhook_delivery
   │  4. enqueue BullMQ job (jobId = deliveryId)
   ▼
BullMQ "webhook-delivery-queue"  (concurrency 10)
   │  sign → SSRF-checked, DNS-pinned HTTPS POST → record result
   ├── 2xx            → success, reset consecutive failures
   ├── error / non-2xx → retry on fixed schedule
   └── last attempt    → failed, maybe auto-disable endpoint
```

Three tables carry the state:

| Table | One row per | Holds |
|---|---|---|
| `webhook_event` | Thing that happened | Type, payload, source, idempotency key |
| `webhook_delivery` | Event × endpoint × attempt chain | Status, attempt number, response code and body, next retry time |
| `webhook` | Customer endpoint | URL, encrypted secret, subscriptions, filters, rate limit, counters |

---

## 1. Events are idempotent

The same real-world event can show up more than once. KumoMTA (the MTA at the heart of our [delivery pipeline](/blog/how-we-built-email-delivery-queue-bullmq)) can log twice, a NATS message can be redelivered, a service can restart mid-handler. If each of those created a new webhook, customers would see duplicate `email.delivered` calls.

So every dispatch carries a stable key. For delivery events it's built from the organization, event type, email ID, KumoMTA record type and record ID:

```typescript
// apps/backend/workflow/src/subscribers/webhook.subscriber.ts
const sourceKey =
  `${orgId}:${webhookType}:${email.id}:${event.type}:${event.id}`;
```

The dispatcher looks the key up before inserting, and the unique constraint on `idempotency_key` catches the race where two replicas insert at once:

```typescript
// apps/backend/workflow/src/lib/webhook-dispatcher.ts (simplified)
const existing = await db.query.webhookEvent.findFirst({
  where: eq(schema.webhookEvent.idempotencyKey, idempotencyKey),
});
if (existing) return { eventId: existing.id, deliveryCount: 0 };

try {
  await db.insert(schema.webhookEvent).values({ id: eventId, idempotencyKey, ... });
} catch {
  // unique violation: a concurrent insert won, reuse it
}
```

On top of that, the dispatcher subscribes in the NATS queue group `webhook-dispatcher`, so only one workflow replica handles each event in the first place.

---

## 2. Fan-out with per-endpoint settings

For each active endpoint subscribed to the event type, the dispatcher applies that endpoint's settings before creating a delivery.

| Setting | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `maxRetries` | 7 | Total attempts including the first, clamped to 1–7 |
| `rateLimitEnabled` | `true` | Turns the outbound rate limit on |
| `maxRequestsPerMinute` | 60 | Outbound POSTs per endpoint per minute |
| `filteringOptions.matchConditions` | none | Only deliver if each listed `data` field equals the value |
| `filteringOptions.excludeFields` | none | Strip these top-level keys from `data` |

### Rate limits delay, they don't drop

The outbound limit is a fixed one-minute window in Redis. When an endpoint is over its cap, the delivery isn't discarded. Its first attempt is delayed until the window resets:

```typescript
// apps/backend/workflow/src/lib/webhook-dispatcher.ts (simplified)
const bucket = Math.floor(Date.now() / 60_000);
const key = `reloop:webhook-out:${hook.id}:${bucket}`;
const count = await redis.increment(key);
if (count === 1) await redis.expire(key, 65);

if (isWebhookRateLimited(count, hook.maxRequestsPerMinute)) {
  delayMs = rateLimitDelayMs(await redis.ttl(key)); // at least 1 s
}
```

If Redis is unavailable, the check fails open and the delivery goes out. Losing a rate limit for a minute is better than losing events.

### Filters

Filtering is shallow on purpose. A customer who only wants bounces (say, to mirror our [bounce processing](/blog/email-bounce-processing-automation) into their own database) can set:

```json
{
  "filteringOptions": {
    "matchConditions": { "status": "bounced" },
    "excludeFields": ["subject"]
  }
}
```

The excluded fields are removed from the stored delivery payload too, not just the outgoing request, so sensitive fields never sit in our delivery logs.

---

## 3. Signing

Every POST is signed with the endpoint's secret (`whsec_…`, stored encrypted and decrypted only inside the worker). The signed string is the Unix timestamp, a dot, and the exact raw body:

```typescript
// packages/webhook-delivery/src/signer.ts
  return createHmac("sha256", secret).update(`${ts}.${rawBody}`).digest("hex");
}
```

The request carries three headers:

| Header | Example |
|---|---|
| `Reloop-Id` | `whev_01h…` (same as the body's `id`) |
| `Reloop-Timestamp` | `1753185600` |
| `Reloop-Signature` | `t=1753185600,v1=5257a8…` |

Two details matter here:

- **The body is serialized once.** The worker builds the envelope, calls `JSON.stringify` once, signs that string and sends that same string. Re-serializing between signing and sending is the classic way to ship signatures that never verify.
- **Customers can't override the security headers.** Endpoints can add custom headers, but names like `Reloop-Signature`, `Content-Type`, `Host` and `Authorization` are reserved and silently dropped.

On the receiving side, verify against the **raw** body, use a constant-time compare, and reject timestamps older than five minutes to block replays. The full snippet is in the [webhook verification docs](/docs/webhooks/verify-webhooks-requests).

---

## 4. Sending without becoming an SSRF proxy

A webhook URL is user input that makes our servers send HTTP requests. Without care, someone could point it at `http://169.254.169.254/` or an internal service and use us to reach it.

The HTTP client in `packages/webhook-delivery` does three things:

1. **HTTPS only** in production.
2. **Resolve, then validate.** The hostname is resolved, and every address is checked against private ranges (`10/8`, `172.16/12`, `192.168/16`, loopback, IPv6 ULA) and always-blocked ranges (link-local `169.254/16`, CGNAT `100.64/10`, multicast, `0.0.0.0`).
3. **Pin the IP.** The request connects to the exact IP that passed validation, while still sending the original hostname for TLS SNI and the `Host` header. This closes the DNS-rebinding gap where a hostname resolves to a public IP during the check and a private one during the request.

```typescript
// packages/webhook-delivery/src/http-client.ts (simplified)
lib.request({
  hostname: resolved.pinnedIp,
  servername: parsed.hostname, // TLS SNI
  headers: { ...headers, Host: parsed.host },
  lookup: (_h, _o, cb) => cb(null, resolved.pinnedIp, resolved.family),
  timeout: 10_000,
});
```

Requests time out after 10 seconds, and stored response bodies are truncated at 8,192 characters.

<Callout type="warning">
  SSRF-blocked URLs are **not retried**. A private IP won't become public on attempt 5, so the delivery fails immediately with a `fix` telling the customer to use a public HTTPS URL.
</Callout>

---

## 5. Retries on a fixed schedule

We tried exponential backoff first. It's fine for jobs, but bad for humans debugging webhooks: "when is the next try?" shouldn't need a calculator. So retries follow a fixed, documented schedule, implemented as a custom BullMQ backoff:

```typescript
// packages/webhook-delivery/src/retry-schedule.ts
  5_000,           // before attempt 2
  5 * 60_000,      // before attempt 3
  30 * 60_000,     // before attempt 4
  2 * 60 * 60_000, // before attempt 5
  5 * 60 * 60_000, // before attempt 6
  10 * 60 * 60_000 // before attempt 7
] as const;
```

| Attempt | Delay after the previous failure | Time since first try (approx.) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Immediate | 0 |
| 2 | 5 seconds | 5 s |
| 3 | 5 minutes | 5 min |
| 4 | 30 minutes | 35 min |
| 5 | 2 hours | 2 h 35 min |
| 6 | 5 hours | 7 h 35 min |
| 7 | 10 hours | 17 h 35 min |

The early retries catch blips like a deploy or a cold start. The late ones cover a real outage that someone has to wake up and fix.

Any network error, timeout or non-2xx response counts as a failure. Each attempt writes the response status, a truncated body, the duration and the next retry time to `webhook_delivery`, so the dashboard can show exactly what happened.

The BullMQ job ID is the delivery ID. Enqueueing the same delivery twice is a no-op, so a restart in the middle of the fan-out can't create duplicate jobs.

---

## 6. Auto-disable broken endpoints

An endpoint that's been deleted or misconfigured will fail forever. Retrying every event 7 times against it wastes work and floods the delivery log.

After each **terminal** outcome (success, or failure on the last attempt) the worker updates the endpoint's counters in one statement:

```typescript
// apps/backend/workflow/src/handlers/webhook-delivery.handler.ts (simplified)
consecutiveFailures: succeeded
  ? 0
  : sql`${schema.webhook.consecutiveFailures} + 1`,
```

When `consecutiveFailures` reaches 10 (`WEBHOOK_DISABLE_AFTER_CONSECUTIVE_FAILURES`), the endpoint is marked `failed` and stops receiving new deliveries. One success in between resets the counter, so a flaky endpoint stays enabled. Re-enable it from the dashboard once it's fixed.

---

## 7. Replays

Sometimes you want an event again: you fixed a bug in your handler, or you restored a database. Replay creates a **new** delivery row linked to the original and enqueues it with the endpoint's current `maxRetries`. The original delivery's history is never changed, which keeps the audit trail honest.

Replays are refused while the endpoint is disabled, failed or paused, with a `why` explaining which.

---

## What we'd tell anyone building this

| Lesson | Why |
|---|---|
| Store the event before you deliver it | Replays and debugging need the original payload |
| Make the event idempotent at the source | Duplicates are cheaper to prevent than to explain |
| Sign the exact bytes you send | Re-serialization breaks signatures |
| Resolve, validate and pin IPs | Validating the hostname alone leaves a DNS-rebinding hole |
| Use a fixed, published retry schedule | Customers can reason about it |
| Disable after repeated terminal failures | Protects you and the customer's logs |
| Never mutate history on replay | The delivery log is an audit trail |

---

## FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Are Reloop webhooks delivered exactly once?">
    At least once. Events are deduplicated at the source, but a delivery can
    still be retried after your server processed it and failed to respond in
    time. Use the `Reloop-Id` header to make your handler idempotent.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Does a 4xx response get retried?">
    Yes. Any non-2xx response is retried on the schedule. Only SSRF-blocked
    or non-HTTPS URLs fail immediately. Return 2xx as soon as you've stored
    the event, and do slow work asynchronously.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can I lower the number of retries?">
    Yes. Set `maxRetries` on the endpoint to anything from 1 to 7. Only the
    first rows of the schedule apply.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Which events can I subscribe to?">
    Email lifecycle (`email.sent`, `email.delivered`, `email.bounced`,
    `email.complained`, `email.opened`, `email.clicked`, `email.received`
    and more), plus domain, API key and contact events. See
    [event types](/docs/webhooks/event-types). `email.received` is what lets
    an [AI agent read and reply to email](/blog/build-ai-agent-sends-emails).
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# Reloop on Coolify: Self-Hosted Email Without the Complexity

Path: /blog/reloop-coolify-setup
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-coolify-setup
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-coolify-setup.md

Deploy Reloop on Coolify with the official template: requirements, the two domains to set, DNS and PTR, first sign-in, system email, tracking domains, updates and the mistakes to avoid.

**If you already run Coolify, it's the easiest way to self-host Reloop.** Reloop ships an official Coolify template. You paste one YAML file, set two domains, and click Deploy. Coolify generates every secret, provisions Postgres and Redis, and issues TLS certificates.

This guide covers the whole path: requirements, deploy, DNS, first sign-in, system email, and the handful of Coolify-specific gotchas that trip people up. At the end there's a short section on the reverse direction: sending Coolify's own mail through Reloop.

---

## Why Coolify and Reloop fit together

[Coolify](https://coolify.io) is an open-source, self-hosted platform-as-a-service. Think Heroku or Render, but on your own server. It gives you a UI for Docker Compose stacks, databases, environment variables, backups and HTTPS.

[Reloop](/blog/introducing-reloop) is open-source email infrastructure: API, SMTP relay, inboxes, campaigns and webhooks. It runs as a Docker Compose stack.

Put them together and you get your own email platform managed from the same dashboard as the rest of your apps. No shell scripts, no hand-written Caddy config.

---

## Requirements

| Requirement | Value |
|---|---|
| Coolify | v4 with the default Traefik proxy |
| Architecture | x86_64 (the dashboard and links images are amd64 only) |
| RAM | 8 GB for Reloop and Coolify together |
| Disk | 50 GB (the images alone take about 22 GB) |
| Ports | `25`, `465` and `587` open, inbound and outbound |
| DNS | Three hostnames pointing at the server |

<Callout type="warning">
  Many hosting providers [block port 25](/blog/smtp-ports-explained) by default. Reloop delivers to other mail servers on outbound 25 and receives on inbound 25, so ask your provider to open it **before** you deploy. Also ask for a PTR (reverse DNS) record for the server IP pointing to your Reloop hostname.
</Callout>

Throughout this guide we'll use `reloop.example.com` as the Reloop hostname and `203.0.113.10` as the server IP. Replace both with your own.

---

## Step 1: Add the DNS records

Do this first so certificates can be issued as soon as the stack starts.

```text
reloop.example.com            A    203.0.113.10
link.reloop.example.com       A    203.0.113.10
inbound.reloop.example.com    A    203.0.113.10
reloop.example.com            TXT  "v=spf1 ip4:203.0.113.10 -all"
```

| Record | What it's for |
|---|---|
| `reloop.example.com` | Dashboard and API |
| `link.reloop.example.com` | Click and open tracking, unsubscribe pages |
| `inbound.reloop.example.com` | MX target for mail your domains receive |
| SPF TXT | Authorizes this server to send; each sending domain's `include:` resolves to it |

---

## Step 2: Create the resource

1. In Coolify, open your project and choose **New Resource → Docker Compose**. Older versions call it **Docker Compose Empty**.
2. Paste the contents of the official template, [`install/coolify/reloop.yaml`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/reloop-labs/reloop/main/install/coolify/reloop.yaml), and save.

The template runs the same stack as the [one-command VPS installer](/blog/self-hosted-email-infrastructure): the Reloop backend services, the dashboard, link tracking, Postgres, Redis and NATS.

---

## Step 3: Set exactly two domains

Before the first deploy, replace Coolify's generated domains on these two services:

| Service | Domain |
|---|---|
| `proxy` | `https://reloop.example.com` |
| `links` | `https://link.reloop.example.com` |

Coolify will warn that `proxy` requires port 80 and `links` requires port 3005. Choose **Use this port anyway**. Traffic still reaches those ports and your URLs stay clean. If you choose **Keep required port**, Coolify throws away the domain you just entered.

Leave every other service **without** a domain.

<Callout type="tip">
  Set the real domains before you add any sending domain in the Reloop dashboard. Reloop writes the DNS records it shows you when a domain is created, so a domain added while the instance still runs on Coolify's temporary `sslip.io` address will keep pointing there.
</Callout>

---

## Step 4: Deploy

Click **Deploy**. The first deploy downloads about 5 GB of images, which unpack to about 22 GB.

Coolify stops any deploy that runs longer than 10 minutes. On a slow connection the first one can time out before the stack starts. That's fine: click **Deploy** again. Images that already downloaded are kept, so the second attempt picks up where the first left off.

Coolify generates the database password, Redis password and every Reloop secret, and stores them under **Environment Variables**.

**Don't change any generated value after the first deploy.**

- The database password is fixed once Postgres initializes.
- Changing the tracking or preferences secrets breaks links in mail you've already sent.
- Changing the webhook key breaks the signature on every existing webhook.

---

## Step 5: First sign-in

1. In Coolify, open **Environment Variables** and copy `SERVICE_PASSWORD_64_SETUPKEY`.
2. Open `https://reloop.example.com/dashboard/setup` and paste it.
3. Create the first administrator: name, email and password.
4. Name your first organization.

The setup key works once. If you think it leaked before you used it, change the variable and restart. The old key stops working.

---

## Step 6: Configure system email (don't skip this)

Setup signs you in with a session that lasts 7 days. After that, Reloop signs you in with an emailed code. If system email isn't configured, you can't get back in.

Set these under **Environment Variables**, then restart:

| Variable | Value |
|---|---|
| `RELOOP_SENDER_DOMAIN` | The domain system mail is sent from (always required) |
| `SMTP_HOST`, `SMTP_PORT`, `SMTP_USER`, `SMTP_PASSWORD`, `SMTP_SECURE` | Any SMTP provider you already use |
| `RELOOP_API_KEY` | Or, instead of SMTP: an API key from this instance, once the sender domain is verified |

The neat option is the last one: verify a domain in your new instance, create an API key, and let Reloop send its own sign-in codes.

---

## Step 7: Add a sending domain and send

In the Reloop dashboard, go to **Domains**, add the domain you'll send from (for example `mail.acme.com`), and add the SPF, DKIM, DMARC and MX records it shows. Coolify-hosted Reloop doesn't support auto-populating DNS, so add them by hand. The [SPF, DKIM and DMARC guide](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide) explains each one.

Then create an API key and send from your app. A fresh server IP has no reputation yet, so ramp volume up slowly with an [IP warming schedule](/blog/ip-warming-guide). Point the SDK at your instance:

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({
  apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY!,
  baseUrl: "https://reloop.example.com",
});

await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
  to: "you@example.com",
  subject: "Hello from Coolify",
  html: "<p>Reloop is running.</p>",
});
```

---

## Useful settings

All optional. Coolify lists each one under **Environment Variables** with its default.

| Variable | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `DISABLE_SIGNUP` | `true` | Blocks public registration; invited users can still join |
| `DISABLE_ORG_CREATION` | `false` | Stops users creating more organizations |
| `APP_NAME` | `Reloop` | Instance name shown in system email |
| `S3_ENDPOINT`, `S3_ACCESS_KEY`, `S3_SECRET_KEY`, `S3_BUCKET` | empty | S3-compatible storage for template images and attachments |
| `DNS_RESOLVERS` | `8.8.8.8,8.8.4.4` | Resolvers used to verify domain records |
| `RELOOP_VERSION` | `latest` | Image tag for every Reloop service |

Keep `RELOOP_VERSION` on `latest` so the public-facing dashboard and links services get security fixes.

### Custom tracking domains

When a sending domain has click or open tracking on, it gets a `link.` CNAME pointing at `link.reloop.example.com`, so tracked links use your customer's own hostname. Coolify's proxy only issues certificates for domains it knows about, so add each tracking hostname to the `links` service:

```text
https://link.reloop.example.com,https://link.customer.com
```

Keep your own `link.` domain **first**. Reloop uses the first one as the CNAME target for new domains.

---

## Updates and backups

Updating pulls the latest images and restarts. A `migrate` service runs first and updates the database schema before the backend starts.

1. **Back up first.** Open the `postgres` service → **Backups**. Schedule daily backups, and run one on demand before every update.
2. **Redeploy** to pull new images.
3. **When a release changes `reloop.yaml`**, paste the new file under **Edit Compose File** and replace the `proxy` service's Caddyfile under **Persistent Storage**.
4. **Clean up old images.** Each update leaves about 4 GB behind. Turn on Coolify's Docker cleanup, or run `docker image prune`.

---

## Mistakes to avoid

| Don't | Why |
|---|---|
| Connect the stack to Coolify's predefined network | It exposes the internal SMTP injection API, NATS and Rspamd to every other resource |
| Deploy on arm64 | The dashboard and links images are amd64 only |
| Route mail ports through Coolify's proxy | SMTP auth needs the TLS session to reach the `smtp` container directly |
| Add sending domains before setting real domains | Their DNS records will point at the temporary `sslip.io` address |
| Change generated secrets | Breaks the database, sent links or webhook signatures |

If campaigns, automations or inbox replies fail right after deploy, the server probably can't reach its own HTTPS address yet. Those features call `https://reloop.example.com` from inside the stack. They start working once Coolify has issued the certificate.

---

## The other direction: send Coolify's mail through Reloop

Coolify itself sends [password resets](/blog/password-reset-email-best-practices), deployment alerts and backup notifications. Point it at Reloop SMTP (hosted or your own instance) under **Settings → Email**:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Host | `smtp.reloop.sh` (or your own instance) |
| Port | `587` |
| Encryption | StartTLS |
| Username | Your Reloop API key (`rl_…`) |
| Password | The same API key |
| From address | `coolify@yourdomain.com` |

Apps you deploy on Coolify can use the same key. Add `RELOOP_API_KEY` as a secret under the app's **Environment Variables** and redeploy. More in the [Coolify integration docs](/docs/integrations/coolify).

---

## FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Can I run Reloop on the same Coolify server as my other apps?">
    Yes, as long as the server has 8 GB of RAM and 50 GB of disk free for
    Reloop. Don't connect Reloop to Coolify's shared predefined network.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Why does the first deploy fail?">
    Usually Coolify's 10-minute deploy timeout while downloading about 5 GB of
    images. Click Deploy again. Downloaded images are kept.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Do I need a separate SMTP provider?">
    No. Reloop sends directly from your server on port 25. You only need an
    external SMTP provider for system email if you prefer not to use a
    Reloop API key for it, or if your host won't open port 25.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Coolify or the one-command installer?">
    If you already use Coolify, use the template: you manage Reloop beside
    everything else. On a fresh server with nothing else on it, the
    [one-command installer](/self-host) is simpler and issues tracking
    domain certificates automatically.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# Best Mailchimp Alternatives in 2026: Stop Paying for Contacts You Never Email

Path: /blog/best-mailchimp-alternatives
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-mailchimp-alternatives
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-mailchimp-alternatives.md

The best Mailchimp alternatives of 2026 compared: Reloop, Brevo, Mailjet, Loops, Customer.io, Elastic Email and Listmonk on pricing model, free tiers, automations, transactional email, inbound and self-hosting.

**The short version:** if your email starts in your product (sign-ups, receipts, onboarding sequences), **Reloop** is the best Mailchimp alternative: it prices by emails sent instead of contacts stored, puts transactional mail, campaigns and automations in one API, and is open source. If your marketing team wants an all-in-one suite with SMS and a CRM, look at **Brevo**. If you want a free, self-hosted newsletter tool, **Listmonk** is hard to beat.

We build Reloop, so factor that in. Every competitor fact below comes from our researched head-to-head posts, which link each provider's own pricing page, and each section says where that tool beats us.

---

## Why teams leave Mailchimp

Mailchimp is a good product for marketers. The reasons people look elsewhere are mostly about fit and price, not quality:

1. **You pay for contacts, not sends.** Mailchimp's free tier covers 250 contacts and 500 sends a month. Essentials starts at $13 a month for 500 contacts, and your monthly sends are capped at 10× your contact count. Every stored contact counts, even ones you never email.
2. **That model hurts SaaS products.** A product that stores 20,000 users but emails the 3,000 active ones this week pays for all 20,000.
3. **Transactional email is a separate add-on.** Mandrill (Mailchimp Transactional) is only sold on top of a paid Standard or Premium plan, billed in blocks of 25,000 emails. See [best Mandrill alternatives](/blog/best-mandrill-alternatives).
4. **It's hosted only.** You can't self-host it or read the code.

If none of those apply (a small newsletter run by a marketer, with no product email), Mailchimp may still be the right tool. We say so at the end.

---

## Top picks at a glance

| Category | Pick | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Best overall for product teams** | Reloop | Per-email pricing, transactional + campaigns + automations in one API, open source |
| **Best all-in-one marketing suite** | Brevo | Email, SMS, WhatsApp, CRM and live chat, priced by sends |
| **Best for marketers who want a bigger free tier** | Mailjet | 6,000 emails a month free, strong drag-and-drop editor |
| **Best lifecycle tool for SaaS marketers** | Loops | Polished, focused onboarding and lifecycle flows |
| **Best multi-channel engagement** | Customer.io | Journeys across email, push, in-app and SMS |
| **Best budget no-code newsletters** | Elastic Email | Separate marketing app with paid newsletters and checkouts |
| **Best free self-hosted newsletter tool** | Listmonk | Single Go binary, AGPLv3, bring your own SMTP |

---

## The comparison table

| | Reloop | Brevo | Mailjet | Loops | Customer.io | Elastic Email (Marketing) | Listmonk |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Pricing basis** | Emails sent | Emails sent | Emails sent | Contacts stored | Profiles stored | Contacts + emails | Free software + your SMTP |
| **Free tier** | 6,000 / mo (200 / day) | 300 / day | 6,000 / mo (200 / day) | 1,000 contacts, 4,000 sends | No free plan listed | 1,000 contacts, 3,000 emails | Free (self-host) |
| **Entry paid plan** | **$10 for 50,000 emails** | From $9 for 5,000 | Starter $9 | $49 / mo | $100 / mo (5,000 profiles) | $29 (2,500 contacts, 37,500 emails) | Server + SMTP cost |
| **Automations** | Every plan | Standard, from $18 | Premium plan | Yes (core focus) | Yes (Journeys) | Starter and Pro | No drip sequences |
| **Drag-and-drop editor** | Yes | Yes | Yes | Visual editor | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| **Transactional API** | Yes | Yes | Yes | Limited | Yes | Separate Email API product | Yes (`/api/tx`) |
| **Inbound email** | Mailboxes, API, MCP, IMAP | Webhook | Parse API | No | No | On the Email API Pro plan | No |
| **Open source / self-host** | Yes (Apache 2.0) | No | No | No | No | No | Yes (AGPLv3) |

Reloop's prices are on [reloop.sh/pricing](/pricing). Competitor prices come from each provider's pricing page, linked in our head-to-head posts below. They all change; check before you commit.

---

## How we evaluated

We looked at what actually decides a Mailchimp replacement:

1. **Pricing model.** Per contact, per profile or per email sent. This matters more than the headline price.
2. **Who runs it.** Is it built for marketers with no developer help, or for product teams sending from code?
3. **Automations.** Are lifecycle sequences included, or gated behind a higher plan?
4. **Transactional email.** Can the same tool send receipts and password resets, or do you need a second vendor?
5. **Inbound and replies.** Can people reply to your emails into something you can work with?
6. **Lock-in.** Can you leave, or run it yourself?

---

## 1. Reloop: best overall for product teams

[Reloop](/alternatives/mailchimp) is open-source email infrastructure: a transactional API, SMTP relay, contacts, broadcast campaigns, event-triggered automations and inbound mailboxes in one product. Use it hosted, or run the same code on your own server.

**Pricing:** Free is 6,000 emails a month (200 a day). Pro is $10 for 50,000. Growth is $20 for 100,000 and includes a dedicated IP. Extra mail costs $0.50 per 1,000. Or skip the subscription and buy pay-as-you-go credits at $0.50 per 1,000, valid for 6 months. Contacts are free to store. Self-hosting is free under Apache 2.0.

**Strengths**

- **Priced by sends, not contacts.** Store 20,000 users, email 3,000, pay for 3,000.
- **One API for everything your product sends:** transactional mail, campaigns and automations share one suppression list, so a hard bounce on a campaign is suppressed for receipts too.
- **Event-triggered automations on every plan.** Your app tracks an event like `user.signed_up`, and Reloop runs delays, conditions and email steps. See [welcome sequences that convert](/blog/welcome-email-sequences-that-convert).
- A visual drag-and-drop template builder, plus HTML and React Email.
- **Inbound mail as real mailboxes**, readable over the API, the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) or IMAP.
- Reloop Cloud runs on Hetzner, a German hosting company, with EU data centers. Or [self-host](/self-host) it.

**Weaknesses**

- Mailchimp's template library, landing pages and sign-up forms are more extensive.
- No A/B testing for campaigns yet.
- Fewer native integrations with e-commerce and CRM tools.

**Best for:** SaaS and product teams whose email starts in their code, and anyone paying Mailchimp for a large, quiet list.

Full breakdown: [Reloop vs Mailchimp](/blog/reloop-vs-mailchimp) · [Compare page](/compare/mailchimp)

## 2. Brevo: best all-in-one marketing suite

[Brevo](https://www.brevo.com/) (formerly Sendinblue) is a marketing suite from Paris: email, SMS, WhatsApp, live chat and a sales CRM in one account. Like Reloop, and unlike Mailchimp, it charges for emails sent rather than contacts stored.

**Pricing:** free for 300 emails a day. Starter begins at $9 for 5,000 emails. Standard, which adds automations, starts at $18. Professional starts at $499 for 150,000 emails. Exact prices at 50k and 100k come from a volume slider on its pricing page.

**Strengths**

- More channels than any other tool here: SMS and WhatsApp alongside email.
- A mature drag-and-drop editor, templates, landing pages, sign-up forms and A/B testing.
- The free plan's 300 emails a day is generous for small senders.

**Weaknesses**

- Automations need Standard.
- Gets expensive at higher volumes compared with developer-focused tools.
- Hosted only.

**Best for:** marketing-led teams that want one bill for email, SMS and CRM.

## 3. Mailjet: best for marketers who want a bigger free tier

[Mailjet](https://www.mailjet.com/) started in France and is now owned by Sinch. It does marketing and transactional mail with a strong drag-and-drop editor.

**Pricing:** free for 6,000 emails a month (200 a day). Starter is $9. After the September 2026 update, Essential is $19 for 15,000 and $40 for 50,000; Premium is $29 for 15,000, $59 for 50,000, $112 for 100,000 and $265 for 250,000.

**Strengths**

- One of the two biggest free tiers in this list (6,000 a month, the same as Reloop's).
- A polished editor, brand kit, forms and landing pages for non-developers.
- Subaccounts for agencies managing several brands.

**Weaknesses**

- Automations, team management and dedicated IPs are Premium features.
- $40 to $59 at 50,000 emails, vs $10 on Reloop.
- Inbound arrives through the Parse API as a webhook, not a mailbox.

**Best for:** small marketing teams that send under 6,000 emails a month, or agencies with many brands.

## 4. Loops: best lifecycle tool for SaaS marketers

[Loops](https://loops.so/) is a focused, polished tool for SaaS lifecycle email: onboarding flows, product announcements and newsletters.

**Pricing:** free for 1,000 contacts and 4,000 sends a month. Paid plans start at $49 a month, and 100,000 contacts costs $399 a month. Like Mailchimp, it prices by contacts stored.

**Strengths**

- Lifecycle email is its whole product, and it's pleasant to use.
- Designed for marketers in SaaS companies, not generic small businesses.
- The free tier suits a small list you email often.

**Weaknesses**

- Contact-based pricing, so the bill grows with signups, like Mailchimp's.
- Limited transactional API and no SMTP relay.
- No inbound email. Hosted only.

**Best for:** SaaS marketing teams that already send transactional mail elsewhere and want a lifecycle tool on top.

## 5. Customer.io: best multi-channel engagement

[Customer.io](https://customer.io/) is a customer engagement platform. Its Journeys builder runs campaigns across email, push, in-app messages and SMS, with deep segmentation.

**Pricing:** Essentials starts at $100 a month for 5,000 profiles and 1 million emails, then $0.009 per extra profile. Premium starts at $1,000 a month, billed annually. Its pricing page lists no free plan.

**Strengths**

- True multi-channel journeys in one workflow.
- Deep segmentation across people, accounts and event history.
- Liquid templates and a visual builder that lifecycle teams can run without engineers.

**Weaknesses**

- Priced by profiles: about $505 a month at 50,000 profiles on Essentials list price.

## 6. Elastic Email: best budget no-code newsletters

**Pricing (Email Marketing):** free for up to 1,000 contacts and 3,000 emails a month, with 1 automation. Starter is $29 a month for up to 2,500 contacts and 37,500 emails, with automations, paid newsletters and checkouts. Pro is $49 with unlimited automations, webhooks and sub-accounts.

**Strengths**

**Weaknesses**

## 7. Listmonk: best free self-hosted newsletter tool

[Listmonk](https://listmonk.app/) is an open-source newsletter and mailing list manager (AGPLv3): a single Go binary plus Postgres. It doesn't send mail itself; it hands each message to an SMTP server you configure.

**Pricing:** free software with no hosted plan. You pay for a small server and your SMTP provider.

**Strengths**

- Very light: its homepage cites a 7+ million email campaign at a peak of 57 MB of RAM.
- Lists with single and double opt-in, SQL segmentation, and visual, WYSIWYG, Markdown and HTML editors.
- No per-contact fees, ever.

**Weaknesses**

- Needs an external SMTP provider, which owns your deliverability.
- No drip sequences or event-triggered automations.
- No inbound email. You run and maintain it.

**Best for:** technical teams that want a free newsletter tool and already have a sending provider. It works well on top of Reloop's SMTP relay.

Full breakdown: [Reloop vs Listmonk](/blog/reloop-vs-listmonk)

---

## How to choose

Answer these in order and stop at the first "yes":

1. **Does your email start in your product** (sign-ups, receipts, lifecycle sequences), or do you store far more contacts than you email? → Reloop.
2. **Do you need SMS, WhatsApp and a CRM in the same tool?** → Brevo.
3. **Do you message users across push, in-app and SMS with complex segments?** → Customer.io.
4. **Do you want a focused SaaS lifecycle tool and already have transactional mail elsewhere?** → Loops.
5. **Do you send under 6,000 emails a month and want a marketer-friendly editor?** → Mailjet.
6. **Do you want cheap no-code newsletters with paid subscriptions?** → Elastic Email.
7. **Do you want free, self-hosted newsletters and have SMTP sorted?** → Listmonk.

<Callout type="tip">
  Count two numbers before you choose: how many contacts you'll store, and how many emails you'll actually send. If the first is much bigger than the second, a per-email tool (Reloop, Brevo, Mailjet) will almost always cost less than a per-contact one (Mailchimp, Loops, Customer.io).
</Callout>

### When to stay on Mailchimp

- Your email is run by marketers with no engineering help, and you rely on its template library, landing pages and forms.
- Your store, CRM and forms already plug into Mailchimp's integrations.
- You send a newsletter or two a month to a few hundred contacts, where contact pricing is cheap.

---

## Switching from Mailchimp

The steps are similar for every tool here:

1. **Export your audience**, including unsubscribed and cleaned contacts, so they stay suppressed in the new tool.
2. **Verify your sending domain.** Add the new DKIM record and merge the new provider into your existing SPF record. Never publish a second SPF record. Our [SPF, DKIM and DMARC guide](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide) covers it.
3. **Rebuild templates.** Mailchimp uses merge tags like `*|FNAME|*`. In Reloop, placeholders use triple braces: `{{{first_name}}}`.
4. **Recreate automations**, triggered by events from your app where possible.
5. **Warm up gradually.** Send to your most engaged contacts first and grow volume over one to two weeks.

If you have product email too, use separate subdomains for marketing and transactional mail (for example `news.acme.com` and `mail.acme.com`) so each keeps its own reputation.

# Reloop vs Cloudflare Email Service (2026): Which to Use for Sending

Path: /blog/reloop-vs-cloudflare-email
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-cloudflare-email
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-cloudflare-email.md

Reloop vs Cloudflare Email Service compared: pricing at 3k to 250k emails a month, the Workers binding vs an HTTP API, DNS requirements, events, inbound email, marketing mail and lock-in.

**Cloudflare now sends email.** Its Email Service adds outbound sending to the Email Routing product many teams already use for inbound, and from a Worker it's one binding and one `send()` call. **If your app lives entirely on Workers and only sends transactional mail, it's a strong, cheap option.** Reloop is the better fit when you need marketing mail, templates, contacts and automations, real inboxes, a domain that isn't on Cloudflare DNS, or the option to self-host.

We build Reloop, so weigh this accordingly. Every Cloudflare fact below links to Cloudflare's own docs, checked in October 2026. Where Cloudflare wins, we say so.

---

## The 30-second comparison

| | **Reloop** | **Cloudflare Email Service** |
|---|---|---|
| Status | Generally available | Sending in public beta, Routing GA |
| Free tier | 6,000 / mo, 200 / day | Sending to your own verified addresses only |
| Paid entry point | $10 / mo for 50k | Workers Paid ($5 / mo minimum), 3,000 emails included |
| Price per extra 1,000 | $0.50 | $0.35 |
| Domain DNS | Any DNS provider | Must use Cloudflare DNS |
| Marketing email | Yes (campaigns) | No, transactional only |
| Templates | Yes, `{{{variables}}}` | Not documented |
| Contacts, campaigns, automations | Yes | No |
| Events | Signed HTTP webhooks | Cloudflare Queues |
| Inbound email | Stored mailboxes, API, MCP, IMAP | Email Routing to addresses or Workers |
| Dedicated IP | Included on Growth ($20) | Not documented |
| Open source / self-host | Yes (Apache 2.0) | No |

Sources: Cloudflare's [pricing](https://developers.cloudflare.com/email-service/platform/pricing/), [overview](https://developers.cloudflare.com/email-service/), [FAQ](https://developers.cloudflare.com/email-service/reference/faq/) and [getting started](https://developers.cloudflare.com/email-service/get-started/send-emails/) pages. Reloop's prices are on [reloop.sh/pricing](/pricing).

---

## Where Cloudflare Email Service stands today

Cloudflare's [changelog](https://developers.cloudflare.com/email-service/platform/changelog/) tells the story:

- **April 16, 2026:** Email Sending enters public beta, through a Workers binding and a REST API.
- **June 8, 2026:** authenticated SMTP submission (beta) on `smtp.mx.cloudflare.net:465`.
- **July 15, 2026:** sending lifecycle events published to Cloudflare Queues.
- **September 25, 2026:** suppressions can be scoped to a single sending domain.

Email Routing, the inbound side, has been generally available for years. Sending is still labeled beta on the [overview page](https://developers.cloudflare.com/email-service/). That's worth knowing if you need a vendor SLA for your password resets today.

---

## Pricing at real volumes

Cloudflare's model is simple: sending to arbitrary recipients **requires the Workers Paid plan** (a $5 a month account minimum, which also covers Workers, KV, Durable Objects and more). That plan includes **3,000 emails a month, then $0.35 per 1,000**. Bounced emails count toward the quota; sends rejected by the API don't. ([pricing](https://developers.cloudflare.com/email-service/platform/pricing/))

| Monthly volume | Reloop | Cloudflare (incl. $5 Workers Paid) |
|---|---|---|
| 3,000 | $0 | $5 |
| 50,000 | **$10** | about $21 |
| 100,000 | **$20** | about $39 |
| 250,000 | $20 + $75 overage = $95 | **about $91** |

The Cloudflare figures are our math from the published rate: `$5 + (volume − 3,000) × $0.35 / 1,000`.

What this means:

- **Below about 200k emails a month, Reloop is cheaper**, mostly because our Growth plan includes 100k for $20.
- **Above about 200k, Cloudflare's $0.35 rate wins** over our $0.50 overage. If you already pay for Workers, the $5 isn't extra and the crossover comes a little earlier.
- **Reloop has a real free tier.** Cloudflare's free plan only lets you send to destination addresses you've verified in your own account, which is fine for alerts to yourself but not for users.

If you self-host Reloop, there's no per-email fee at all. See [self-hosted email infrastructure](/blog/self-hosted-email-infrastructure).

---

## Developer experience on Workers

This is Cloudflare's best argument. Add a binding to `wrangler.jsonc`:

```jsonc
{
  "send_email": [{ "name": "EMAIL" }]
}
```

Then send from any handler:

```typescript
// Cloudflare Email Service
const { messageId } = await env.EMAIL.send({
  from: "welcome@acme.com",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Welcome",
  html: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
  text: "Thanks for signing up.",
});
```

No API key to store, no package to install. Errors are thrown with a `code` such as `E_SENDER_NOT_VERIFIED` or `E_RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`. ([Workers API](https://developers.cloudflare.com/email-service/api/send-emails/workers-api/))

Reloop from a Worker is one `fetch` call, or the SDK with the `nodejs_compat` flag. Our [Cloudflare Workers guide](/blog/send-email-cloudflare-workers) covers both:

```typescript
// Reloop

const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: env.RELOOP_API_KEY });

const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <welcome@mail.acme.com>",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Welcome",
  html: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
});
```

You do store one secret (`wrangler secret put RELOOP_API_KEY`). In return, the same code runs unchanged on Vercel, Fly.io, a Node server or a cron job, and errors come back as values with `message`, `why` and `fix` instead of exceptions.

Outside Workers, both have options. Cloudflare offers a [REST API](https://developers.cloudflare.com/email-service/api/send-emails/rest-api/) (`POST /client/v4/accounts/{account_id}/email/sending/send` with a Cloudflare API token) and SMTP. Reloop offers the REST API, SDKs for Node, Python, Go, PHP, Ruby, Rust, Java, .NET and Elixir, and an SMTP relay at `smtp.reloop.sh`.

| | Reloop | Cloudflare |
|---|---|---|
| Workers integration | `fetch` or SDK + secret | Native binding, no secret |
| REST API | Yes | Yes |
| SMTP | Yes | Yes (beta, port 465) |
| Official SDKs | 9 languages | Workers binding |
| Errors | Returned as values (`message`, `why`, `fix`) | Thrown, with `code` |
| Idempotent retries | `Idempotency-Key` header | Not documented |
| Stored templates | Yes | Not documented |

Cloudflare caps each email at 50 recipients across to, cc and bcc, and at 5 MiB including attachments ([limits](https://developers.cloudflare.com/email-service/platform/limits/)). New Cloudflare accounts also start on a "conservative daily quota" that grows over time, and higher limits go through a request form.

---

## The DNS requirement

Cloudflare's getting-started guide is explicit: **"You must be using Cloudflare DNS to use Email Service."** ([source](https://developers.cloudflare.com/email-service/get-started/send-emails/)) Onboarding a domain adds bounce MX records, SPF, DKIM (selector `cf-bounce._domainkey`) and DMARC on a `cf-bounce` subdomain. ([domains](https://developers.cloudflare.com/email-service/configuration/domains/))

If your DNS is already on Cloudflare, that's a non-issue and setup takes minutes. If it's on Route 53, Google Cloud DNS, Vercel or your registrar, you'd have to move the whole zone just to send email.

Reloop works with any DNS provider: publish one DKIM record (`reloop._domainkey`) and merge `include:reloop.sh` into your SPF record.

---

## Events and webhooks

Cloudflare publishes six sending events (`message.delivered`, `message.deferred`, `message.bounced`, `message.failed`, `message.rejected`, `message.complained`) **to a Cloudflare Queue**, which you consume with a Worker or an HTTP pull consumer. ([event subscriptions](https://developers.cloudflare.com/email-service/reference/event-subscriptions/)) That's elegant if you're on Workers; from anywhere else you're polling.

Reloop pushes signed HTTP webhooks (`email.delivered`, `email.bounced`, `email.complained`, `email.opened`, `email.clicked`, `email.received` and more) to any URL, signed with HMAC-SHA256 in the `Reloop-Signature` header and retried on failure. See [building a webhook delivery system](/blog/building-webhook-delivery-system) for how that works.

Both maintain a suppression list for bounces and complaints. Cloudflare's can be scoped per sending domain; Reloop's is shared across transactional mail and campaigns, so one bounce protects both.

---

## Inbound email

Cloudflare's [Email Routing](https://developers.cloudflare.com/email-service/get-started/route-emails/) is excellent and free: unlimited inbound mail, forwarded to verified addresses or handed to a Worker's `email()` handler, which can reply in-thread. What you do with the message after that (store it, thread it, search it) is your code.

Reloop receives mail into **mailboxes**. Messages are stored, threaded, spam-scored with Rspamd, and readable over the API, the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) or IMAP. Reply in-thread with one call. Hosted plans include 3 inboxes on Free, 5 on Pro and 10 on Growth; self-hosted is unlimited.

| | Reloop | Cloudflare |
|---|---|---|
| Receive on your domain | Yes | Yes |
| Price | Included per plan | Free, unlimited |
| Stored mailboxes with threads | Yes | Build it (for example, Workers + R2) |
| Reply in thread | API call | `message.reply()` in a Worker |
| MCP and IMAP access | Yes | No |

If you're building [AI agents that read and answer email](/blog/build-ai-agent-sends-emails), Reloop gives you the inbox; with Cloudflare you build one.

---

## Marketing, contacts and automations

Cloudflare's FAQ is clear: **"Email Service supports transactional email only."** No newsletters, product announcements or drip campaigns.

Reloop covers both sides with one suppression list: contacts with custom properties, groups and subscription channels, scheduled broadcast campaigns, and event-triggered automations (`reloop.automations.start`) for onboarding and dunning sequences. See [welcome sequences that convert](/blog/welcome-email-sequences-that-convert).

---

## Lock-in

Cloudflare Email Service ties sending to Cloudflare DNS, Workers Paid and, for events, Cloudflare Queues. That's a fine trade if you're committed to the platform.

Reloop is Apache 2.0. Start on Reloop Cloud, move to your own server with the [one-command installer](/self-host), and point the SDK's `baseUrl` at your instance. Nothing else in your code changes.

---

## Where Cloudflare is the better choice

- **You're all-in on Workers** and your DNS is already on Cloudflare. The binding is the least code you'll ever write to send email.
- **You send high transactional volume.** Above roughly 200k emails a month, $0.35 per 1,000 beats our overage rate.
- **You only need inbound forwarding.** Email Routing is free and unlimited.
- **You want one vendor and one bill** for compute, storage and email.

For more ways to send from Workers, see our roundup of the [best Cloudflare Email Service alternatives](/blog/best-cloudflare-email-alternatives).

## Where Reloop is the better choice

- **Your DNS isn't on Cloudflare**, or your app runs on more than Workers.
- **You send under ~200k a month** and want the lower bill and a real free tier.
- **You need marketing mail, templates, contacts or automations** alongside transactional.
- **You want inboxes**, for support or AI agents, with MCP and IMAP.
- **You want signed HTTP webhooks** instead of a queue consumer.
- **You need open source or self-hosting.**
- **You need a generally available product today** rather than a beta.

---

## Using both, or switching

You don't have to choose all at once. A common setup: keep **Email Routing** for forwarding `hello@` to your team, and send through Reloop from your Workers.

To move transactional sending from Cloudflare to Reloop:

1. **Add your domain in Reloop**, publish the `reloop._domainkey` DKIM record and merge `include:reloop.sh` into your SPF record. Don't create a second SPF record.
2. **Store the key** with `wrangler secret put RELOOP_API_KEY`.
3. **Replace `env.EMAIL.send(...)`** with `reloop.mail.send(...)` or the `fetch` helper from our [Workers guide](/blog/send-email-cloudflare-workers). Rename `replyTo` to `reply_to`, and check `emailError` instead of catching exceptions.
4. **Swap the Queue consumer** for a webhook endpoint that verifies `Reloop-Signature`.
5. **Import suppressions** from Cloudflare so you don't email addresses that already bounced or complained.
6. **Ramp traffic** over a few days, then remove the `send_email` binding.

# Best Transactional Email APIs in 2026: In-Depth Comparison and Top Picks

Path: /blog/best-transactional-email-apis-2026
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-transactional-email-apis-2026
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-transactional-email-apis-2026.md

The best transactional email APIs of 2026 compared: Reloop, Resend, Postmark, Amazon SES, SendGrid and Mailgun on pricing at 50k and 100k emails, deliverability, inbound, marketing, self-hosting and developer experience.

**The short version:** for most developer teams in 2026, **Reloop** is the best all-round transactional email API: a modern API, inbound mailboxes, campaigns, and the lowest price per email of any full platform, with the option to self-host. **Postmark** is the pick if transactional deliverability is the only thing you care about. **Amazon SES** is the cheapest raw pipe if you're on AWS and happy to build the rest yourself.

We build Reloop, so factor that in. Every price below comes from each provider's public pricing page, and each section says plainly where that provider beats us.

---

## Top picks at a glance

| Category | Pick | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Best overall** | Reloop | Full platform, $10 for 50k, open source |
| **Best for cost at scale** | Reloop (platform) / Amazon SES (raw pipe) | $0.50 per 1k with a product around it, or $0.10 per 1k with nothing around it |
| **Best for deliverability-focused transactional** | Postmark | Long transactional-only track record, separate message streams |
| **Best for AWS-native teams** | Amazon SES | IAM, SNS and Lambda integration, lowest list price |
| **Best for marketing + transactional** | Reloop | Campaigns, automations and transactional on one suppression list |
| **Best developer experience on a hosted-only API** | Resend | Clean API, React Email, big ecosystem |
| **Best for enterprise procurement** | SendGrid | Twilio contracts, subusers, IP pools |
| **Best open source / self-hosted** | Reloop | Apache 2.0, one-command install |

---

## How we evaluated

We scored each API on six things that actually change your bill or your week:

1. **Price at real volumes.** Free tiers look alike. We compared 50k and 100k emails a month, plus overage.
2. **Developer experience.** Time from install to delivered email, SDK quality, how readable errors are.
3. **Deliverability tooling.** Suppression, bounce handling, dedicated IPs, separation of transactional and bulk traffic.
4. **Inbound email.** Can you receive and reply, and do you get a webhook or a real mailbox?
5. **Breadth.** Templates, campaigns, automations, contacts. Fewer tools to glue together means fewer things to break.
6. **Lock-in.** Can you leave, or run it yourself, if pricing or policy changes?

We didn't score "deliverability rate". Inbox placement depends mostly on your own domain setup and list hygiene, and no provider publishes comparable numbers. Get [SPF, DKIM and DMARC](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide) right first and every provider here will reach the inbox.

---

## 1. Reloop: best overall

Reloop is open-source email infrastructure: a transactional API, SMTP relay, inbound mailboxes, campaigns, automations and webhooks in one product. Use it hosted at [reloop.sh](https://reloop.sh) or run the same code on your own server.

**Pricing:** Free is 6,000 emails a month (200 a day). Pro is $10 for 50,000. Growth is $20 for 100,000 and includes a dedicated IP. Extra mail costs $0.50 per 1,000. Self-hosting is free under Apache 2.0.

**Strengths**

- Lowest price of any full platform here: $10 vs $20 (Resend) and $19.95 (SendGrid) at 50k.
- **Inbound as real mailboxes.** Mail is stored and threaded, spam-scored, and readable over the API, the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) or IMAP. That makes it the natural fit for AI agents and support inboxes.
- Transactional, campaigns and event-triggered automations share one API key and one suppression list.
- Errors return `message`, `why` and `fix`, so most failures explain themselves.
- Official SDKs for Node, Python, Go, PHP, Ruby, Rust, Java, .NET and Elixir.
- Fully self-hostable with a [one-command installer](/self-host) or [Coolify](/blog/reloop-coolify-setup).

**Weaknesses**

- Younger than SendGrid, Mailgun or Postmark. Fewer years of edge cases and community answers.
- No A/B testing for campaigns yet.
- Self-hosting means owning IP reputation and uptime yourself.

**Best for:** startups and product teams that want one email platform at a low price, especially if they need inbound mail or might self-host later.

---

## 2. Resend: best hosted developer experience

Resend made "an email API that feels like Stripe" the norm, and its React Email project made writing templates in JSX mainstream.

**Pricing:** Free is 3,000 a month (100 a day). Pro is $20 for 50,000. 100,000 costs $35 a month. Overage is $0.90 per 1,000.

**Strengths**

- Excellent docs and onboarding.
- React Email is first-class.
- A large ecosystem of examples, templates and integrations.
- Broadcasts and audiences for simple marketing sends.

**Weaknesses**

- $35 at 100k vs $20 on Reloop, and a dedicated IP needs the $90 Scale plan plus a $30/mo add-on.
- Hosted only. No self-hosting, no source.
- Inbound arrives as a webhook per message, not a mailbox you can thread and reply from.
- A dedicated IP needs the $90 Scale plan plus a $30/mo add-on.

**Best for:** small teams that want a polished hosted API and expect to stay under 50k emails a month.

Full breakdown: [Reloop vs Resend](/blog/reloop-vs-resend).

---

## 3. Postmark: best for deliverability-focused transactional

Postmark has been transactional-first for over a decade and is known for fast, reliable delivery of password resets and receipts. It separates traffic into **message streams**, so bulk mail can't drag down your transactional reputation.

**Pricing:** a free developer plan with 100 emails a month that never expires. Basic starts at $15 for 10,000 emails, with overage at $1.80 per 1,000; Pro and Platform lower the overage to $1.30 and $1.20. Inbound processing needs Pro or above. Dedicated IPs start at $50 a month per IP for senders above 300,000 emails a month.

**Strengths**

- Strong reputation for transactional deliverability.
- Message streams keep transactional and broadcast traffic apart, with up to 15 streams on Basic.
- Clear bounce taxonomy and good activity logs.
- Excellent support.

**Weaknesses**

- The most expensive per email in this list once you pass the base tier.
- Very small free tier (100 a month).
- Inbound requires a higher plan.
- Hosted only.

**Best for:** teams where a delayed password reset costs real money and budget is secondary.

---

## 4. Amazon SES: best for AWS-native teams

SES is AWS's raw email service. It's the cheapest way to send at volume, and it's a building block, not a product.

**Pricing:** $0.10 per 1,000 emails à la carte, plus $0.12 per GB of attachments. Receiving costs $0.10 per 1,000. Dedicated IPs are $24.95 a month each. New AWS accounts get up to $200 in Free Tier credits for six months.

**Strengths**

- Lowest list price per email by a wide margin.
- Deep AWS integration: IAM, SNS, EventBridge, Lambda, S3.
- Scales to very high volume.

**Weaknesses**

- No real dashboard for logs, templates or campaigns. You build that yourself.
- New accounts start in a sandbox and need production access approval.
- Inbound is receipt rules that drop mail into S3 or trigger Lambda, not a mailbox.
- Bounce and complaint handling is yours to wire up through SNS.

**Best for:** AWS-heavy teams with engineering time to build the surrounding tooling.

<Callout type="tip">
  You can get SES pricing with a real product on top: Reloop can route outbound mail through SES (or any SMTP provider) while you keep Reloop's API, logs, templates and suppression list.
</Callout>

---

## 5. SendGrid: best for enterprise procurement

SendGrid, now part of Twilio, sends an enormous share of the world's email and has every enterprise checkbox.

**Pricing:** no permanent free plan; new accounts get a 60-day trial at 100 emails a day. Essentials is $19.95 for 50,000 and $34.95 for 100,000. Pro, which adds a dedicated IP, subusers and SSO, starts at $89.95. Marketing Campaigns is a separate plan.

**Strengths**

- Proven at very high volume, with IP pools and subuser management.
- Mature enterprise compliance programme and procurement path through Twilio.
- Handlebars logic (`{{#if}}`, `{{#each}}`) inside dynamic templates.
- Email validation API on higher plans.

**Weaknesses**

- Two products (Email API and Marketing Campaigns) with separate plans.
- An older API surface and a dashboard that shows its age.
- No free tier after the trial.
- Hosted only.

**Best for:** larger companies already on Twilio that need enterprise contracts more than developer ergonomics.

Full breakdown: [Reloop vs SendGrid](/blog/reloop-vs-sendgrid).

---

## 6. Mailgun: best for validation and detailed logs

Mailgun, now part of Sinch, is a long-standing developer email API with strong routing and log tooling.

**Pricing:** a free plan at 100 emails a day. Basic is $15 for 10,000. Foundation is $35 for 50,000, with overage from $1.30 per 1,000.

**Strengths**

- Mature email validation (priced as an add-on).
- Inbound routes that match on patterns and forward or POST messages.
- Detailed event logs and search.
- Handlebars templates.

**Weaknesses**

- Campaign tooling is a separate Sinch product.
- Dedicated IPs are a paid add-on.
- Hosted only.

**Best for:** teams that need validation and log search alongside sending, and are happy on a hosted service.

---

## Developer experience, side by side

The modern APIs look almost identical. Here's one send on Reloop, Resend and SES:

```typescript
// Reloop
const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY! });
const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Welcome",
  html: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
});

// Resend
const resend = new Resend(process.env.RESEND_API_KEY);
const { data, error } = await resend.emails.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@acme.com>",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Welcome",
  html: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
});

// Amazon SES (AWS SDK v3)
const ses = new SESv2Client({ region: "us-east-1" });
await ses.send(
  new SendEmailCommand({
    FromEmailAddress: "hello@acme.com",
    Destination: { ToAddresses: ["user@example.com"] },
    Content: {
      Simple: {
        Subject: { Data: "Welcome" },
        Body: { Html: { Data: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>" } },
      },
    },
  }),
);
```

Reloop and Resend are a near find-and-replace apart. SES needs more ceremony, plus IAM credentials and production access. Postmark, SendGrid and Mailgun sit in between.

Every provider here also offers SMTP. If your app or framework already speaks SMTP, switching is a host, port and credential change. On Reloop that's `smtp.reloop.sh` on port 587, with your API key as both username and password.

---

## How to choose

Answer these in order and stop at the first "yes":

1. **Do you need to self-host or read the source?** → Reloop.
2. **Do you need to receive email into mailboxes, for an AI agent or a support inbox?** → Reloop.
3. **Are you all-in on AWS with time to build tooling, and cost per email is everything?** → Amazon SES.
4. **Is transactional deliverability the only metric, with budget to match?** → Postmark.
5. **Do you need enterprise contracts through Twilio?** → SendGrid.
6. **Do you need email validation and log search above all?** → Mailgun.
7. **Do you want a polished hosted API and expect to stay small?** → Resend.
8. **None of the above, and you want the most for the money?** → Reloop.

<Callout type="info">
  Price your volume twelve months out, not today. Switching providers means re-verifying DNS and re-warming reputation, so pick the one that still makes sense at 10× your current volume.
</Callout>

    Amazon SES has the lowest list price at $0.10 per 1,000 emails, but it's
    a raw sending service with no dashboard or templates. Among full
    platforms, Reloop is cheapest: $10 for 50,000 and $20 for 100,000, then
    $0.50 per 1,000.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Which email API has the best deliverability?">
    Postmark has the strongest reputation for transactional delivery, helped
    by strict separation of transactional and bulk streams. In practice your
    own SPF, DKIM, DMARC and list hygiene matter more than the provider. All
    six here will reach the inbox with a well-configured domain.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Is there an open-source alternative to SendGrid and Resend?">
    Yes. Reloop is open source under Apache 2.0, with the same kind of
    modern API, and you can run it on your own server or use the hosted
    version.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Which email API is best for AI agents?">
    One that gives agents a real mailbox to read and reply from, not just an
    inbound webhook. Reloop provides mailboxes with threads over the API, an
    MCP server and IMAP. See
    [email infrastructure for AI agents](/blog/email-infrastructure-for-ai-agents).
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Do I need a dedicated IP?">
    Usually not until you send a few hundred thousand emails a month
    consistently. Below that, a well-managed shared pool performs better
    because a dedicated IP needs steady volume to keep its reputation. Read
    the [IP warming guide](/blog/ip-warming-guide) before you get one.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# BIMI: Show Your Logo in the Gmail Inbox

Path: /blog/bimi-email-setup-guide
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/bimi-email-setup-guide
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/bimi-email-setup-guide.md

A complete BIMI setup guide: DMARC enforcement, the SVG Tiny PS logo, VMC vs CMC certificates, the default._bimi DNS record, which inboxes show logos, and how to debug a logo that won't appear.

**BIMI shows your logo next to your emails in Gmail, Apple Mail, Yahoo and a few other inboxes.** To get it you need three things: DMARC at enforcement (`p=quarantine` or `p=reject` with `pct=100`), your logo as an SVG Tiny PS file, and for Gmail and Apple Mail a mark certificate (VMC or CMC). Then you publish one TXT record at `default._bimi.yourdomain.com`.

The DNS part takes five minutes. The certificate is what takes time, so start there if you want the logo in Gmail. This guide covers every step and the reasons logos don't show up.

---

## What BIMI is (and isn't)

BIMI stands for Brand Indicators for Message Identification. It's a DNS record that tells mailbox providers where to find your logo, and optionally a certificate proving you're allowed to use it.

It is **not** a deliverability shortcut. A BIMI record won't move you from spam to inbox (if that's your problem, start with [why emails land in spam](/blog/why-emails-land-in-spam-fix)). What it does:

- Puts your logo in the inbox list instead of a grey letter avatar
- Makes phishing that imitates your brand easier to spot
- Adds a blue verified checkmark in Gmail if you have a VMC

The real benefit is the prerequisite. BIMI requires DMARC enforcement, and getting there means you've authenticated every service that sends as your domain. That alone improves deliverability and blocks spoofing.

---

## Which inboxes show BIMI logos

| Mailbox provider | Shows BIMI logos | Certificate needed |
|---|---|---|
| Gmail | Yes | VMC or CMC. A VMC adds the blue checkmark |
| Apple Mail (iCloud, iOS, macOS) | Yes | VMC |
| Yahoo Mail / AOL | Yes | Not required; a self-asserted logo can show |
| Fastmail | Yes | Check their current policy |
| La Poste, Zone, AU (KDDI) | Yes | Varies |
| Microsoft Outlook / Outlook.com | No | - |

Sources: the [BIMI Group's provider list](https://bimigroup.org/where-is-my-bimi-logo-displayed/) and [Google Workspace's BIMI setup page](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/security/set-up-bimi). Providers can always decline to show a logo if they don't trust the sender's reputation, even with everything configured correctly.

---

## Step 1: Get DMARC to enforcement

This is the requirement most domains fail. Your DMARC record must use `p=quarantine` or `p=reject`, and must apply to 100% of mail.

```text
_dmarc.yourdomain.com  TXT  "v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; pct=100; rua=mailto:dmarc@yourdomain.com"
```

| Policy | BIMI eligible |
|---|---|
| `p=none` | No |
| `p=quarantine; pct=50` | No |
| `p=quarantine` (pct defaults to 100) | Yes |
| `p=reject` | Yes |

Don't jump straight to `reject`. Moving to enforcement before every sender is authenticated means your own invoices, CRM emails or support replies start landing in spam. The safe path:

1. Publish `p=none` with a `rua` reporting address.
2. Read the aggregate reports for two to four weeks. Find every service sending as your domain.
3. Add SPF and DKIM for each one: your email API, Google Workspace or Microsoft 365, your CRM, your helpdesk.
4. Move to `p=quarantine`, watch reports for another week or two, then optionally `p=reject`.

The [SPF, DKIM and DMARC setup guide](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide) walks through each step. If you send with Reloop, your domain page shows the exact SPF and DKIM records and whether they verify.

<Callout type="warning">
  If your organizational domain has `sp=none` (subdomain policy), subdomains you send from may not qualify. Check both the subdomain you send from and the root domain's policy.
</Callout>

---

## Step 2: Make an SVG Tiny PS logo

BIMI logos must be in **SVG Tiny Portable/Secure (SVG Tiny PS)**, a restricted SVG profile. A normal SVG exported from Figma or Illustrator will not work as-is.

Gmail's requirements:

- SVG Tiny PS: `version="1.2"` and `baseProfile="tiny-ps"` on the root `<svg>`
- A `<title>` element with your company name
- Square aspect ratio, with the logo centered on a **solid** background
- Minimum 96 × 96 pixels, in absolute units
- Under 32 KB
- No scripts, external links, raster images, animations or `x=`/`y=` on the root element

A minimal valid structure:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" version="1.2" baseProfile="tiny-ps"
     viewBox="0 0 96 96" width="96" height="96">
  <title>Acme</title>
  <rect width="96" height="96" fill="#000000"/>
  <!-- your logo paths, centered -->
</svg>
```

Design for a circle. Most inboxes crop the logo into a circle, so keep the mark inside the middle ~70% of the square.

Converting an existing logo:

1. Export a clean SVG (paths only, text converted to outlines).
2. Remove any embedded bitmaps, gradients that reference external resources, and `<script>` or `<style>` blocks that pull in fonts.
3. Edit the root element to add `version="1.2"` and `baseProfile="tiny-ps"`, remove `x` and `y`, and add a `<title>`.
4. Host it at a stable HTTPS URL, for example `https://yourdomain.com/bimi/logo.svg`.

If you're getting a VMC or CMC, the certificate authority will usually check or prepare the SVG for you, since the logo is embedded in the certificate.

---

## Step 3: Get a VMC or CMC (for Gmail and Apple Mail)

A mark certificate proves you're entitled to use the logo. Two types exist:

| | VMC (Verified Mark Certificate) | CMC (Common Mark Certificate) |
|---|---|---|
| Proof required | A **registered trademark** for the logo | Evidence the logo has been publicly used for at least a year |
| Gmail | Logo + blue checkmark | Logo, no checkmark |
| Apple Mail | Logo | Not supported |
| Time to get | Weeks once you hold the trademark. Registering the trademark itself often takes 6–12 months | Usually days to weeks |
| Typical issuers | DigiCert, Sectigo, GlobalSign, Entrust | DigiCert, Sectigo, GlobalSign, Entrust |

Pick based on what you have:

- **You already have a registered trademark for the logo:** get a VMC. You get Gmail, Apple Mail and the checkmark.
- **No trademark:** get a CMC for Gmail now, and file a trademark if you want the checkmark and Apple Mail later.
- **You only care about Yahoo:** you can skip the certificate entirely.

Certificates are annual purchases. The issuer gives you a PEM file. Host it at an HTTPS URL next to your logo, for example `https://yourdomain.com/bimi/certificate.pem`.

---

## Step 4: Publish the BIMI record

Add a TXT record at `default._bimi` on the domain in your From address.

**With a certificate:**

```text
default._bimi.yourdomain.com  TXT  "v=BIMI1; l=https://yourdomain.com/bimi/logo.svg; a=https://yourdomain.com/bimi/certificate.pem"
```

**Without a certificate (Yahoo and others that accept self-asserted logos):**

```text
default._bimi.yourdomain.com  TXT  "v=BIMI1; l=https://yourdomain.com/bimi/logo.svg; a="
```

| Tag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `v=BIMI1` | Version, required, must come first |
| `l=` | HTTPS URL of the SVG Tiny PS logo |
| `a=` | HTTPS URL of the VMC or CMC PEM file. Empty if you have none |

When the logo is embedded in the certificate, Gmail uses the certificate's copy. Keep the `l=` file identical to it anyway.

If you send from a subdomain like `mail.yourdomain.com`, publish the record on that subdomain (`default._bimi.mail.yourdomain.com`) or rely on the organizational domain's record, which providers fall back to.

---

## Step 5: Check it

Use the free [Reloop BIMI checker](/tools/bimi-checker). It looks up `default._bimi` for your domain, validates the `v=`, `l=` and `a=` tags, checks that DMARC is at enforcement with `pct=100`, and fetches the logo to run SVG Tiny PS checks.

Then send a real email to a Gmail and a Yahoo address. Logos can take up to 48 hours to appear after everything is in place, and providers cache them, so changes aren't instant.

---

## Why your BIMI logo isn't showing

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Nothing anywhere | DMARC is `p=none` or `pct` is under 100 | Move to `p=quarantine` with `pct=100` |
| Shows in Yahoo, not Gmail | No VMC or CMC | Get a certificate and add it as `a=` |
| Shows in Gmail, not Apple Mail | You have a CMC | Apple Mail needs a VMC |
| Checker says logo invalid | Not SVG Tiny PS, has `x`/`y` on root, or over 32 KB | Re-export and fix the root element |
| Some emails show it, others don't | A different service sends some mail and fails DMARC alignment | Authenticate that service's SPF/DKIM for your domain |
| Logo shows with wrong crop | Logo not centered for a circle | Shrink the mark to the middle ~70% |
| Recently fixed, still missing | Provider cache | Wait up to 48 hours |

Also remember that mailbox providers can choose not to show logos for senders with poor reputation, [high complaint rates](/blog/gmail-yahoo-bulk-sender-requirements), or very low volume. A new domain gets there by [warming up gradually](/blog/ip-warming-guide). BIMI rewards senders who are already doing the basics right.

---

## BIMI and Reloop

[Reloop](/blog/introducing-reloop) doesn't need anything special for BIMI. The logo is tied to the domain in your From address, not to the sending service. As long as the mail you send through Reloop passes DMARC (which it does once the SPF and DKIM records from your domain page are verified), BIMI works for it automatically.

A quick pre-flight for a Reloop sending domain:

1. Domain verified in Reloop, DKIM passing.
2. DMARC at `p=quarantine` or `p=reject`, `pct=100`.
3. `default._bimi` record published, logo and certificate on HTTPS.
4. [BIMI checker](/tools/bimi-checker) passes.

The free [auth checker](/tools/auth-checker) will confirm SPF, DKIM and DMARC for the domain first, if you're not sure where you stand.

---

## FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Do I need a trademark for BIMI?">
    Only for a VMC, which gives you the Gmail checkmark and Apple Mail
    support. A CMC needs proof that the logo has been in public use for at
    least a year instead, and works in Gmail without a checkmark. Yahoo
    doesn't require a certificate at all.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Does BIMI improve deliverability?">
    Not directly. BIMI requires DMARC enforcement, and enforcement does help
    by blocking spoofing and pushing you to authenticate every sender. The
    logo itself may improve recognition and opens, but it won't fix spam
    placement.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Does Outlook support BIMI?">
    Not at the time of writing. Outlook shows its own sender images for some
    brands, but it doesn't read BIMI records.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="How much does a VMC cost?">
    VMCs and CMCs are sold as annual certificates by the certificate
    authorities listed above. Prices change and vary by issuer, so compare
    current quotes. Budget for the trademark separately if you don't have one.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can I use BIMI on a subdomain?">
    Yes. Publish `default._bimi` on the subdomain you send from, or let it
    fall back to the organizational domain's record. DMARC enforcement has to
    apply to the subdomain either way.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>
