# Reloop vs Loops (2026): Pricing, Features and Which to Choose

Path: /blog/reloop-vs-loops
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-loops
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-loops.md

Reloop vs Loops compared honestly: per-email vs per-contact pricing at 1k to 100k contacts, lifecycle automations, transactional API and SMTP, inbound inboxes, self-hosting, plus how to switch.

**Loops and Reloop both send the emails a SaaS product needs: onboarding sequences, product announcements and account mail.** The big difference is how you pay. **Loops bills by how many contacts you store. Reloop bills by how many emails you send.** At 100,000 contacts that's $399 a month on Loops versus $20 to $70 on Reloop for most sending patterns. Reloop also covers the transactional side (REST API and SMTP), receives mail into real inboxes, and is open source.

Loops is a polished, focused tool for lifecycle marketing, and for some teams that focus is exactly the point. We build Reloop, so weigh this accordingly. Loops' prices below come from [loops.so/pricing](https://loops.so/pricing), and where Loops is the better pick, we say so.

---

## The 30-second comparison

| | **Reloop** | **Loops** |
|---|---|---|
| Pricing basis | Emails sent | Contacts stored |
| Free tier | 6,000 emails / mo, 200 / day | 1,000 contacts, 4,000 sends / mo |
| Entry paid plan | **$10** / mo (50,000 emails) | $49 / mo |
| At 100,000 | **$20** / mo (100,000 emails) | $399 / mo (100,000 contacts) |
| Extra volume | $0.50 per 1,000 emails | Next contact tier |
| Transactional REST API | Yes | Limited |
| SMTP relay | Yes | No |
| Lifecycle automations | Yes | Yes (core focus) |
| Broadcasts | Yes | Yes |
| Inbound email / agent inbox | Yes | No |
| Sending engine | Own MTA (KumoMTA) | Third-party infrastructure |
| Open source / self-host | Yes (Apache 2.0) | No |

Reloop's prices are on [reloop.sh/pricing](/pricing). Both change; check before you commit.

---

## Pricing: contacts vs emails

This is the decision for most teams, so it's worth getting right.

**Loops charges for your list.** Every contact you store counts, whether they opened an email last week or haven't logged in for a year. Your bill grows with signups, not with how much you send.

**Reloop charges for sends.** Store as many contacts as you like. You pay for the emails that go out, and nothing at all for the software if you self-host.

Here's what that means for a product with **100,000 contacts**, depending on how often you email them:

| Emails per contact per month | Emails sent | Reloop | Loops |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (monthly newsletter) | 100,000 | $20 | $399 |
| 2 | 200,000 | $20 + $50 overage = **$70** | $399 |
| 4 (weekly) | 400,000 | $20 + $150 overage = **$170** | $399 |

Reloop's Growth plan includes 100,000 emails for $20. Each extra 1,000 costs $0.50.

At the small end, the free tiers favor different shapes. Loops gives you 1,000 contacts and 4,000 sends a month. Reloop gives you 6,000 emails a month with a 200-a-day cap and no limit on contacts. A side project with a large, quiet waitlist fits Reloop's free tier better; a tiny list you email often fits Loops'.

<Callout type="tip">
  Per-contact pricing quietly punishes growth. A launch that brings in 20,000 signups raises your Loops bill even if you never email most of them. Before you choose, model next year's list size, not today's.
</Callout>

---

## Automations and lifecycle email

Lifecycle email is Loops' core focus, and it shows. Building onboarding flows is pleasant and the product is designed around that one job.

Reloop's automations cover the same ground: an **event trigger**, then **delays**, **conditions** and **email steps**. Your app tracks an event, and the contact enters every automation that event triggers:

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY! });

const { automationError } = await reloop.automations.start({
  event: "user.signed_up",
  email: user.email,
  firstName: user.name,
  properties: { plan: user.plan },
});
if (automationError) console.error(automationError);
```

Passing `email` creates the contact if it doesn't exist yet. Conditions can read event properties (for example `trigger.plan`), so trial and paid users can get different welcome emails. Our [welcome sequence guide](/blog/welcome-email-sequences-that-convert) builds a full four-email onboarding flow this way.

Around that, Reloop has contacts with custom properties, groups, subscription channels so people can opt out of one kind of mail without losing all of it, and scheduled broadcast campaigns.

| | Reloop | Loops |
|---|---|---|
| Event-triggered automations | Yes | Yes |
| Delays and conditions | Yes | Yes |
| Broadcasts / newsletters | Yes | Yes |
| Template editing | HTML, React Email, stored templates with `{{{variables}}}` | HTML / visual editor |

If your marketing team wants to build emails visually without touching code, that's a point for Loops.

---

## Transactional email: one tool or two

Password resets, receipts, magic links and invoices need to arrive in seconds, every time. They're also where developers spend most of their integration time.

Loops' transactional support is limited and it has no SMTP relay, so many teams that use Loops for lifecycle mail add a second vendor (often Resend or Postmark) for transactional sends. That means two bills, two sets of DNS records, two dashboards and two suppression lists that can disagree.

Reloop handles both in one place:

```typescript
const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
  to: user.email,
  subject: "Reset your password",
  html: `<p><a href="${resetUrl}">Reset your password</a></p>`,
});
```

- **REST API** with SDKs for Node, Python, Go, PHP, Ruby, Rust, Java, .NET and Elixir.
- **SMTP relay** at `smtp.reloop.sh` for frameworks, CMSs and tools that only speak SMTP.
- **Signed webhooks** for delivered, bounced and complained events, verified with HMAC-SHA256 in the `Reloop-Signature` header.
- **One sender reputation and one suppression list** for transactional and marketing mail. A user who hard-bounces on a receipt won't get your next newsletter.

---

## Receiving email and agent inboxes

Loops is outbound only.

Reloop receives mail into **mailboxes**. Messages are stored, threaded and spam-scored, and readable through the API, the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) or IMAP. You can reply in-thread with one call.

That matters for reply handling ("just reply to this email"), support addresses, and AI agents that need their own address to read and answer mail. See [build an AI agent that reads and replies to email](/blog/build-ai-agent-sends-emails).

---

## Deliverability and data ownership

Reloop runs its own MTA (KumoMTA), with per-domain throttling and automatic pauses when bounce or complaint rates spike. Loops sends through third-party email infrastructure. Both verify your domain and sign webhooks.

The bigger difference is where your data lives:

- **Loops** is closed SaaS. You can export contacts as CSV.
- **Reloop** is Apache 2.0. You can start on Reloop Cloud and later move to your own server with the [one-command installer](/self-host) or [Coolify](/blog/reloop-coolify-setup). Point the SDK's `baseUrl` at your instance and your code stays the same.

Self-hosting means owning IP warm-up and uptime yourself, so most teams should start hosted. It's useful to have the option for data residency, security reviews and price protection.

---

## Where Loops is the better choice

Being honest about it:

- **Your list is small and you email it often.** Under 1,000 contacts, Loops' free tier allows 4,000 sends a month.
- **Marketers own email, not engineers.** Loops is built around a visual, marketing-first workflow, and that focus makes it pleasant for non-developers.
- **You already run transactional mail elsewhere** and only want a lifecycle tool on top.

Considering more than these two? Our roundup of the [best Loops alternatives](/blog/best-loops-alternatives) covers other lifecycle tools for SaaS.

## Where Reloop is the better choice

- **Your contact list is large or growing fast.** Paying per send instead of per contact is usually far cheaper: $20 vs $399 at 100,000.
- **You want transactional and lifecycle mail in one product**, with one domain setup and one suppression list.
- **You need SMTP**, inbound inboxes, or email for AI agents.
- **You want open source** or the option to self-host.

---

## Switching from Loops to Reloop

1. **Add your sending domain** in Reloop and publish the DKIM record (`reloop._domainkey`). Merge `include:reloop.sh` into your existing SPF record rather than adding a second SPF record.
2. **Export your contacts** from Loops as CSV and import them into Reloop. Map custom fields to contact properties and keep unsubscribed contacts unsubscribed.
3. **Rebuild templates.** Paste in your HTML or React Email components and change placeholders to triple braces: `{{{first_name}}}`.
4. **Recreate your loops as automations.** Create an event for each trigger (for example `user.signed_up`), then add the same delays, conditions and email steps.
5. **Swap the tracking calls** in your app for `reloop.automations.start`, and send transactional mail with `reloop.mail.send`.
6. **Run both in parallel** for a week or two, then remove Loops' DNS records.

# Email Provider Comparison: Resend vs SendGrid vs Reloop

Path: /blog/email-provider-comparison-2026
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/email-provider-comparison-2026
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/email-provider-comparison-2026.md

Resend vs SendGrid vs Reloop in 2026: pricing at 3k, 50k and 100k emails a month, developer experience, inbound and agent inboxes, self-hosting, and which one fits your team.

**Short answer:** pick **Resend** if you want a polished hosted API and don't mind paying more per email as you grow. Pick **SendGrid** if you're already deep in the Twilio ecosystem or need its long enterprise track record. Pick **Reloop** if you want the same modern developer experience at a lower price, plus inbound mail, agent inboxes, and the option to self-host the whole stack.

We build Reloop, so read this with that in mind. We've tried to keep every claim checkable: pricing comes from each provider's public pricing page, and where a competitor is better, we say so.

---

## The 30-second comparison

| | **Reloop** | **Resend** | **SendGrid** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Free tier | 6,000 / mo (200 / day) | 3,000 / mo (100 / day) | 60-day trial, 100 / day |
| 50,000 emails / mo | **$10** | $20 | $19.95 |
| 100,000 emails / mo | **$20** | $35 | $34.95 |
| Overage per 1,000 | **$0.50** | $0.90 | Plan upgrade |
| Open source | Yes (Apache 2.0) | No | No |
| Self-host | Yes | No | No |
| Inbound + agent inbox | Yes | Inbound via webhooks | Inbound Parse webhook |
| Marketing / campaigns | Yes | Broadcasts | Marketing Campaigns (separate plan) |
| SMTP relay | Yes | Yes | Yes |

Prices are list prices for hosted plans as published on [resend.com/pricing](https://resend.com/pricing), [sendgrid.com/pricing](https://sendgrid.com/pricing/) and [reloop.sh/pricing](/pricing). Check them before you sign anything; providers change tiers often.

---

## What actually matters when choosing an email API

Every serious provider ships the basics: a REST API, SMTP, SPF/DKIM support, webhooks for delivery events, and SDKs for the usual languages. If a provider is missing any of those, skip it.

The real differences show up in five places:

1. **Price at your volume.** Free tiers look similar. The real gap opens at 50k–500k emails a month.
2. **Developer experience.** How long from `npm install` to a delivered email? How readable are errors?
3. **Deliverability controls.** Dedicated IPs, suppression lists, bounce handling, warm-up.
4. **What else it does.** Receiving mail, campaigns, automations, contact management.
5. **Lock-in.** Can you move, or run it yourself, if pricing or policy changes?

Let's go through each provider against those.

---

## Resend

Resend popularised the "email API that feels like Stripe" style. The docs are clean, the Node SDK is tiny, and its React Email project made writing templates in JSX normal.

**Where Resend is strong**

- Excellent onboarding and docs. You'll send your first email in minutes.
- React Email integration is first-class.
- A focused product. It does sending very well and doesn't try to be a CRM.

**Where it falls short**

- **Price as you scale.** The free tier is half the size of ours (3,000 vs 6,000 a month), the first paid tier is $20 for 50k, and 100k emails costs $35 a month on Pro. Overage is $0.90 per 1,000.
- **Hosted only.** There's no self-hosted option, so data residency and vendor risk are on their terms.
- **Inbound is webhook-based.** You receive a POST per message rather than a mailbox your app or agent can read, thread, and reply from.

**Best for:** small teams that want a great hosted sending API and expect modest volume.

For more options in the same space, see the [best Resend alternatives](/blog/best-resend-alternatives).

---

## SendGrid

SendGrid has been around since 2009 and is now part of Twilio. It sends a huge share of the world's transactional email and has every enterprise checkbox you can think of.

**Where SendGrid is strong**

- Proven at very high volume, with dedicated IP pools and sub-user management.
- Mature compliance story (SOC 2, HIPAA-eligible configurations, SSO).
- Marketing Campaigns, Inbound Parse and an Email Validation API exist in one account.

**Where it falls short**

- **The permanent free plan is gone.** New accounts get a 60-day trial, then pay.
- **Complexity.** Two products (Email API and Marketing Campaigns) with separate plans, legacy v2/v3 APIs, and a dashboard that shows its age.
- **Account reviews.** New accounts can be held for manual review before sending is enabled, which can delay a launch.
- **Hosted only**, like Resend.

**Best for:** larger companies already on Twilio that need enterprise procurement more than developer ergonomics.

If you're leaving, we wrote a step-by-step [SendGrid migration guide](/blog/migrating-from-sendgrid), and our roundup of the [best SendGrid alternatives](/blog/best-sendgrid-alternatives) compares where else you could go.

---

## Reloop

Reloop is open-source email infrastructure: transactional API, SMTP relay, campaigns, automations, webhooks and agent inboxes in one product. You can use the hosted version at [reloop.sh](https://reloop.sh) or run the same code on your own servers.

**Where Reloop is strong**

- **Price.** Pro is $10 for 50k emails and Growth is $20 for 100k, with $0.50 per extra 1,000. That's 2–4× cheaper than the alternatives at the same volume.
- **Two-way email.** Every domain can receive mail into real mailboxes with threads, so AI agents and humans can read and reply, over the API, the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server), or IMAP.
- **Transactional and marketing together.** Contacts, groups, templates, campaigns and event-triggered automations share one API key and one suppression list.
- **Self-hosting.** Everything is Apache 2.0. Deploy with Docker Compose on a [$5 VPS](/blog/self-host-email-5-dollars), [Coolify](/blog/reloop-coolify-setup) or [Fly.io](/blog/reloop-flyio-deployment).
- **Bring your own SMTP.** Route sends through SES, Postmark or any SMTP provider while keeping Reloop's API, logs and templates.

**Where it falls short**

- **Younger product.** Reloop launched in 2025. SendGrid has fifteen years of edge cases behind it.
- **No A/B testing yet** for campaigns.
- **Self-hosting is real work.** You own IP reputation, warm-up and uptime. The hosted plan exists for teams that don't want that.

**Best for:** startups and developer teams that want a modern API, care about cost, and want the option to own their infrastructure later.

---

## Pricing at real volumes

Free tiers are a marketing number. Here's what the hosted plans cost at three realistic monthly volumes.

| Monthly volume | Reloop | Resend | SendGrid |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3,000 | $0 | $0 | Trial, then paid |
| 50,000 | $10 | $20 | $19.95 |
| 100,000 | $20 | $35 | $34.95 |
| 250,000 | $20 + $75 overage = **$95** | $35 + $135 overage = $170 | Pro tier |

At 100k emails a month, Reloop costs **$240 a year**. The same volume on Resend is **$420 a year**, or $1,440 with a dedicated IP (Scale plus the $30 add-on).

If you self-host Reloop, the software is free and your cost is the server plus your time. For most teams under a few million emails a month, the hosted plan is cheaper than an engineer's afternoon.

<Callout type="tip">
  Price your **projected** volume twelve months out, not today's. Switching providers mid-growth means re-verifying domains and re-warming reputation.
</Callout>

## Developer experience, side by side

All three have a Node SDK. Here's sending one email with each.

**Resend**

```typescript

const resend = new Resend(process.env.RESEND_API_KEY);

await resend.emails.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@acme.com>",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Welcome",
  html: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
});
```

**SendGrid**

```typescript

sgMail.setApiKey(process.env.SENDGRID_API_KEY!);

await sgMail.send({
  from: "hello@acme.com",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Welcome",
  html: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
});
```

**Reloop**

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY! });

const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Welcome",
  html: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
});
```

The calls are nearly identical, which is the point: switching between modern providers is mostly a find-and-replace. Reloop returns errors as values (`emailError`) instead of throwing, and every API error includes a `message`, `why`, `fix` and docs `link`, so you know what to change without opening a support ticket.

---

## Deliverability

Deliverability is mostly about **your** domain and list, not the provider. Any of these three will land in the inbox if you:

- Publish [SPF, DKIM and DMARC](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide)
- Keep bounces and complaints low with automatic suppression
- [Warm up](/blog/ip-warming-guide) new domains and IPs gradually
- Separate transactional and marketing traffic

Where providers differ is how much they do for you. SendGrid offers dedicated IPs on higher plans. Resend offers dedicated IPs as an add-on. Reloop includes a dedicated IP on Growth, auto-suppresses hard bounces and complaints across transactional and marketing sends, and runs a [free domain reputation checker](/tools/domain-reputation-checker) you can use before you send anything.

---

## Lock-in and data ownership

This is the biggest structural difference.

With Resend and SendGrid, your sending history, templates, suppression lists and contacts live in their database. If prices rise or your account is suspended, you export what you can and start over.

With Reloop, the code is open. You can start hosted, export everything, and move to your own servers without changing your integration. Just point the SDK's `baseUrl` at your instance. That also matters for data residency: if you need email bodies to stay in the EU or on-prem, you can.

Read more in [why we open-sourced our email infrastructure](/blog/why-we-open-sourced-email-infrastructure).

---

## Which one should you pick?

- **You're a solo developer or small team sending under 3,000 emails a month:** any of them. Pick the docs you like most.
- **You're growing past 50k emails a month and cost matters:** Reloop. Same DX, a fraction of the price.
- **You need inbound email for an AI agent or support inbox:** Reloop. Real mailboxes, not just webhooks.
- **You need data residency or air-gapped deploys:** Reloop self-hosted. It's the only one of the three you can run yourself.
- **You're an enterprise on Twilio with procurement already approved:** SendGrid.
- **You want the most established hosted API and React Email is central to your stack:** Resend. (React Email also works with Reloop.)

# Password Reset Email: Best Practices and Template

Path: /blog/password-reset-email-best-practices
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/password-reset-email-best-practices
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/password-reset-email-best-practices.md

How to build a secure password reset email: token design, expiry, rate limiting, link vs code, subject lines and copy, a full HTML and plain-text template, sending code and deliverability tips.

**A good password reset email arrives in seconds, contains one link that works once and expires within an hour, and does not reveal whether an account exists.** Everything else, from copy to design, comes after those three rules.

Password resets are the email users need most urgently and trust least. If one is slow, lands in spam or looks like phishing, the user gives up or opens a support ticket. If it is built carelessly, it becomes the easiest way to take over an account.

This guide covers the security side (tokens, expiry, rate limits), the email itself (subject, copy, a full template) and how to make sure it reaches the inbox.

---

## The password reset flow

1. User enters their email on a "Forgot password" form.
2. Your server **always** shows the same message: "If an account exists, we sent a link."
3. If the account exists, generate a token, store its **hash**, and email the link.
4. User clicks the link and sets a new password.
5. Server checks the token, updates the password, **deletes the token** and ends other sessions.
6. Send a **"Your password was changed"** confirmation.

Steps 2, 5 and 6 are the ones most implementations skip.

---

## Security best practices

### 1. Generate tokens with a secure random source

Use at least 32 random bytes from a cryptographically secure generator. Never use `Math.random()`, timestamps, user IDs or anything an attacker could guess.

```typescript

  const token = randomBytes(32).toString("base64url"); // goes in the email
  const tokenHash = createHash("sha256").update(token).digest("hex"); // goes in the DB
  return { token, tokenHash };
}
```

### 2. Store only the hash

Treat reset tokens like passwords. If your database leaks, plain-text tokens let an attacker reset any account with a pending request. A SHA-256 hash is enough here because the token is already high-entropy, so you do not need bcrypt.

```sql
CREATE TABLE password_reset_tokens (
  id          uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  user_id     uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  token_hash  text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  expires_at  timestamptz NOT NULL,
  used_at     timestamptz
);
```

### 3. Expire tokens quickly

**15 to 60 minutes** is the usual range. OWASP recommends short-lived tokens, and most users click within a few minutes. Show the expiry in the email so users know to act.

### 4. Make tokens single-use

Mark the token used (or delete it) in the same transaction that updates the password. Also delete every other outstanding reset token for that user, so older emails stop working.

### 5. Do not reveal whether an account exists

Return the same response, with the same status code and roughly the same timing, for known and unknown addresses. Otherwise your reset form tells attackers which emails have accounts.

To keep the timing the same, put the send on a background queue instead of awaiting it in the request.

<Callout type="info">
  Optional but useful: when the address has no account, send a short "Someone asked to reset a password for this address, but there is no account" email. It helps users who signed up with a different address. Rate-limit it hard so it cannot be used to spam strangers.
</Callout>

### 6. Rate limit requests

Limit by **email address** (for example 3 requests per hour) and by **IP** (for example 20 per hour). This prevents mailbombing a victim and protects your sender reputation. Every reset email that goes unopened counts against you.

### 7. End other sessions after a reset

A reset often happens because someone else has the password. Revoke existing sessions and refresh tokens, and offer to keep only the current device signed in.

### 8. Never email the password itself

Do not send a new temporary password, and never send the old one. Email is not a secure channel, and it sits in inboxes for years.

---

## Link or code?

| | Magic link | 6-digit code |
|---|-----------|--------------|
| **UX on same device** | One click | Copy and paste |
| **UX across devices** (request on laptop, email on phone) | Opens on the wrong device | Works anywhere |
| **Mobile apps** | Needs universal links or deep links | Simple text field |
| **Security** | Long random token, hard to guess | Short, so needs strict attempt limits |
| **Email scanners** | Corporate link scanners can "click" it | Not affected |

**Use a link** for web apps. **Use a code** for mobile apps or when users often switch devices. A code must expire faster (10 to 15 minutes) and lock after about 5 wrong attempts.

### Link scanners and single-use tokens

Microsoft Defender, Mimecast and other security gateways open links before the user does. If a **GET** request to your reset URL consumes the token, the user's click fails. Make the link open a page with the new password form, and consume the token only when that form is **submitted** (POST).

---

## Writing the email

### Subject lines

Keep them plain and recognisable. Users search their inbox for "reset" and "password".

- `Reset your Acme password`
- `Your Acme password reset link`
- `Reset your password (expires in 30 minutes)`

Avoid urgency and alarm, like `URGENT: Account security action required`. That is what phishing looks like, and spam filters agree.

### Copy that works

```
Hi Ada,

We received a request to reset the password for your Acme account
(ada@example.com).

[Reset password]

This link expires in 30 minutes and can only be used once.

If you did not ask for this, you can ignore this email. Your password
will not change.

Requested from Chrome on macOS, Berlin, Germany, at 14:32 UTC.
```

What makes it work:

- **Names the product and the account email.** Users with several accounts know which one.
- **One clear button.** No newsletter links, social icons or upsells.
- **States the expiry.**
- **Tells users what to do if it was not them.** Reassure them: ignoring the email is safe.
- **Shows request details** (device, approximate location, time). This helps users spot attacks.
- **Includes the raw URL** as a fallback for clients that break buttons.

---

## Password reset email template

This template uses Reloop's `{{{variable}}}` placeholders, so you can paste it into a [Reloop template](/docs/learn/templates) and send it by ID. It uses tables and inline styles, so it renders in Outlook and Gmail. You can also preview and edit it in the [email HTML editor](/tools/email-html-editor).

```html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8" />
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1" />
    <title>Reset your password</title>
  </head>
  <body style="margin:0;padding:0;background:#f4f4f5;font-family:-apple-system,Segoe UI,Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif;">
    <table role="presentation" width="100%" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" style="background:#f4f4f5;padding:32px 16px;">
      <tr>
        <td align="center">
          <table role="presentation" width="100%" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" style="max-width:480px;background:#ffffff;border-radius:8px;padding:32px;">
            <tr>
              <td style="font-size:20px;font-weight:600;color:#18181b;padding-bottom:16px;">
                Reset your {{{product_name}}} password
              </td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
              <td style="font-size:15px;line-height:24px;color:#3f3f46;padding-bottom:24px;">
                Hi {{{first_name}}}, we received a request to reset the password
                for <strong>{{{email}}}</strong>. Click the button below to choose
                a new one.
              </td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
              <td style="padding-bottom:24px;">
                <a href="{{{reset_url}}}" style="display:inline-block;background:#18181b;color:#ffffff;text-decoration:none;font-size:15px;font-weight:600;padding:12px 24px;border-radius:6px;">
                  Reset password
                </a>
              </td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
              <td style="font-size:14px;line-height:22px;color:#52525b;padding-bottom:16px;">
                This link expires in {{{expires_in}}} and can only be used once.
                If you did not ask for a reset, ignore this email. Your password
                will not change.
              </td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
              <td style="font-size:13px;line-height:20px;color:#71717a;padding-bottom:16px;">
                Requested from {{{request_device}}}, {{{request_location}}}.
              </td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
              <td style="font-size:12px;line-height:18px;color:#a1a1aa;word-break:break-all;">
                Button not working? Paste this link into your browser:<br />
                {{{reset_url}}}
              </td>
            </tr>
          </table>
        </td>
      </tr>
    </table>
  </body>
</html>
```

And the plain-text version:

```
Reset your {{{product_name}}} password

Hi {{{first_name}}}, we received a request to reset the password for {{{email}}}.

Reset your password: {{{reset_url}}}

This link expires in {{{expires_in}}} and can only be used once.
If you did not ask for a reset, ignore this email. Your password will not change.

Requested from {{{request_device}}}, {{{request_location}}}.
```

If you leave out the text part, Reloop generates one from the HTML so the message still goes out as `multipart/alternative`. Writing your own gives you control over the wording.

<Callout type="warning">
  Template variables are inserted as-is, without HTML escaping. Escape user-controlled values such as `first_name` before you pass them, or someone can sign up with a name containing HTML or a fake link.
</Callout>

---

## Sending the email

With the [Reloop Node.js SDK](/blog/send-email-nodejs) (`reloop-email` 2.3 or later):

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY ?? "" });

  to: string;
  firstName: string;
  token: string;
  device: string;
  location: string;
}): Promise<void> {
  const resetUrl = `https://app.acme.com/reset-password?token=${params.token}`;

  const { emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
    from: "Acme <security@auth.acme.com>",
    to: params.to,
    subject: "Reset your Acme password",
    template: {
      id: process.env.RELOOP_RESET_TEMPLATE_ID ?? "",
      variables: {
        product_name: "Acme",
        first_name: escapeHtml(params.firstName),
        email: params.to,
        reset_url: resetUrl,
        expires_in: "30 minutes",
        request_device: escapeHtml(params.device),
        request_location: escapeHtml(params.location),
      },
    },
    tags: [{ name: "type", value: "password_reset" }],
  });

  if (emailError) {
    // Log it, but do not tell the user. The response must look the same either way.
    console.error("Password reset email failed", emailError.status, emailError.body.message);
  }
}

function escapeHtml(value: string): string {
  return value
    .replace(/&/g, "&amp;")
    .replace(/</g, "&lt;")
    .replace(/>/g, "&gt;")
    .replace(/"/g, "&quot;");
}
```

The SDK returns `{ response, emailError }` instead of throwing, so a failed send never crashes the request.

**Retrying from a queue?** Send the request with an [`Idempotency-Key` header](/docs/api/idempotency) based on the token's database ID, for example `password-reset-<token id>`. A retry then returns the original result instead of sending a second email. A new reset request creates a new token, so it gets a new key and a new email.

---

## Make sure it reaches the inbox

A reset email that lands in spam is the same as no email.

1. **Authenticate your domain.** SPF, DKIM and an aligned DMARC record are required by Gmail, Yahoo and Outlook. See the [setup guide](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide) and the [bulk sender requirements](/blog/gmail-yahoo-bulk-sender-requirements).
2. **Use a dedicated transactional subdomain.** Send security mail from something like `auth.acme.com`, separate from newsletters on `news.acme.com`. A bad campaign then cannot drag your reset emails into spam. See [subdomain vs root domain](/docs/guides/subdomain-vs-root).
3. **Turn off click tracking for security mail.** Click tracking rewrites links through a redirect domain. That makes the link look less trustworthy, adds a hop, and puts the token in another system's logs. In Reloop, click and open tracking are set per domain on the domain's **Configuration** tab, so turn them off on your auth subdomain ([domain settings](/docs/learn/domain)).
4. **Do not use link shorteners.** bit.ly, tinyurl.com and similar links are a classic phishing signal. Reloop rejects sends that contain them with `Disallowed URL in email body`. Link straight to your own domain.
5. **No unsubscribe header.** Password resets are transactional and exempt from one-click unsubscribe rules. An unsubscribe link here only lets users block mail they need.
6. **Keep it short and image-free.** One button, a fallback link and almost no images. Large images and many links look like marketing.
7. **Send in under 10 seconds.** Users request a second reset after about 30 seconds, and then the first link no longer works. Use a fast queue and monitor delivery time.
8. **Suppress hard bounces.** Reloop keeps a [suppression list](/docs/guides/suppression-list) per organization so you do not keep sending to dead addresses.

Before you launch, send one through the [deliverability tester](/tools/deliverability-tester) to check authentication and spam signals.

---

## The confirmation email

After the password changes, send a second email to the **same address**:

```
Subject: Your Acme password was changed

Hi Ada,

The password for your Acme account (ada@example.com) was changed on
7 April 2026 at 14:35 UTC from Chrome on macOS, Berlin, Germany.

If this was you, you don't need to do anything.

If it wasn't you, secure your account now: https://app.acme.com/account-recovery
```

This is how users find out their account was taken over. Send it even when the change came from the settings page rather than a reset link. When the email address itself changes, send the notice to the **old** address too.

---

## Password reset email not received? Checklist

- [ ] Request reached your server (check logs, rate limiter and bot protection)
- [ ] Account lookup used normalised email (lowercase, trimmed)
- [ ] Send succeeded (check the [email logs](/docs/learn/logs))
- [ ] Address is not on the suppression list from a past bounce
- [ ] Domain authenticated, test with the [auth checker](/tools/auth-checker)
- [ ] Not in spam or the Promotions tab
- [ ] Corporate gateway did not quarantine it (ask the user's IT team)
- [ ] Token was not consumed by a link scanner (consume on POST, not GET)

---

## FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="How long should a password reset link be valid?">
    Between 15 and 60 minutes is the common range. Shorter is safer, but too
    short frustrates users who check email later. 30 minutes is a good
    default. Codes should expire faster, around 10 to 15 minutes.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Should the reset email say if the account does not exist?">
    Not on the website. The form should show the same message for every
    address. You can optionally email the address to say no account exists,
    because only the owner of that inbox sees it.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Why does my reset link say expired when users click it right away?">
    Usually a link scanner opened it first and your server consumed the token
    on a GET request. Show the password form on GET and only consume the token
    when the form is submitted. A second cause is users requesting the email
    twice, which invalidates the first link.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Do password reset emails need an unsubscribe link?">
    No. They are transactional messages that the user asked for. Gmail and
    Yahoo require one-click unsubscribe only for marketing and subscribed mail.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Should I hash password reset tokens?">
    Yes. Store a SHA-256 hash and compare against it, the same way you would
    never store plain passwords. A leaked database should not give an attacker
    working reset links.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can I send password reset emails from Supabase or Firebase through my own provider?">
    Yes. Both let you set custom SMTP credentials for auth emails. Point them at
    Reloop's SMTP relay so reset emails come from your own authenticated
    domain instead of a shared default sender.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# How to Use Email to Reduce Churn: Sequences That Work

Path: /blog/email-reduce-churn-sequences
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/email-reduce-churn-sequences
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/email-reduce-churn-sequences.md

The four email sequences that reduce SaaS churn: inactivity check-ins, failed payment recovery, pre-renewal reminders and cancellation win-backs. Timing, subject lines, and how to build each one as an automation in Reloop.

**Email reduces churn when it reacts to a signal, not a calendar.** The four sequences worth building are: an inactivity check-in when usage drops, failed payment recovery when a card declines, a reminder before an annual renewal, and a short win-back after someone cancels. Each one starts from an event in your app, checks whether the problem is already fixed before every follow-up, and stops as soon as it is.

This guide walks through each sequence with timing, example subject lines and what each email is for, then shows how to build them as automations in Reloop. It's the other end of the lifecycle from [welcome sequences](/blog/welcome-email-sequences-that-convert), which do the same job for new signups.

---

## Two kinds of churn, two kinds of email

| | Voluntary churn | Involuntary churn |
|---|---|---|
| What happens | The customer decides to leave | The card fails and nobody notices |
| Early signal | Usage drops, key feature unused | `invoice.payment_failed` from your billing provider |
| Right email | Helpful, personal, from a person | Clear, transactional, one link to update the card |
| Who should send it | Customer success or a founder | Billing, automatically |

Involuntary churn is the easiest win. The customer still wants your product; their card expired. A short, clear sequence recovers a meaningful share of these with almost no effort, and it's often the first churn email worth building.

---

## Sequence 1: inactivity check-in

**Trigger:** an active user hasn't done your core action in a set number of days. Pick the number from your own data: if healthy users act weekly, 14 days of silence is a real signal.

| # | When | Goal | Example subject |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | When inactivity is detected | Ask, don't sell | Quick question about your Acme setup |
| 2 | +4 days, if still inactive | Remove a blocker or show what's new | Three things that changed since you last logged in |
| 3 | +10 days, if still inactive | Offer a human | Want me to take a look? |

Rules for this sequence:

- **Plain text from a person.** "I noticed you haven't run a report in a couple of weeks, did something break?" gets honest replies.
- **Never guilt-trip.** No "We miss you!" with a sad illustration.
- **Stop the moment they come back.** Check before every follow-up.

The replies are the real value here. They tell you why people drift away, which is input for the product, not just for the email.

---

## Sequence 2: failed payment recovery (dunning)

**Trigger:** your billing provider reports a failed charge, for example Stripe's `invoice.payment_failed` webhook.

| # | When | Goal | Example subject |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Immediately | Tell them, one link to fix it | Your payment for Acme didn't go through |
| 2 | +3 days, if still unpaid | Remind, mention what they'll lose | Action needed: update your card to keep your workspace |
| 3 | +7 days, if still unpaid | Final notice with a date | Your Acme account will be paused on March 14 |
| 4 | When paid | Confirm and thank | You're all set: payment received |

Rules for this sequence:

- **Transactional tone.** Facts, the amount, the date, one button to the billing page. No marketing.
- **Link straight to the card form.** Not to the login page, not to the dashboard home.
- **Say exactly what happens and when.** "Paused on March 14" is clearer than "soon."
- **Check before each reminder.** Nobody should get "update your card" after they already did.

Most billing providers also retry the card on their own schedule. Line your emails up with those retries so the reminder lands just before the next attempt.

<Callout type="tip">
  Send dunning from your transactional subdomain, not your marketing one. These emails must reach the inbox even if a newsletter has been marked as spam. If they're already landing in junk, start with [why emails land in spam](/blog/why-emails-land-in-spam-fix).
</Callout>

---

## Sequence 3: pre-renewal reminder

**Trigger:** an annual plan renews in 30 days.

| # | When | Goal | Example subject |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 30 days before renewal | Remind, show the value they got | Your Acme plan renews on June 1 |
| 2 | 7 days before renewal | Last reminder with the amount | Reminder: $1,200 renewal on June 1 |

This one feels counter-intuitive: why remind people they're about to pay? Because a surprise annual charge is how you get angry cancellations, refund requests and chargebacks. A clear reminder with a [short summary of what they used](/blog/transactional-email-as-growth-channel) this year turns renewal into a non-event. In some places, renewal reminders for subscriptions are also a legal requirement, so check the rules where your customers are.

---

## Sequence 4: cancellation and win-back

**Trigger:** the customer cancels.

| # | When | Goal | Example subject |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Immediately | Confirm, explain what happens to their data | Your Acme subscription is cancelled |
| 2 | +1 day | Ask why, one question | One question before you go |
| 3 | +30 days | Show what changed, if anything did | We fixed the thing you mentioned |
| 4 | +60 days | Open door, no pressure | Your Acme data is still here |

Rules for this sequence:

- **Make email 1 purely transactional.** Confirm the cancellation, the end date, and how to export data. No "are you sure?" upsell.
- **Ask one question in email 2.** A single reply or a one-click reason gets far more answers than a survey.
- **Only send email 3 if you have something real to say.** If they left over a missing feature and you shipped it, that's worth an email. A generic discount usually isn't.
- **Stop after two win-back attempts.** Then leave them alone.

---

## The pattern behind all four

Every sequence above has the same shape:

1. **An event** from your app or billing provider starts it.
2. **A first email** goes out immediately.
3. **A wait**, then **a check**: is the problem still there?
4. **A follow-up only if it is.**
5. **A hard stop** after a few attempts.

The check is what makes these sequences work. Without it you're spamming people who already fixed the problem, which is the fastest way to turn a retention email into an unsubscribe.

---

## Build them in Reloop

Reloop runs these as **automations**: a trigger event, then send, delay and condition steps. Conditions read the contact's current data when the step runs, so your app only has to keep one property up to date for each check.

### 1. Keep a health property on the contact

Create [contact properties](/docs/learn/contacts/properties) for the states you check, for example `billing_status` and `engagement`. Update them from your app whenever they change:

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY! });

// e.g. from your Stripe webhook handler
await reloop.contacts.update(contactId, {
  properties: { billing_status: "past_due" },
});

// later, when invoice.paid arrives
await reloop.contacts.update(contactId, {
  properties: { billing_status: "active" },
});
```

### 2. Track the event that starts the sequence

Create a trigger (for example `billing.payment_failed`) under **Automation → Triggers**, then send it from your billing webhook:

```typescript
const { automationError } = await reloop.automations.start({
  event: "billing.payment_failed",
  email: customer.email,
  properties: { amount: "$49.00", plan: "Pro" },
});
if (automationError) console.error(automationError);
```

### 3. Build the dunning automation

Payment can fail more than once in a customer's lifetime, so turn on re-entry with `restart`: a new failure cancels any run still in progress and starts fresh.

```typescript
const stillPastDue = {
  type: "rule",
  field: "contact.billing_status",
  operator: "eq",
  value: "past_due",
} as const;

await reloop.automations.create({
  name: "Failed payment recovery",
  status: "active",
  reentry: "restart",
  steps: [
    { key: "start", type: "trigger", config: { eventName: "billing.payment_failed" } },
    { key: "notice", type: "send_email", config: { template: { id: "tmpl_payment_failed" } } },

    { key: "wait_1", type: "delay", config: { amount: 3, unit: "days" } },
    { key: "check_1", type: "condition", config: stillPastDue },
    { key: "reminder", type: "send_email", config: { template: { id: "tmpl_update_card" } } },

    { key: "wait_2", type: "delay", config: { amount: 4, unit: "days" } },
    { key: "check_2", type: "condition", config: stillPastDue },
    { key: "final", type: "send_email", config: { template: { id: "tmpl_final_notice" } } },
  ],
  connections: [
    { from: "start", to: "notice" },
    { from: "notice", to: "wait_1" },
    { from: "wait_1", to: "check_1" },
    { from: "check_1", to: "reminder", type: "condition_met" },
    { from: "reminder", to: "wait_2" },
    { from: "wait_2", to: "check_2" },
    { from: "check_2", to: "final", type: "condition_met" },
  ],
});
```

If the customer pays, your webhook sets `billing_status` to `active`, the next condition doesn't match, and the sequence ends on its own.

The "payment received" confirmation is a single [transactional email](/blog/transactional-email-best-practices), so send it straight from your `invoice.paid` handler with `reloop.mail.send` rather than through the automation.

### 4. Reuse the shape for the others

| Sequence | Trigger event | Condition before follow-ups | Re-entry |
|---|---|---|---|
| Inactivity check-in | `user.went_inactive` | `contact.engagement` `eq` `inactive` | `restart` |
| Failed payment | `billing.payment_failed` | `contact.billing_status` `eq` `past_due` | `restart` |
| Pre-renewal | `billing.renewal_upcoming` | none (always send) | `parallel` (one per renewal) |
| Cancellation win-back | `subscription.canceled` | `contact.billing_status` `eq` `canceled` | `once` |

Detecting inactivity is your app's job: a nightly job that finds users with no core action in N days, sets `engagement` to `inactive` and tracks `user.went_inactive`. When they come back, set it to `active` and the check-in sequence stops.

<Callout type="info">
  Automation steps send each template with its default variable values. Write these emails so they read well without per-user data. For an email that needs specifics, like the exact amount and card ending, send it from your webhook handler with `reloop.mail.send` and `template.variables`.
</Callout>

Unsubscribed contacts leave automations at their next step. Make sure purely transactional notices (payment failed, cancellation confirmed) still reach people who opted out of marketing by sending those directly from your app.

---

## How to tell if it's working

| Sequence | Measure |
|---|---|
| Inactivity check-in | Share of contacts whose `engagement` returns to `active` within 30 days |
| Failed payment | Recovered revenue ÷ revenue at risk |
| Pre-renewal | Refund and chargeback rate on renewals |
| Win-back | Reactivations within 90 days of cancelling |

Compare against a period before the sequence existed. Each automation's enrollment history shows which step every contact reached, which tells you where people respond and where they drop off.

---

## FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Which churn sequence should I build first?">
    Failed payment recovery. It's the simplest, it needs no copywriting
    finesse, and it recovers customers who never meant to leave.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Should churn emails offer a discount?">
    Usually not as the first move. A discount in the first email teaches
    customers to cancel to get one. Ask what's wrong first. If price really
    is the reason, a targeted offer later in the sequence is reasonable.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="How do I stop a sequence when the user fixes the problem?">
    Put a condition before every follow-up that checks a contact property
    your app keeps current, such as `billing_status`. When the property
    changes, the condition fails and the contact finishes the automation.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Are dunning emails transactional?">
    Yes. They're about an account the customer already has and a payment
    they owe, so treat them as transactional: plain, factual, and sent from
    your transactional subdomain.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# How to Send Email with SvelteKit (2026)

Path: /blog/send-email-sveltekit
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/send-email-sveltekit
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/send-email-sveltekit.md

Send transactional email from SvelteKit 2 and Svelte 5 with Reloop: a server-only client, form actions with progressive enhancement, +server.ts API routes, error handling, templates and deployment.

**To send email from SvelteKit, call Reloop only from server code:** a form action in `+page.server.ts` or an endpoint in `+server.ts`. Keep the client in `src/lib/server/` and read the API key from `$env/static/private`, and SvelteKit will refuse to bundle either into the browser.

This guide builds both patterns end to end on SvelteKit 2 and Svelte 5: install, a shared client, a contact form with progressive enhancement, a JSON endpoint for webhooks and cron, error handling, templates and deploys.

Using another framework? See the [Next.js](/blog/send-email-nextjs-app-router), [Remix](/blog/send-email-remix) or plain [Node.js](/blog/send-email-nodejs) guides.

---

## What you'll build

| Pattern | File | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| **Form action** | `src/routes/contact/+page.server.ts` | Contact forms, signup, password reset, anything triggered from your own UI |
| **API endpoint** | `src/routes/api/send/+server.ts` | Webhooks, cron jobs, mobile apps, other services |

Both run only on the server and both use the same Reloop call. Use form actions for your UI. Use `+server.ts` when something outside your app needs a URL to POST to.

---

## Prerequisites

1. A SvelteKit 2 project (`npx sv create my-app` if you're starting fresh)
2. A Reloop account and an API key from the [dashboard](https://reloop.sh/dashboard). Keys start with `rl_`.
3. A verified sending domain. See [connect a domain](/docs/guides/connect-domain) and the [SPF, DKIM and DMARC guide](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide).

---

## 1. Install the SDK

<InstallSdkCode />

The package is [`reloop-email`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/reloop-email). It's written in TypeScript, so you get types for every field without extra packages.

---

## 2. Add the API key

Create `.env` in the project root:

```env
RELOOP_API_KEY=rl_your_api_key_here
```

SvelteKit splits environment variables into public and private:

| Module | Visible in the browser? | Use for the Reloop key? |
|---|---|---|
| `$env/static/private` | No | **Yes** |
| `$env/dynamic/private` | No | Yes, if the value is only known at runtime |
| `$env/static/public` | Yes (needs `PUBLIC_` prefix) | **Never** |
| `$env/dynamic/public` | Yes | **Never** |

If you import a private module from client-side code, the build fails. That's the guardrail you want.

<Callout type="warning">
  Never prefix the key with `PUBLIC_`. Anything public ends up in the JavaScript bundle. If a key ever leaks, rotate it in the dashboard and redeploy.
</Callout>

---

## 3. Create a server-only client

Put the client in `src/lib/server/`. SvelteKit won't let any file under that folder be imported into code that runs in the browser.

```typescript
// src/lib/server/reloop.ts

```

The constructor takes an options object: `{ apiKey }`, plus an optional `baseUrl` if you [self-host Reloop](/blog/self-hosted-email-infrastructure).

---

## 4. Send from a form action

Form actions are the most natural fit. They work without JavaScript, and `use:enhance` upgrades them to a smooth in-page submit when JavaScript is available.

### The action

```typescript
// src/routes/contact/+page.server.ts

  default: async ({ request }) => {
    const data = await request.formData();
    const email = String(data.get("email") ?? "").trim().toLowerCase();
    const message = String(data.get("message") ?? "").trim();

    if (!email.includes("@")) {
      return fail(400, { email, message, error: "Enter a valid email." });
    }
    if (message.length < 10) {
      return fail(400, { email, message, error: "Tell us a bit more." });
    }

    const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
      from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
      to: email,
      reply_to: "support@acme.com",
      subject: "We got your message",
      html: `<p>Thanks for reaching out. We'll reply within one business day.</p>`,
      text: "Thanks for reaching out. We'll reply within one business day.",
      tags: [{ name: "type", value: "contact_confirmation" }],
    });

    if (emailError) {
      console.error("Reloop send failed", emailError.status, emailError.body);
      return fail(502, { email, message, error: "Couldn't send. Try again." });
    }

    return { success: true, id: response.messageId };
  },
} satisfies Actions;
```

A few things worth noting:

- `reloop.mail.send` doesn't throw on API errors. It returns `{ response, emailError }`, so failures are a normal branch in your code.
- `emailError.body` carries Reloop's structured error: a `message`, `why`, `fix` and docs `link`. Log it on the server. Don't send it to the user.
- `fail()` returns the submitted values, so the form can be re-filled after a validation error.
- `from` must be on a domain you've verified in Reloop.

### The page

```svelte
<!-- src/routes/contact/+page.svelte -->
<script lang="ts">

  let { form }: PageProps = $props();
  let sending = $state(false);
</script>

{#if form?.success}
  <p>Thanks! Check your inbox for a confirmation.</p>
{:else}
  <form
    method="POST"
    use:enhance={() => {
      sending = true;
      return async ({ update }) => {
        await update();
        sending = false;
      };
    }}
  >
    <input name="email" type="email" value={form?.email ?? ""} required />
    <textarea name="message" required>{form?.message ?? ""}</textarea>

    {#if form?.error}<p class="error">{form.error}</p>{/if}

    <button disabled={sending}>{sending ? "Sending…" : "Send"}</button>
  </form>
{/if}
```

This uses Svelte 5 runes: `$props()` for the action result and `$state()` for the pending flag. Without JavaScript, the form still posts and the page re-renders with `form` filled in.

---

## 5. Send from a `+server.ts` endpoint

Use an endpoint when the caller isn't your own UI: a Stripe webhook, a cron job, a mobile app, [an AI agent](/blog/build-ai-agent-sends-emails).

```typescript
// src/routes/api/send/+server.ts

type Body = { to?: string; name?: string };

  if (request.headers.get("x-internal-secret") !== INTERNAL_SEND_SECRET) {
    error(401, "Unauthorized");
  }

  const body = (await request.json().catch(() => ({}))) as Body;
  const to = body.to?.trim().toLowerCase();
  if (!to?.includes("@")) error(400, "Field `to` must be an email");

  const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
    from: "Acme <onboarding@mail.acme.com>",
    to,
    subject: body.name ? `Welcome, ${body.name}` : "Welcome to Acme",
    html: "<p>Your account is ready.</p>",
    text: "Your account is ready.",
  });

  if (emailError) {
    console.error("Reloop send failed", emailError.status, emailError.body);
    error(502, "Failed to send email");
  }

  return json({ ok: true, messageId: response.messageId });
};
```

Test it locally:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:5173/api/send \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "x-internal-secret: $INTERNAL_SEND_SECRET" \
  -d '{"to":"you@example.com","name":"Ada"}'
```

<Callout type="warning">
  A public endpoint that sends email to any address is an open relay. Always gate it with a session check, a shared secret, or a verified webhook signature, and rate-limit it.
</Callout>

In SvelteKit 2, `error()` throws for you, so there's no `throw` keyword in front of it.

---

## 6. Form action or endpoint?

| Question | Form action | `+server.ts` |
|---|---|---|
| Triggered by a form in this app? | Yes | No |
| Needs to work without JavaScript? | Yes | No |
| Called by webhooks, cron or other services? | No | Yes |
| Needs a stable public URL? | No | Yes |
| Same Reloop call? | Yes | Yes |

Most apps end up using both: actions for product UI, endpoints for integrations.

---

## 7. Use a template instead of inline HTML

Inline HTML is fine for a contact form. For anything you'll iterate on (welcome emails, receipts, [password resets](/blog/password-reset-email-best-practices)), keep the design in a Reloop template and send variables from code.

```typescript
await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
  to: user.email,
  subject: "Reset your password",
  template: {
    id: "tmpl_password_reset",
    variables: { name: user.name, reset_url: resetUrl },
  },
});
```

Templates use `{{variable}}` placeholders. Designers can edit them in the dashboard without a deploy.

---

## 8. Fields you'll use most

```typescript
await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>", // required, verified domain
  to: ["a@example.com", "b@example.com"], // string or array, up to 50
  subject: "Order shipped", // required
  html: "<p>Your order is on its way.</p>",
  text: "Your order is on its way.", // plain-text fallback
  reply_to: "support@acme.com",
  cc: "ops@acme.com",
  bcc: "archive@acme.com",
  scheduled_at: "2026-02-25T09:00:00Z", // send later (ISO 8601)
  tags: [{ name: "type", value: "shipping" }],
  attachments: [{ filename: "invoice.pdf", content: base64Pdf }],
});
```

The full list is in the [send email API reference](/docs/api/mail/post-api-mail-v1send).

---

## 9. Deploying

The SDK sends over `fetch`, so it runs on any SvelteKit adapter: `adapter-node`, Vercel, Netlify and Cloudflare.

| Adapter | Where to set `RELOOP_API_KEY` | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `adapter-node` | Server environment or `.env` | Read at build with `static`, at runtime with `dynamic` |
| Vercel | Project → Settings → Environment Variables | Redeploy after adding |
| Netlify | Site configuration → Environment variables | Redeploy after adding |
| Cloudflare | `wrangler secret put RELOOP_API_KEY` | Use `$env/dynamic/private` for runtime secrets |

`$env/static/private` inlines the value at build time. If your platform only exposes secrets at runtime, import from `$env/dynamic/private` instead:

```typescript
// src/lib/server/reloop.ts

```

For Cloudflare specifics, see [sending email from Cloudflare Workers](/blog/send-email-cloudflare-workers).

---

## Production checklist

- [ ] API key only in private env, never `PUBLIC_`
- [ ] Client lives in `src/lib/server/`
- [ ] Sending domain verified with SPF, DKIM and DMARC
- [ ] `emailError` handled and logged server-side
- [ ] Public endpoints gated and rate-limited
- [ ] Plain-text version included alongside HTML

## FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Can I send email from a +page.ts or a component?">
    No. `+page.ts` and components can run in the browser. Send only from
    `+page.server.ts`, `+layout.server.ts`, `+server.ts` or `hooks.server.ts`.
    The browser calls those, never Reloop directly.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can I use SMTP with Nodemailer instead of the SDK?">
    Yes. Point Nodemailer at `smtp.reloop.sh` on port 587 with your API key as
    both username and password. See the [SMTP docs](/docs/examples/smtp/introduction).
    The SDK is simpler on serverless platforms because it's a single HTTPS
    request.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="How do I send a welcome email right after signup?">
    Call `reloop.mail.send` inside the form action or endpoint that creates the
    user, after the database write succeeds. For multi-step onboarding, start a
    Reloop automation from that same spot instead.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="How do I test without emailing real people?">
    Send to your own address while developing, and use tags like
    `{ name: "env", value: "dev" }` so you can filter test sends in the logs.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# Reloop vs Plunk (2026): Open-Source Email Platforms Compared

Path: /blog/reloop-vs-plunk
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-plunk
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-plunk.md

Reloop vs Plunk, two open-source email platforms compared: hosted pricing, licenses, self-hosting requirements, sending infrastructure, inbound email and automations, plus how to switch.

**Reloop and Plunk are both open-source email platforms that do more than send.** Each gives you a transactional API, SMTP, contacts, campaigns, automations and inbound email, on a hosted cloud or on your own server. The differences are in the details: **Plunk sends through Amazon SES and charges per email with no plan tiers; Reloop runs its own MTA, costs less once you pass a few thousand emails, and stores inbound mail in real inboxes that agents can work from.** Plunk's pricing is the simplest in the market, and its AGPL license is a deliberate choice worth understanding.

We build Reloop, so weigh this accordingly. Plunk facts below come from [Plunk's pricing page](https://www.useplunk.com/pricing), [docs](https://docs.useplunk.com) and [GitHub repository](https://github.com/useplunk/plunk). Where Plunk is the better pick, we say so.

---

## The 30-second comparison

| | **Reloop** | **Plunk** |
|---|---|---|
| License | Apache 2.0 | AGPL-3.0 |
| Free tier | 6,000 / mo, 200 / day | 1,000 / mo, with Plunk branding |
| Paid pricing | Plans: $10 for 50k, $20 for 100k | $0.001 per email, no base fee |
| 50,000 emails / mo | **$10** | about $50 |
| 100,000 emails / mo | **$20** | about $100 |
| Dedicated IP | Included on Growth ($20) | Not offered on the hosted plan |
| Sending path | Own MTA (KumoMTA) | Amazon SES |
| Self-host needs | Your server | Your server + an AWS SES account |
| Transactional API and SMTP | Yes | Yes |
| Contacts, segments, campaigns | Yes | Yes |
| Automations | Event-triggered, with delays and conditions | Workflows with triggers, delays and conditions |
| Inbound email | Mailboxes with threads, API, MCP, IMAP | Inbound with routing rules |
| Agent inbox | Yes | No |

Plunk's prices are from [useplunk.com/pricing](https://www.useplunk.com/pricing); Reloop's are on [reloop.sh/pricing](/pricing). Both change, so check before you commit.

---

## Pricing at real volumes

The two products price in different ways. Plunk charges a flat **$0.001 per email** (that's $1 per 1,000) with no base fee and no plan tiers, plus a free tier of 1,000 emails a month that carries Plunk branding. Reloop has a free tier of 6,000 a month, then flat plans with overage.

| Monthly volume | Reloop | Plunk (approx.) |
|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | $0 | $0 (branded) |
| 3,000 | $0 | about $3 |
| 50,000 | $10 | about $50 |
| 100,000 | $20 | about $100 |
| 200,000 | $20 + $50 overage = $70 | about $200 |

Plunk figures are per-email list price, rounded; check Plunk's page for exactly how the free allowance applies once you upgrade.

What this means in practice:

- **At very low or spiky volume, Plunk's model is hard to beat for simplicity.** You never pay for capacity you don't use, and Plunk offers a monthly spend cap.
- **At steady volume, Reloop is cheaper.** From about 10,000 emails a month on, a Reloop plan costs less than the same mail at $1 per 1,000.
- **On both, self-hosting removes the platform fee.** On Plunk you still pay AWS for SES sending. On Reloop you pay for the server only.

<Callout type="tip">
  Price the volume you expect in a year, not today's. Moving providers later means re-verifying DNS and rebuilding reputation, so pick the one that still makes sense at 10× your current volume.
</Callout>

---

## Open source: Apache 2.0 vs AGPL-3.0

Both projects publish their full source, but the licenses behave differently.

- **Plunk is AGPL-3.0.** You can self-host and modify it freely. If you modify Plunk and let others use it over a network, the AGPL requires you to share those modifications under the same license. For a company running it internally that's often fine; for one embedding it in a product, check with your legal team.
- **Reloop is Apache 2.0.** It's a permissive license: you can modify it, embed it and run it as part of a commercial product without publishing your changes, as long as you keep the license and notices.

Neither is "more open". They make different trade-offs, and AGPL is a reasonable choice for a project that wants improvements to flow back.

---

## Self-hosting: what you actually run

This is the biggest technical difference.

**Plunk is built on Amazon SES.** Its [self-hosting guide](https://docs.useplunk.com/self-hosting/introduction) lists Docker and Docker Compose, a domain with subdomains for each service, and an AWS SES account. The [environment variables](https://docs.useplunk.com/self-hosting/environment-variables) mark PostgreSQL, Redis and the SES credentials as required, and the bundled setup includes MinIO for file storage. In practice that means:

1. Getting your AWS account out of the SES sandbox, which AWS reviews by hand.
2. Creating an IAM user for sending and domain identities.
3. Wiring an SNS topic and configuration set so bounces, complaints and deliveries flow back to Plunk.

**Reloop brings its own MTA.** Reloop sends through KumoMTA running on your server, so there's no third-party sending account to apply for. You install it with the [one-command installer](/self-host) or on [Coolify](/blog/reloop-coolify-setup), point DNS at it, and send.

The trade-off cuts both ways:

| | Reloop self-hosted | Plunk self-hosted |
|---|---|---|
| Sending infrastructure | Your own IPs via KumoMTA | Amazon SES |
| IP reputation | You own it and warm it up | SES handles it |
| Extra cloud account | None | AWS (SES, IAM, SNS) |
| Per-email cost | None | SES rates |
| Data stays on your server | All of it | App data yes; mail passes through SES |

If you'd rather not think about IP warm-up at all, SES doing the sending is a genuine advantage for Plunk. If you want no dependency on AWS, or mail that never leaves your infrastructure, Reloop's model fits better. Our [self-hosted email infrastructure guide](/blog/self-hosted-email-infrastructure) covers what owning IP reputation really involves.

---

## Developer experience

Both APIs are small and easy to call.

**Plunk**

```typescript
const res = await fetch("https://next-api.useplunk.com/v1/send", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.PLUNK_SECRET_KEY}`,
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    to: "user@example.com",
    subject: "Welcome",
    body: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
  }),
});
```

**Reloop**

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY! });

const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Welcome",
  html: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
});
```

| | Reloop | Plunk |
|---|---|---|
| Auth | `x-api-key` header or SDK | `Authorization: Bearer` with a secret key (`sk_`) |
| HTML field | `html` | `body` |
| Template variables | `{{{first_name}}}` | `{{ firstName }}`, values in `data` |
| Event tracking | `reloop.automations.start({ event, email })` | `POST /v1/track` with `event` and `email` |
| Errors | `message`, `why` and `fix` | Error codes |
| Webhooks | Signed with `Reloop-Signature` (HMAC-SHA256) | See Plunk docs |

Plunk has a nice touch for frontend use: public keys (`pk_`) can only call `/v1/track`, so you can track events from the browser without exposing a sending key.

Reloop's error shape is our one strong opinion. When a send fails, the error says **why** and **how to fix it**:

```json
{
  "message": "Domain not found",
  "why": "The domain mail.acme.com was not found or is not authorized for your organization",
  "fix": "Ensure the domain is registered and verified in your dashboard"
}
```

---

## Automations, campaigns and contacts

Here the two are closer than any other pair we've compared. Both cover:

- **Contacts** with custom fields and activity history.
- **Segments or groups** to target part of your list.
- **Campaigns** for newsletters and product updates.
- **Event-triggered automations** with delays and conditional branches.

Both start an automation the same way: your app sends an event (`user.signed_up`) with the contact's email, and the contact is created if it doesn't exist. See our [welcome sequence guide](/blog/welcome-email-sequences-that-convert) for a worked example on Reloop.

Reloop also has **subscription channels**, so a contact can opt out of product updates while still getting billing mail.

---

## Inbound email and agent inboxes

Both can receive email on your domain.

- **Plunk** receives inbound mail and processes it with routing rules.
- **Reloop** receives mail into **mailboxes**: messages are stored, threaded, spam-scored with Rspamd, and readable over the API, the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) or IMAP. You can reply in-thread with one call.

If you're building an AI agent that reads and answers email, or a shared inbox where humans and agents work the same threads, Reloop's mailboxes save you building storage and threading yourself. See [build an AI agent that reads and replies to email](/blog/build-ai-agent-sends-emails).

---

## Where Plunk is the better choice

- **Your volume is low or unpredictable.** Paying $1 per 1,000 emails with no base fee and a spend cap is as simple as pricing gets.
- **You want SES to own deliverability when self-hosting.** No IP warm-up, no MTA to tune; Amazon handles the sending reputation.
- **You prefer AGPL** so that improvements to the platform stay open.
- **You track events from the browser.** Plunk's public `pk_` keys are scoped to tracking only.

If you're evaluating more open-source and hosted platforms, see the [best Plunk alternatives](/blog/best-plunk-alternatives).

## Where Reloop is the better choice

- **You send more than about 10,000 emails a month.** Flat plans ($10 for 50k, $20 for 100k) cost a fraction of per-email pricing.
- **You want a larger free tier** without branding: 6,000 a month.
- **You want to self-host without AWS.** Reloop sends with its own MTA, so there's no SES sandbox review or SNS wiring.
- **You need inbound mail as real inboxes**, especially for AI agents over MCP or IMAP.
- **You need a dedicated IP** on the hosted plan.
- **You want a permissive license** to embed the platform in your own product.

---

## Switching from Plunk to Reloop

1. **Add your domain in Reloop** and publish the DKIM record (`reloop._domainkey`). Merge `include:reloop.sh` into your existing SPF record rather than adding a second one.
2. **Swap the send call.** Replace `POST /v1/send` with `reloop.mail.send`, and rename `body` to `html`.
3. **Move templates.** Change `{{ firstName }}` placeholders to triple braces: `{{{first_name}}}`.
4. **Swap event tracking.** Replace `/v1/track` calls with `reloop.automations.start({ event, email })`, and recreate your workflows as Reloop automations listening for the same event names.
5. **Import contacts** with their custom fields, and import unsubscribes so you never mail someone who opted out.
6. **Point webhooks** at a handler that verifies the `Reloop-Signature` header.
7. **Ramp traffic** from 10% to 100% over a week or two, then remove the old DNS records.

Our [SendGrid migration guide](/blog/migrating-from-sendgrid) covers the same steps in more detail, including a traffic-split flag and a suppression import script.

---

  <Accordion title="Are Reloop and Plunk both open source?">
    Yes. Reloop is Apache 2.0 and Plunk is AGPL-3.0. Both can be self-hosted

    share modifications if you offer a modified version over a network.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Does self-hosted Plunk need AWS?">
    Yes. Plunk's self-hosting guide requires an AWS SES account for sending,
    along with PostgreSQL and Redis. Self-hosted Reloop sends through its own
    MTA, so no AWS account is needed.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Which is cheaper on the hosted plans?">
    It depends on volume. Plunk charges $0.001 per email with no base fee, so
    it's cheap for tiny or irregular volumes. From around 10,000 emails a
    month, Reloop's plans cost less: $10 for 50k and $20 for 100k.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can both receive email?">
    Yes. Plunk processes inbound mail with routing rules. Reloop stores it in
    threaded mailboxes you can read over the API, MCP or IMAP, and reply to in
    one call.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Do my Plunk templates work in Reloop?">
    The HTML does. Change the placeholders from `{{ firstName }}` to
    `{{{first_name}}}` and pass the values as template variables.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>
