# How to Automate Invoice Processing From Email With AI (Step by Step)

Path: /blog/automate-invoice-processing-from-email
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/automate-invoice-processing-from-email
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/automate-invoice-processing-from-email.md

Stop digging through inboxes for invoices. Give invoices one email address, then let AI read each PDF and pull out the vendor, amount and due date into your spreadsheet or accounting tool. Plain-English guide with the code a developer needs.

**To automate invoice processing from email, send every invoice to one dedicated address, such as `invoices@yourdomain.com`. Then have a small program read each new email, pass the PDF to an AI model, and save the vendor, amount and due date to your spreadsheet or accounting tool.** Reloop handles the inbox part: it receives the email, keeps the original with its attachments, and notifies your program the moment an invoice arrives. The AI model does the reading.

The first half of this guide needs no technical skills at all and already fixes the most common problem: invoices scattered across everyone's inbox. The second half is for whoever builds the automation, explained so that anyone can follow what is happening.

---

## Sound familiar?

If you pay bills for a business, you probably know at least one of these:

- **It's the end of the month and you're searching** three inboxes for "invoice", "receipt" and "bill", hoping you didn't miss one.
- **A supplier sent the invoice to someone who was on holiday**, and you only found out when the payment reminder arrived.
- **You type the same five details** (vendor, invoice number, date, amount, due date) from every PDF into a spreadsheet or Xero/QuickBooks, by hand.
- **One typo** turns $1,250.00 into $125.00, and nobody notices until the accounts don't add up.
- **A late fee** appears because a due date was buried in an attachment nobody opened.
- **Your accountant keeps asking** for receipts you're sure you received somewhere.

None of these is really a "data entry" problem. The underlying issue is that **invoices arrive in too many places and are read too late.** So the fix comes in two parts: one place to collect them, then automatic reading.

---

## How it works, in plain English

```
Supplier emails an invoice
        ↓
invoices@yourdomain.com          ← one address for every invoice (Reloop)
        ↓
"New invoice arrived!"           ← Reloop instantly notifies your program
        ↓
AI reads the PDF                 ← pulls out vendor, amount, due date…
        ↓
Saved to your spreadsheet,       ← and anything unclear is flagged
accounting tool or database        for a person to check
```

Being clear about who does what:

| Step | Who does it |
|------|-------------|
| Receiving the email and keeping the PDF | **Reloop** |
| Telling your program a new email arrived | **Reloop** (a webhook) |
| Reading the PDF and pulling out the details | **An AI model** you connect, such as Claude |
| Saving the details where you want them | **Your program** (a short script) |
| Approving and paying the bill | **You**. Nothing in this setup pays anyone. |

<Callout type="info">
  Reloop is email infrastructure, not accounting software. It does not read invoices by itself and it does not connect to your bank. It gets every invoice email into one reliable place and hands it to your automation, which is exactly the part that is usually missing.
</Callout>

---

## Part 1: One inbox for every invoice (no code)

This part takes about fifteen minutes and is worth doing even if you never automate anything else.

### Step 1: Create the address

Follow our [step-by-step guide to receiving email on your own domain](/blog/receive-email-on-your-own-domain). In short:

1. Add a domain in the [Reloop dashboard](https://reloop.sh/dashboard). If your main domain already uses Gmail or Outlook, use a subdomain such as `billing.yourdomain.com` so your existing email is untouched.
2. Add the one MX record Reloop shows you at your DNS provider.
3. Create a mailbox, for example `invoices@billing.yourdomain.com`.

The free plan includes 3 inboxes, so this costs nothing to try.

### Step 2: Get invoices sent there

- **Tell your suppliers.** Send them the new address and ask them to update their billing contact. Most billing systems (Stripe, Shopify, AWS, Google, etc.) let you set a separate billing email in account settings.
- **Forward what still lands elsewhere.** In Gmail, create a filter (for example, emails with "invoice" in the subject and an attachment) that forwards to the new address. Gmail first sends a confirmation code to the new address; you'll see it in the Reloop inbox.

<Callout type="warning">
  Many Microsoft 365 organisations block automatic forwarding to outside addresses by default. If your Outlook forwarding rule doesn't seem to work, ask your IT admin to allow forwarding to that one address, or forward invoices by hand until they do.
</Callout>

### Step 3: Read it like a normal inbox

Add the mailbox to Apple Mail, Outlook or Thunderbird over IMAP (server `imap.reloop.sh`, port `993`), with a Reloop API key as the password. Invoices and their PDFs show up like any other email. Your whole finance team can watch the same inbox.

**Already better:** every invoice is in one place, nothing depends on one person's inbox, and month-end means opening one folder.

---

## Part 2: Let AI read the invoices (for whoever builds it)

This part needs someone comfortable running a small Node.js script: a developer, a technical co-founder, or a freelancer. You can hand them this page. Each step starts with what it does in plain English.

### What you need

- The invoice mailbox from Part 1
- A Reloop API key and a webhook (set up in the dashboard)
- An API key for an AI model. This example uses [Claude](https://www.anthropic.com/api), which reads PDFs directly.
- Somewhere to run the code: any server or serverless function that can receive a web request

```bash
npm install reloop-email @anthropic-ai/sdk mailparser zod
```

### Step 1: Get notified when an invoice arrives

*In plain English: instead of checking the inbox every few minutes, Reloop calls your program the moment an email arrives.*

In the dashboard, create a webhook that subscribes to the `email.received` event and points to your program's URL. Each notification looks like this:

```json
{
  "type": "email.received",
  "data": {
    "email_id": "in_123456789",
    "mailbox_id": "mb_123456789",
    "from": "billing@supplier.com",
    "to": ["invoices@billing.yourdomain.com"],
    "subject": "Invoice INV-2041 from Supplier Ltd",
    "has_attachments": true,
    "is_spam": false
  }
}
```

The notification tells you *that* an invoice arrived, not what is in it. Your program fetches the email itself in the next step.

### Step 2: Get the PDF out of the email

*In plain English: Reloop keeps an exact copy of every email exactly as it was received, attachments included. Your program downloads that copy and unpacks the PDF from it.*

```typescript

async function getInvoiceFiles(emailId: string) {
  const { message, messageError } = await reloop.inbox.messages.getRaw(emailId);
  if (messageError) throw messageError;

  const email = await simpleParser(message.raw);
  const pdfs = email.attachments.filter((a) => a.contentType === "application/pdf");

  return { email, pdfs };
}
```

`reloop.inbox.messages.getRaw` returns the full original email. The open-source [mailparser](https://nodemailer.com/extras/mailparser/) library turns it into a subject, a body and a list of attachments, each with its file contents.

Some invoices are not PDFs at all: many SaaS receipts are just the text of the email. The next step handles both.

### Step 3: Ask the AI to read it

*In plain English: you send the PDF to the AI with a short form to fill in (vendor, amount, due date…). It sends the form back completed. If something isn't on the invoice, it leaves that field empty instead of guessing.*

```typescript

const anthropic = new Anthropic();

const InvoiceSchema = z.object({
  is_invoice: z.boolean(),
  vendor_name: z.string().nullable(),
  invoice_number: z.string().nullable(),
  invoice_date: z.string().nullable(), // YYYY-MM-DD
  due_date: z.string().nullable(),     // YYYY-MM-DD
  currency: z.string().nullable(),     // e.g. USD, EUR
  subtotal: z.number().nullable(),
  tax: z.number().nullable(),
  total: z.number().nullable(),
});

type Invoice = z.infer<typeof InvoiceSchema>;

async function readInvoice(pdf: Buffer | null, emailText: string): Promise<Invoice | null> {
  const content: Anthropic.ContentBlockParam[] = [];
  if (pdf) {
    content.push({
      type: "document",
      source: { type: "base64", media_type: "application/pdf", data: pdf.toString("base64") },
    });
  }
  content.push({
    type: "text",
    text:
      "Extract the invoice details. Use null for anything not clearly stated; never guess. " +
      "Set is_invoice to false if this is not an invoice or receipt.\n\n" +
      `Email text:\n${emailText}`,
  });

  const response = await anthropic.messages.parse({
    model: "claude-opus-5-5",
    max_tokens: 16000,
    messages: [{ role: "user", content }],
    output_config: { format: zodOutputFormat(InvoiceSchema) },
  });

  if (response.stop_reason === "refusal") return null; // send to manual review
  return response.parsed_output;
}
```

Two details matter here:

- **"Use null, never guess."** A blank field is easy to spot and fill in. A confidently wrong amount isn't.
- **`is_invoice`.** Newsletters, "your invoice is ready" notifications without the actual invoice, and marketing emails will reach the address too. This lets your program skip them.

### Step 4: Check it, then save it

*In plain English: the program runs a few common-sense checks. Anything that passes goes into your spreadsheet. Anything that looks off is marked "needs review" for a person.*

```typescript
function needsReview(inv: Invoice): string[] {
  const problems: string[] = [];
  if (!inv.vendor_name) problems.push("missing vendor");
  if (inv.total === null) problems.push("missing total");
  if (!inv.due_date) problems.push("missing due date");
  if (inv.subtotal !== null && inv.tax !== null && inv.total !== null &&
      Math.abs(inv.subtotal + inv.tax - inv.total) > 0.01) {
    problems.push("subtotal + tax doesn't equal total");
  }
  return problems;
}
```

Then save it wherever your team already works: a row in Google Sheets, a draft bill in your accounting software through its API, or a table in your own database. Always store the `email_id` with the row so anyone can open the original email in one click.

### Step 5: Put it together

```typescript

  const raw = await req.text();
  if (!verify(raw, req.headers.get("Reloop-Signature") ?? "", process.env.RELOOP_WEBHOOK_SECRET!)) {
    return new Response("Bad signature", { status: 401 });
  }

  const event = JSON.parse(raw);
  if (event.type !== "email.received" || event.data.is_spam) {
    return new Response("skipped");
  }

  // Reply straight away, do the slow work in the background
  await queue.add("process-invoice", { emailId: event.data.email_id });
  return new Response("ok");
}

async function processInvoice(emailId: string) {
  if (await alreadyProcessed(emailId)) return; // the same notification can arrive twice

  const { email, pdfs } = await getInvoiceFiles(emailId);
  const files = pdfs.length > 0 ? pdfs.map((p) => p.content) : [null];

  for (const file of files) {
    const invoice = await readInvoice(file, email.text ?? "");
    if (!invoice) {
      await saveForReview(emailId, ["AI could not read this one"]);
    } else if (invoice.is_invoice) {
      await saveInvoice(emailId, invoice, needsReview(invoice));
    }
  }
}
```

The signature check (`verify`) is the same function shown in our [receiving email guide](/blog/receive-email-on-your-own-domain). It proves the request really came from Reloop and not from someone pretending.

---

## Mistakes that cause real problems

Most of these come from treating the AI as if it can't be wrong.

| Mistake | What happens | Do this instead |
|---------|--------------|-----------------|
| Paying automatically from the extracted data | A misread amount or a fake invoice gets paid | Keep a human approval step before any payment |
| Trusting any email that says "invoice" | Invoice fraud: a lookalike sender with new bank details | Only accept known vendors automatically. Treat changed bank details as a phone-call check, every time. |
| Doing the AI work inside the webhook request | Slow PDFs time out and the notification is retried | Reply `ok` immediately and process in a background job |
| Not checking for duplicates | The same invoice is recorded twice when a webhook is retried or a supplier resends | Skip an `email_id` you've already processed, and flag repeated vendor + invoice number pairs |
| Letting the AI fill gaps | Invented dates or amounts look real | Ask for `null` when unsure and send those to review |
| Ignoring emails with several PDFs | Only the first invoice is recorded | Loop over every PDF attachment, as in Step 5 |
| Throwing away the original | No proof for your accountant or auditor | Store the `email_id` with every row; the original stays in the mailbox |

<Callout type="warning">
  AI extraction is very good on clear, typed invoices and less reliable on blurry phone photos of paper receipts or handwritten bills. Start with every invoice going through review, see how often corrections are needed on your own invoices, and only then decide what can skip review.
</Callout>

---

## Is it worth it for you?

**Probably yes if** you receive more than a handful of invoices a month, several people currently receive them, or you've paid a late fee or lost a receipt in the last year. Part 1 alone is worth doing at any size.

**Probably not yet if** you get three invoices a month from the same suppliers. A shared inbox (Part 1) is enough; the automation would take longer to build than it saves.

**Something to be aware of:** the AI model is billed separately by its provider, per invoice it reads. Check their pricing against your monthly invoice volume before you switch it on for everything.

## FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Do I need to know how to code?">
    Not for Part 1. Creating the invoice inbox, pointing suppliers at it and
    reading it in Outlook or Apple Mail needs no code. Automatic reading of
    the invoices (Part 2) needs a short program, so you'll need a developer
    or a technical teammate for that part.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Does Reloop read the invoices itself?">
    No. Reloop receives the emails, keeps the originals with their
    attachments, and notifies your program when one arrives. An AI model
    that you connect, such as Claude, reads the invoice. Your program decides
    where the details are saved.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can it handle invoices that are in the email body, not a PDF?">
    Yes. When there's no PDF attached, the example in Step 5 sends the email's
    text to the AI instead. Many SaaS receipts work this way.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can it connect to Xero or QuickBooks?">
    Your program can, because both have APIs for creating draft bills.
    Reloop doesn't have a built-in Xero or QuickBooks connection. A common
    approach is to create the bill as a draft so someone approves it inside
    the accounting tool.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Is it safe to send invoices to an AI model?">
    Invoices contain business and sometimes personal data, so check the AI
    provider's data and retention terms and your own obligations (for example,
    GDPR) before you start. Keep the API keys for the mailbox restricted to
    that one invoice address.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="What if a supplier sends a fake or altered invoice?">
    Automation doesn't remove that risk, and it can make it easier to miss if
    payments happen without review. Keep a person approving payments, only
    trust known vendors automatically, and always confirm changed bank
    details by phone with a number you already have.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# Building in Public: Lessons From Growing Reloop

Path: /blog/building-in-public-lessons
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/building-in-public-lessons
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/building-in-public-lessons.md

What we've learned building Reloop, an open-source email platform, in public since July 2025: shipping order, rewriting early, public changelogs, docs as product, writing for AI agents, and what open source changes.

**Building in public is mostly a discipline, not a marketing tactic.** For us it has meant an open repository, a public changelog for everything we ship, docs written before people ask, and saying plainly what Reloop doesn't do yet. Those habits have shaped the product more than any launch.

Reloop's first commit landed on July 31, 2025, and we [introduced it publicly](/blog/introducing-reloop) that September. Since then the repository has grown to more than 5,900 commits, 21 backend services, 66 public changelog entries and over 370 documentation pages. Here's what we've learned along the way. Every number in this post comes from the repo, so you can check it.

---

## What "in public" means for us

"Building in public" gets used loosely, so here's what we actually do:

| Practice | Where you can see it |
|---|---|
| Source code is open (Apache 2.0) | [github.com/reloop-labs/reloop](https://github.com/reloop-labs/reloop) |
| Every notable release gets a changelog entry | [/changelog](/changelog) |
| Docs ship with the feature, not after | [/docs](/docs) |
| Pricing is public, including what self-hosting costs | [/pricing](/pricing) |
| Comparisons say where competitors are better | [/compare](/compare) |
| The product is usable by AI agents, not just humans | [/llms.txt](/llms.txt), MCP server |

We don't publish revenue dashboards or daily metrics threads. That's a valid version of building in public, but it's not ours. Ours is: you can read the code, see what changed, and know what you're getting.

---

## Lesson 1: Ship the boring core first

Our first month of changelog entries, from August 2025, reads like a list of things nobody tweets about:

- Domain DNS verification for [SPF, DKIM and DMARC](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide)
- KumoMTA as the SMTP engine
- DNS record status badges and quick copy
- A "send test email" tool in the dashboard

No campaigns, no AI, no automations. Just: can you verify a domain and get an email delivered?

That order was deliberate. Email infrastructure lives or dies on deliverability. A beautiful campaign builder on top of mail that lands in spam is worthless. Getting authentication and the MTA right first meant everything we built later inherited a working foundation.

**What we'd tell others:** find the part of your product that has to be boring and correct, and ship that before anything people will screenshot.

---

## Lesson 2: Rewrite early, while it's cheap

In September 2025, about six weeks in, we migrated the data layer to Drizzle ORM on PostgreSQL. In November 2025 we built background jobs on Inngest. Today that event layer runs on NATS JetStream [inside our own stack](/blog/how-we-built-email-delivery-queue-bullmq).

Each of those was a rewrite of something that already worked. They were worth it because:

- **Self-hosting changes the constraints.** A dependency that's fine for a hosted SaaS becomes a problem when every self-hoster has to run it too. Moving the event bus into the stack meant one less external service for people deploying Reloop themselves.
- **Early rewrites are small.** Changing the ORM with a few thousand lines of code is an afternoon of pain. Changing it a year later is a quarter.
- **Doing it in public keeps you honest.** When the changelog says "Migration to Drizzle ORM & PostgreSQL", you have to actually finish it.

**What we'd tell others:** if an early architectural choice is wrong for where the product is going, change it now. The cost only goes up.

---

## Lesson 3: A public changelog is a forcing function

We've published 66 changelog entries since August 2025. A few things happen when every release has to be written up:

1. **You ship smaller.** A changelog entry needs a clear "what changed". That pushes features into shippable pieces instead of month-long branches.
2. **You think about the user's next step.** A feature written up for strangers has to make sense on its own. That's why entries like "[Webhook Retry Engine](/blog/building-webhook-delivery-system) & Test Delivery Tool" pair the capability with the way to try it.
3. **Users can see momentum.** For an infrastructure product, people need to trust it's maintained before they put password resets on it. A dated changelog is the most honest proof.

The changelog isn't marketing copy. It's a record. Entries say what shipped, not what's coming.

---

## Lesson 4: Docs are part of the product

Our docs site has more than 370 pages. A lot of them are unglamorous: DNS setup for GoDaddy, Namecheap, Cloudflare, Route 53, Hetzner, Porkbun and others; troubleshooting pages for SPF conflicts, MX conflicts and domains that won't verify.

Those pages exist because domain setup is where most people get stuck with any email provider. Every guide we write is one fewer person who gives up at the DNS step.

Two rules we follow:

- **Write the doc when you ship the feature.** If it can't be explained clearly, the feature probably isn't done.
- **Errors link to docs.** Every Reloop API error returns a `message`, a `why`, a `fix` and a `link` to the relevant page. The docs are where the error message sends you, so they have to be right.

---

## Lesson 5: Write for AI agents, not just people

In mid-2026 we shipped the [Reloop MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server), standardized `llms.txt` and `skill.md` endpoints, and copy-paste setup prompts for AI coding tools like Cursor, Claude Code and Windsurf.

A growing share of developers meet a new API through their coding assistant rather than through the docs homepage. If the assistant can't find accurate information about your product, it guesses, and the guesses are usually wrong.

What that looks like in practice:

- An [`llms.txt`](/llms.txt) index of the docs, so agents can find the right page
- Markdown versions of pages, which are cheaper and cleaner for models to read
- An OpenAPI spec generated from the code, so it can't drift from the real API
- An MCP server so an agent can send email, manage templates and [read an inbox](/blog/build-ai-agent-sends-emails) directly

**What we'd tell others:** treat "can an AI assistant use our product correctly?" as a real acceptance test.

---

## Lesson 6: Open source changes who you're accountable to

Reloop is licensed under Apache 2.0 and can be [self-hosted with a single install command](/blog/self-hosted-email-infrastructure). That changes the relationship with users in ways we didn't fully expect.

- **People read the code before they trust it.** Security reviews and "how does this actually work?" questions are answered by the source, not by a sales call.
- **Self-hosters run it in places you don't.** Different networks, DNS resolvers and hosting providers. That's why the self-hosting docs go into detail on things like outbound DNS and port 25.
- **You can't hide limitations.** If a feature isn't there, anyone can see it isn't there. So we say so: our [comparison pages](/compare) mark features we don't have yet, like A/B testing, as "No".

We wrote more about the decision in [why we open-sourced our email infrastructure](/blog/why-we-open-sourced-email-infrastructure).

---

## Lesson 7: Be honest about what's not done

The easiest way to lose trust in public is to overclaim. So we've adopted a few rules for everything we publish, including this blog:

| We do | We don't |
|---|---|
| Cite pricing from public pages and link to them | Quote competitor prices from memory |
| Say "we build Reloop" in comparison posts | Pretend to be a neutral review site |
| Mark beta features as beta | Announce features before they ship |
| Use numbers from the repo or the product | Invent growth metrics |

This post follows the same rules. You won't find a revenue chart here, because we haven't published one.

---

## Follow along

If you want to see what we ship next:

- Watch or star the [GitHub repo](https://github.com/reloop-labs/reloop)
- Read the [changelog](/changelog)
- Subscribe to the [blog feed](/blog/feed.xml)

And if you're building something in public yourself, our advice is short: ship the boring parts first, write it all down, and don't claim anything you can't link to.

---

  </Accordion>

  </Accordion>

  </Accordion>

# Reloop vs Postal (2026): Self-Hosted Mail Servers Compared

Path: /blog/reloop-vs-postal
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-postal
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-postal.md

Reloop vs Postal compared honestly: two open-source, self-hosted email platforms. Architecture, requirements, sending API, inbound mail, webhooks, marketing features and when each one is the right pick.

**Reloop and Postal are both open-source email platforms you can run on your own server.** Both send over SMTP and an HTTP API, fire webhooks, sign mail with DKIM and keep a suppression list. The difference is scope: **Postal is a focused mail delivery server, and it's very good at that job. Reloop is a full email platform: sending, real inboxes your agents can read and reply from, contacts, campaigns and automations, and it's also available as a hosted service if you don't want to run it yourself.**

We build Reloop, so weigh this accordingly. Every Postal fact below links to [Postal's own docs](https://docs.postalserver.io/) or [its GitHub repository](https://github.com/postalserver/postal), and where Postal is the better pick, we say so.

---

## The 30-second comparison

| | **Reloop** | **Postal** |
|---|---|---|
| License | Apache 2.0 | MIT |
| Language | TypeScript (Bun) | Ruby |
| Hosted option | Yes (free tier, from $10/mo) | No, self-host only |
| Self-host | Yes, one-command installer | Yes, Docker + CLI |
| Sending engine | KumoMTA | Postal's own MTA |
| Database | PostgreSQL | MariaDB 10.6+ |
| HTTP send API | Yes | Yes |
| SMTP submission | Yes | Yes |
| Webhooks | Yes, HMAC-signed | Yes |
| IP pools | Dedicated IPs | Multiple IP pools with routing rules |
| Inbound email | Mailboxes with threads, API, MCP, IMAP | Forward to HTTP endpoint, SMTP server or address |
| Agent inbox | Yes | No |
| Contacts, campaigns, automations | Yes | No |
| Stored templates | Yes | No |
| Open and click tracking | Yes | Yes |

Postal's feature set is from its [feature list](https://docs.postalserver.io/welcome/feature-list). Reloop's is on [reloop.sh](/) and in [the docs](/docs).

---

## What each one is

**Postal** describes itself as "a complete and fully featured mail delivery platform for use by websites & web servers", an open-source alternative to Sendgrid, Mailgun or Postmark that you run on your own infrastructure. It has been around for years, is written in Ruby, has around 17k GitHub stars, and is released under the MIT license. There is no official hosted version: if you use Postal, you run Postal.

**Reloop** is open-source email infrastructure under Apache 2.0: an email API and SMTP relay, plus inbound mailboxes, contacts, broadcast campaigns, event-triggered automations and webhooks. You can use it hosted on [Reloop Cloud](/pricing) or run the same code yourself with the [self-host installer](/self-host).

So the honest framing is: **Postal replaces the sending part of SendGrid or Mailgun. Reloop replaces the sending part and the tools you'd usually bolt on next to it.**

---

## Running it yourself

Both run on a single Linux server with Docker. Neither is "free" in effort: you own IP reputation, warm-up, blocklist monitoring and uptime either way.

| | Reloop | Postal |
|---|---|---|
| Minimum hardware | 2 vCPUs, 4 GB RAM, 35 GB disk | 2 CPU cores, 4 GB RAM, 25 GB disk |
| Install | `curl -fsSL https://reloop.sh/install.sh \| sudo bash` | `postal bootstrap`, `postal initialize`, `postal make-user`, `postal start` |
| Database | PostgreSQL (bundled) | MariaDB 10.6+ (MySQL not supported) |
| Reverse proxy and TLS | Caddy (bundled) | Caddy (recommended in the docs) |
| What runs | API services, dashboard, KumoMTA, PostgreSQL, Redis, NATS, Caddy | Postal web, SMTP and worker processes, MariaDB |

Postal's numbers are from its [prerequisites page](https://docs.postalserver.io/getting-started/prerequisites) and [installation guide](https://docs.postalserver.io/getting-started/installation). Reloop's are from our [self-hosting guide](/blog/self-hosted-email-infrastructure).

**Postal is the lighter install.** It does less, so it runs less. Reloop runs more containers because it ships more of the product: inboxes, campaigns, automations and the dashboard for all of them. If you only need an MTA with a web UI, Postal's footprint is a real advantage.

Both need outbound port 25 open, which many cloud providers block by default. Check that before you pick a host.

<Callout type="tip">
  Whichever you pick, the hard part of self-hosting is reputation, not installation. Plan a 2–4 week warm-up and set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC before your first real send. Our [IP warming guide](/blog/ip-warming-guide) has a day-by-day schedule.
</Callout>

---

## Sending email

Both accept mail over SMTP and an HTTP API.

**Postal**

Postal's HTTP API authenticates with an `X-Server-API-Key` header and sends through `POST /api/v1/messages/message` ([API docs](https://docs.postalserver.io/developer/api)):

```typescript
const res = await fetch("https://postal.example.com/api/v1/messages/message", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
    "X-Server-API-Key": process.env.POSTAL_API_KEY!,
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
    to: ["user@example.com"],
    subject: "Welcome",
    html_body: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
  }),
});

const { status, data } = await res.json();
// status is "success" or "error"; data.messages maps each recipient to an id
```

**Reloop**

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({
  apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY!,
  // Self-hosted? Point it at your own instance:
  // baseUrl: "https://mail.example.com",
});

const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Welcome",
  html: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
});
```

A few differences:

| | Reloop | Postal |
|---|---|---|
| Official SDKs | Node, Python, Go, PHP, Ruby, Rust, Java, .NET, Elixir | HTTP API, plus community clients |
| Error format | `message`, `why` and `fix` | `status: "error"` with a code and message |
| Stored templates | Yes, sent by ID with `{{{variables}}}` | No, send the rendered body |
| React Email | Pass a component or rendered HTML | Pass rendered HTML |
| Same API hosted and self-hosted | Yes | Self-hosted only |

That last row is the practical one. With Reloop you can start on the hosted free tier, then move to your own server by changing `baseUrl`. Nothing else in your code changes.

---

## Deliverability controls

This is where Postal has a lot of depth for a pure MTA. Its [feature list](https://docs.postalserver.io/welcome/feature-list) includes:

- **Multiple IP pools**, with rules that route specific senders or recipients to specific IPs
- **Per-server send rate limits**
- DKIM signing, a built-in suppression list, and automated DNS checks
- **Development mode**, which holds messages instead of delivering them while you test
- Click and open tracking, message tagging, and full message and queue history with search

Reloop sends through KumoMTA with per-destination throttling and automatic pauses when bounce or complaint rates spike. It handles bounces and complaints, keeps one suppression list across transactional mail and campaigns, and includes a dedicated IP on the hosted Growth plan. Read [how bounce processing works](/blog/email-bounce-processing-automation).

If fine-grained IP pool routing is your main requirement, for example you run mail for many separate brands or clients and need to isolate their reputations, Postal's model is built for exactly that.

---

## Receiving email

Both receive mail on your domain. What happens next is very different.

**Postal** routes inbound mail. A message can be forwarded to an **HTTP endpoint** (as form data or JSON, raw or parsed, with replies and signatures optionally split out of the body), to another **SMTP server**, or to an **email address**. It runs spam and virus checks with SpamAssassin, rspamd and ClamAV. Storing, threading and replying is up to your application.

**Reloop** receives mail into **mailboxes**. Messages are stored, threaded, spam-scored with Rspamd, and readable over the API, the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) or IMAP. You can reply in-thread with one call, and there's an `email.received` webhook if you also want push notifications.

| | Reloop | Postal |
|---|---|---|
| Receive on your domain | Yes | Yes |
| Forward to your app over HTTP | Yes (`email.received` webhook) | Yes |
| Stored mailboxes with threads | Yes | No |
| Reply in thread via API | Yes | Build it yourself |
| IMAP access | Yes | No |
| MCP access for AI agents | Yes | No |

If you're building an AI agent that handles email, a support inbox, or "reply to this email" features, Reloop saves you from building the storage and threading layer. See [build an AI agent that reads and replies to email](/blog/build-ai-agent-sends-emails).

---

## Webhooks

Both send webhooks for delivery events.

- **Postal** sends events such as `MessageSent`, `MessageDelayed`, `MessageDeliveryFailed`, `MessageHeld`, `MessageBounced`, `MessageLinkClicked`, `MessageLoaded` and `DomainDNSError`, and keeps 7 days of webhook request history in the UI ([webhook docs](https://docs.postalserver.io/developer/webhooks)).
- **Reloop** sends `email.delivered`, `email.bounced`, `email.complained`, `email.opened`, `email.clicked`, `email.received` and more, signed with HMAC-SHA256 in the `Reloop-Signature` header and retried with backoff. See [how we built webhook delivery](/blog/building-webhook-delivery-system).

---

## Beyond sending: contacts, campaigns and automations

Postal deliberately stops at mail delivery. For newsletters, onboarding sequences or product announcements, you'd pair it with another tool and keep the two suppression lists in sync yourself.

Reloop includes:

- **Contacts** with custom properties, groups and subscription channels
- **Broadcast campaigns** with scheduling
- **Event-triggered automations**: delays, conditions and email steps that start when your app tracks an event like `user.signed_up`
- **Stored templates** with `{{{variables}}}`

All of it shares one suppression list with your transactional mail. See [welcome sequences that convert](/blog/welcome-email-sequences-that-convert) for a worked example.

---

## Where Postal is the better choice

Being honest about it:

- **You want a pure MTA and nothing more.** Postal is mature, does one job, and has a smaller footprint to run and secure.
- **You run mail for many tenants** and need multiple IP pools with per-sender or per-recipient routing rules.
- **You prefer MIT** over Apache 2.0, or your team already runs Ruby and MariaDB and is comfortable operating them.
- **You already run Postal** and it's working. Migrating a stable mail server for features you don't need isn't worth the warm-up.

For more self-hosted mail servers and platforms, see our roundup of the [best Postal alternatives](/blog/best-postal-alternatives).

## Where Reloop is the better choice

- **You want a hosted option** today, with the freedom to self-host later on the same API.
- **You need inbound mail as real inboxes**, especially for AI agents, with IMAP and MCP access.
- **You want transactional mail, campaigns and automations** in one product with one suppression list.
- **You want official SDKs** in your language instead of calling a raw HTTP API.

---

## Switching from Postal to Reloop

1. **Install or sign up.** Run the [self-host installer](/self-host) on a new server, or create a hosted account. Keep Postal running for now.
2. **Add your domain** and publish Reloop's DKIM record (`reloop._domainkey`). Merge `include:reloop.sh` into your SPF record if you send hosted. Don't add a second SPF record.
3. **Swap the send call.** Replace `POST /api/v1/messages/message` with `reloop.mail.send`, and rename `html_body` → `html` and `plain_body` → `text`. SMTP senders only need new host and credentials.
4. **Move inbound routes.** For each Postal route, create a Reloop mailbox, or keep your HTTP handler and subscribe it to `email.received`.
5. **Port webhooks.** Map `MessageSent` → `email.delivered`, `MessageBounced` and `MessageDeliveryFailed` → `email.bounced`, `MessageLinkClicked` → `email.clicked` and `MessageLoaded` → `email.opened`, and verify the `Reloop-Signature` header.
6. **Import suppressions** so you don't re-mail addresses that bounced on Postal.
7. **Ramp traffic** from 10% to 100% over one to two weeks while the new IP warms up, then retire Postal's DNS records and server.

Our [SendGrid migration guide](/blog/migrating-from-sendgrid) walks through the traffic split and suppression import in more detail.

# Gmail & Yahoo Bulk Sender Requirements: 2026 Checklist

Path: /blog/gmail-yahoo-bulk-sender-requirements
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/gmail-yahoo-bulk-sender-requirements
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/gmail-yahoo-bulk-sender-requirements.md

Every rule Gmail, Yahoo and Microsoft Outlook enforce on email senders: SPF, DKIM, DMARC alignment, one-click unsubscribe, spam rate limits and PTR records, with a checklist you can run today.

**Gmail, Yahoo and Outlook now reject or junk mail that is not authenticated.** If you send more than 5,000 messages a day to any of them, you need SPF, DKIM, an aligned DMARC record, one-click unsubscribe on marketing mail, and a spam complaint rate under 0.3%. Smaller senders still need SPF or DKIM, valid reverse DNS and TLS.

Google and Yahoo announced these rules together in October 2023 and started enforcing them in February 2024. Microsoft followed for Outlook.com, Hotmail and Live addresses in May 2025. Enforcement has only tightened since: what began as temporary errors is now outright rejection.

This guide lists every requirement, who it applies to, and how to check each one. The checklist at the end works for any provider, including [Reloop](/features/transaction-emails).

---

## Who counts as a bulk sender?

| Mailbox provider | Bulk threshold | What counts |
|------------------|----------------|-------------|
| **Gmail** | ~5,000 messages in a 24-hour period | Mail to personal `@gmail.com` and `@googlemail.com` addresses from the same primary domain |
| **Yahoo** | No fixed number published | Yahoo applies the rules to "bulk senders" by volume and pattern |
| **Outlook / Hotmail / Live** | More than 5,000 messages a day | Mail to Microsoft consumer addresses |

Three details catch people out:

1. **Gmail counts by primary domain.** Mail from `mail.acme.com` and `news.acme.com` adds up under `acme.com`.
2. **Once Gmail classifies you as bulk, you stay bulk.** One busy day with a product launch is enough. Dropping back under 5,000 does not undo it.
3. **Transactional and marketing mail share the count.** Password resets and receipts count toward the 5,000 threshold even though they are exempt from the unsubscribe rule.

The safe move is to meet the bulk sender rules from day one. None of them are hard to set up, and all of them improve inbox placement even at low volume.

---

## Requirements for every sender

These apply even if you send ten emails a day.

### 1. SPF or DKIM on your sending domain

At least one of them must pass. In practice, set up both: DKIM survives forwarding, SPF does not. Our [SPF, DKIM and DMARC setup guide](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide) walks through the exact records.

### 2. Valid forward and reverse DNS (PTR)

The IP address that connects to Gmail must have a PTR record, and that hostname must resolve back to the same IP. If you use an email API, your provider handles this. If you run your own MTA, check it:

```bash
dig -x 203.0.113.10 +short
# mta1.mail.example.com.
dig mta1.mail.example.com +short
# 203.0.113.10
```

### 3. TLS for the connection

Gmail requires TLS when it receives your mail. Every modern provider supports this. A self-hosted Postfix with an expired certificate is the usual way to fail it.

### 4. Spam complaint rate below 0.3%

Google measures the share of your delivered mail that users mark as spam, as reported in [Google Postmaster Tools](https://postmaster.google.com). Aim for **under 0.1%**. At 0.3% and above, Gmail stops giving you mitigation help and starts filtering hard.

### 5. RFC 5322 compliant messages

That means one `From` header, a valid `Message-ID` and a `Date` header, among others. Hand-built MIME strings are where this breaks. Use a library or an API.

### 6. Do not impersonate Gmail

Never put a `@gmail.com` address in the `From` header when sending through a third party. Gmail's own DMARC policy is `p=quarantine`, so those messages get filtered.

---

## Extra requirements for bulk senders

### 7. SPF **and** DKIM, both passing

Bulk senders need both, not one or the other.

### 8. A DMARC record, at least `p=none`

Publish a TXT record at `_dmarc.yourdomain.com`:

```
v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@yourdomain.com
```

`p=none` meets the requirement. It only asks for reports and does not change delivery. Move to `p=quarantine` and then `p=reject` once the reports show only your own services sending.

### 9. DMARC alignment

This is the requirement most teams miss. The domain in your visible `From` address must **match** the domain that passed SPF or DKIM.

| From address | DKIM signing domain (`d=`) | Aligned? |
|--------------|---------------------------|----------|
| `hello@acme.com` | `acme.com` | Yes |
| `hello@acme.com` | `mail.acme.com` | Yes (relaxed alignment, same organizational domain) |
| `hello@acme.com` | `sendgrid.net` | **No** |
| `hello@acme.com` | `amazonses.com` | **No** |

If your provider signs with its own domain, your mail passes DKIM but fails alignment. Use a provider that signs with **your** domain. Reloop does this by default when you [verify a domain](/docs/learn/domain).

### 10. One-click unsubscribe for marketing mail

Marketing and subscribed messages need two headers defined in [RFC 8058](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8058):

```
List-Unsubscribe: <https://acme.com/unsubscribe?token=abc123>, <mailto:unsubscribe@acme.com?subject=unsubscribe>
List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click
```

Gmail and Yahoo then show their own "Unsubscribe" button next to the sender name. When a user clicks it, the provider sends a `POST` request to your HTTPS URL. Your endpoint must unsubscribe the user **without** a login, confirmation page or second click.

Two more rules apply:

- **Honor the request within two days.**
- **Keep a visible unsubscribe link in the body too.** The header does not replace it.

Both headers must also be covered by your DKIM signature, or Gmail ignores them. Reloop's MTA includes `List-Unsubscribe` and `List-Unsubscribe-Post` in the signed header set, and [campaigns](/features/email-marketing) add both headers automatically for each recipient.

<Callout type="info">
  Transactional mail such as password resets, receipts and security alerts is **exempt** from the one-click unsubscribe rule. Do not add an unsubscribe header to a login code: users will click it and stop receiving mail they need.
</Callout>

---

## What Outlook added in 2025

Microsoft's rules for Outlook.com, Hotmail.com and Live.com took effect on **May 5, 2025**, for domains sending more than 5,000 messages a day:

- SPF must pass for the sending domain
- DKIM must pass
- DMARC must exist with at least `p=none` and align with SPF or DKIM

Non-compliant mail first went to Junk. It is now rejected with:

```
550 5.7.515 Access denied, sending domain [example.com] does not meet the required authentication level.
```

Microsoft also asks, but does not yet enforce, a working unsubscribe link, valid `From` and `Reply-To` addresses, and list hygiene. See our guide on [avoiding the Outlook spam folder](/docs/guides/avoid-outlook-spam).

---

## What happens when you fail

Gmail and Outlook return SMTP errors that tell you exactly which rule you broke. These are the ones you will see in your [bounce logs](/blog/email-bounce-processing-automation):

| Error | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `550 5.7.26` | Unauthenticated: the message failed DMARC or had no SPF/DKIM pass |
| `421 4.7.27` / `550 5.7.27` | SPF did not pass |
| `550 5.7.30` | DKIM did not pass (bulk senders) |
| `421 4.7.32` / `550 5.7.32` | `From` domain not aligned with SPF or DKIM |
| `421 4.7.28` | Rate limited: unusual volume or a high spam rate |
| `550 5.7.515` | Outlook: domain does not meet authentication requirements |

A `4xx` code is temporary and the message will be retried. A `5xx` code is a permanent failure. If `5xx` codes for authentication pile up, stop sending and fix DNS before you retry. Repeated failures damage your [domain reputation](/tools/domain-reputation-checker).

---

## The checklist

Work through this list once per sending domain.

- [ ] **SPF** record published and passing ([check with the auth checker](/tools/auth-checker))
- [ ] **DKIM** signing with **your** domain, 2048-bit key
- [ ] **DMARC** record at `_dmarc.yourdomain.com`, at least `p=none`, with a `rua` address
- [ ] `From` domain **aligned** with the DKIM `d=` domain
- [ ] **PTR record** valid for every sending IP
- [ ] **TLS** on all outbound connections
- [ ] **One-click unsubscribe** headers on marketing and newsletter mail, covered by DKIM
- [ ] **Visible unsubscribe link** in the body of marketing mail
- [ ] Unsubscribes processed **within 48 hours**
- [ ] **Spam rate under 0.1%**, monitored in Google Postmaster Tools
- [ ] Domain **not on any blocklist** ([blocklist checker](/tools/blocklist-checker))
- [ ] Transactional and marketing mail on **separate subdomains** so one cannot sink the other ([subdomain vs root](/docs/guides/subdomain-vs-root))

Then send a real message to the [deliverability tester](/tools/deliverability-tester). It shows the SPF, DKIM and DMARC results and the headers the receiving server actually saw.

---

## How to keep your spam rate low

Authentication gets you through the door. The spam complaint rate decides whether you stay in the inbox.

1. **Only send to people who asked.** Double opt-in for newsletters. Never buy lists.
2. **Block throwaway addresses at signup.** Disposable inboxes inflate bounces and never engage. See [how to block disposable emails](/blog/block-disposable-emails-at-signup).
3. **Suppress hard bounces and complainers immediately.** Reloop keeps a [suppression list](/docs/guides/suppression-list) per organization automatically.
4. **Make unsubscribing easier than complaining.** If the unsubscribe link is hidden, users press "Report spam" instead, and that counts against you.
5. **Warm up new domains and IPs.** Jumping from zero to 50,000 a day looks like a compromised account. Follow the [IP warming guide](/blog/ip-warming-guide).
6. **Sunset inactive contacts.** Stop mailing people who have not opened in 6 to 12 months.

For a full diagnosis when mail is already landing in spam, read [why emails land in spam and how to fix it](/blog/why-emails-land-in-spam-fix).

---

## FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Do the Gmail requirements apply if I send fewer than 5,000 emails a day?">
    The basic rules do: SPF or DKIM, valid reverse DNS, TLS, a spam rate under
    0.3% and RFC 5322 compliant messages. DMARC, alignment and one-click
    unsubscribe are only required above 5,000 a day, but you should set them up
    anyway. Gmail filters unauthenticated mail more aggressively at any volume.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Does one-click unsubscribe apply to transactional email?">
    No. Google and Yahoo exempt transactional messages such as password resets,
    receipts, order updates and security alerts. The rule covers marketing and
    subscribed mail like newsletters and promotions.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Is DMARC p=none enough?">
    It meets the Gmail, Yahoo and Outlook requirement. It does not protect your
    domain from spoofing, because receivers still deliver failing mail. Use
    p=none to collect reports, then move to p=quarantine and p=reject once only
    your own services appear in them.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="How do I check my spam complaint rate?">
    Add and verify your domain in Google Postmaster Tools. It shows the user
    reported spam rate for mail delivered to Gmail. Yahoo offers a Complaint
    Feedback Loop, and Microsoft offers SNDS and JMRP for Outlook.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="What does error 550 5.7.26 mean?">
    Gmail rejected the message because it was not authenticated. Either DMARC
    failed, or neither SPF nor DKIM passed for your domain. Check that your DKIM
    record is published and that your From domain aligns with the signing
    domain.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Does Reloop handle these requirements for me?">
    Reloop signs mail with DKIM using your own domain, gives you the SPF and
    DMARC records to publish, sends over TLS from IPs with valid PTR records,
    and adds one-click unsubscribe headers to campaign mail. You still publish
    the DNS records and keep your list clean.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# Best SendGrid Alternatives in 2026: Cheaper, Simpler and Open Source

Path: /blog/best-sendgrid-alternatives

The best SendGrid alternatives in 2026 compared: Reloop, Resend, Postmark, Amazon SES, Mailgun, MailerSend, Brevo and Mailjet on price at 50k and 100k emails, free tiers, inbound, marketing and how to migrate.

**The short version:** if you're leaving SendGrid to pay less and get a simpler API, **Reloop** is the strongest all-round replacement: $10 for 50,000 emails, a permanent free tier, inbound mailboxes, campaigns on the same plan, and open source. If you only care about transactional deliverability, look at **Postmark**. If you're on AWS and want the cheapest raw pipe, **Amazon SES**.

We build Reloop, so weigh that. Every price below comes from the providers' public pricing pages, linked in our head-to-head posts, and each section says where that provider beats us.

---

## Why teams leave SendGrid

SendGrid, now part of Twilio, is proven at enormous volume. The reasons people look elsewhere are consistent:

- **No permanent free plan.** New accounts get 100 emails a day for a 60-day trial, then you pay.
- **The features growing teams want sit on Pro.** A dedicated IP, subusers and SSO start at $89.95 a month.
- **Two products, two plans.** The Email API and Marketing Campaigns are billed separately.
- **An older API.** The v3 payload nests recipients inside a `personalizations` array that most developers look up every time.
- **Hosted only.** No source, no self-hosting, no way to run it yourself if pricing or policy changes.

If none of that bothers you and you need Twilio's enterprise contracts, SendGrid may still be the right call. Otherwise, here are the alternatives.

## 1. Reloop: best overall SendGrid alternative

Reloop is open-source email infrastructure: a transactional API, SMTP relay, inbound mailboxes, contacts, campaigns, automations and webhooks in one product. Use it hosted, or run the same code on your own server.

**Pricing:** Free is 6,000 emails a month (200 a day) with no end date. Pro is $10 for 50,000. Growth is $20 for 100,000 and includes a dedicated IP. Extra mail costs $0.50 per 1,000. Self-hosting is free under Apache 2.0. Pay-as-you-go credits are also available at $0.50 per 1,000, valid for 6 months.

**Why it fits SendGrid users**

- **Roughly half the price.** $10 vs $19.95 at 50k, $20 vs $34.95 at 100k. With a dedicated IP, it's $20 on Reloop against $89.95 on SendGrid Pro.
- **One product.** Transactional email, campaigns and event-triggered automations share one API key and one suppression list. No second Marketing Campaigns plan.
- **A flat API.** One request, one message, no `personalizations` array. Errors return `message`, `why` and `fix`.
- **Inbound as real mailboxes.** Where SendGrid's Inbound Parse POSTs each message to your URL, Reloop stores and threads mail, scores spam, and lets you read and reply over the API, the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) or IMAP.
- **Open source and self-hostable**, so you're never locked in. Reloop Cloud runs on Hetzner, a German hosting company, with EU data centers.

**Where SendGrid is still ahead**

- **Template logic.** SendGrid's dynamic templates run full Handlebars (`#if`, `#each`). Reloop templates substitute variables like `{{{first_name}}}` with defaults; loops and conditions happen in your code.
- **Enterprise procurement.** Subusers, IP pools and a mature Twilio compliance programme.
- **Track record.** Reloop is younger, with fewer years of community answers.

**Best for:** startups and product teams that want SendGrid's sending without its pricing, especially if they also need inbound mail or might self-host.

Full breakdown: [Reloop vs SendGrid](/blog/reloop-vs-sendgrid) · [SendGrid alternative overview](/alternatives/sendgrid) · [Feature comparison](/compare/sendgrid)

---

## 2. Resend: best hosted developer experience

Resend set the bar for a modern email API and created React Email.

**Pricing:** Free is 3,000 a month (100 a day). Pro is $20 for 50,000. 100,000 costs $35. Overage is $0.90 per 1,000.

**Strengths:** excellent docs and onboarding, first-class React Email, a large ecosystem of examples, and Broadcasts for simple marketing sends.

**Weaknesses:** $35 at 100k is about the same as SendGrid Essentials, a dedicated IP needs the $90 Scale plan plus a $30/mo add-on, inbound is a webhook per message, and it's hosted only.

**Best for:** small teams that want a polished API and will stay under 50k emails a month.

Full breakdown: [Reloop vs Resend](/blog/reloop-vs-resend) · [Resend alternatives](/blog/best-resend-alternatives)

---

## 3. Postmark: best for transactional deliverability

Postmark has been transactional-first for over a decade. **Message streams** keep transactional and broadcast traffic apart, so a newsletter can't hurt your password resets.

**Pricing:** a free developer plan of 100 emails a month. Basic is $15 for 10,000, with overage at $1.80 per 1,000; Pro and Platform lower that to $1.30 and $1.20. Inbound needs Pro or above. Dedicated IPs are $50 a month per IP for senders above 300,000 a month.

**Strengths:** strong transactional reputation, clear bounce handling, excellent support.

**Weaknesses:** the most expensive per email here once you pass 10,000, a tiny free tier, and hosted only.

**Best for:** teams where a delayed receipt or reset costs real money and budget is secondary.

Full breakdown: [Reloop vs Postmark](/blog/reloop-vs-postmark)

---

## 4. Amazon SES: cheapest raw sending

SES is AWS's sending pipe. It's the cheapest per email by a wide margin, and it's a building block, not a product.

**Pricing:** $0.10 per 1,000 emails plus $0.12 per GB of outbound data. Dedicated IPs are $24.95 a month. New AWS accounts get up to $200 in Free Tier credits for six months.

**Strengths:** lowest list price, deep AWS integration (IAM, SNS, EventBridge, Lambda), scales to huge volume.

**Weaknesses:** new accounts start in a sandbox, and you build bounce handling, logs, templates and any dashboard yourself.

**Best for:** AWS-heavy teams with engineering time to build the tooling SendGrid gave them.

<Callout type="tip">
  You can combine the two: Reloop can route outbound mail through SES (or any SMTP provider) while you keep Reloop's API, logs, templates and suppression list.
</Callout>

Full breakdown: [Reloop vs Amazon SES](/blog/reloop-vs-aws-ses)

---

## 5. Mailgun: best for inbound routing and logs

Mailgun, now part of Sinch, is a long-standing developer API with strong log search and inbound routes.

**Pricing:** a 100-a-day free trial. Basic is $15 for 10,000. Foundation is $35 for 50,000, with overage from $1.30 per 1,000.

**Strengths:** inbound routes that match patterns and forward or POST messages, detailed event logs, Handlebars templates, and email validation as an add-on.

**Weaknesses:** more expensive than SendGrid Essentials at 50k, dedicated IPs are an add-on, campaigns are a separate Sinch product, and it's hosted only.

**Best for:** teams that need routing and log search more than a low price.

Full breakdown: [Reloop vs Mailgun](/blog/reloop-vs-mailgun) · [Mailgun alternatives](/blog/best-mailgun-alternatives)

---

## 6. MailerSend: best for a visual builder

MailerSend comes from the team behind MailerLite and is built for teams where non-developers edit emails.

**Pricing:** free for 500 emails a month. Hobby is $7 for 5,000. Starter is $35 for 50,000 and $68 for 100,000, with $1.30 per 1,000 overage at those tiers. Professional, which unlocks the dedicated IP add-on, is $110 for 50k.

**Strengths:** a drag-and-drop template builder, SMS in the US and Canada, and a clean dashboard.

**Weaknesses:** a small free tier, marketing lives in a separate product (MailerLite), and inbound is forwarded rather than stored.

**Best for:** teams where designers or marketers own transactional templates.

Full breakdown: [Reloop vs MailerSend](/blog/reloop-vs-mailersend)

---

## 7. Brevo: best for marketing-led teams

Brevo (formerly Sendinblue) is an all-in-one marketing suite from Paris with a transactional API.

**Pricing:** free for 300 emails a day. Starter begins at $9 for 5,000 emails, and Standard, with automations, starts at $18. Larger volumes are priced on a slider.

**Strengths:** email, SMS, WhatsApp, CRM and live chat in one product, with an editor marketers can use alone.

**Weaknesses:** costs rise quickly with volume compared with developer APIs, dedicated IPs are on higher tiers, and inbound is a webhook.

**Best for:** teams that left SendGrid mainly for Marketing Campaigns and want a broader marketing suite.

Full breakdown: [Reloop vs Brevo](/blog/reloop-vs-brevo)

---

## 8. Mailjet: best EU-based ESP

Mailjet, now owned by Sinch, combines transactional and marketing email with a strong drag-and-drop editor.

**Pricing:** free for 6,000 emails a month (200 a day). At 50,000 it's $40 on Essential or $59 on Premium; 100,000 on Premium is $112.

**Strengths:** tied with Reloop for the most generous free tier here, a good visual editor, and long GDPR experience.

**Weaknesses:** automations and the dedicated IP need Premium, and above the free tier it's several times Reloop's price.

**Best for:** small senders under 6,000 a month, or teams that want a visual editor with EU hosting.

Full breakdown: [Reloop vs Mailjet](/blog/reloop-vs-mailjet) · [Mailjet alternatives](/blog/best-mailjet-alternatives)

---

## How to choose

- **"We want SendGrid's features for less."** Reloop. It's $10 at 50k, and the dedicated IP is $20 instead of $89.95.
- **"Our templates depend on Handlebars logic."** Stay on SendGrid, or move the logic into your code and use Reloop or Resend.
- **"Only transactional deliverability matters."** Postmark.
- **"We're all-in on AWS and have engineers to spare."** Amazon SES, or SES behind Reloop.
- **"Marketers edit the emails."** MailerSend, Brevo or Mailjet.
- **"We receive mail too, or run AI agents that read and reply."** Reloop, the only option here with stored, threaded mailboxes.
- **"We need to self-host or read the source."** Reloop, the only open-source option here.

---

## Migrating off SendGrid

The steps are the same whichever provider you pick:

1. **Verify your domain** with the new provider. For Reloop, publish the `reloop._domainkey` DKIM record and merge `include:reloop.sh` into your existing SPF record. Never publish a second SPF record.
2. **Export your suppressions** (bounces, blocks, spam reports, unsubscribes) from SendGrid and import them, so you don't email people who already said no.
3. **Swap the client.** Replace `sgMail.send` and flatten the `personalizations` array into one request per message.
4. **Move templates.** In Reloop, placeholders use triple braces, like `{{{first_name}}}`, and Handlebars logic moves into your code.
5. **Point webhooks** at a new handler. Reloop events are named `email.delivered`, `email.bounced` and so on, and are signed in the `Reloop-Signature` header.
6. **Ramp traffic** from 10% to 100% over one to two weeks, watching bounce and complaint rates.

Our [SendGrid migration guide](/blog/migrating-from-sendgrid) walks through each step with code, including a traffic-split flag and a suppression import script.

  <Accordion title="Is there a free SendGrid alternative?">

# Reloop vs Resend (2026): Pricing, Features and Which to Choose

Path: /blog/reloop-vs-resend
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-resend
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-resend.md

Reloop vs Resend compared honestly: pricing at 3k to 250k emails a month, developer experience, inbound and agent inboxes, deliverability, self-hosting and lock-in, plus how to switch.

**Reloop and Resend feel almost the same to code against.** Both give you a clean REST API, a small SDK, React Email support, webhooks and SMTP. The differences are underneath: **Reloop costs about half as much at 50k emails and about 40% less at 100k (far less if you need a dedicated IP), receives mail into real inboxes your agents can reply from, and is open source, so you can run it yourself.** Resend is the more established hosted product with a larger ecosystem.

We build Reloop, so weigh this accordingly. Every price below is from the public pricing pages, and where Resend is the better pick, we say so.

---

## The 30-second comparison

| | **Reloop** | **Resend** |
|---|---|---|
| Free tier | 6,000 / mo, 200 / day | 3,000 / mo, 100 / day |
| 50,000 emails / mo | **$10** | $20 |
| 100,000 emails / mo | **$20** | $35 |
| Overage per 1,000 | **$0.50** | $0.90 |
| Dedicated IP | Included on Growth ($20) | $30/mo add-on on Scale ($90+), from 3,000 emails a day |
| Open source | Yes (Apache 2.0) | No |
| Self-host | Yes | No |
| Sending path | Own MTA (KumoMTA) | Amazon SES |
| Inbound email | Mailboxes with threads, API, MCP, IMAP | Webhook per message |
| Agent inbox | Yes | No |
| Contacts and broadcasts | Yes | Yes |
| Automations | Yes | Limited |
| React Email | Yes | Yes (they created it) |
| SMTP relay | Yes | Yes |

Resend's prices are from [resend.com/pricing](https://resend.com/pricing). Reloop's are on [reloop.sh/pricing](/pricing). Both change; check before you commit.

---

## Pricing at real volumes

Reloop's free tier is double Resend's: 6,000 emails a month capped at 200 a day, vs 3,000 and 100. The gap widens the moment you pay.

| Monthly volume | Reloop | Resend | Difference per year |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3,000 | $0 | $0 | $0 |
| 50,000 | $10 | $20 | $120 |
| 100,000 | $20 | $35 | **$180** |
| 150,000 | $20 + $25 overage = $45 | $35 + $45 overage = $80 | $420 |
| 100,000 with a dedicated IP | $20 | $90 Scale + $30 add-on = $120 | **$1,200** |

Two things drive the difference:

- **Reloop has a $10 tier.** Resend's first paid plan is $20 for 50k.
- **Reloop's 100k plan is $20, Resend's is $35.** A dedicated IP is included on Reloop Growth; on Resend it needs the $90 Scale plan plus a $30/mo add-on. Above that, extra mail costs $0.50 per 1,000 on Reloop vs $0.90 on Resend.

And if you self-host Reloop, there's no per-email fee at all. You pay for the server. See [self-hosted email infrastructure](/blog/self-hosted-email-infrastructure) for what that really involves.

<Callout type="tip">
  Price the volume you expect in a year, not today's. Moving providers later means re-verifying DNS and rebuilding reputation, so pick the one that still makes sense at 10× your current volume.
</Callout>

---

## Developer experience

This is where the two are closest. Resend set the bar for a modern email API, and Reloop's API follows the same shape on purpose.

**Resend**

```typescript

const resend = new Resend(process.env.RESEND_API_KEY);

const { data, error } = await resend.emails.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@acme.com>",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Welcome",
  html: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
});
```

**Reloop**

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY! });

const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Welcome",
  html: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
});
```

Both return errors as values instead of throwing. A few differences worth knowing:

| | Reloop | Resend |
|---|---|---|
| Error format | `message`, `why` and `fix` | `name` and `message` |
| Field style | `reply_to`, `scheduled_at` (snake_case) | `replyTo`, `scheduledAt` (camelCase in Node) |
| Idempotent retries | `Idempotency-Key` header | `Idempotency-Key` header |
| Stored templates | Yes, sent by ID with `{{{variables}}}` | Yes |
| React Email | Pass a component or rendered HTML | Pass a component or rendered HTML |
| Official SDKs | Node, Python, Go, PHP, Ruby, Rust, Java, .NET, Elixir | Most major languages |

Reloop's error shape is our one strong opinion here. When a send fails, the error tells you **why** it failed and **how to fix it**, so you rarely need to open the docs:

```json
{
  "message": "Domain not found",
  "why": "The domain mail.acme.com was not found or is not authorized for your organization",
  "fix": "Ensure the domain is registered and verified in your dashboard"
}
```

Resend's docs and onboarding are excellent, and its ecosystem of examples and integrations is larger. That's a real advantage if your team leans heavily on copy-paste examples.

---

## Receiving email and agent inboxes

This is the biggest functional difference.

**Resend** can receive email on your domain and deliver each message to your webhook. What you do with it after that (storage, threading, replies) is up to you.

**Reloop** receives mail into **mailboxes**. Messages are stored, threaded, spam-scored with Rspamd, and readable over the API, the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) or IMAP. You can reply in-thread with one call, and there's an `email.received` webhook if you want push notifications too.

That matters if you're building:

- **AI agents that handle email.** Give an agent its own address, let it read the thread and reply. See [build an AI agent that reads and replies to email](/blog/build-ai-agent-sends-emails).
- **Support or shared inboxes** where humans and agents work the same threads.
- **Reply handling** for transactional mail ("reply to this email to comment").

| | Reloop | Resend |
|---|---|---|
| Receive on your domain | Yes | Yes |
| Stored mailboxes with threads | Yes | No |
| Reply in thread via API | Yes | Build it yourself |
| Inbound spam scoring | Yes (Rspamd) | Not documented |
| MCP access for agents | Yes | Not for inboxes |
| IMAP access | Yes | No |

---

## Marketing, contacts and automations

Both products now go beyond transactional mail.

- **Resend** has Audiences and Broadcasts for sending newsletters and announcements to a contact list.
- **Reloop** has contacts with custom properties, groups, subscription channels, broadcast campaigns with scheduling, and **event-triggered automations**: delays, conditions and email steps that run when your app tracks an event like `user.signed_up`.

If you want onboarding or dunning sequences without adding another tool, Reloop covers that. See [welcome sequences that convert](/blog/welcome-email-sequences-that-convert) for a worked example.

Neither offers A/B testing on campaigns today.

---

## Deliverability

Deliverability mostly comes down to your own domain setup and list hygiene. Both providers handle the fundamentals: SPF, DKIM, DMARC guidance, bounce and complaint events, open and click tracking, and suppression of bad addresses.

The differences:

- **Sending path.** Resend sends through Amazon SES. Reloop runs its own MTA (KumoMTA), with per-domain throttling and automatic pauses when bounce or complaint rates spike. Read [how bounce processing works](/blog/email-bounce-processing-automation).
- **Dedicated IPs.** Reloop includes one on Growth ($20/mo). On Resend, a dedicated IP is a $30/mo add-on on the Scale plan (from $90), available once you send more than 3,000 emails a day.
- **Tools.** Reloop ships free [domain reputation](/tools/domain-reputation-checker), [blocklist](/tools/blocklist-checker) and [auth](/tools/auth-checker) checkers you can run before you send.

---

## Self-hosting and lock-in

Resend is hosted-only. Your templates, logs, contacts and suppression lists live in Resend's database.

Reloop is Apache 2.0. You can:

1. Start on Reloop Cloud.
2. Move to your own server later with the [one-command installer](/self-host) or [Coolify](/blog/reloop-coolify-setup).
3. Keep the same API. Point the SDK's `baseUrl` at your instance and nothing else in your code changes.

That's useful for data residency (EU-only, on-prem), for security reviews that need to read the code handling your users' mail, and as insurance against price changes or account suspensions.

Self-hosting isn't free in effort. You own IP reputation, warm-up and uptime. Most teams should start hosted and treat self-hosting as an option, not a requirement.

---

## Where Resend is the better choice

Being honest about it:

- **You want the most established hosted API** with the largest set of community examples, and you'll stay well under 50k emails a month where the price gap is small.
- **Your team is already on Resend** and happy. Migrating for a $10/month difference isn't worth the DNS work.

Weighing more than these two? See our roundup of the [best Resend alternatives](/blog/best-resend-alternatives).

## Where Reloop is the better choice

- **You're past 50k emails a month** and cost matters.
- **You need inbound mail as real inboxes**, especially for AI agents.
- **You want transactional mail, campaigns and automations** in one product with one suppression list.
- **You need open source or self-hosting** for compliance, residency or peace of mind.

---

## Switching from Resend to Reloop

Because the APIs are so similar, most of the work is DNS.

1. **Add your domain in Reloop** and publish the DKIM record (`reloop._domainkey`). Merge `include:reloop.sh` into your existing SPF record. Don't add a second SPF record.
2. **Swap the client.** Replace `resend.emails.send` with `reloop.mail.send`, and rename `replyTo` → `reply_to` and `scheduledAt` → `scheduled_at`.
3. **Move templates.** Change placeholders to triple braces: `{{{first_name}}}`.
4. **Point webhooks** at a new handler. Reloop events are named `email.delivered`, `email.bounced`, `email.complained` and so on, and are signed with HMAC-SHA256 in the `Reloop-Signature` header.
5. **Ramp traffic** from 10% to 100% over a week or two, then remove Resend's DNS records.

Our [SendGrid migration guide](/blog/migrating-from-sendgrid) covers the same steps in more detail, including a traffic-split flag and a suppression import script that work just as well when coming from Resend.

---

# Pay as You Go vs Monthly: How to Choose the Right Email Plan

Path: /blog/pay-as-you-go-vs-monthly-email-pricing
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/pay-as-you-go-vs-monthly-email-pricing
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/pay-as-you-go-vs-monthly-email-pricing.md

Credits or a monthly plan? Worked numbers for every volume from 6,000 to 150,000 emails a month, the 26,000-email break-even point, and when bursty sending makes credits the cheaper choice.

Reloop has two ways to pay past the [free tier](/blog/reloop-free-tier): **credits** you buy once, or a **monthly plan**. Both cost $0.50 per 1,000 emails at the margin, so the right choice comes down to one question:

**Is your volume steady, or does it spike?**

This guide gives you the numbers to answer it. For what each option includes, see [introducing pay as you go](/blog/introducing-pay-as-you-go) and [introducing monthly plans](/blog/introducing-monthly-plans).

## The short answer

- **Under 6,000 emails a month:** stay on **Free**. It costs nothing and never expires.
- **Under about 26,000 a month, or spiky volume:** buy **credits**.
- **Steady 26,000 to 66,000 a month:** **Pro**, $10 / month.
- **Steady 66,000 to 250,000 a month:** **Growth**, $20 / month.
- **Over 250,000 a month:** talk to us about **Enterprise**.

The rest of this post shows where those lines come from.

## How each option is priced

**Credits.** $0.50 per 1,000 emails, valid for 6 months. Your free 6,000 each month is used first, so you only spend credits on what goes past it.

**Pro.** $10 a month for 50,000 emails, then $0.50 per 1,000.

**Growth.** $20 a month for 100,000 emails, then $0.50 per 1,000.

Monthly allowances reset every billing period. Credits carry over for 6 months. That one difference decides most cases.

## Steady volume: the numbers

If you send roughly the same amount every month, here is what each option costs per month:

| Emails / month | Credits | Cheapest plan | Best choice |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6,000 | $0 | $0 (Free) | Free |
| 10,000 | $2 | $10 (Pro) | Credits |
| 20,000 | $7 | $10 (Pro) | Credits |
| 26,000 | $10 | $10 (Pro) | Either |
| 30,000 | $12 | $10 (Pro) | Pro |
| 50,000 | $22 | $10 (Pro) | Pro |
| 75,000 | $34.50 | $20 (Growth) | Growth |
| 100,000 | $47 | $20 (Growth) | Growth |
| 150,000 | $72 | $45 (Growth) | Growth |

Credits cost `(emails - 6,000) / 1,000 × $0.50`. The free 6,000 is why credits win at low volume: at 20,000 emails you only pay for 14,000.

**Break-even with Pro is 26,000 emails a month.** That's 6,000 free plus 20,000 on credits ($10). Below it, credits are cheaper. Above it, Pro is.

**Pro to Growth is around 66,000.** Past 50,000, Pro charges $0.50 per 1,000 on top of $10. At about 66,000 emails Pro reaches $18, and Growth's flat $20 for 100,000 becomes the better deal, with more inboxes, domains and a dedicated IP.

<Callout type="tip">
  Plan for the volume you expect in three months, not today. If you're at 20,000 and growing fast, you'll cross 26,000 soon and Pro will be cheaper.
</Callout>

## Spiky volume: where credits win

Steady averages hide the real advantage of credits: **they don't reset every month.**

Take an app that sends 5,000 emails most months and 40,000 in a launch month, twice a year.

**On Pro:** 6 months × $10 = **$60**, and most of the 50,000 allowance goes unused in quiet months.

**On credits:** quiet months are covered by the free 6,000. Each launch month needs 34,000 on credits. Two launches = 68,000 emails = **$34**.

Same sending, about half the cost. The more your volume swings, the bigger the gap.

Credits also fit:

- **Seasonal businesses.** Big in November and December, quiet the rest of the year.
- **New products.** You don't know your volume yet, and you don't want a subscription before you do.
- **Agencies and side projects.** Many small projects that each send in bursts.
- **One-off sends.** A migration notice or a policy update to your whole user base.

## When a monthly plan wins

- **Steady volume above 26,000 a month.** Pro is simply cheaper.
- **You want a fixed bill.** The same charge every month is easier to budget and expense.
- **You need Growth's extras.** 10 agent inboxes, 10 webhooks, 10 domains, 3 of your own SMTP servers and a dedicated IP.
- **You'd rather not watch a balance.** Plans keep sending and charge $0.50 per 1,000 past the allowance, so there's nothing to top up.

## A quick way to decide

1. **Look at your last 3 to 6 months of sending.** Your current provider's dashboard shows it, or check Reloop's analytics if you're already here.
2. **Find your average and your peak.**
3. **If your average is under 26,000, buy credits.** Size the pack to cover 6 months of sending past 6,000 a month.
4. **If your average is over 26,000 and your peak is less than double it, pick a plan.** Pro up to about 66,000, Growth above.
5. **If your peak is several times your average, run both numbers.** Credits usually win.

You can switch whenever your volume changes. Your domains, templates, contacts and API keys stay the same, so there's nothing to migrate.

## FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Is pay as you go more expensive per email?">
    No. Credits and plan overage both cost $0.50 per 1,000 emails. The
    difference is that a plan charges a fixed fee for an allowance that resets
    monthly, while credits last 6 months.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Do I still get the free 6,000 emails with credits?">
    Yes. Each month the free 6,000 is used first and credits only cover what
    goes past it.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Is there a daily limit on credits?">
    No. The 200-a-day cap only applies to the free tier. While you hold
    credits there is no daily cap.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="What if I buy credits and then need a plan?">

  </Accordion>
