# Self-Hosted Email Infrastructure: When and How

Path: /blog/self-hosted-email-infrastructure
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/self-hosted-email-infrastructure
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/self-hosted-email-infrastructure.md

When self-hosting email infrastructure is worth it, what it really costs, and how to deploy Reloop on your own server with one command: requirements, DNS, port 25, reputation and upgrades.

**Self-host your email infrastructure when you have a hard reason to:** data residency, security review of the code that touches your users' mail, or volume high enough that per-email pricing hurts. If none of those apply, a hosted provider is cheaper once you count your own time.

If you do have a reason, self-hosting in 2026 is far easier than it used to be. This guide covers when it's worth it, what you're signing up for, and how to run Reloop on your own server with one command.

---

## When self-hosting makes sense

Most teams should not run their own mail stack. These are the cases where it pays off.

| Reason | What it looks like in practice |
|---|---|
| **Data residency** | Email bodies, logs and contacts must stay in the EU, in-country, or on-prem for GDPR, HIPAA or a customer contract. |
| **Security review** | Your security team needs to audit the code that handles password resets, invoices and inbound mail. |
| **Cost at scale** | You send millions of emails a month and per-email pricing is a real line item. |
| **No vendor risk** | You can't afford an account suspension or a surprise price change blocking signups. |
| **Air-gapped or private networks** | Internal tools that send to internal mailboxes and never touch the public internet. |

## When it doesn't

- You send fewer than a few hundred thousand emails a month. Hosted plans cost less than an hour of engineering time.
- Nobody on the team wants to own DNS, IP reputation and on-call for a mail server.
- You need to send from day one at high volume. A brand-new IP needs [weeks of warm-up](/blog/ip-warming-guide).

A useful middle ground: **start on a hosted plan and move later.** With open-source infrastructure, the API is the same in both places, so moving is a config change, not a rewrite.

---

## What "email infrastructure" actually includes

People underestimate this. Sending a message over SMTP is the easy part. A production email stack needs:

1. **An API** your app calls, with auth, rate limits and idempotency.
2. **A queue** so a traffic spike doesn't drop mail.
3. **An MTA** (mail transfer agent) that talks SMTP to Gmail, Outlook and everyone else, with per-domain throttling and retries.
4. **DKIM signing** and the DNS records to back it up.
5. **Bounce and complaint processing**, plus a suppression list so you stop mailing dead addresses.
6. **Inbound mail**: an MX server, spam filtering and somewhere to store what arrives.
7. **Tracking and webhooks** for delivered, bounced, opened and clicked events.
8. **A dashboard** to debug "why didn't this email arrive?"

Building that from Postfix and cron jobs is a multi-month project. Reloop ships all of it as one open-source stack.

---

## What you get with Reloop

Reloop is Apache 2.0. The self-hosted version is the same code that runs [reloop.sh](https://reloop.sh), minus the parts that only make sense for a hosted business, like billing.

- **Transactional API and SDKs** for Node, Python, Go, PHP, Ruby and more
- **SMTP relay** on ports 465 and 587 for apps that only speak SMTP
- **KumoMTA** as the outbound and inbound MTA
- **Rspamd** spam scoring for inbound mail
- **Agent and human inboxes** with threads, readable over the API, MCP or IMAP
- **Campaigns, contacts, groups and automations**
- **Webhooks** with signed payloads and retries
- **Templates**, logs and delivery metrics in a dashboard

On a self-hosted install there are no plan limits. The installer sets `SELF_HOSTED=true`, which turns off sending quotas and caps on inboxes, domains and organizations. Sending isn't metered.

---

## Requirements

| Resource | Minimum | Recommended |
|---|---|---|
| CPU | 2 vCPUs | 4+ vCPUs |
| RAM | 4 GB | 8 GB |
| Disk | 35 GB | 50 GB NVMe |
| OS | Ubuntu 22.04 / 24.04, Debian 12 / 13 | Same |
| Ports | 25, 465, 587, 80, 443 | Same |

The disk floor is higher than you might expect because the container images total about 22 GB. The installer checks this up front and refuses to start on a smaller disk rather than failing halfway through a download.

<Callout type="warning">
  Many cloud providers (AWS, GCP, Azure, DigitalOcean on new accounts) block port 25 by default. You need it open to receive mail. Ask your provider to unblock it **before** you deploy, and ask for a PTR (reverse DNS) record pointing your server IP at your Reloop hostname.
</Callout>

Providers that are friendly to mail servers include Hetzner (after a short account review), OVH, and most dedicated-server hosts. If you can't get port 25 open for outbound mail, you can still self-host the API, dashboard and inboxes and route outbound mail through an SMTP provider such as Amazon SES.

---

## Deploy with one command

On a fresh Ubuntu or Debian server:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://reloop.sh/install.sh | sudo bash
```

Prefer to read it first? You should:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://reloop.sh/install.sh -o install.sh
less install.sh
sudo bash install.sh
```

The installer asks for a handful of things:

- **Primary domain**, for example `reloop.example.com`, where the dashboard and API live
- **TLS contact email** for Let's Encrypt
- Whether you're **behind an existing reverse proxy** (Caddy, Nginx, Traefik)
- Optional **S3-compatible storage** for template images and attachments

Everything else is generated for you: database and Redis passwords, the auth secret, the webhook encryption key and the internal service secret. They're written to `/opt/reloop/.env` with `0600` permissions.

When it finishes, you'll have 20 containers running: 14 Reloop backend services, the dashboard, the link-tracking service, PostgreSQL, Redis, NATS and Caddy. Only Caddy and the mail ports are exposed to the internet. The database and event bus stay on the internal Docker network.

```text
/opt/reloop/
├── .env                 # configuration and secrets
├── docker-compose.yml   # the production stack
├── Caddyfile            # reverse proxy and TLS
└── backups/             # automatic DB dumps before schema changes
```

---

## DNS: two layers

There are two sets of DNS records, and mixing them up is the most common setup mistake.

### 1. Records for the Reloop server itself

The installer prints these at the end:

```text
reloop.example.com            A    203.0.113.10
link.reloop.example.com       A    203.0.113.10
inbound.reloop.example.com    A    203.0.113.10
reloop.example.com            TXT  "v=spf1 ip4:203.0.113.10 -all"
```

- The apex serves the dashboard and API.
- `link.` serves click and open tracking and unsubscribe pages.
- `inbound.` is the MX target for mail your domains receive.
- The SPF record authorizes your server's IP to send.

### 2. Records for each domain you send from

Add a sending domain under **Domains** in the dashboard. Reloop generates the exact SPF, DKIM, DMARC and MX records for it. Add them at your DNS host, then click verify.

If you're new to these, read the [SPF, DKIM and DMARC setup guide](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide). It's the single biggest factor in whether your mail lands in the inbox.

---

## Point your app at your own instance

The SDK is the same one you'd use with Reloop Cloud. Set `baseUrl` to your server:

```typescript

  apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY!,
  baseUrl: "https://reloop.example.com",
});

const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Your login link",
  html: "<p>Click to sign in.</p>",
});
```

Because the API is identical, you can develop against Reloop Cloud and deploy against your own instance, or the other way round.

---

## Day-two operations

Running a mail server is mostly boring once it's set up. These are the things you'll actually do.

```bash
reloop status            # container health
reloop logs mail         # follow one service's logs
reloop restart           # apply .env changes
reloop update            # pull the new version and redeploy
```

`reloop update` takes a database backup before applying schema changes, so a bad upgrade can be rolled back.

### Protect your reputation

A new IP has no reputation, and mailbox providers treat unknown senders with suspicion. In the first few weeks:

- **Warm up gradually.** Start with your most engaged recipients and ramp volume over 2–4 weeks. See the [IP warming schedule](/blog/ip-warming-guide).
- **Separate traffic.** Send transactional and marketing mail from different subdomains so a campaign complaint doesn't hurt password resets.
- **Watch bounces and complaints.** Reloop suppresses hard bounces and spam complaints automatically. Keep complaints under 0.1%.
- **Check blocklists.** Run your IP and domain through the free [blocklist checker](/tools/blocklist-checker) after launch.

### Back up the right things

PostgreSQL holds everything that matters: contacts, templates, logs and inbox messages. Back up the database and `/opt/reloop/.env` (your secrets and DKIM keys depend on it). Containers are disposable. Data isn't.

---

## Self-hosted vs hosted: the real cost

| | Reloop Cloud | Self-hosted Reloop |
|---|---|---|
| Software | Free tier, then $10–$20/mo for 50k–100k | Free (Apache 2.0) |
| Server | Included | $10–$40/mo VPS |
| Setup time | Minutes | An hour, plus DNS propagation |
| IP reputation | Shared pool, already warm | Yours to build |
| Upgrades | Automatic | `reloop update` |
| Data location | Our infrastructure | Wherever you put it |
| Plan limits | Per plan | None |

The software is free either way. What you're really choosing is who runs it.

If you want the cheapest possible setup, we wrote a step-by-step guide to [self-hosting email for $5 a month](/blog/self-host-email-5-dollars). If you already run Coolify, see [Reloop on Coolify](/blog/reloop-coolify-setup).

---

## FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Is self-hosted Reloop the same as Reloop Cloud?">
    Same code, same API, same dashboard. The self-hosted install leaves out
    billing, the public docs site and the public email tools, and it removes
    plan limits.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can I run it without port 25?">
    You need inbound port 25 to receive mail. For sending, you can route
    outbound mail through an SMTP provider like Amazon SES if your host
    blocks outbound port 25.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Does it run on Kubernetes?">
    The supported path is Docker Compose on a single server, plus guides for
    Coolify, Dokploy, CapRover and Railway. Every service is a container, so
    you can move it to Kubernetes, but you'll own that configuration.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can I migrate from Reloop Cloud to self-hosted later?">
    Yes. Change the SDK's `baseUrl`, move your domains, and update your DNS
    records. Your application code doesn't change.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# Reloop vs Customer.io (2026): Pricing, Features and Which to Choose

Path: /blog/reloop-vs-customer-io
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-customer-io
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-customer-io.md

Reloop vs Customer.io compared honestly: per-email vs per-profile pricing at 10k to 100k profiles, journeys vs automations, transactional API and SMTP, inbound inboxes, self-hosting, plus how to switch.

**Customer.io is a customer engagement platform, and Reloop is email infrastructure.** Both can send onboarding sequences triggered by events from your app, broadcasts and transactional mail. They are built for different teams, and they charge differently. **Customer.io bills by the profiles you store, starting at $100 a month. Reloop bills by the emails you send, starting at $10.** At 50,000 profiles that's roughly $505 a month on Customer.io's entry plan versus $10 to $45 on Reloop for most sending patterns. Reloop also adds an SMTP relay, real inboxes for inbound mail, and an open-source license.

Customer.io does far more than email: push, in-app messages, SMS, deep segmentation and data pipelines. If you need those, it's the stronger product. We build Reloop, so weigh this accordingly. Customer.io's prices below come from [customer.io/pricing](https://customer.io/pricing), and where Customer.io is the better pick, we say so.

---

## The 30-second comparison

| | **Reloop** | **Customer.io** |
|---|---|---|
| Pricing basis | Emails sent | Profiles stored (people and objects) |
| Free tier | 6,000 emails / mo, 200 / day | No free plan on the pricing page |
| Entry paid plan | **$10** / mo (50,000 emails) | $100 / mo (5,000 profiles, 1M emails) |
| Extra volume | $0.50 per 1,000 emails | $0.009 per extra profile, $0.12 per 1,000 extra emails |
| Next plan | $20 / mo (100,000 emails, dedicated IP) | Premium, from $1,000 / mo billed annually |
| Channels | Email | Email, push, in-app, SMS (SMS priced separately) |
| Event-triggered automations | Yes | Yes (Journeys) |
| Transactional API | Yes | Yes |
| SMTP relay | Yes | No |
| Inbound email / agent inbox | Yes | No |
| Template language | `{{{variables}}}` | Liquid |
| Open source / self-host | Yes (Apache 2.0) | No |

Reloop's prices are on [reloop.sh/pricing](/pricing). Both change; check before you commit.

---

## Pricing: profiles vs emails

**Customer.io charges for your audience.** The Essentials plan starts at $100 a month and includes 5,000 profiles and 1 million emails. Each profile beyond that costs $0.009, and profiles include objects (like companies or accounts) as well as people. A signup who never comes back still counts.

**Reloop charges for sends.** Store as many contacts as you like. You pay for the emails that go out.

Here's the Essentials list price against Reloop for a product that emails each contact about twice a month:

| Profiles | Customer.io Essentials | Emails sent (2 per contact) | Reloop |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5,000 | $100 | 10,000 | **$10** |
| 10,000 | $100 + $45 = $145 | 20,000 | **$10** |
| 50,000 | $100 + $405 = $505 | 100,000 | **$20** |
| 100,000 | $100 + $855 = $955 | 200,000 | $20 + $50 overage = **$70** |

The Customer.io column is the published starting price plus $0.009 per profile over 5,000. Larger accounts usually move to Premium or negotiate, so treat it as a ceiling for Essentials, not a quote.

<Callout type="tip">
  Profile-based pricing grows with signups, not with value. A launch that adds 30,000 free users raises a Customer.io bill by $270 a month even if most of them never get past the welcome email. Model next year's list size before you choose.
</Callout>

---

## Automations: Journeys vs Reloop automations

Customer.io's **Journeys** are its core product. The workflow builder is visual and cross-channel. One campaign can send an email, wait, branch on an attribute, push a mobile notification and update a profile. Segmentation is deep, with segments built from attributes, events and objects.

Reloop's automations cover the email side of that: an **event trigger**, then **delays**, **conditions** and **email steps**. Your app tracks an event, and the contact enters every automation that listens for it.

**Customer.io**

```javascript
const { CustomerIO } = require("customerio-node");
const cio = new CustomerIO({ apiKey: process.env.CIO_API_KEY });

await cio.identify("user_123", { email: "ada@example.com" });
await cio.track("user_123", { name: "signed_up" });
```

**Reloop**

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY! });

const { automationError } = await reloop.automations.start({
  event: "user.signed_up",
  email: "ada@example.com",
  firstName: "Ada",
  properties: { plan: "trial" },
});
if (automationError) console.error(automationError);
```

Passing `email` creates the contact if it doesn't exist yet, so there's no separate identify call. Conditions can read event properties (for example `trigger.plan`), so trial and paid users can get different emails. Our [welcome sequence guide](/blog/welcome-email-sequences-that-convert) builds a four-email onboarding flow this way.

| | Reloop | Customer.io |
|---|---|---|
| Event-triggered flows | Yes | Yes |
| Delays and conditions | Yes | Yes |
| Push, in-app, SMS steps | No | Yes |
| Segments from events and objects | Groups and contact properties | Yes, much deeper |
| Broadcasts | Yes | Yes |
| Subscription preferences | Channels per contact | Subscription center |

If your lifecycle program spans mobile push, in-app messages and SMS, Customer.io does that and Reloop doesn't.

---

## Transactional email

Both send password resets, receipts and magic links from your code.

Customer.io's transactional API sends a template you build in its dashboard. You call `https://api.customer.io/v1/send/email` with an App API key, a `transactional_message_id`, the recipient and `message_data` for the Liquid variables:

```javascript
await cio.sendEmail({
  to: "ada@example.com",
  identifiers: { id: "user_123" },
  transactional_message_id: 5,
});
```

Reloop sends either raw HTML or a stored template:

```typescript
const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
  to: "ada@example.com",
  subject: "Reset your password",
  html: `<p><a href="${resetUrl}">Reset your password</a></p>`,
});
```

A few differences worth knowing:

- **SMTP relay.** Reloop runs one at `smtp.reloop.sh` for frameworks, CMSs and tools that only speak SMTP. Customer.io doesn't offer one.
- **Templates.** Customer.io uses Liquid (`{{customer.first_name}}`), which supports loops and filters. Reloop substitutes `{{{first_name}}}` placeholders and also accepts React Email components or your own rendered HTML.
- **Errors.** Reloop's errors include `message`, `why` and `fix`, so a failed send tells you what to change.
- **Webhooks.** Reloop signs delivered, bounced and complained events with HMAC-SHA256 in the `Reloop-Signature` header.

---

## Receiving email and agent inboxes

Customer.io is outbound. It doesn't host mailboxes for replies.

Reloop receives mail into **mailboxes**. Messages are stored, threaded and spam-scored, and readable through the API, the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) or IMAP. You can reply in-thread with one call.

That matters for "just reply to this email" flows, support addresses, and AI agents that need their own address to read and answer mail. See [build an AI agent that reads and replies to email](/blog/build-ai-agent-sends-emails).

---

## Deliverability and data ownership

Reloop runs its own MTA (KumoMTA), with per-domain throttling and automatic pauses when bounce or complaint rates spike. The Growth plan ($20/mo) includes a dedicated IP. Both products handle SPF, DKIM, bounces, complaints and suppression for you.

The larger difference is where your data lives:

- **Customer.io** is closed SaaS. Data warehouse sync is a Premium feature.
- **Reloop** is Apache 2.0. Start on Reloop Cloud and later move to your own server with the [one-command installer](/self-host) or [Coolify](/blog/reloop-coolify-setup). Point the SDK's `baseUrl` at your instance and your code stays the same.

Self-hosting means owning IP warm-up and uptime, so most teams should start hosted. The option is useful for data residency, security reviews and price protection.

---

## Where Customer.io is the better choice

Being honest about it:

- **You message users on more than email.** Push, in-app and SMS in the same journey is what Customer.io is built for.
- **Your segmentation is complex.** Segments across people, accounts and event history, managed by a growth or lifecycle team, are Customer.io's strength.
- **Marketers own the program.** The visual Journeys builder and Liquid templates let non-engineers run sophisticated campaigns without a developer.
- **You need warehouse sync** and are already on a Premium-sized budget.

If you're shopping around, our guide to the [best Customer.io alternatives](/blog/best-customer-io-alternatives) covers other lifecycle tools.

## Where Reloop is the better choice

- **Email is your only channel**, and paying $100+ a month for a multi-channel platform doesn't make sense.
- **Your list is large or growing fast.** Paying per email instead of per profile is usually far cheaper: $20 vs about $505 at 50,000 profiles.
- **You want transactional mail, SMTP and lifecycle emails in one product**, with one domain setup and one suppression list.
- **You need inbound inboxes**, email for AI agents, or open source and self-hosting.

---

## Switching from Customer.io to Reloop

1. **Add your sending domain** in Reloop and publish the DKIM record (`reloop._domainkey`). Merge `include:reloop.sh` into your existing SPF record rather than adding a second one.
2. **Export your people** from Customer.io as CSV and import them as Reloop contacts. Map attributes to contact properties, and keep unsubscribed people unsubscribed.
3. **Rebuild templates.** Paste in your HTML and change Liquid placeholders to triple braces: `{{customer.first_name}}` becomes `{{{first_name}}}`. Liquid loops and filters need to move into your code before the send.
4. **Recreate email Journeys as automations.** Create an event for each trigger (for example `user.signed_up`), then add the same delays, conditions and email steps. Push, in-app and SMS steps have no Reloop equivalent.
5. **Swap the calls.** Replace `identify` plus `track` with `reloop.automations.start`, and `sendEmail` with `reloop.mail.send`.
6. **Run both in parallel** for a week or two, then remove Customer.io's DNS records.

---

## FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Why is Customer.io more expensive than Reloop?">
    Customer.io is priced by profiles stored, starting at $100 a month for
    5,000 profiles, plus $0.009 for each extra profile. Reloop is priced by
    emails sent: $10 for 50,000 and $20 for 100,000, whatever the size of
    your list.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can Reloop replace Customer.io?">
    For email, yes: event-triggered automations, broadcasts, transactional
    sends and SMTP. If your journeys also use push, in-app messages or SMS,
    Reloop doesn't cover those channels.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Does Customer.io have a free plan?">
    No free plan is listed on its pricing page; paid plans start at $100 a
    month. Reloop's free tier sends 6,000 emails a month with no limit on
    contacts.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Do Liquid templates work in Reloop?">
    Not directly. Reloop substitutes `{{{variable}}}` placeholders. Simple
    Liquid variables convert one-to-one; loops and filters should be rendered
    in your code, or with React Email, before you send.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can I self-host Customer.io?">
    No. Customer.io is a hosted service. Reloop is Apache 2.0 and can run on
    your own server with the same API.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# Best Mailjet Alternatives in 2026: Cheaper Plans, Same Two Jobs

Path: /blog/best-mailjet-alternatives
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-mailjet-alternatives
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-mailjet-alternatives.md

The best Mailjet alternatives of 2026 compared: Reloop, Brevo, MailerSend, Mailgun, Elastic Email, Lettermint and Resend on price at 50k and 100k emails, automations, inbound mail, EU hosting and self-hosting.

**The short version:** if you're leaving Mailjet because of price, **Reloop** does the same two jobs (transactional and marketing mail) for $10 at 50,000 emails instead of $40 or $59, with automations on every plan. If you want a marketer-friendly suite with SMS and a CRM, look at **Brevo**. If you need an EU company on EU hosting, look at **Lettermint**.

We build Reloop, so weigh our entry accordingly. Every price below comes from the provider's own pricing page, and each section says where that provider beats us.

---

## Why teams look for a Mailjet alternative

Mailjet is a mature platform with a good drag-and-drop editor, and its free tier (6,000 emails a month) is bigger than most. People still leave, usually for one of these reasons:

- **The September 2026 price update.** Essential is now $19 for 15k and $40 for 50k; Premium is $29, $59 and $112 at 15k, 50k and 100k ([Mailjet pricing](https://www.mailjet.com/pricing/)).
- **Features are gated by plan.** Segmentation starts on Essential. Automations, team management and the dedicated IP need Premium, even if you only send 15,000 emails a month.
- **Inbound is a webhook, not a mailbox.** The Parse API posts each message to your endpoint. Storing, threading and replying is up to you.
- **Hosted only.** There's no way to run Mailjet yourself.

If none of those bother you, staying on Mailjet is a reasonable choice. If they do, here are the alternatives.

Sources: [mailjet.com/pricing](https://www.mailjet.com/pricing/), [reloop.sh/pricing](/pricing), [brevo.com/pricing](https://www.brevo.com/pricing/), [mailersend.com/pricing](https://www.mailersend.com/pricing), [mailgun.com/pricing](https://www.mailgun.com/pricing/), [elasticemail.com/email-api-pricing](https://elasticemail.com/email-api-pricing), [lettermint.co/pricing](https://lettermint.co/pricing), [resend.com/pricing](https://resend.com/pricing). "Slider" means the provider prices that volume interactively. Mailgun's 100k figure is its Scale plan ($90 for 100,000).

## 1. Reloop: best overall Mailjet alternative

Reloop is open-source email infrastructure: a transactional API, SMTP relay, contacts, campaigns, event-triggered automations, inbound mailboxes and webhooks in one product. Use it hosted, or run the same code on your own server.

**Pricing:** Free is 6,000 emails a month (200 a day). Pro is $10 for 50,000. Growth is $20 for 100,000 and includes a dedicated IP. Extra mail costs $0.50 per 1,000, and pay-as-you-go credits cost the same $0.50 per 1,000 and stay valid for 6 months. Self-hosting is free under Apache 2.0.

**Strengths**

- **$10 vs $40 or $59 at 50k, and $20 vs $112 at 100k.** Every plan gets the same product; plans differ only by volume.
- **Automations on every plan.** Trigger sequences from your app with one call, no Premium upgrade needed. See [welcome sequences that convert](/blog/welcome-email-sequences-that-convert).
- **Inbound as real mailboxes.** Mail is stored, threaded, spam-scored and readable over the API, the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) or IMAP. Hosted plans include 3, 5 or 10 inboxes on Free, Pro and Growth.
- **European hosting.** Reloop Cloud runs on Hetzner, a German hosting company, with EU data centers.
- Open source, so you can [self-host](/self-host) later without changing your code.

**Weaknesses**

- **No drag-and-drop editor.** Templates are code or HTML. If marketers build your emails, Mailjet or Brevo will feel friendlier.
- Younger than Mailjet, with fewer years of community answers.

**Best for:** teams sending more than the free tier who want transactional mail and campaigns in one place at a fraction of the price.

Full breakdown: [Reloop vs Mailjet](/blog/reloop-vs-mailjet).

**Pricing:** free for 300 emails a day. Starter begins at $9 for 5,000 emails, and Standard, which adds automations, starts at $18. Larger volumes are priced on a slider.

**Strengths**

- A builder marketers can use without developers.

**Weaknesses**

## How to choose

- **"Price went up and we send 50k+ a month."** Reloop: $10 at 50k, $20 at 100k.
- **"Our marketers build every email in the visual editor."** Brevo, or stay on Mailjet.
- **"We need automations but don't want to pay for Premium."** Reloop includes them on every plan.
- **"Our policy requires an EU-registered provider."** Lettermint. Reloop Cloud runs on Hetzner with EU data centers, and you can self-host it on EU hardware.
- **"We want to reply to inbound mail, or let an AI agent do it."** Reloop's mailboxes. See [email infrastructure for AI agents](/blog/email-infrastructure-for-ai-agents).
- **"We send under 6,000 a month and plan to stay there."** Mailjet and Reloop both give 6,000 a month free; pick on features.

---

## Switching from Mailjet

1. **Export contacts, unsubscribes and bounces** from Mailjet so you don't email people who opted out.
2. **Verify your domain** with the new provider. Merge its SPF include into your existing record (never publish two SPF records) and add its DKIM record. Our [SPF, DKIM and DMARC guide](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide) covers it.
3. **Rebuild templates.** Mailjet's `{{var:name}}` placeholders become the new provider's syntax. On Reloop that's `{{{name}}}`.
4. **Swap the client** in your code, or just change the SMTP host if you send over SMTP.
5. **Move webhooks** to the new event names.
6. **Ramp traffic** over one to two weeks while you watch bounce and complaint rates.

# Best Lettermint Alternatives in 2026: EU-Friendly Email APIs Compared

Path: /blog/best-lettermint-alternatives
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-lettermint-alternatives
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-lettermint-alternatives.md

The best Lettermint alternatives of 2026 compared: Reloop, Sweego, MailPace, Brevo and Mailjet, plus Postmark and Resend, on EU hosting, pricing at 50k and 100k emails, inbound mail, campaigns and self-hosting.

**The short version:** **Reloop** is the strongest Lettermint alternative for most teams: it's hosted on Hetzner with EU data centers, costs $10 for 50,000 emails instead of €40, and adds real inboxes, campaigns and automations, with the option to self-host. **Sweego** is the pick if you need a French company and SMS. **MailPace** fits if you want no tracking at all. **Brevo** and **Mailjet** are the established EU marketing suites.

Lettermint is a good product. It's a Dutch company on EU infrastructure, ISO 27001 certified, with a clean API. People look elsewhere for a few honest reasons:

- **Price at volume.** 50,000 emails is €40 on Starter and 100,000 lands in the €85 tier.
- **Inbound is a webhook, not a mailbox.** If you want stored threads you can reply from, or agents that read mail, you build that yourself.
- **No contacts or automations** in its docs, only a broadcast sending route.
- **Hosted only.** You can't run it on your own servers.

We build Reloop, so weigh our entry accordingly. Every competitor fact below comes from our head-to-head posts, each of which links the provider's own pricing and docs.

## 1. Reloop: best overall Lettermint alternative

[Reloop](/) is open-source email infrastructure: a transactional API and SMTP relay, inbound mailboxes, contacts, campaigns, event-triggered automations and signed webhooks. **Reloop Cloud runs on Hetzner, a German hosting company, with EU data centers**, and comes with a [DPA](/dpa) based on the EU Standard Contractual Clauses. ## Switching from Lettermint

1. **Sign the new provider's DPA** and update your records of processing.
2. **Verify your sending domain.** Add the new DKIM record and merge the provider's include into your existing SPF record; never publish a second SPF record. Our [SPF, DKIM and DMARC guide](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide) covers it.
3. **Export your suppressions** from Lettermint and import them, so you don't email people who bounced or complained.
4. **Swap the client and webhooks.** On Reloop, the API key goes in `x-api-key`, templates use `{{{variable}}}`, and webhooks are signed in the `Reloop-Signature` header.
5. **Ramp traffic** over one to two weeks while watching bounce and complaint rates, then remove Lettermint's DNS records.

# Reloop vs SendGrid (2026): Pricing, Features and Which to Choose

Path: /blog/reloop-vs-sendgrid
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-sendgrid
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-sendgrid.md

Reloop vs SendGrid compared honestly: pricing at 50k and 100k emails, API and SMTP, inbound mail, campaigns, deliverability tooling, compliance, self-hosting, and when SendGrid is still the better pick.

**Short answer:** choose **SendGrid** if you need enterprise procurement checkboxes, subuser management, or Handlebars logic in your templates, and you're already inside Twilio. Choose **Reloop** if you want a simpler API at roughly half the price, real mailboxes for inbound mail and AI agents, transactional and marketing email in one product, and the option to self-host the whole stack.

We build Reloop, so weigh this accordingly. Pricing comes from [SendGrid's public pricing page](https://www.twilio.com/en-us/products/email-api/pricing) and [ours](/pricing). Where SendGrid is better, we say so.

---

## The 30-second comparison

| | **Reloop** | **SendGrid** |
|---|---|---|
| Free | 6,000 / mo, 200 / day, no time limit | 100 / day for a 60-day trial |
| 50,000 emails / mo | **$10** (Pro) | $19.95 (Essentials) |
| 100,000 emails / mo | **$20** (Growth) | $34.95 (Essentials) |
| Dedicated IP, subusers, SSO tier | Dedicated IP on Growth ($20) | Pro, from $89.95 |
| Extra volume | $0.50 per 1,000 | Move up a tier |
| Open source | Yes, Apache 2.0 | No |
| Self-host | Yes | No |
| Inbound mail | Mailboxes with threads, API, MCP, IMAP | Inbound Parse webhook |
| Marketing | Campaigns and automations, same plan | Marketing Campaigns, separate plans |
| Template logic | Variables only (`{{{name}}}`) | Full Handlebars (`#if`, `#each`) |
| Enterprise compliance | DPA; self-host for data control | Mature enterprise program |

---

## Pricing at real volumes

| Monthly volume | Reloop | SendGrid |
|---|---|---|
| 3,000 | $0 | Trial for 60 days, then paid |
| 50,000 | $10 | $19.95 |
| 100,000 | $20 | $34.95 |
| 100,000 with a dedicated IP | $20 | from $89.95 (Pro) |
| 250,000 | $20 + $75 overage = $95 | Higher Essentials or Pro tier |

Two things stand out.

**The free tier.** SendGrid no longer has a permanent free plan. New accounts get 100 emails a day for 60 days. Reloop's free tier is 6,000 emails a month with no end date, which is enough for a side project or a staging environment indefinitely.

**The dedicated IP jump.** On SendGrid, the features most growing teams eventually want (a dedicated IP, subusers, SSO, 2,500 free email validations) start on Pro at $89.95 a month. Reloop's Growth plan includes a dedicated IP at $20.

At 100,000 emails a month, Reloop is **$240 a year** and SendGrid Essentials is **about $420 a year**. With a dedicated IP, the gap is $240 versus roughly $1,080.

<Callout type="tip">
  List prices change. Check both pricing pages for your exact volume before deciding, and ask SendGrid sales about commit discounts if you send millions a month.
</Callout>

---

## Developer experience

Both have a REST API, SMTP relay, webhooks and SDKs for the major languages. The difference is shape and age.

**SendGrid**

```typescript

sgMail.setApiKey(process.env.SENDGRID_API_KEY!);

await sgMail.send({
  from: { email: "hello@acme.com", name: "Acme" },
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Your receipt",
  html: "<p>Thanks for your order.</p>",
  categories: ["receipt"],
});
```

**Reloop**

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY! });

const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@acme.com>",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Your receipt",
  html: "<p>Thanks for your order.</p>",
  tags: [{ name: "category", value: "receipt" }],
});
```

Under the SDK, SendGrid's v3 payload nests recipients and per-recipient data inside a `personalizations` array. It's powerful (one request can carry many different messages) but it's the part of SendGrid most developers have to look up every time. Reloop's payload is flat: one request, one message.

Errors differ too. Reloop returns errors as values instead of throwing, and every API error has a `message`, a `why`, a `fix` and a docs `link`. Retries are safe with an `Idempotency-Key` header, so a timeout never means a duplicate email.

### SMTP

| | Reloop | SendGrid |
|---|---|---|
| Host | `smtp.reloop.sh` | `smtp.sendgrid.net` |
| Port | 587 (STARTTLS) | 587 |
| Username | Your API key | `apikey` |
| Password | Your API key | Your API key |

### Templates

This is one place SendGrid is ahead. SendGrid dynamic templates use full Handlebars, so you can write `{{#if}}` and `{{#each}}` inside the template. Reloop templates support variable substitution with `{{{name}}}` placeholders and default values, plus a visual editor and versioning, but no logic. With Reloop, loops and conditionals happen in your code before you send.

---

## Sending and receiving

SendGrid receives mail through **Inbound Parse**: you point MX records at SendGrid and it POSTs each message to your URL. Storage, threading and replies are up to you.

Reloop treats inbound as a first-class feature. Every domain can receive mail into **mailboxes** with threads. You can:

- Read and reply over the API or SDK (`inbox.messages.reply`)
- Give an AI agent access through the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server)
- Open the same mailbox in a mail client over IMAP
- Get an `email.received` webhook for each message, signed with the same `Reloop-Signature` HMAC as outbound events

If you're building a support inbox, an AI agent that answers email, or anything conversational, this saves you from building a mail store. See [building an AI agent that reads and replies to email](/blog/build-ai-agent-sends-emails).

---

## Marketing and automations

SendGrid's marketing product, Marketing Campaigns, is sold on separate plans from the Email API. Many teams end up with two bills and two places where contacts live.

Reloop puts it in one product under one API key:

- **Contacts, groups and custom properties**
- **Campaigns** to a group, with scheduling and engagement stats
- **Automations** triggered by events from your app, with delay and condition steps
- **Channels** (subscription topics) so users can opt out of one kind of email without leaving everything
- **One suppression list** shared by transactional and marketing sends

What SendGrid has that Reloop doesn't yet: A/B testing in campaigns and a longer list of marketing integrations.

---

## Deliverability tooling

Both handle the essentials: DKIM signing, bounce and complaint processing, suppression lists, and click and open tracking.

**Where SendGrid is stronger:** IP pools and subuser-level IP assignment for large senders, and an Email Address Validation API included on Pro and above.

**What Reloop adds:**

- Automatic protection when reputation dips: sending pauses if bounce or complaint rates cross safe thresholds, instead of letting a bad list burn your domain. See [how bounce processing works](/blog/email-bounce-processing-automation).
- Free public tools for [domain reputation](/tools/domain-reputation-checker), [blocklists](/tools/blocklist-checker), [SPF/DKIM/DMARC](/tools/auth-checker) and [temporary email detection](/tools/temp-email-checker).
- Bring your own SMTP provider. Route sends through SES or another relay while keeping Reloop's API, templates and logs.

Neither will rescue a bad list. If you're seeing spam-folder placement, start with [why emails land in spam](/blog/why-emails-land-in-spam-fix).

---

## Compliance and enterprise: where SendGrid wins

Be clear-eyed here. SendGrid is part of Twilio, a public company with a long-established compliance program, enterprise contracts, SSO, subusers for agencies and multi-brand companies, and Premier support tiers. If your procurement team needs a specific certification report or a vendor with a decade of enterprise history, SendGrid is the safer choice today.

Reloop offers a [DPA](/dpa) for the hosted service. For strict data requirements, the stronger answer is self-hosting: run Reloop on your own servers and your email data never leaves your infrastructure. No hosted vendor, SendGrid included, can offer that.

---

## Self-hosting and lock-in

SendGrid is hosted only. Your templates, suppression lists, contacts and logs live in Twilio's systems. If pricing changes or an account review pauses sending, your options are to wait or to migrate.

Reloop is open source under Apache 2.0. You can:

- Start on the hosted plan
- Move to your own server later with [one command](/blog/self-hosted-email-infrastructure) or [Coolify](/blog/reloop-coolify-setup)
- Keep the same API: change the SDK's `baseUrl` and nothing else in your code

Self-hosted installs have no plan limits and no per-email fees. You do take on IP reputation, warm-up and uptime yourself.

---

## Switching from SendGrid

Most teams finish the code changes in an afternoon. SMTP users change four settings. API users swap the client and flatten the payload. The careful part is moving your suppression list first and ramping traffic over a week or two while both providers run.

We wrote the full playbook: [Migrating from SendGrid to Reloop](/blog/migrating-from-sendgrid). It covers DNS, suppressions, field mapping, templates, webhooks and the cutover schedule.

---

## Which should you pick?

| If you… | Pick |
|---|---|
| Want the lowest price at 50k–500k emails a month | Reloop |
| Need a free tier that doesn't expire | Reloop |
| Need inbound mailboxes, a support inbox or an AI email agent | Reloop |
| Want transactional and marketing in one plan | Reloop |
| Need to self-host or keep data on your own infrastructure | Reloop |
| Rely on Handlebars logic inside templates | SendGrid |
| Manage many brands or clients with subusers and IP pools | SendGrid |
| Need an established enterprise compliance program for procurement | SendGrid |
| Already run on Twilio with a negotiated commit | SendGrid |

If neither is quite right, our roundup of the [best SendGrid alternatives](/blog/best-sendgrid-alternatives) compares the wider field.

# Reloop vs Elastic Email (2026): Pricing, Features and Which to Choose

Path: /blog/reloop-vs-elastic-email
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-elastic-email
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-elastic-email.md

Reloop vs Elastic Email compared: Email API and Email Marketing plans, pricing at 3k to 250k emails a month, developer experience, inbound mail, dedicated IPs, self-hosting, and how to switch.

**Elastic Email is one of the longest-running budget email providers, and it sells two separate products: an Email API for developers and an Email Marketing app for newsletters.** Reloop puts transactional email, campaigns, automations and inboxes in one product. **It costs about half as much at 50k emails, includes a dedicated IP on its $20 plan, receives mail into real inboxes, and is open source, so you can run it yourself.** Elastic Email has the more mature drag-and-drop marketing tools.

We build Reloop, so weigh this accordingly. Elastic Email's prices below are from its [Email API pricing](https://elasticemail.com/email-api-pricing) and [Email Marketing pricing](https://elasticemail.com/pricing) pages, and where Elastic Email is the better pick, we say so.

---

## The 30-second comparison

| | **Reloop** | **Elastic Email (Email API)** |
|---|---|---|
| Free tier | 6,000 / mo, 200 / day | 3,000 / mo, 100 / day |
| 50,000 emails / mo | **$10** | $19 (Starter) or $49 (Pro) |
| 100,000 emails / mo | **$20** | Set by a volume slider |
| Dedicated IP | Included on Growth ($20) | Add-on: $40/mo on Starter, $50/mo on Pro |
| Inbound email | Mailboxes with threads, API, MCP, IMAP | Inbound processing on Pro |
| Webhooks | All plans | Pro |
| Log retention | Plan-based | 3 days (Free, Starter), 7 days (Pro) |
| Marketing and automations | Included in the same product | Separate Email Marketing plans |
| Open source | Yes (Apache 2.0) | No |
| Self-host | Yes | No |
| SMTP relay | Yes | Yes |

Both pricing pages change; check them before you commit.

---

## Pricing at real volumes

Reloop's free tier is twice the size: 6,000 emails a month with a 200-a-day cap, vs 3,000 a month and 100 a day on Elastic Email. Elastic Email's free API plan keeps logs for 3 days and has no dedicated IP or inbound processing.

At 50,000 emails a month:

| | Reloop | Elastic Email |
|---|---|---|
| Plan | Pro, $10 | Starter, $19 |
| With inbound and webhooks | $10 | Pro, $49 |
| With a dedicated IP | Growth, $20 (100k emails) | Starter $19 + $40 = $59, or Pro $49 + $50 = $99 |

Above 50,000 emails, Elastic Email prices both API plans with a volume slider that runs up to 10 million emails a month. The exact numbers depend on where you set it, so check the [calculator](https://elasticemail.com/email-api-pricing) for your volume. Reloop's 100k plan is $20, and every extra 1,000 emails costs $0.50, so 250,000 emails is $20 + $75 = **$95**.

Two things drive the difference at low and mid volume:

- **Webhooks and inbound sit on Elastic Email's $49 Pro plan.** On Reloop they're on every plan, including Free.
- **A dedicated IP is an add-on on Elastic Email** ($40 or $50 a month). Reloop includes one on Growth at $20.

At very high volume, Elastic Email's slider may come out cheaper per email than Reloop's $0.50 per 1,000 overage. If you send millions of emails a month and only need sending, price both at your real volume. If you self-host Reloop, there's no per-email fee at all; you pay for the server.

<Callout type="tip">
  Price the features you'll need in a year, not just the volume. Webhooks, inbound mail and a dedicated IP move Elastic Email from $19 to $49 or more, while Reloop includes them.
</Callout>

---

## Developer experience

Elastic Email's v4 REST API lives at `https://api.elasticemail.com/v4` and authenticates with an `X-ElasticEmail-ApiKey` header. Transactional mail goes to `POST /emails/transactional`.

**Elastic Email**

```typescript
const res = await fetch("https://api.elasticemail.com/v4/emails/transactional", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
    "X-ElasticEmail-ApiKey": process.env.ELASTIC_EMAIL_API_KEY!,
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    Recipients: { To: ["user@example.com"] },
    Content: {
      From: "Acme <hello@acme.com>",
      Subject: "Welcome",
      Body: [{ ContentType: "HTML", Content: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>" }],
    },
  }),
});
```

**Reloop**

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY! });

const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Welcome",
  html: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
});
```

The differences worth knowing:

| | Reloop | Elastic Email |
|---|---|---|
| Field style | snake_case (`reply_to`) | PascalCase (`Recipients`, `Content`, `ReplyTo`) |
| Body | `html` and `text` fields | `Body` array of `{ ContentType, Content }` |
| Template variables | `{{{first_name}}}` | `{firstname}` merge fields, values passed in `Merge` |
| Stored templates | Sent by ID | Sent by `TemplateName` |
| Error format | `message`, `why` and `fix` | JSON error response |
| Official SDK | `reloop-email` and SDKs for Python, Go, PHP, Ruby, Rust, Java, .NET, Elixir | Generated clients on [GitHub](https://github.com/ElasticEmail) |

Reloop's errors tell you **why** a send failed and **how to fix it**:

```json
{
  "message": "Domain not found",
  "why": "The domain mail.acme.com was not found or is not authorized for your organization",
  "fix": "Ensure the domain is registered and verified in your dashboard"
}
```

---

## Receiving email and agent inboxes

Elastic Email includes **inbound email processing on its Pro plan**: mail sent to your domain is parsed and forwarded to your app.

Reloop receives mail into **mailboxes**. Messages are stored, threaded, spam-scored with Rspamd, and readable over the API, the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) or IMAP. You can reply in-thread with one call, and the `email.received` webhook notifies your app.

| | Reloop | Elastic Email |
|---|---|---|
| Receive on your domain | All plans | Pro ($49) |
| Stored mailboxes with threads | Yes | No |
| Reply in thread via API | Yes | Build it yourself |
| MCP access for AI agents | Yes | No |
| IMAP access | Yes | No |

If you're building support inboxes or [an AI agent that reads and replies to email](/blog/build-ai-agent-sends-emails), this is the biggest functional gap.

---

## Marketing, contacts and automations

This is where Elastic Email is strongest. Its **Email Marketing** product is a separate set of plans:

- **Free:** up to 1,000 contacts and 3,000 emails a month, with 1 automation.
- **Starter ($29/mo):** up to 2,500 contacts and 37,500 emails a month, with automations, paid newsletters and checkouts.
- **Pro ($49/mo):** the same visible contact tier, plus unlimited automations, unlimited custom fields, webhooks and sub-accounts.

It comes with a drag-and-drop designer and a gallery of pre-designed templates, aimed at marketers who don't write code.

Reloop keeps marketing and transactional mail in **one product with one suppression list**: contacts with custom properties, groups, subscription channels, scheduled broadcast campaigns, and event-triggered automations with delays and conditions. You start them from your app:

```typescript
await reloop.automations.start({
  event: "user.signed_up",
  email: user.email,
});
```

See [welcome sequences that convert](/blog/welcome-email-sequences-that-convert) for a worked example. If your marketing team wants a visual newsletter builder with paid-newsletter checkouts, Elastic Email's marketing app has more to offer today.

---

## Deliverability

Deliverability mostly comes down to your own domain setup and list hygiene. Both providers handle SPF and DKIM, bounces, complaints, open and click tracking, and suppression.

- **Sending path.** Reloop runs its own MTA (KumoMTA), with per-domain throttling and automatic pauses when bounce or complaint rates spike. See [how bounce processing works](/blog/email-bounce-processing-automation).
- **Dedicated IPs.** Included on Reloop's Growth plan; a $40 to $50 monthly add-on on Elastic Email.
- **Logs.** Elastic Email's API plans keep logs for 3 days (Free, Starter) or 7 days (Pro). Short retention makes it harder to debug a delivery complaint from last week.
- **Tools.** Reloop ships free [domain reputation](/tools/domain-reputation-checker), [blocklist](/tools/blocklist-checker) and [auth](/tools/auth-checker) checkers.

---

## Self-hosting and lock-in

Elastic Email is hosted-only. Reloop is Apache 2.0:

1. Start on Reloop Cloud.
2. Move to your own server later with the [one-command installer](/self-host) or [Coolify](/blog/reloop-coolify-setup).
3. Keep the same API by pointing the SDK's `baseUrl` at your instance.

Self-hosting means you own IP reputation, warm-up and uptime. Most teams should start hosted and keep self-hosting as an option. See [self-hosted email infrastructure](/blog/self-hosted-email-infrastructure) for what it involves.

---

## Where Elastic Email is the better choice

- **You send millions of emails a month and only need sending.** Its volume slider goes to 10 million emails, and at that scale it may cost less per email than Reloop's hosted overage. Price both.
- **Your marketing team wants a no-code newsletter tool** with a drag-and-drop designer, template gallery, paid newsletters and checkouts.
- **You need sub-accounts** to separate clients, which Elastic Email lists on Pro.

Comparing more budget senders? Read our roundup of the [best Elastic Email alternatives](/blog/best-elastic-email-alternatives).

## Where Reloop is the better choice

- **You're at 50k to a few hundred thousand emails a month** and want the lower price.
- **You need webhooks, inbound mail or a dedicated IP** without moving to a $49 plan or paying an add-on.
- **You need inbound mail as real inboxes**, especially for AI agents.
- **You want transactional mail, campaigns and automations in one product** instead of two subscriptions.
- **You need open source or self-hosting.**

---

## Switching from Elastic Email to Reloop

1. **Add your domain in Reloop** and publish the DKIM record (`reloop._domainkey`). Merge `include:reloop.sh` into your existing SPF record rather than adding a second one.
2. **Swap the client.** Replace the `/v4/emails/transactional` call with `reloop.mail.send`, and map `Recipients.To` → `to`, `Content.From` → `from`, `Content.Subject` → `subject`, and the HTML `Body` entry → `html`.
3. **Move templates.** Change merge fields to triple braces: `{firstname}` becomes `{{{first_name}}}`, and pass values as template variables instead of `Merge`.
4. **Move contacts and suppressions.** Export your contacts and any unsubscribed or bounced addresses from Elastic Email and import them into Reloop so nobody who opted out is emailed again.
5. **Point webhooks** at a new handler. Reloop events are named `email.delivered`, `email.bounced`, `email.complained` and so on, signed with HMAC-SHA256 in the `Reloop-Signature` header.
6. **Ramp traffic** from 10% to 100% over a week or two, then remove Elastic Email's DNS records.

Our [SendGrid migration guide](/blog/migrating-from-sendgrid) covers the same steps in more detail, including a traffic-split flag and a suppression import script.

---

# How to Send Email in Next.js App Router (2026)

Path: /blog/send-email-nextjs-app-router
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/send-email-nextjs-app-router
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/send-email-nextjs-app-router.md

Send transactional email from Next.js App Router with Reloop: complete Server Action and Route Handler examples, env setup, error handling, and Vercel deploy.

**To send email in Next.js App Router, call Reloop only on the server**, from a [Server Action](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/building-your-application/data-fetching/server-actions-and-mutations) or a [Route Handler](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/building-your-application/routing/route-handlers). Never put your API key in a Client Component or public env var.

This guide covers both patterns end-to-end: install, shared client, form + Server Action, API route + `fetch`, error handling, and deploy on Vercel.

---

## What you will build

| Approach | Best for | File shape |
|----------|----------|------------|
| **Server Action** | Forms, signup, password reset, any UI in the same Next app | `app/actions/send-email.ts` + client form |
| **Route Handler (API)** | Webhooks, mobile clients, external services, cron, AI tools | `app/api/send-email/route.ts` |

Both run on the server. Both use the same Reloop SDK call. Pick Server Actions for app UI. Pick Route Handlers when something outside your React tree needs HTTP.

---

## Prerequisites

1. A Next.js app on the **App Router** (this guide uses `app/`, not `pages/`)
2. A Reloop account and API key from the [dashboard](https://reloop.sh/dashboard) (keys look like `rl_…`)
3. A verified sending domain (see [connect a domain](/docs/guides/connect-domain) and [SPF / DKIM / DMARC](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide))

Optional but useful: the [Node.js SDK docs](/docs/examples/nodejs/nextjs) and full [send mail API](/docs/api/mail/post-api-mail-v1send).

---

## 1. Install the SDK

<InstallSdkCode />

Package: [`reloop-email`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/reloop-email) · source: [reloop-labs/reloop-node](https://github.com/reloop-labs/reloop-node)

---

## 2. Add the API key (server only)

Create or edit `.env.local` in the project root:

```env
RELOOP_API_KEY=rl_your_api_key_here
```

Rules that matter:

- Use `RELOOP_API_KEY` (no `NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefix). Public vars are bundled into the browser.
- Do not commit `.env.local`. Keep it in `.gitignore`.
- On Vercel, add the same key under **Project → Settings → Environment Variables** (see [Vercel integration](/docs/integrations/vercel)).

<Callout type="warning">
  If the key appears in browser Network tabs or client bundles, treat it as leaked: rotate it in the dashboard and redeploy.
</Callout>

---

## 3. Create a shared Reloop client

One client file keeps Server Actions and Route Handlers identical.

```typescript
// lib/reloop.ts

if (!process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY) {
  throw new Error("Missing RELOOP_API_KEY");
}

  apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY,
});
```

Initialize with an object: `{ apiKey: string }`. Optional: `baseUrl` if you [self-host](/self-host) Reloop.

---

## 4. Method A: Server Action (forms & app UI)

### When to use this

- Contact form, welcome email after signup, magic link, [password reset](/blog/password-reset-email-best-practices)
- Call site is a React Server Component or Client Component in **this** app
- You want progressive enhancement with `<form action={...}>` and no hand-written `fetch`

### Action

```typescript
// app/actions/send-welcome-email.ts
"use server";

  | { ok: true; messageId?: string }
  | { ok: false; error: string };

  email: string,
  name?: string,
): Promise<SendWelcomeResult> {
  const to = email.trim().toLowerCase();

  if (!to || !to.includes("@")) {
    return { ok: false, error: "Enter a valid email address." };
  }

  try {
    const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
      from: "Acme <onboarding@mail.yourdomain.com>",
      to,
      subject: name ? `Welcome, ${name}` : "Welcome to Acme",
      html: `<p>Thanks for signing up${name ? `, ${name}` : ""}.</p>
             <p>You're ready to go.</p>`,
      text: `Thanks for signing up${name ? `, ${name}` : ""}. You're ready to go.`,
      reply_to: "support@yourdomain.com",
      tags: [{ name: "type", value: "welcome" }],
    });

    if (emailError) {
      console.error("Reloop send failed", emailError);
      return { ok: false, error: "Could not send email. Try again." };
    }

    return { ok: true, messageId: response?.messageId };
  } catch (err) {
    console.error("Reloop send threw", err);
    return { ok: false, error: "Could not send email. Try again." };
  }
}
```

Notes:

- `"use server"` must be at the top of the file (or above the exported function).
- Return a **safe** result to the client. Log Reloop details server-side; do not dump API errors into the UI.
- `from` must use a domain you verified in Reloop.

### Client form that calls the action

```tsx
// app/signup/welcome-form.tsx
"use client";

  const [message, setMessage] = useState<string | null>(null);
  const [pending, startTransition] = useTransition();

  return (
    <form
      className="space-y-3"
      onSubmit={(e) => {
        e.preventDefault();
        const form = e.currentTarget;
        const data = new FormData(form);
        const email = String(data.get("email") ?? "");
        const name = String(data.get("name") ?? "");

        startTransition(async () => {
          const result = await sendWelcomeEmail(email, name || undefined);
          setMessage(
            result.ok
              ? "Check your inbox for a welcome email."
              : result.error,
          );
          if (result.ok) form.reset();
        });
      }}
    >
      <input name="name" type="text" placeholder="Name" />
      <input name="email" type="email" required placeholder="you@company.com" />
      <button type="submit" disabled={pending}>
        {pending ? "Sending…" : "Create account"}
      </button>
      {message ? <p>{message}</p> : null}
    </form>
  );
}
```

### Form Action without client JS (optional)

You can also bind the action directly:

```tsx
// app/contact/page.tsx

async function contactAction(formData: FormData) {
  "use server";
  const email = String(formData.get("email") ?? "");
  await sendWelcomeEmail(email);
}

  return (
    <form action={contactAction}>
      <input name="email" type="email" required />
      <button type="submit">Send</button>
    </form>
  );
}
```

Server Actions work for same-origin app flows. For external HTTP callers, use a Route Handler.

---

## 5. Method B: Route Handler (API route)

### When to use this

- Stripe / Clerk / Supabase webhooks that should fire an email
- Mobile apps, desktop clients, or another backend posting JSON
- Cron jobs, n8n, Zapier, or AI agents that call HTTP
- You need a stable URL like `POST /api/send-email`

### Route Handler

```typescript
// app/api/send-email/route.ts

type Body = {
  to?: string;
  subject?: string;
  html?: string;
  text?: string;
  name?: string;
};

  let body: Body;

  try {
    body = (await request.json()) as Body;
  } catch {
    return NextResponse.json({ error: "Invalid JSON body" }, { status: 400 });
  }

  const to = body.to?.trim().toLowerCase();
  if (!to || !to.includes("@")) {
    return NextResponse.json(
      { error: "Field `to` must be a valid email" },
      { status: 400 },
    );
  }

  const subject = body.subject?.trim() || "Hello from Next.js";
  const html =
    body.html?.trim() ||
    `<p>Hi${body.name ? ` ${body.name}` : ""},</p><p>This was sent from a Next.js Route Handler.</p>`;
  const text =
    body.text?.trim() ||
    `Hi${body.name ? ` ${body.name}` : ""}, This was sent from a Next.js Route Handler.`;

  try {
    const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
      from: "Acme <hello@mail.yourdomain.com>",
      to,
      subject,
      html,
      text,
      reply_to: "support@yourdomain.com",
      tags: [{ name: "source", value: "api-route" }],
    });

    if (emailError) {
      console.error("Reloop send failed", emailError);
      return NextResponse.json(
        { error: "Failed to send email" },
        { status: 502 },
      );
    }

    return NextResponse.json({
      ok: true,
      id: response?.id,
      messageId: response?.messageId,
    });
  } catch (err) {
    console.error("Reloop send threw", err);
    return NextResponse.json(
      { error: "Failed to send email" },
      { status: 500 },
    );
  }
}
```

### Call it from the browser or another service

```typescript
// From a Client Component or any HTTP client
const res = await fetch("/api/send-email", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    to: "user@example.com",
    name: "Ada",
    subject: "Your receipt",
    html: "<p>Thanks for your purchase.</p>",
    text: "Thanks for your purchase.",
  }),
});

const data = await res.json();
if (!res.ok) throw new Error(data.error ?? "Send failed");
```

cURL for local testing:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/send-email \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"to":"you@example.com","name":"Ada","subject":"Test from Next.js"}'
```

### Protect the route

An open send endpoint is an open relay. At minimum:

1. Require a session / auth check for user-triggered sends
2. Or require a shared secret header for webhooks and cron
3. Rate-limit by IP or user id

Example secret gate for internal callers:

```typescript
// inside POST, before sending
const secret = request.headers.get("x-internal-secret");
if (secret !== process.env.INTERNAL_SEND_SECRET) {
  return NextResponse.json({ error: "Unauthorized" }, { status: 401 });
}
```

Add `INTERNAL_SEND_SECRET` to `.env.local` and Vercel the same way as the API key.

---

## 6. Server Action vs Route Handler: pick one

| Question | Prefer Server Action | Prefer Route Handler |
|----------|----------------------|----------------------|
| Triggered by a form in this Next app? | Yes | No |
| Need a public HTTP URL for webhooks / mobile / cron? | No | Yes |
| Want zero client `fetch` boilerplate? | Yes | No |
| Called from non-Next code? | No | Yes |
| Same Reloop SDK? | Yes | Yes |
| Safe for `RELOOP_API_KEY`? | Yes (server) | Yes (server) |

You can use **both** in one app: Server Actions for product UI, Route Handlers for integrations.

---

## 7. Full `mail.send` fields you will use most

```typescript
const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.yourdomain.com>", // required, verified domain
  to: "user@example.com",                   // string or string[]
  subject: "Order confirmed",               // required
  html: "<p>Your order shipped.</p>",       // HTML body
  text: "Your order shipped.",              // plain-text fallback
  reply_to: "support@yourdomain.com",
  cc: "ops@yourdomain.com",
  bcc: "archive@yourdomain.com",
  tags: [{ name: "type", value: "receipt" }],
});
```

More options (attachments, templates, scheduling, headers) are on the [send email API reference](/docs/api/mail/post-api-mail-v1send).

Always send both `html` and `text` when you can. You get better deliverability, and clients that block HTML still get a readable message. See [transactional email best practices](/blog/transactional-email-best-practices).

---

## 8. Runtime: Node vs Edge

- Prefer the default **Node.js** runtime for the Reloop SDK.
- Edge Runtime is a restricted environment. If you must run on Edge, call Reloop’s **HTTP API** with `fetch` instead of relying on Node-only modules, the same idea as the [Cloudflare Workers guide](/blog/send-email-cloudflare-workers).

```typescript
// Edge-friendly alternative (no SDK)

  const body = await request.json();

  const res = await fetch("https://reloop.sh/api/mail/v1/send", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
      "x-api-key": process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY!,
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      from: "Acme <hello@mail.yourdomain.com>",
      to: body.to,
      subject: body.subject,
      html: body.html,
      text: body.text,
    }),
  });

  const data = await res.json();
  return Response.json(data, { status: res.status });
}
```

For most App Router apps on Vercel, stick with the SDK on Node.

---

## 9. Deploy on Vercel

1. Push the app and import it in [Vercel](https://vercel.com)
2. Add env vars: `RELOOP_API_KEY` (and `INTERNAL_SEND_SECRET` if you use it)
3. Redeploy so server functions pick up the vars
4. Send a test from production; confirm delivery in the [Reloop logs](https://reloop.sh/dashboard/logs)

Details: [Vercel + Reloop](/docs/integrations/vercel).

---

## 10. Common mistakes

1. **`NEXT_PUBLIC_RELOOP_API_KEY`**: exposes the key. Use server-only `RELOOP_API_KEY`.
2. **Calling Reloop from a Client Component**: keys and secrets belong in Server Actions / Route Handlers only.
3. **Unverified `from` domain**: verify DNS first ([domain guide](/docs/guides/connect-domain)).
4. **Open `/api/send-email`**: always authenticate or use a shared secret.
5. **Wrong constructor**: use `new Reloop({ apiKey })`, not a bare string, for the current SDK.
6. **Ignoring `emailError`**: check it (or catch throws) and return a safe user message.
7. **HTML only**: include `text` as a fallback.

---

## 11. FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Can I send email from a Client Component?">
    Not directly. Client Components can **call** a Server Action or `fetch` your
    Route Handler. The Reloop SDK and API key stay on the server.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Server Action or API route for a contact form?">
    Server Action. Less plumbing, works with `<form action>`, and stays
    same-origin by default.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="How do I send after signup with Auth.js / Clerk / Supabase?">
    In the server-side callback or server action that creates the user, call
    `sendWelcomeEmail(user.email)`. Do not wait for the client to “remember” to
    hit an API.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Does this work with React Email?">
    Yes. Render your React Email template to HTML on the server, then pass the
    string as `html` to `reloop.mail.send`.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Where do I see delivery status?">
    In the Reloop dashboard logs, and via [webhooks](/docs/webhooks) for
    delivered, bounced, opened, and clicked events.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# Best MailPace Alternatives in 2026: Privacy-Friendly Email APIs Compared

Path: /blog/best-mailpace-alternatives
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-mailpace-alternatives
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-mailpace-alternatives.md

The best MailPace alternatives of 2026 compared: Reloop, Lettermint, Sweego, Mailjet and Brevo, plus Postmark and Resend, on EU hosting, tracking, pricing at 50k and 100k emails, campaigns, dedicated IPs and self-hosting.

**The short version:** **Reloop** is the strongest MailPace alternative once you send more than 10,000 emails a month: it's hosted on Hetzner with EU data centers, costs $10 for 50,000 emails instead of $50, lets you switch tracking off per domain, and adds campaigns, automations, inboxes and a dedicated IP. **Lettermint** is the pick for an EU company with ISO 27001. **Sweego** fits French hosting plus SMS. **Postmark** is the non-EU choice for transactional-only deliverability.

MailPace is a small, principled product: EU-hosted, run by a UK company, and it never tracks opens or clicks. People look elsewhere for honest reasons:

- **Price past 10,000 emails.** $50 at 50,000 and $100 at 100,000.
- **Transactional only.** Marketing and newsletters are prohibited, so you need a second provider for campaigns.
- **Shared IPs only.** No dedicated IP at any volume.
- **No open or click data** when your product team does want it.
- **Inbound is a JSON webhook**, not a mailbox you can read and reply from.

We build Reloop, so weigh our entry accordingly. Every competitor fact below comes from our head-to-head posts, each of which links the provider's own pricing and docs.

---

| **Best French option with SMS** | Sweego | French company on French data centers |
| **Best established EU ESP** | Mailjet | EU data centers, transactional and marketing |
| **Best EU marketing suite** | Brevo | Email, SMS, WhatsApp and CRM |
| **Best non-EU for transactional deliverability** | Postmark | Transactional focus, message streams (US company) |

## 1. Reloop: best overall MailPace alternative

[Reloop](/) is open-source email infrastructure: a transactional API and SMTP relay, inbound mailboxes, contacts, campaigns, event-triggered automations and signed webhooks. **Reloop Cloud runs on Hetzner, a German hosting company, with EU data centers**, and comes with a [DPA](/dpa) based on the EU Standard Contractual Clauses. The same Apache 2.0 code [self-hosts](/self-host) on your own EU server if you want full control.

**Pricing:** free for 6,000 emails a month (200 a day). Pro is $10 for 50,000, Growth is $20 for 100,000 with a dedicated IP, and overage is $0.50 per 1,000. Or skip the plan and buy prepaid credits at $0.50 per 1,000, valid for 6 months.

**On tracking:** open and click tracking are per-domain settings. They're on for new domains, and you can switch either off, so no pixel or rewritten links are added. That gives you MailPace's privacy stance where you need it, and data where you want it.

**Strengths**

- **$10 vs $50 at 50k, and $20 vs $100 at 100k.**
- **Transactional and marketing in one product**, with one suppression list.
- **A dedicated IP on Growth**, which MailPace doesn't offer.
- **Inbound mail as real mailboxes** with threads, over the API, [MCP](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) or IMAP. Hosted plans include 3, 5 or 10 inboxes on Free, Pro and Growth.

**Weaknesses**

- Tracking is on by default for new domains; you have to switch it off, where MailPace never offers it.
- At around 10,000 emails a month the price is the same as MailPace.

**Best for:** teams that have outgrown MailPace's volume or scope but still want EU hosting. Full comparison: [Reloop vs MailPace](/blog/reloop-vs-mailpace).

---

## 2. Lettermint: best EU company with ISO 27001

[Lettermint](https://lettermint.co/) is Lettermint B.V., a Dutch company running on EU infrastructure (UpCloud in the Netherlands, encrypted backups on OVHcloud in Germany), and certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022.

**Pricing:** free for 300 emails a month. 10,000 is €10 on Starter, 50,000 is €40, and 100,000 falls in the €85 tier for 125,000. See [lettermint.co/pricing](https://lettermint.co/pricing).

**Strengths:** EU company and EU hosting, ISO 27001, transactional, broadcast and inbound on one plan, SSO with SCIM from Starter.

**Weaknesses:** inbound is a webhook, no contacts or automations in its docs, hosted only.

**Best for:** EU companies whose security review asks both "where" and "who". Full comparison: [Reloop vs Lettermint](/blog/reloop-vs-lettermint).

More options: [Lettermint alternatives](/blog/best-lettermint-alternatives)

## 3. Sweego: best French option with SMS

[Sweego](https://www.sweego.io/) is a French email and SMS API from Mindbaz SAS, hosted on OVHcloud and Scaleway in France.

**Pricing:** free for 100 emails a day. Individual starts at €10 for 20,000 to 50,000 emails; Startup at €79 for 100,000 to 200,000. See [sweego.io/pricing](https://www.sweego.io/pricing).

**Strengths:** French company and hosting, SMS in the same account, dedicated IPs from Startup.

**Weaknesses:** no campaigns or automations, inbound by webhook on paid plans, hosted only.

**Best for:** French teams that need transactional email and SMS. Full comparison: [Reloop vs Sweego](/blog/reloop-vs-sweego).

More options: [Sweego alternatives](/blog/best-sweego-alternatives)

---

## 4. Mailjet: best established EU ESP

[Mailjet](https://www.mailjet.com/), now owned by Sinch, stores customer data in Google Cloud data centers in Frankfurt and Saint-Ghislain.

**Pricing:** free for 6,000 emails a month (200 a day). $40 on Essential or $59 on Premium at 50,000; $112 on Premium at 100,000. See [mailjet.com/pricing](https://www.mailjet.com/pricing/).

**Strengths:** transactional and marketing in one account, a mature visual editor, a generous free tier.

**Weaknesses:** automations need Premium, and tracking is part of the standard product.

**Best for:** teams that want MailPace's EU hosting plus marketing. Full comparison: [Reloop vs Mailjet](/blog/reloop-vs-mailjet).

---

## 5. Brevo: best EU marketing suite

[Brevo](https://www.brevo.com/) runs from Paris, with servers in the EU on OVH and Google Cloud.

**Pricing:** free for 300 emails a day. Starter from $9 for 5,000 emails, Standard from $18; larger volumes on a slider at [brevo.com/pricing](https://www.brevo.com/pricing/).

**Strengths:** email, SMS, WhatsApp and CRM with a drag-and-drop editor.

**Weaknesses:** a marketing-first product, pricier at higher volumes than developer APIs.

**Best for:** marketing-led EU teams. Full comparison: [Reloop vs Brevo](/blog/reloop-vs-brevo).

## Non-EU options worth knowing

- **[Postmark](/blog/reloop-vs-postmark):** a US company with a strong transactional deliverability reputation and separate message streams. $15 for 10,000 on Basic, then $1.80 per 1,000, so about $87 at 50k.
- **[Resend](/blog/reloop-vs-resend):** a US company with a polished API. Free for 3,000 a month; $20 for 50k and $35 for 100k.

For EU personal data, both need a DPA and a transfer mechanism such as SCCs. See our [EU email API guide](/blog/eu-email-api-providers-2026).

## How to choose

- **"We're past 10,000 emails a month and want EU hosting."** Reloop.
- **"We never want tracking, and our volume is small."** Stay on MailPace.
- **"We need campaigns as well as transactional."** Reloop, Mailjet or Brevo.
- **"We need a dedicated IP."** Reloop on Growth, or Sweego from Startup.
- **"Our review requires an EU company and ISO 27001."** Lettermint.
- **"We need SMS."** Sweego or Brevo.

---

## Switching from MailPace

1. **Sign the new provider's DPA.**
2. **Verify your sending domain** with the new DKIM record, and merge the new include into your existing SPF record. See our [SPF, DKIM and DMARC guide](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide).
3. **Decide on tracking.** On Reloop, switch open and click tracking off per domain if you want to keep MailPace's behavior.
4. **Move suppressions, client code and webhooks.** Reloop templates use `{{{variable}}}`, and webhooks are signed in the `Reloop-Signature` header.
5. **Ramp traffic** over one to two weeks, then remove MailPace's DNS records.

# Best Mandrill Alternatives in 2026: Transactional Email Without a Mailchimp Plan

Path: /blog/best-mandrill-alternatives
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-mandrill-alternatives
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-mandrill-alternatives.md

The best Mandrill (Mailchimp Transactional) alternatives of 2026 compared: Reloop, Postmark, Resend, SendGrid, Mailgun, Amazon SES and MailerSend on price at 50k and 100k, templates, inbound, dedicated IPs and self-hosting.

**The short version:** Mandrill, now sold as Mailchimp Transactional, can't be bought on its own. It's an add-on to a paid Mailchimp Standard or Premium plan, billed in blocks of 25,000 emails. If you only need transactional email, **Reloop** is a standalone API with a free tier and $10 for 50,000 emails (Mandrill is $40 in blocks, plus the Mailchimp plan). **Postmark** is the closest match on transactional focus, and **Amazon SES** is the cheapest raw pipe.

We build Reloop, so weigh our pick accordingly. Every competitor price below comes from the provider's public pricing page, linked in each section, and each section says where that provider beats us.

---

## Why developers look for a Mandrill alternative

Mandrill is a solid sending API. It supports Mailchimp merge tags and Handlebars, inbound routes and dedicated IPs. Developers leave for reasons that are mostly about packaging:

- **It requires a Mailchimp marketing plan.** Transactional is "available as an add-on to Standard and Premium plans", and Essentials isn't eligible. If you never send newsletters, you're paying for a plan you don't use.
- **Blocks, not usage.** You buy whole blocks of 25,000 emails at $20 each (cheaper only past 500k a month). A month with 26,000 emails needs two blocks.
- **No real free tier.** Up to 500 trial sends, then you pay.
- **Dedicated IPs are an extra $29.95 a month.**
- **Inbound is a webhook.** Routes post each message to your endpoint; storage, threading and replies are yours to build.
- **Hosted only, tied to your Mailchimp account.**

If you already pay for Mailchimp Standard and send millions of emails a month, Mandrill's per-block price gets competitive. Otherwise, here are the options.

| **Closest modern developer experience** | Resend | Clean API, React Email |
| **Best Handlebars templating** | SendGrid | Full Handlebars logic, enterprise program |
| **Best for inbound routing** | Mailgun | Mature API and pattern-based routes |
| **Cheapest raw sending** | Amazon SES | $0.10 per 1,000, build the rest yourself |

## 1. Reloop: best overall Mandrill alternative

Reloop is open-source email infrastructure: a transactional API, SMTP relay, inbound mailboxes, contacts, campaigns, automations and webhooks in one product. Use it hosted (Reloop Cloud runs on Hetzner, a German hosting company, with EU data centers) or run the same code on your own server.

**Strengths**
