- **$10 vs $40 in blocks at 50k**, before Mandrill's Mailchimp plan; $20 vs $80 at 100k.
- **A dedicated IP included at $20**, instead of $29.95 a month extra.
- **Inbound as real mailboxes.** Mail is stored, threaded, spam-scored with Rspamd, and readable over the API, the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) or IMAP, with one-call replies. Hosted plans include 3, 5 or 10 inboxes on Free, Pro and Growth.
- If you do want marketing mail later, campaigns and event-triggered automations are in the same account, with one suppression list.

**Weaknesses**

- **No template logic.** Reloop substitutes `{{{variable}}}` placeholders but doesn't run `{{#if}}` or `{{#each}}`. Resolve those in code and pass the result as a variable. Mandrill's Handlebars is more powerful here.
- At millions of emails a month, Mandrill's lowest block price ($10 per 25,000, or $0.40 per 1,000) can undercut Reloop's overage if you already pay for Mailchimp.
- Open and click tracking are on for new domains; switch them off per domain if you don't want them.

**Best for:** developers who only need transactional email and don't want to pay for a Mailchimp plan to get it.

Full comparison: [Reloop vs Mandrill](/blog/reloop-vs-mandrill).

---

## 2. Postmark: best transactional reputation

Postmark has been transactional-first for over a decade. Its **message streams** keep bulk mail from hurting your transactional reputation.

**Pricing:** 100 emails a month free. Basic is $15 for 10,000, then $1.80 per extra 1,000: about $87 at 50k and $177 at 100k. Dedicated IPs are $50 a month for senders above 300,000 a month.

**Strengths:** strong reputation for inbox placement, message streams, excellent docs, and no marketing plan required.

**Weaknesses:** more than Mandrill's blocks at 50k and above. Inbound needs Pro. Templates use Mustachio, so Handlebars templates need rewriting. Hosted only.

**Best for:** low-volume senders who value reputation and docs over price.

Full comparison: [Reloop vs Postmark](/blog/reloop-vs-postmark) · [Best Postmark alternatives](/blog/best-postmark-alternatives)

---

## 3. Resend: closest modern developer experience

Resend made the clean, Stripe-style email API the norm, and its React Email project made JSX templates mainstream.

**Pricing:** Free is 3,000 a month (100 a day). Pro is $20 for 50,000 and $35 for 100,000. Overage is $0.90 per 1,000.

**Strengths:** excellent docs, first-class React Email, a large ecosystem of examples.

**Weaknesses:** $35 at 100k vs $20 on Reloop. Inbound is a webhook per message. A dedicated IP needs the $90 Scale plan plus a $30/mo add-on. Hosted only.

**Best for:** teams rewriting their email layer anyway who want to build templates in React.

Full comparison: [Reloop vs Resend](/blog/reloop-vs-resend).

More options: [Resend alternatives](/blog/best-resend-alternatives)

---

## 4. SendGrid: best Handlebars templating

SendGrid (Twilio) supports full Handlebars logic (`#if`, `#each`) in dynamic templates, which makes it the easiest landing spot if your Mandrill templates rely on it.

**Pricing:** a 60-day trial at 100 emails a day. Essentials is $19.95 for 50,000 and $34.95 for 100,000. Dedicated IPs, subusers and SSO start on Pro from $89.95.

**Strengths:** Handlebars templates move over with the least rewriting, a mature enterprise program, subusers and IP pools.

**Weaknesses:** no permanent free plan, marketing is on separate plans, inbound is the Inbound Parse webhook. Hosted only.

**Best for:** teams with logic-heavy Handlebars templates and enterprise procurement needs.

Full comparison: [Reloop vs SendGrid](/blog/reloop-vs-sendgrid) · [SendGrid alternative page](/alternatives/sendgrid)

More options: [SendGrid alternatives](/blog/best-sendgrid-alternatives)

---

## 5. Mailgun: best for inbound routing

Mailgun is one of the original developer email APIs. Its **inbound routes** match incoming mail by pattern and forward it, much like Mandrill's routes.

**Pricing:** a trial at 100 emails a day. Basic is $15 for 10,000; Foundation is $35 for 50,000. Overage starts at $1.30 per 1,000. Dedicated IPs are a paid add-on.

**Strengths:** Handlebars templates, flexible inbound routing that maps closely to Mandrill's, built-in email validation.

**Weaknesses:** around $100 at 100k with overage. Marketing is a separate Sinch product. Hosted only.

**Best for:** teams that rely on Mandrill's inbound routes and want the most similar model.

Full comparison: [Reloop vs Mailgun](/blog/reloop-vs-mailgun).

---

## 6. Amazon SES: cheapest raw sending

SES is the lowest list price in email: $0.10 per 1,000. It's a sending pipe, not a product.

**Pricing:** $0.10 per 1,000 emails plus $0.12 per GB of outbound data. New AWS accounts get $200 in Free Tier credits for the first 6 months.

**Strengths:** cheapest per email at any volume, deep AWS integration.

**Weaknesses:** you build bounce and complaint handling, suppression, logs and dashboards yourself. You also need to leave the SES sandbox before you can email real users.

**Best for:** AWS-native teams with engineers to own the glue, or senders at millions of emails a month.

Full comparison: [Reloop vs Amazon SES](/blog/reloop-vs-aws-ses).

---

## 7. MailerSend: best with a visual builder

MailerSend is a transactional API from the team behind MailerLite, with a drag-and-drop builder, SMS and email verification.

**Pricing:** Free is 500 emails a month. Hobby is $7 for 5,000. Starter is $35 for 50,000 and $68 for 100,000, with overage at $1.30 per 1,000.

**Strengths:** non-developers can edit templates without touching code; SMS and verification from the same vendor.

**Weaknesses:** inbound is forwarded, not stored, and each forward counts against your quota. Hosted only.

**Best for:** teams where marketers or support staff own the transactional templates.

Full comparison: [Reloop vs MailerSend](/blog/reloop-vs-mailersend).

---

## How to choose

- **"We don't use Mailchimp for marketing."** Any standalone API here removes the plan cost. Reloop is $10 at 50k.
- **"Our templates are full of Handlebars logic."** SendGrid or Mailgun keep Handlebars. With Reloop, move the logic into code.
- **"We rely on inbound routes."** Mailgun is the closest model; Reloop goes further with stored, threaded mailboxes.
- **"We send millions a month and already pay for Mailchimp."** Run the numbers; Mandrill's lowest blocks, SES or ZeptoMail may win on raw cost.
- **"Legal wants source code or self-hosting."** Reloop is the only option here that's open source.

<Callout type="tip">
  Mandrill blocks are bought in whole units of 25,000. Before you compare, check your real monthly volume over the last six months. If it swings between 20k and 60k, per-1,000 overage pricing will usually save more than the headline numbers suggest.
</Callout>

---

## Switching from Mandrill

1. **Add your sending domain** in the new provider and publish its DKIM record. Merge the new SPF include into your existing record; never publish a second SPF record.
2. **Swap the client.** On Reloop, replace `messages.send({ message })` with `reloop.mail.send`. `from_email` becomes `from`, and the `to` array of `{ email, type }` becomes addresses, with `cc` and `bcc` as separate fields.
3. **Map template placeholders.** On Reloop, `*|FNAME|*` and `{{fname}}` both become `{{{fname}}}`; resolve `{{#if}}` and `{{#each}}` in code.
4. **Switch SMTP** if you use it: on Reloop, host `smtp.reloop.sh`, port 587 with STARTTLS, API key as username and password.
5. **Import suppressions.** Export your Mandrill rejection list and import it, so you don't re-mail bounced or complaining addresses.
6. **Rewrite webhook handlers.** Mandrill batches events in `mandrill_events` signed with `X-Mandrill-Signature`; Reloop sends single JSON events signed in `Reloop-Signature`.
7. **Ramp traffic** from 10% to 100% over a week or two, then cancel the Mandrill add-on.

The [Reloop vs Mandrill](/blog/reloop-vs-mandrill) post has the full mapping, and the [SendGrid migration guide](/blog/migrating-from-sendgrid) shows a traffic-split flag you can reuse.

# Build an AI Agent That Reads and Replies to Email

Path: /blog/build-ai-agent-sends-emails
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/build-ai-agent-sends-emails
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/build-ai-agent-sends-emails.md

Give an AI agent its own mailbox: receive mail with Reloop's email.received webhook, read the thread, draft a reply with Claude, require human approval, and send from the same thread. Or connect Claude to Reloop's MCP server with one command.

**A useful email agent doesn't just send. It has its own address, reads what arrives, replies in the same thread, and asks a human before anything risky goes out.** With Reloop, the agent gets a real mailbox, an `email.received` webhook when mail lands, and API calls to read the thread and reply. The model only decides what to say.

There are two ways to build this. If you want an assistant like Claude or Claude Code to work your inbox for you, connect [Reloop's MCP server](#the-fast-path-connect-claude-with-mcp) with one command. If you're building the agent into your own product, follow the [build it yourself](#build-it-yourself-the-architecture) sections below.

---

## What the agent needs

Sending email from an LLM is one tool call. A working email agent needs much more:

| Capability | Why it matters | Reloop piece |
|---|---|---|
| Its own address | Replies come back to the agent, not a no-reply void | Mailbox on your domain |
| A trigger when mail arrives | The agent reacts instead of polling | `email.received` webhook |
| Full conversation context | The model needs the thread, not one message | `inbox.threads.get` |
| Replying in-thread | Recipients see one conversation, not scattered emails | `inbox.messages.reply` |
| An undo window | A human can stop a bad send | `undoWindowSeconds` + `cancelPending` |
| Spam signal | Don't let spammers drive your agent | `is_spam` on every inbound message |
| An audit trail | Know what the agent sent and why | Inbox sent folder and email logs |

---

## The fast path: connect Claude with MCP

Reloop runs a hosted [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) at `https://reloop.sh/mcp`. Any MCP client can use it, and you sign in with your Reloop account instead of pasting an API key.

In Claude Code:

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http reloop https://reloop.sh/mcp
```

Then run `/mcp`, choose **reloop**, and authenticate. In Claude on the web or desktop, add a custom connector under **Settings → Connectors** with the same URL.

The inbox tools the agent gets include:

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `list_mailboxes` | Find the mailboxes in your organization |
| `list_inbox_threads` | Conversations, newest first, with folder and search filters |
| `get_inbox_thread` | Every message in one conversation |
| `get_inbox_message` | One message with its body and attachments |
| `reply_to_inbox_message` | Reply in-thread, to the sender or everyone |
| `send_mailbox_email` | Start a new conversation from a mailbox |
| `cancel_pending_mailbox_send` | Cancel a scheduled send or one still in its undo window |
| `move_inbox_thread` | Archive, trash or restore a conversation |

Now you can ask: *"Go through unread threads in support@, draft replies to anything about billing, and show me each one before you send."*

<Callout type="warning">
  Sending email is real and can't be undone. MCP clients ask you to approve each tool call. Read the recipients and the text before you approve a reply.
</Callout>

That's enough for a personal assistant. For an agent that runs inside your product, unattended, you'll want the architecture below.

---

## Build it yourself: the architecture

```text
 customer ──email──▶ support@mail.acme.com  (Reloop mailbox)
                            │
                  email.received webhook
                            ▼
                    your /api/agent route
                            │
          inbox.threads.get ── full conversation
                            │
                    Claude drafts a reply
                            │
            ┌───────────────┴────────────────┐
     safe + confident                  anything else
            │                                 │
  inbox.messages.reply             save draft → human approves
                                              │
                                    inbox.messages.reply
```

Four steps: create a mailbox, subscribe to inbound mail, let the model draft, and decide when a human must approve.

---

## 1. Create a mailbox for the agent

In the dashboard, open your verified domain and create a mailbox such as `support@mail.acme.com`. Or do it from code:

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY! });

const { mailbox, mailboxError } = await reloop.inbox.mailboxes.create({
  domainId: "dom_…",
  email: "support@mail.acme.com",
  displayName: "Acme Support",
});
if (mailboxError) throw mailboxError;
```

Receiving must be on for the domain, which adds an MX record pointing at Reloop. The free plan includes three agent inboxes. Pro includes five and Growth includes ten. [How to give an AI agent its own email address](/blog/give-ai-agent-email-address) covers the domain and mailbox setup in more detail.

---

## 2. Get notified when mail arrives

Create a webhook in the dashboard that subscribes to `email.received`. Every inbound message triggers a POST like this:

```json
{
  "id": "whev_…",
  "type": "email.received",
  "created_at": "2026-06-16T12:00:00.000Z",
  "data": {
    "email_id": "in_…",
    "mailbox_id": "mb_…",
    "from": "customer@example.com",
    "from_name": "Dana",
    "to": ["support@mail.acme.com"],
    "subject": "Can't download my invoice",
    "thread_id": "thr_…",
    "has_attachments": false,
    "is_spam": false,
    "status": "received"
  }
}
```

Verify the `Reloop-Signature` header before you trust the payload. The [webhook verification guide](/docs/webhooks/verify-webhooks-requests) has a copy-paste helper.

---

## 3. Read the thread and draft a reply

The handler loads the conversation, gives it to the model, and asks for a structured decision rather than free text.

```typescript
// app/api/agent/route.ts

const Decision = z.object({
  action: z.enum(["reply", "escalate", "ignore"]),
  category: z.enum(["billing", "how_to", "bug", "sales", "other"]),
  confidence: z.number().min(0).max(1),
  reply: z.string().max(3000).optional(),
});

  const raw = await req.text();
  const valid = verifyReloopWebhook({
    secret: process.env.RELOOP_WEBHOOK_SECRET!,
    rawBody: raw,
    signatureHeader: req.headers.get("Reloop-Signature") ?? "",
  });
  if (!valid) return new Response("Bad signature", { status: 401 });

  const event = JSON.parse(raw);
  if (event.type !== "email.received" || event.data.is_spam) {
    return new Response("skipped");
  }

  const { message, messageError } = await reloop.inbox.messages.get(
    event.data.email_id,
  );
  if (messageError) throw messageError;

  // Never answer automated mail: it's how agents end up in reply loops.
  const auto = Object.entries(message.headers ?? {}).find(
    ([key]) => key.toLowerCase() === "auto-submitted",
  )?.[1];
  if (auto && auto.toLowerCase() !== "no") {
    return new Response("auto-reply ignored");
  }

  const { thread, threadError } = await reloop.inbox.threads.get(
    event.data.thread_id,
  );
  if (threadError) throw threadError;

  const history = thread.messages
    .map((m) => `[${m.direction}] ${m.fromEmail}: ${m.preview ?? ""}`)
    .join("\n");

  const { output: decision } = await generateText({
    model: anthropic("claude-sonnet-5-5"),
    output: Output.object({ schema: Decision }),
    system:
      "You are Acme's support agent. Reply only with facts from the help " +
      "center below. If unsure, or if money, refunds or account access are " +
      "involved, choose escalate. Never promise anything.\n\n" +
      HELP_CENTER,
    prompt:
      `Conversation so far:\n${history}\n\n` +
      `Latest message from ${message.fromEmail}:\n${message.textBody ?? ""}`,
  });

  await handleDecision(message.id, decision);
  return new Response("ok");
}
```

Notes on this design:

- **The model returns a decision, not an action.** Your code decides what happens next. That keeps the model away from the send button.
- **Spam and auto-replies are filtered before the model runs.** That saves tokens and stops out-of-office loops.
- **The system prompt limits the agent to known facts.** An email agent that makes up refund policies is worse than no agent.

---

## 4. Human in the loop

Not every reply should go out on its own. A simple policy:

```typescript
const AUTO_SEND = new Set(["how_to"]);

async function handleDecision(messageId: string, d: z.infer<typeof Decision>) {
  if (d.action === "ignore") return;

  const safe =
    d.action === "reply" &&
    d.reply &&
    AUTO_SEND.has(d.category) &&
    d.confidence >= 0.85;

  if (safe) {
    const { message, messageError } = await reloop.inbox.messages.reply(messageId, {
      text: d.reply!,
    });
    if (messageError) throw messageError;
    return;
  }

  // Everything else waits for a person.
  await db.drafts.insert({
    messageId,
    category: d.category,
    reply: d.reply ?? null,
    status: "needs_review",
  });
}
```

When a teammate approves a draft in your review screen, call the same `reloop.inbox.messages.reply(messageId, { text })`. The reply lands in the original thread with the right `In-Reply-To` headers, so the customer sees one conversation.

| Category | Auto-send? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| How-to questions | Yes, if confident | Low risk, answer is in the docs |
| Bug reports | Draft only | Needs a human to confirm and log it |
| Billing and refunds | Never | Money and policy decisions |
| Sales inquiries | Draft only | Tone and pricing matter |
| Anything uncertain | Escalate | The default when in doubt |

### Add an undo window to new emails

When the agent starts a *new* conversation (a follow-up, a reminder), send it from the mailbox with an undo window:

```typescript
const { message, messageError } = await reloop.inbox.messages.send({
  mailboxId: "mb_…",
  to: "customer@example.com",
  subject: "Following up on your download issue",
  text: followUp,
  undoWindowSeconds: 300,
});
if (messageError) throw messageError;

// Within 5 minutes, a reviewer can still stop it:
await reloop.inbox.messages.cancelPending(message.id);
```

The email stays pending for five minutes. Show it in your review queue, and cancel it if anything looks wrong.

---

## Guardrails that matter

| Guardrail | How |
|---|---|
| Skip spam | Check `is_spam` on the webhook before calling the model |
| Prevent reply loops | Ignore messages with an `Auto-Submitted` header; cap replies per thread |
| Rate limits | Cap agent sends per hour and per recipient |
| No invented facts | Ground the prompt in your docs; escalate when the answer isn't there |
| No money decisions | Billing, refunds and account access always go to a human |
| Prompt injection | Treat email bodies as untrusted data; the model can't pick recipients or call arbitrary tools |
| Audit trail | Every agent reply is in the mailbox's sent folder and Reloop's logs |

<Callout type="tip">
  Start in draft-only mode for a week. Review every draft, then turn on auto-send for the one category where the agent was right almost every time.
</Callout>

---

## What to build next

- **Learn from outcomes.** Subscribe to `email.opened`, `email.clicked` and replies on the thread, and feed them back into the agent's context.
- **Label and route.** Use `inbox.threads.update` to mark threads important, or archive resolved ones with `inbox.threads.archive`.
- **Send one-way notifications.** For alerts from a chat assistant or background job, see [Vercel AI SDK + Reloop](/blog/vercel-ai-sdk-reloop-notifications).
- **Give humans the same inbox.** People can work the same mailbox in the Reloop dashboard, so the agent and your team share one queue.

For the infrastructure side (MX records, threading, storage, IMAP), read [how the infrastructure for an email agent works](/blog/email-infrastructure-for-ai-agents). If you're weighing hosted agent inbox providers, see [Reloop vs AgentMail](/blog/reloop-vs-agentmail).

---

## FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Should I use MCP or build my own agent?">
    MCP is the fastest way for you, personally, to work your inbox with
    Claude or Claude Code, with approval on every call. Build your own when
    the agent runs unattended inside your product and you need fixed rules
    for what it can send.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can the agent use my existing support address?">
    Yes, if the domain's MX points to Reloop. Many teams start with a
    subdomain like `support.acme.com` so their main mailbox provider is
    untouched.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Which model should I use?">
    Any model the AI SDK supports. We use Claude for support-style replies
    because it follows grounding instructions well. Keep the structured
    decision step whichever model you pick.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="How do I stop the agent replying to other bots?">
    Ignore messages that carry an `Auto-Submitted` header other than `no`,
    skip `is_spam` messages, and cap the number of agent replies per thread.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# Best Plunk Alternatives in 2026: Open-Source and Hosted Email Platforms Compared

Path: /blog/best-plunk-alternatives
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-plunk-alternatives
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-plunk-alternatives.md

The best Plunk alternatives in 2026 compared: Reloop, useSend, Loops, Resend, Listmonk and Amazon SES on pricing at steady volume, automations, inbound email, licensing and self-hosting without AWS.

**The short version:** Plunk is an open-source platform for transactional mail, campaigns and automations. If you want the same scope for less at steady volume, inbound mail in real inboxes, or self-hosting without AWS, **Reloop** is the closest alternative. **useSend** is the other open-source option on SES, **Loops** is the polished hosted tool for lifecycle email, and **Listmonk** covers self-hosted newsletters.

Plunk does a lot right: simple pricing, automations, inbound routing and an open codebase. Teams usually look elsewhere because of:

- **Per-email pricing at steady volume.** $1 per 1,000 emails is simple, but it's about $50 at 50k and $100 at 100k.
- **A branded free tier.** The free 1,000 emails a month carry Plunk branding.
- **Self-hosting needs Amazon SES.** You need an AWS account out of the SES sandbox, an IAM user and an SNS topic for events.
- **The AGPL license**, which some companies' legal teams avoid.

We build Reloop, so weigh this accordingly. Prices and facts come from our researched head-to-head posts and each provider's own site, and each section says where that alternative beats us.

---

## Top picks at a glance

| Category | Pick | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Best overall Plunk alternative** | Reloop | Same scope, $10 for 50k, inboxes, Apache 2.0 |
| **Best open source on SES** | useSend | Resend-style API, $0.40 per 1,000 transactional |
| **Best hosted lifecycle email** | Loops | Polished automations for SaaS, priced by contacts |
| **Best hosted developer API** | Resend | Clean API, React Email |
| **Best self-hosted newsletters** | Listmonk | Fast, light, bring any SMTP |
| **Cheapest raw pipe** | Amazon SES | $0.10 per 1,000, build the rest |

---

## The comparison table

| | Plunk | Reloop | useSend | Loops | Resend | Listmonk |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **License** | AGPL-3.0 | Apache 2.0 | AGPL-3.0 | Closed | Closed | AGPLv3 |
| **Pricing basis** | Per email | Plans by email volume | Per email ($10 minimum) | Contacts stored | Plans by email volume | Self-host only |
| **Free tier** | 1,000 / mo, branded | 6,000 / mo (200 / day) | 3,000 / mo (100 / day) | 1,000 contacts, 4,000 sends | 3,000 / mo (100 / day) | N/A |
| **~50,000 emails / mo** | about $50 | **$10** | $20 | From $49 (by contacts) | $20 | Server + SMTP |
| **~100,000 emails / mo** | about $100 | **$20** | $40 | $399 at 100k contacts | $35 | Server + SMTP |
| **Automations** | Yes | Yes | Not listed | Yes, core focus | Limited | No drip sequences |
| **Inbound email** | Routing rules | Mailboxes, API, MCP, IMAP | Roadmap | No | Webhook | No |
| **SMTP relay** | Yes | Yes | Yes | No | Yes | Needs one |
| **Self-host without AWS** | No (SES) | Yes | No (SES) | No | No | Yes (any SMTP) |

Plunk and useSend figures are our math from their per-email rates. Loops prices by contacts, not emails, so its column depends on list size.

---

## 1. Reloop: best overall Plunk alternative

[Reloop](/) covers the same ground as Plunk: a transactional API, SMTP, contacts, campaigns, event-triggered automations and inbound email. It's open source under Apache 2.0 and runs its own mail server.

Starting an automation looks almost identical to Plunk's `/v1/track` call:

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY! });

const { automationError } = await reloop.automations.start({
  event: "user.signed_up",
  email: user.email,
});
```

**Pricing:** free for 6,000 emails a month (200 a day) with no branding. Pro is $10 for 50,000, Growth is $20 for 100,000 with a dedicated IP, then $0.50 per 1,000. Pay-as-you-go credits are also $0.50 per 1,000, valid for 6 months. Self-hosting has no per-email fee.

**Strengths**

- **Cheaper at steady volume.** From about 10,000 emails a month on, a flat plan costs less than $1 per 1,000.
- **No AWS when self-hosting.** KumoMTA sends from your own server, so there's no SES sandbox, IAM or SNS setup, and mail never passes through a third party. Install with [one command](/self-host).
- **Inbound into real inboxes**, threaded and spam-scored, readable over the API, the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) or IMAP, so agents and humans can reply in-thread.
- **Subscription channels**, so a contact can opt out of product updates while still getting billing mail.
- **Apache 2.0**, with no copyleft obligations. Reloop Cloud runs on Hetzner, a German hosting company, with EU data centers.

**Weaknesses**

- **You own IP reputation when self-hosting.** With Plunk, SES handles warm-up.
- No browser-safe public tracking key like Plunk's `pk_` keys; track events from your server.

**Best for:** teams with steady volume, anyone who needs inbound mail as inboxes, and self-hosters who want to avoid AWS. Full comparison: [Reloop vs Plunk](/blog/reloop-vs-plunk).

---

## 2. useSend: best open source on SES

[useSend](https://usesend.com) (formerly Unsend) is an open-source Resend alternative under AGPL-3.0, sending through Amazon SES, with contacts, campaigns and a hosted cloud.

**Pricing:** free for 3,000 a month (100 a day). Paid is usage-based with a $10 monthly minimum: $0.0004 per transactional email and $0.001 per marketing email.

**Strengths:** cheaper than Plunk for transactional mail, a Resend-style API, and SES handles reputation when self-hosted.

**Weaknesses:** still beta, inbound is on the roadmap, automations aren't listed, and self-hosting needs the same AWS setup as Plunk.

**Best for:** high-volume transactional senders on SES. Full comparison: [Reloop vs useSend](/blog/reloop-vs-usesend).

More options: [useSend alternatives](/blog/best-usesend-alternatives)

---

## 3. Loops: best hosted lifecycle email

[Loops](https://loops.so) is a polished, hosted tool for SaaS lifecycle email: onboarding sequences, product announcements and broadcasts.

**Pricing:** free for 1,000 contacts and 4,000 sends a month, then from $49 a month. It bills by contacts stored: 100,000 contacts is $399 a month, however much you send.

**Strengths:** a focused, well-designed automation builder that non-developers enjoy using.

**Weaknesses:** closed source and hosted only, limited transactional API, no SMTP relay, no inbound, and contact-based pricing grows with your list, not your sending.

**Best for:** marketing-led SaaS teams that want a polished lifecycle tool and will pair it with a separate transactional provider. Full comparison: [Reloop vs Loops](/blog/reloop-vs-loops). See also [Loops alternative](/alternatives/loops).

More options: [Loops alternatives](/blog/best-loops-alternatives)

---

## 4. Resend: best hosted developer API

[Resend](https://resend.com) is a hosted email API with a clean SDK, React Email and Broadcasts for audiences.

**Pricing:** free for 3,000 a month (100 a day), $20 for 50k, $35 for 100k, then $0.90 per 1,000.

**Strengths:** excellent developer experience and docs, a large ecosystem.

**Weaknesses:** closed source and hosted only, limited automations, inbound is a webhook per message.

**Best for:** developer teams that want a polished hosted API and don't need open source. Full comparison: [Reloop vs Resend](/blog/reloop-vs-resend). See also [Resend alternative](/alternatives/resend).

---

## 5. Listmonk: best self-hosted newsletters

[Listmonk](https://listmonk.app) is a newsletter and mailing list manager under AGPLv3: a single Go binary plus Postgres that sends through any SMTP server you provide.

**Pricing:** free and self-hosted only; you pay for the server and your SMTP provider.

**Strengths:** very fast and light, SQL segmentation, a mature campaign UI, and no AWS requirement.

**Weaknesses:** doesn't send mail itself, no drip sequences or inbound.

**Best for:** self-hosted newsletters. Pair it with an SMTP backend such as Reloop. Full comparison: [Reloop vs Listmonk](/blog/reloop-vs-listmonk).

More options: [Listmonk alternatives](/blog/best-listmonk-alternatives)

---

## 6. Amazon SES: cheapest raw pipe

[Amazon SES](https://aws.amazon.com/ses/) is what Plunk sends through. Using it directly removes the platform layer and its fee.

**Pricing:** $200 in AWS credits for the first 6 months, then $0.10 per 1,000 plus $0.12 per GB outbound.

**Strengths:** the lowest per-email price, and Amazon manages reputation.

**Weaknesses:** no contacts, campaigns, automations or inbox UI. You build the product Plunk gave you.

**Best for:** AWS teams with engineers to spare. Full comparison: [Reloop vs Amazon SES](/blog/reloop-vs-aws-ses). See also [Amazon SES alternative](/alternatives/aws-ses).

---

## How to choose

- **"Plunk's bill grows with our volume."** Reloop. $10 for 50k and $20 for 100k.
- **"We want to self-host without AWS."** Reloop, or Listmonk for newsletters only.
- **"We need agents or support to reply to inbound mail."** Reloop, with stored mailboxes, MCP and IMAP.
- **"We send millions of transactional emails on SES."** useSend.
- **"Marketing wants a polished hosted automation tool."** Loops, with a separate transactional provider.
- **"Our lawyers avoid AGPL."** Reloop (Apache 2.0), or the hosted options.

---

## Switching from Plunk

1. **Add your domain** in the new provider and publish its DKIM record. Merge its SPF include into your existing record rather than adding a second one.
2. **Swap the send call.** Plunk's `POST /v1/send` maps to Reloop's `reloop.mail.send`.
3. **Swap event tracking.** Plunk's `POST /v1/track` with `event` and `email` becomes `reloop.automations.start({ event, email })`, called from your server.
4. **Rebuild automations** in Reloop with the same triggers, delays and conditions.
5. **Move templates.** Plunk's `{{ firstName }}` becomes `{{{firstName}}}` in Reloop.
6. **Export contacts and suppressions** and import them, so you don't email anyone who bounced or unsubscribed.
7. **Ramp traffic** over one to two weeks, then remove the old DNS records.

# Why Your Emails Land In Spam & How to Fix It

Path: /blog/why-emails-land-in-spam-fix
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/why-emails-land-in-spam-fix
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/why-emails-land-in-spam-fix.md

The definitive guide to diagnosing and fixing email spam folder placement, covering authentication, content, reputation, list hygiene, and ISP-specific issues.

**Email deliverability does not fail with an HTTP 404 error or a readable stack trace. It fails silently by routing your mission-critical messages into the recipient's spam folder.**

When auth tokens, password reset links, invoices, and user notifications land in spam, your business is effectively down for those users. Because SMTP technically completes message handoff without an error code, deliverability regressions are notoriously difficult to detect and debug without a systematic methodology.

This guide walks you through every major root cause of spam folder placement, provides exact CLI commands and tools to diagnose your sending path, and details the concrete steps required to fix each issue permanently.

## Start with a spam score baseline

**Before debugging individual infrastructure components, establish an objective spam score baseline.**

Send a test email from your production or staging environment to [mail-tester.com](https://mail-tester.com). The service executes automated SpamAssassin heuristics, analyzes message MIME structure, and checks DNSBL blacklists to return a score from 0 to 10.

- **Score 9.0 to 10.0**: **Optimal deliverability baseline** required for transactional infrastructure.
- **Score 7.0 to 8.9**: **Active deliverability risks**: minor configuration warnings, missing headers, or slight content penalties.
- **Score Below 7.0**: **Severe deliverability failure**: failing authentication, blacklisted IP, or broken MIME structure.

In parallel, register your sending domain with [Google Postmaster Tools](https://postmaster.google.com). It provides proprietary Gmail telemetry directly from Google, including **domain reputation**, **IP reputation**, **spam complaint rates**, and **authentication success rates**.

## Cause 1: Missing or broken email authentication

**Probability: Very High. Over 70% of inbox placement failures stem from authentication misconfigurations.**

Major mailbox providers ([Google, Yahoo, and Microsoft](https://blog.google/products/gmail/gmail-security-authentication-spam-protection/)) enforce mandatory authentication for all senders. If your messages fail or lack [SPF, DKIM, or DMARC](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide), inbox providers will aggressively route your traffic to spam or drop it at the SMTP handshake.

### How to diagnose authentication in DNS

Verify that your DNS records are active and resolving across public resolvers:

```bash
# 1. Verify SPF record
dig TXT yourdomain.com +short | grep spf

# 2. Verify DKIM record (Reloop uses the 'reloop' selector)
dig TXT reloop._domainkey.yourdomain.com +short

# 3. Verify DMARC record
dig TXT _dmarc.yourdomain.com +short
```

You can also paste raw message headers into the [MXToolbox Email Header Analyzer](https://mxtoolbox.com/EmailHeaders.aspx) to inspect how receiving mail transfer agents evaluate your records.

### What healthy authentication headers look like

Inspect the `Authentication-Results` header inside a delivered email:

```http
Authentication-Results: mx.google.com;
  spf=pass (google.com: domain of notifications@yourdomain.com designates 1.2.3.4 as permitted sender) smtp.mailfrom=notifications@yourdomain.com;
  dkim=pass header.i=@yourdomain.com header.s=reloop;
  dmarc=pass (p=REJECT) header.from=yourdomain.com
```

**If any authentication check shows `fail` or `softfail`, resolve authentication before investigating any other deliverability factor.** See our step-by-step [SPF, DKIM, and DMARC complete setup guide](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide).

### The DMARC alignment trap

**An email can pass SPF and DKIM individually while still failing DMARC due to identifier misalignment.**

DMARC requires that the domain in the user-visible `From:` header matches either:
1. The domain in the envelope sender `Return-Path` (**SPF Alignment**)
2. The domain specified in the `d=` tag of a valid `DKIM-Signature` (**DKIM Alignment**)

If you send from `auth@yourdomain.com` but your DKIM signature is signed under a third-party vendor domain without custom domain alignment, DMARC evaluation will fail.

## Cause 2: Sending from a new IP with no reputation

**Probability: High for freshly provisioned servers and new infrastructure.**

Internet Service Providers (ISPs) maintain rolling reputation scores for every sending IP address. **A brand new IP starts with neutral reputation, which anti-abuse filters treat with heightened suspicion.** Jumping immediately to high sending volume from a cold IP triggers automated rate-limiting, temporary deferrals (`421` / `451` SMTP codes), and spam placement.

### Indicators of an IP reputation issue

- Deliverability was flawless on previous infrastructure before migrating to a new server.
- You recently provisioned a dedicated IP address or switched email infrastructure providers.
- [Google Postmaster Tools](https://postmaster.google.com) reports **"Low"** or **"Bad"** IP reputation.

### How to fix it: Structured IP warming

**IP warming is the process of gradually scaling outbound volume over 4 to 6 weeks to establish trusted sender reputation.**

| Week | Recommended Daily Sends | Primary Focus |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Week 1** | **50 – 200 emails/day** | High-intent transactional mail (password resets, welcome emails). |
| **Week 2** | **200 – 500 emails/day** | Active daily users and transactional notifications. |
| **Week 3** | **500 – 1,000 emails/day** | Expand to weekly summaries and invoice dispatches. |
| **Week 4** | **1,000 – 2,500 emails/day** | Begin rolling out product updates to engaged segments. |
| **Week 5** | **2,500 – 5,000 emails/day** | Monitor spam complaint rate; ensure complaints remain < 0.05%. |
| **Week 6+** | **5,000 – 10,000+ emails/day** | Full production capacity with established reputation. |

**During the initial warm-up window, send exclusively to your most engaged recipients.** High open rates and user engagement accelerate positive reputation scoring with mailbox algorithms. Follow our detailed [IP warming schedule guide](/blog/ip-warming-guide).

## Cause 3: High bounce rate

**Probability: Moderate to High, particularly after user imports or list migrations.**

**A bounce rate exceeding 2% is an immediate warning signal to ISPs; a bounce rate over 5% triggers automated throttling or domain blacklisting.** High bounce rates indicate that a sender is not validating email addresses at collection or is sending to stale, unverified databases.

### Distinguishing Hard vs. Soft Bounces

- **Hard Bounces (5xx SMTP errors)**: Permanent delivery failures (e.g. `550 5.1.1 User unknown`, invalid mailbox, nonexistent domain).
- **Soft Bounces (4xx SMTP errors)**: Temporary delivery failures (e.g. `452 Mailbox full`, server busy, transient network timeout).

### How to eliminate bounce penalties

1. **Automatically suppress hard-bounced addresses**: Never retry sending to a hard bounce. [Reloop's delivery engine](/features/deliverability) automatically suppresses hard bounces to protect your domain reputation (see our guide on [email bounce processing automation](/blog/email-bounce-processing-automation)).
2. **Clean lists before you send**: Before campaigns or imports, run addresses through a [free email validator](/tools/email-validator) to catch invalid syntax, disposable domains, and domains with no MX records, so hard bounces never hit your sending reputation.
3. **Verify addresses in real-time at signup**: Prevent typos and invalid domains directly at your registration form (or call Reloop's [email validation API](/features/email-validation) / use the free [bulk email verifier](/tools/email-validator) for CSV imports):
   ```typescript

     // Basic format validation
     const emailRegex = /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/;
     if (!emailRegex.test(email)) return false;

     // Verify domain has active MX records
     const domain = email.split("@")[1];
     try {
       const mxRecords = await resolver.resolveMx(domain);
       return mxRecords && mxRecords.length > 0;
     } catch {
       return false;
     }
   }
   ```
4. **Never purchase or scrape email lists**: Third-party lists contain spam traps (honeypot addresses maintained by anti-spam organizations) that immediately ruin domain reputation.

## Cause 4: High spam complaint rate

**Probability: High for mixed transactional and notification streams.**

A spam complaint occurs whenever a recipient clicks "Report Spam" or "Mark as Spam" in Gmail, Apple Mail, or Outlook.

- **Google & Yahoo Warning Threshold**: **0.10%** (1 complaint per 1,000 delivered emails).
- **Enforcement & Blocking Threshold**: **0.30%** (3 complaints per 1,000 delivered emails).

**Exceeding 0.30% spam complaints will cause mailbox providers to route all subsequent domain traffic directly to the spam folder.**

### How to reduce spam complaints

1. **Isolate transactional from promotional sending**: **Never send marketing blasts from your primary transactional domain.** Isolate critical auth tokens and receipts on a dedicated subdomain (e.g. `auth.yourdomain.com` or `mail.yourdomain.com`) as detailed in our [transactional email best practices](/blog/transactional-email-best-practices).
2. **Implement RFC 8058 One-Click Unsubscribe**: Gmail and Yahoo require one-click unsubscribe headers for non-transactional messages:
   ```typescript

   const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY });

   await reloop.emails.send({
     from: "notifications@yourdomain.com",
     to: user.email,
     subject: "Your weekly analytics digest",
     headers: {
       "List-Unsubscribe": `<https://yourdomain.com/unsubscribe?token=${user.token}>`,
       "List-Unsubscribe-Post": "List-Unsubscribe=One-Click",
     },
     html: "<p>Your weekly digest content...</p>",
   });
   ```
3. **Sunset inactive recipients**: Implement sunset policies for non-essential notifications. If a user has not opened an email in 90 days, reduce sending frequency or require explicit re-opt-in.

## Cause 5: Content triggering Bayesian spam filters

**Probability: Low for standard transactional receipts; Moderate for notification templates.**

Modern spam filters use natural language processing and Bayesian analysis to evaluate message payloads. While keywords alone rarely cause spam placement, poor HTML formatting combined with aggressive promotional phrasing will penalize your delivery score.

### Content practices that degrade inbox placement

- **Missing `text/plain` multipart MIME**: Sending an HTML-only email without an accompanying plain text alternative is a strong spam signal. Reloop automatically generates plain text fallbacks for all outgoing messages.
- **Extreme Image-to-Text Ratio**: Single large promotional images with little or no accompanying text mimic phishing campaigns.
- **Link Text vs. Href Domain Mismatches**: If your link anchor text displays `https://yourdomain.com/login` but the underlying `href` points to an unbranded tracking redirect, filters flag the discrepancy as a potential phishing attempt.
- **Spam Trigger Patterns**: Excessive capitalization in subject lines (`URGENT: RESET NOW`), repetitive punctuation (`$$$`, `!!!`), and deceptive urgency triggers.

## Cause 6: Sending from unmonitored `noreply@` addresses

**Probability: Measurable impact on recipient engagement signals.**

Using `noreply@yourdomain.com` harms deliverability in two distinct ways:
1. **Machine Learning Heuristics**: Mailbox algorithms associate `noreply@` with low-engagement bulk blasts.
2. **Missed Engagement Signals**: When recipients reply to an email (e.g. "Thanks!" or asking a question), mailbox algorithms register that interaction as a strong positive reputation signal. A `noreply@` address blocks this positive feedback loop.

**Best Practice**: Use a recognizable sender address such as `notifications@yourdomain.com` or `team@yourdomain.com`, and set a monitored `Reply-To` header to route inbound responses to your support inbox:

```typescript
await reloop.emails.send({
  from: "Acme Support <notifications@yourdomain.com>",
  replyTo: "support@yourdomain.com",
  to: user.email,
  subject: "Your order confirmation",
  html: "<p>Thank you for your purchase...</p>",
});
```

## Cause 7: Sending IP or domain listed on a DNSBL blacklist

**Probability: High if credentials were leaked, sending servers were compromised, or list hygiene was neglected.**

DNSBLs (DNS-based Blackhole Lists) are shared databases of IP addresses and domains flagged for spam transmission or compromised SMTP servers. If your IP or domain appears on an authoritative blocklist (such as **Spamhaus**, **Barracuda**, or **Spamcop**), major ISPs will reject or spam-folder your mail immediately.

### How to check blacklist status

Run an automated scan across all major DNSBL registries using the [MXToolbox Blacklist Checker](https://mxtoolbox.com/blacklists.aspx). Enter your sending IP address and sending domain.

### How to request delisting

1. **Isolate and fix the root cause**: Identify and patch the compromised SMTP credential, stop the rogue sending loop, or purge the failing email list.
2. **Submit a removal request**: Visit the specific blacklist removal portal (e.g. the [Spamhaus Blocklist Removal Center](https://www.spamhaus.org/removal/)) and provide proof of remediation.
3. **Monitor clearance**: Most reputable blocklists clear listings within 24 to 48 hours once remediation is verified.

## Cause 8: ISP-specific filtering (Gmail, Microsoft 365, Apple)

Each major mailbox provider utilizes proprietary filtering algorithms beyond baseline standards:

### 1. Google (Gmail)
- **Primary Tool**: Monitor [Google Postmaster Tools](https://postmaster.google.com).
- **Tab Placement vs. Spam**: If transactional emails route to the **Promotions** tab instead of **Primary**, this is a classification issue rather than a spam penalty. Keep transactional templates lightweight and free from promotional banners to help Gmail route them to Primary.
- **BIMI Brand Logo**: Implement [BIMI (Brand Indicators for Message Identification)](/blog/bimi-email-setup-guide) with a valid DMARC enforcement policy (`p=quarantine` or `p=reject`) to display your verified company avatar in Gmail inboxes.

### 2. Microsoft (Outlook / Office 365)
- Microsoft maintains stringent IP reputation filtering and relies heavily on [Smart Network Data Services (SNDS)](https://sendersupport.olc.protection.outlook.com/snds/).
- Microsoft frequently returns `550 5.7.1` error codes when an IP reputation drops below acceptable thresholds.

## The 8-Step Deliverability Diagnostic Checklist

When emails are landing in spam, work through this diagnostic sequence in order:

1. **Run a [mail-tester.com](https://mail-tester.com) scan (target score ≥ 9/10)**: Identifies broken MIME syntax, missing DNS tags, and Bayesian spam keyword flags before you touch infrastructure.
2. **Audit raw authentication headers**: Inspect received headers in an actual test inbox to confirm `SPF: PASS`, `DKIM: PASS`, and `DMARC: PASS` with identifier alignment.
3. **Check [Google Postmaster Tools](https://postmaster.google.com) telemetry**: Verify that your Domain Reputation is "Good" or "High" and inspect Gmail-specific spam rates.
4. **Check DNSBL blacklists on [MXToolbox](https://mxtoolbox.com/blacklists.aspx)**: Confirm neither your sending IP nor domain is listed on Spamhaus, Barracuda, or Spamcop.
5. **Review real-time bounce rates in [Reloop Analytics](/features/email-analytics)**: Confirm that your 30-day hard bounce rate is strictly **below 2%** and that auto-suppression is active.
6. **Review your spam complaint rate**: Ensure complaints remain strictly **below 0.10%** (1 per 1,000 sends) to prevent algorithmic ISP filtering.
7. **Audit MIME structure & plain text fallback**: Verify that every outgoing template includes both a valid `text/plain` part and a balanced HTML payload without broken tracking URLs.
8. **Verify ISP-specific routing & tab placement**: Check whether messages are routing to Gmail's Promotions tab vs. spam, and isolate transactional subdomains from promotional lists.

# How to Send Email in Ruby: Net::SMTP, Rails and API

Path: /blog/send-email-ruby
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/send-email-ruby
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/send-email-ruby.md

Send email from Ruby with Net::SMTP, the mail gem, Rails Action Mailer or Sinatra, or with an email API. Copy-paste examples for HTML email, attachments, background jobs and retries without duplicates.

**Ruby can send email with `Net::SMTP`, and Rails apps already have Action Mailer built in.** For anything in production, send through a provider: either over SMTP with Action Mailer or the `mail` gem, or over HTTPS with an email API SDK.

This guide covers plain `Net::SMTP`, the `mail` gem, the Reloop Ruby SDK, Rails and Sinatra, then the production details: attachments, background jobs and safe retries.

Working in another language? See the guides for [Python](/blog/send-email-python) and [Node.js](/blog/send-email-nodejs).

---

## Which approach should you use?

| | `Net::SMTP` / Action Mailer | Email API SDK |
|---|-----------------------------|---------------|
| **Install** | `net-smtp` gem (Rails includes it) | `bundle add reloop` |
| **Transport** | SMTP on port 587 (STARTTLS) | HTTPS on port 443 |
| **Building the message** | `mail` gem or mailer views | A hash with `html`, `text`, `attachments` |
| **Errors** | `Net::SMTPError` subclasses | `Reloop::Error` and `Faraday::Error` |
| **Safe retries** | No, a retry can send twice | Yes, with an idempotency key |
| **Works with Action Mailer and Devise** | Yes, natively | Through SMTP settings |

If you are wiring up Devise emails, Action Mailer views or a third-party gem, use SMTP settings. If you are writing the send call yourself, use the API.

---

## Prerequisites

1. **Ruby 3.1 or later**
2. A **verified sending domain** with [SPF, DKIM and DMARC](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide)
3. An **API key** from the [Reloop dashboard](https://reloop.sh/dashboard). Keys start with `rl_`, and the same key works for the API and SMTP.

```bash
```

Keep the key in the environment, Rails credentials or a secrets manager, never in your code or git.

---

## Method 1: Send email with Net::SMTP

`Net::SMTP` speaks the protocol. Since Ruby 3.1 it ships as a bundled gem rather than part of the standard library, so in a Bundler project add it to your Gemfile:

```bash
bundle add net-smtp
```

Then send a plain-text message:

```ruby
require "net/smtp"

message = <<~MESSAGE
  From: Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>
  To: user@example.com
  Subject: Welcome to Acme
  MIME-Version: 1.0
  Content-Type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8

  Welcome! Thanks for signing up.
MESSAGE

Net::SMTP.start(
  "smtp.reloop.sh", 587,
  user: "reloop",
  secret: ENV.fetch("RELOOP_API_KEY"),
  authtype: :plain,
  starttls: :always,
) do |smtp|
  smtp.send_message(message, "hello@mail.acme.com", "user@example.com")
end
```

The username can be any string. The password is your API key. `starttls: :always` makes the connection fail instead of falling back to plain text if TLS is not available.

### Build HTML email with the mail gem

Writing MIME by hand gets messy once you need HTML, a plain-text fallback or attachments. The `mail` gem (the same one Action Mailer uses) builds the message and sends it over SMTP:

```bash
bundle add mail
```

```ruby
require "mail"

Mail.defaults do
  delivery_method :smtp,
    address: "smtp.reloop.sh",
    port: 587,
    user_name: "reloop",
    password: ENV.fetch("RELOOP_API_KEY"),
    authentication: :plain,
    enable_starttls: true
end

mail = Mail.new do
  from    "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>"
  to      "user@example.com"
  subject "Welcome to Acme"

  # Plain-text body first, then the HTML alternative
  text_part do
    body "Welcome! Thanks for signing up."
  end

  html_part do
    content_type "text/html; charset=UTF-8"
    body "<h1>Welcome!</h1><p>Thanks for signing up.</p>"
  end
end

mail.deliver!
```

### When port 587 is blocked

Some hosts block outbound 587. Reloop also accepts STARTTLS on port **2587** (and 2025), so only the port number changes:

```ruby
Net::SMTP.start(
  "smtp.reloop.sh", 2587,
  user: "reloop",
  secret: ENV.fetch("RELOOP_API_KEY"),
  authtype: :plain,
  starttls: :always,
) do |smtp|
  smtp.send_message(message, "hello@mail.acme.com", "user@example.com")
end
```

Reloop does not offer implicit TLS on port 465, so do not pass `tls: true` to `Net::SMTP`, or `ssl: true` / `tls: true` to the `mail` gem or Action Mailer. If the connection hangs or times out, see [SMTP ports explained](/blog/smtp-ports-explained).

### Handle SMTP errors

```ruby
begin
  Net::SMTP.start(
    "smtp.reloop.sh", 587,
    user: "reloop",
    secret: ENV.fetch("RELOOP_API_KEY"),
    authtype: :plain,
    starttls: :always,
  ) do |smtp|
    smtp.send_message(message, "hello@mail.acme.com", "user@example.com")
  end
rescue Net::SMTPAuthenticationError
  warn "Wrong API key"
rescue Net::SMTPServerBusy => e
  warn "Temporary failure, try again later: #{e.message}"
rescue Net::SMTPFatalError, Net::SMTPSyntaxError => e
  warn "Rejected: #{e.message}"
rescue Net::OpenTimeout, Net::ReadTimeout, SystemCallError => e
  warn "Network error: #{e.message}"
end
```

SMTP codes run the other way from HTTP: `4xx` replies (`Net::SMTPServerBusy`) are temporary and worth retrying, `5xx` replies (`Net::SMTPFatalError`) are permanent.

### Can I send with Gmail from Ruby?

For a personal script, yes: use `smtp.gmail.com` on port 587 with an [App Password](https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/185833). For an app, no. Gmail limits personal accounts to about 500 recipients a day, every message comes from your `@gmail.com` address, and bulk sending gets the account suspended.

---

## Method 2: Send email with the Ruby SDK

### Install

```bash
bundle add reloop
```

Or `gem install reloop` outside Bundler. The gem is `reloop` and you load it with `require "reloop"`.

### Send an email

```ruby
require "reloop"

reloop = Reloop::Client.new(api_key: ENV.fetch("RELOOP_API_KEY"))

begin
  result = reloop.mail.send(
    from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
    to: "user@example.com",
    subject: "Welcome to Acme",
    html: "<h1>Welcome!</h1><p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
    text: "Welcome! Thanks for signing up.",
  )
  puts "Sent: #{result["id"]}"
rescue Reloop::Error => e
  warn "Failed: #{e.message}"
rescue Faraday::Error => e
  warn "Network error: #{e.message}"
end
```

The SDK **raises** on failure. When the API answers with a non-`2xx` status you get a `Reloop::Error` whose message includes the status code and the error body. Connection failures and timeouts surface as `Faraday::Error`, since the SDK uses Faraday for HTTP. On success, `send` returns the parsed JSON response as a hash with string keys, so read the email ID with `result["id"]`.

The SDK passes your hash to the API as JSON, so field names match the [API reference](/docs/api/mail/post-api-mail-v1send) exactly: `reply_to`, `scheduled_at`, `template`, `attachments`.

### Send to several recipients

```ruby
reloop.mail.send(
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
  to: ["ada@example.com", "grace@example.com"],
  cc: "team@acme.com",
  reply_to: "support@acme.com",
  subject: "Your weekly report",
  text: "Here is your report.",
  tags: [{ name: "type", value: "weekly_report" }],
)
```

Every address in `to` sees the others. For personalized mail, send one message per recipient.

### Send a stored template

Keep copy out of your code so non-developers can edit it. Create the template in Reloop, then send it by ID with variables:

```ruby
reloop.mail.send(
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Welcome to Acme",
  template: {
    id: "tmpl_welcome",
    variables: { first_name: "Ada", plan: "Pro" },
  },
)
```

See [templates](/docs/learn/templates) for variables and defaults.

---

## Rails

Action Mailer works with any SMTP provider. Point it at Reloop and your mailers, Devise emails and [password reset emails](/blog/password-reset-email-best-practices) all go through Reloop.

### Store the key in credentials

```bash
bin/rails credentials:edit
```

```yaml
reloop:
  api_key: rl_your_api_key
```

### Configure Action Mailer

```ruby
# config/environments/production.rb
Rails.application.configure do
  config.action_mailer.delivery_method = :smtp
  config.action_mailer.smtp_settings = {
    address: "smtp.reloop.sh",
    port: 587,
    user_name: "reloop",
    password: Rails.application.credentials.dig(:reloop, :api_key),
    authentication: :plain,
    enable_starttls: true,
  }
  config.action_mailer.default_url_options = { host: "acme.com", protocol: "https" }
  config.action_mailer.raise_delivery_errors = true
end
```

Leave `ssl` and `tls` unset: Reloop uses STARTTLS, not implicit TLS. If 587 is blocked, set `port: 2587`.

### Write a mailer

```ruby
# app/mailers/application_mailer.rb
class ApplicationMailer < ActionMailer::Base
  default from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>"
  layout "mailer"
end

# app/mailers/user_mailer.rb
class UserMailer < ApplicationMailer
  def welcome
    @user = params[:user]
    mail(to: @user.email, subject: "Welcome to Acme")
  end
end
```

Add both `app/views/user_mailer/welcome.html.erb` and `app/views/user_mailer/welcome.text.erb`. Action Mailer sees the two templates and sends a multipart email with HTML and a plain-text fallback.

### Send it with deliver_later

```ruby
UserMailer.with(user: @user).welcome.deliver_later
```

`deliver_later` hands the email to Active Job, so the request returns without waiting on SMTP. New Rails 8 apps use Solid Queue in production, which stores jobs in your database so they survive restarts. Use `deliver_now` only in scripts and consoles.

### Use the SDK from Rails

When you want the API instead of SMTP, create one client in an initializer and reuse it:

```ruby
# config/initializers/reloop.rb
RELOOP = Reloop::Client.new(
  api_key: Rails.application.credentials.dig(:reloop, :api_key),
)
```

```ruby
# app/controllers/contacts_controller.rb
class ContactsController < ApplicationController
  def create
    result = RELOOP.mail.send(
      from: "Acme Website <contact@mail.acme.com>",
      to: "support@acme.com",
      reply_to: params.require(:email),
      subject: "New message from #{params[:email]}",
      text: params.require(:message),
    )
    render json: { id: result["id"] }
  rescue Reloop::Error, Faraday::Error
    render json: { error: "Could not send message" }, status: :bad_gateway
  end
end
```

The visitor's address goes in `reply_to`, never in `from`. You can only send from your verified domain, and putting someone else's domain in `from` fails [DMARC](/blog/gmail-yahoo-bulk-sender-requirements). Full example: [Rails guide](/docs/examples/ruby/rails).

---

## Sinatra

```ruby
# app.rb
require "sinatra"
require "json"
require "reloop"

RELOOP = Reloop::Client.new(api_key: ENV.fetch("RELOOP_API_KEY"))

post "/contact" do
  content_type :json
  data = JSON.parse(request.body.read)

  result = RELOOP.mail.send(
    from: "Acme Website <contact@mail.acme.com>",
    to: "support@acme.com",
    reply_to: data["email"],
    subject: "New contact form message",
    text: data["message"],
  )
  { id: result["id"] }.to_json
rescue Reloop::Error, Faraday::Error
  halt 502, { error: "Could not send message" }.to_json
end
```

Prefer SMTP? Use the `mail` gem settings from Method 1 with the same host, port and credentials.

---

## Attachments

With the SDK, pass base64 content:

```ruby
require "base64"

pdf = File.binread("invoice-1042.pdf")

reloop.mail.send(
  from: "Acme Billing <billing@mail.acme.com>",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Your invoice #1042",
  text: "Your invoice is attached.",
  attachments: [{
    filename: "invoice-1042.pdf",
    content: Base64.strict_encode64(pdf),
    content_type: "application/pdf",
  }],
)
```

On Ruby 3.4 and later, `base64` is a bundled gem too. Rails already depends on it; in a plain Bundler project, run `bundle add base64`.

In a Rails mailer, assign to `attachments`:

```ruby
def invoice
  attachments["invoice-1042.pdf"] = File.binread(Rails.root.join("tmp/invoice-1042.pdf"))
  mail(to: params[:user].email, subject: "Your invoice #1042")
end
```

With the `mail` gem, use `add_file`:

```ruby
mail.add_file(filename: "invoice-1042.pdf", content: pdf)
```

Keep attachments small. Many inboxes reject messages over 25 MB, and large files hurt deliverability. For big files, send a signed download link.

---

## Send in the background with Active Job

Sending inside a web request adds latency and fails the request when the provider is slow. `deliver_later` already moves Action Mailer sends into a job. Active Job does not retry failed deliveries on its own (some backends, like Sidekiq, add their own retries), so tell the delivery job which errors are temporary:

```ruby
# app/jobs/retrying_mail_delivery_job.rb
class RetryingMailDeliveryJob < ActionMailer::MailDeliveryJob
  retry_on Net::OpenTimeout, Net::ReadTimeout, Errno::ECONNRESET,
    Errno::ECONNREFUSED, Net::SMTPServerBusy,
    wait: :polynomially_longer, attempts: 5
end

# app/mailers/application_mailer.rb
class ApplicationMailer < ActionMailer::Base
  self.delivery_job = RetryingMailDeliveryJob
  default from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>"
  layout "mailer"
end
```

`wait: :polynomially_longer` needs Rails 7.1 or later. `Net::SMTPFatalError` and `Net::SMTPAuthenticationError` are left out on purpose. An invalid address or a wrong key fails the same way every time.

For API sends, write the job yourself. The rules are the same as for any HTTP API: **retry** network errors (no status at all), `429` and `5xx`. **Do not retry** other `4xx` errors: an invalid address or unverified domain fails the same way every time. The next section shows that job, with an idempotency key so retries are safe.

---

## Retries without duplicate emails

A request times out and your job retries. If the first attempt actually went through, the user gets two emails. The API prevents this with an [`Idempotency-Key` header](/docs/api/idempotency): repeat a request with the same key and Reloop returns the original send instead of sending again.

`Reloop::Error` does not expose the status code as a field, so this job calls the endpoint with `Net::HTTP` to decide what to retry:

```ruby
# app/jobs/send_receipt_job.rb
require "net/http"
require "json"

class SendReceiptJob < ApplicationJob
  class RetryableSendError < StandardError; end

  SEND_URL = URI("https://reloop.sh/api/mail/v1/send")

  retry_on RetryableSendError, wait: :polynomially_longer, attempts: 5

  def perform(order_id, to)
    request = Net::HTTP::Post.new(SEND_URL)
    request["x-api-key"] = Rails.application.credentials.dig(:reloop, :api_key)
    request["Content-Type"] = "application/json"
    request["Idempotency-Key"] = "receipt-#{order_id}"
    request.body = {
      from: "Acme <orders@mail.acme.com>",
      to: to,
      subject: "Receipt for order #{order_id}",
      text: "Thanks for your order.",
    }.to_json

    response = Net::HTTP.start(
      SEND_URL.host, SEND_URL.port,
      use_ssl: true, open_timeout: 10, read_timeout: 30,
    ) { |http| http.request(request) }

    status = response.code.to_i
    return JSON.parse(response.body)["id"] if response.is_a?(Net::HTTPSuccess)

    if status == 429 || status >= 500
      raise RetryableSendError, "Reloop returned #{status}"
    end

    # Other 4xx: do not retry
    raise "Send failed (#{status}): #{response.body}"
  rescue Net::OpenTimeout, Net::ReadTimeout, SocketError, SystemCallError => e
    raise RetryableSendError, e.message
  end
end
```

```ruby
SendReceiptJob.perform_later(order.id, order.email)
```

Base the key on the business event (`receipt-#{order_id}`), not a new UUID per attempt, so retries from any worker are safe. If an attempt failed before the email went out, a retry with the same key sends it.

If you only need deduplication and not status-based retries, the SDK works too. The API also reads the key from an `idempotency_key` field in the body, and the SDK passes it through:

```ruby
reloop.mail.send(
  from: "Acme <orders@mail.acme.com>",
  to: order.email,
  subject: "Receipt for order #{order.id}",
  text: "Thanks for your order.",
  idempotency_key: "receipt-#{order.id}",
)
```

---

## Testing without sending real email

- **Rails:** the test environment uses the `:test` delivery method, which stores emails in `ActionMailer::Base.deliveries` instead of sending them. Call `deliver_now` in mailer tests, or wrap `deliver_later` in `perform_enqueued_jobs`, then assert on the array.
- **Anything else:** stub the client in unit tests, and send to [test addresses](/docs/guides/testing-email-addresses) in staging so you do not hurt your [sender reputation](/blog/why-emails-land-in-spam-fix) with bounces.
- **Local SMTP:** run [Mailpit](https://mailpit.axllent.org) with `docker run -p 1025:1025 -p 8025:8025 axllent/mailpit`. In `config/environments/development.rb`, set `config.action_mailer.delivery_method = :smtp` and `config.action_mailer.smtp_settings = { address: "localhost", port: 1025 }`, with no user name, password or `enable_starttls`. Open `http://localhost:8025` to see the messages.

```ruby
# test/mailers/user_mailer_test.rb
class UserMailerTest < ActionMailer::TestCase
  test "welcome" do
    user = users(:ada)
    UserMailer.with(user: user).welcome.deliver_now

    email = ActionMailer::Base.deliveries.last
    assert_equal [user.email], email.to
    assert_equal "Welcome to Acme", email.subject
  end
end
```

---

## Production checklist

- [ ] API key in Rails credentials, an environment variable or a secrets manager
- [ ] Sending domain verified with SPF, DKIM and DMARC
- [ ] `from` on your verified domain; user addresses in `reply_to`
- [ ] Both HTML and plain-text bodies (`.html.erb` and `.text.erb` views)
- [ ] One shared client, created in an initializer
- [ ] Sending in a job (`deliver_later`, Solid Queue, Sidekiq), not the request
- [ ] Retries only on network errors, `429` and `5xx` (or SMTP `4xx`)
- [ ] Idempotency keys on anything that retries
- [ ] [Webhooks](/features/webhooks) for bounces and complaints
- [ ] Disposable addresses blocked at signup ([how](/blog/block-disposable-emails-at-signup))

## FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="How do I send an HTML email in Ruby?">
    With the mail gem, add a text_part with the plain-text version and an
    html_part with your HTML and a text/html content type. In Rails, add both
    an .html.erb and a .text.erb view for the mailer action. With the Reloop
    SDK, pass html and text keys to mail.send.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Why does Net::SMTP fail with cannot load such file?">
    Since Ruby 3.1, net-smtp is a bundled gem, not part of the default
    standard library. Under Bundler you have to list it in your Gemfile with
    bundle add net-smtp. Rails apps get it through the mail gem.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Should I use port 587 or 465 with Action Mailer?">
    Use 587 with enable_starttls set to true. Port 465 expects implicit TLS,
    which needs ssl or tls set to true instead. Reloop only offers STARTTLS,
    on ports 587, 2587 and 2025, so leave ssl and tls unset.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Why do my Ruby emails go to spam?">
    Usually the sending domain is not authenticated, or the From domain does
    not match the domain that signed the message. Set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC,
    send from your own domain, and always include a plain-text body.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can I use Reloop with Devise emails?">
    Yes. Devise sends through Action Mailer, so the SMTP settings shown above
    route confirmation, password reset and unlock emails through Reloop with
    no code changes.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# Transactional Email as a Growth Channel (Not Just Notifications)

Path: /blog/transactional-email-as-growth-channel
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/transactional-email-as-growth-channel
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/transactional-email-as-growth-channel.md

How to turn receipts, invites, usage alerts and digests into growth without breaking the rules for transactional mail: seven emails to improve, what to add to each, and how to send them with Reloop templates.

**Transactional emails are the emails your users actually wait for and open: receipts, invites, password resets, usage alerts.** That attention makes them one of your best growth channels, as long as the transactional content stays the main point and the growth part is one small, relevant next step. Done right, an invite brings in a new user, a usage alert becomes an upgrade, and a receipt becomes a referral.

This guide covers seven transactional emails worth improving, what to add to each one, the line you shouldn't cross, and how to send them with Reloop.

---

## Why transactional email is underrated

Most teams treat transactional email as plumbing. Someone wires up a password reset during the first sprint, and nobody touches it again.

That's a missed opportunity, for three reasons:

1. **Expected.** The user just did something and is waiting for the email. It doesn't have to compete for attention the way a newsletter does.
2. **In context.** It arrives at the exact moment the user is engaged with your product.
3. **Reaches everyone.** Every active user gets transactional email. Many never read your marketing.

The goal isn't to stuff marketing into receipts. It's to make each transactional email do its job so well that the natural next step is obvious.

---

## The line you shouldn't cross

Transactional email is treated differently by law and by mailbox providers because it's something the user asked for. In the US, the FTC's guidance on CAN-SPAM uses a "primary purpose" test: if the message's main purpose is commercial, it's a commercial email and needs commercial rules, like an opt-out. Other countries have their own versions.

A practical rule of thumb:

| Keep it transactional | Crosses the line |
|---|---|
| Receipt plus "invite your team" link at the bottom | Receipt with a big banner for an unrelated product |
| Usage alert that mentions the plan that fits | "Flash sale!" subject line on a usage alert |
| Invite email that explains what the product does | Invite email that's mostly a feature tour |
| One relevant next step | Three promotions and a newsletter signup |

If you're unsure, ask: would this email still make sense if I removed the growth part? If yes, you're fine. Also keep marketing mail on a separate subdomain, so a campaign that draws complaints can't slow down password resets.

---

## Seven transactional emails to improve

### 1. Team invite

The invite is the only email from you that a brand-new person reads. It's an acquisition email that most teams write as an afterthought.

| Include | Why |
|---|---|
| Who invited them, by name | People trust colleagues, not products |
| What the product does, in one sentence | They've likely never heard of you |
| What they'll see when they accept | Removes uncertainty |
| A single "Accept invite" button | One action |

**Subject:** `Ada invited you to the Acme workspace on Acme Analytics`

### 2. Usage limit alert

When a user approaches a plan limit, they're getting real value. That's the best moment to talk about upgrading, because the reason is concrete.

**Subject:** `You've used 80% of your monthly events`

Show the number, the date it resets, and what happens at 100%. Then mention the plan that fits, with one link. Send at 80% and again at 100%, never more often than that.

### 3. Receipt

Receipts get opened and kept. After the line items, one short line is enough: a referral link, or "Add a teammate for $8/month."

**Subject:** `Receipt for your Acme Pro subscription, May 2026`

### 4. Weekly or monthly digest

A summary of what happened in the user's account ("312 new signups this week, up from 280") reminds people the product is working for them, even when they don't log in. It's one of the best inactivity defences there is, alongside the [churn sequences](/blog/email-reduce-churn-sequences) that react when usage drops.

Only send it when there's something real to report, and let users turn it off in a preference center.

### 5. Milestone

"Your 1,000th invoice sent." Milestones are tiny moments of delight, and they're shareable. A "share this" link or a short note about what power users do next fits naturally.

### 6. Activity notification

"Ada commented on your report." These bring people back into the product. The growth lever is the content: show the actual comment, not just "you have a new notification", so the email is useful on its own and clicking through is the obvious next step.

### 7. Password reset and magic link

Don't add anything here. These must be fast, plain, and only about signing in (our [password reset guide](/blog/password-reset-email-best-practices) covers what belongs in one). The growth play is reliability: a magic link that arrives in two seconds is part of a good first impression. One that [lands in spam](/blog/why-emails-land-in-spam-fix) loses the user.

---

## Measuring it

| Email | Primary metric |
|---|---|
| Team invite | Invite acceptance rate |
| Usage alert | Upgrades within 7 days of the alert |
| Receipt | Clicks on the referral or add-seat link |
| Digest | Logins within 48 hours of sending |
| Milestone | Shares or clicks |
| Activity notification | Click-through to the item |

Opens are unreliable because of privacy features like Apple Mail Privacy Protection, so measure clicks and the action that follows. Tag each send so you can split the numbers by email type.

---

## Send them with Reloop

Transactional growth emails carry per-user data: a name, a usage number, a date. The cleanest setup is one [template](/docs/learn/templates) per email, with variables, sent from your app at the moment the event happens.

### 1. Create a template with variables

In the Reloop dashboard, create a template for the usage alert, or [have AI draft it](/blog/ai-generate-transactional-email-templates) for you. Template variables use triple braces and can have a default:

```html
<p>Hi {{{first_name}}},</p>
<p>
  You've used <strong>{{{used}}}</strong> of your
  <strong>{{{limit}}}</strong> monthly events. Your usage resets on
  {{{reset_date}}}.
</p>
<p>
  At 100%, new events are queued until the reset.
  The {{{suggested_plan}}} plan includes {{{suggested_limit}}} events.
</p>
<p><a href="{{{upgrade_url}}}">Compare plans</a></p>
```

### 2. Send it when the threshold is crossed

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY! });

  const percent = Math.round((usage.used / usage.limit) * 100);

  const { emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
    from: "Acme <billing@mail.acme.com>",
    to: user.email,
    subject: `You've used ${percent}% of your monthly events`,
    template: {
      id: "tmpl_usage_alert",
      variables: {
        first_name: user.firstName ?? "there",
        used: usage.used.toLocaleString(),
        limit: usage.limit.toLocaleString(),
        reset_date: usage.resetsOn,
        suggested_plan: "Growth",
        suggested_limit: "1,000,000",
        upgrade_url: "https://acme.com/settings/billing",
      },
    },
    tags: [{ name: "type", value: "usage_alert" }],
  });

  if (emailError) console.error(emailError);
}
```

Call it from wherever you count usage, and store which thresholds you've already alerted on so each user gets the 80% email once per cycle.

### 3. Make retries safe

Usage checks often run in background jobs that retry. Add an `Idempotency-Key` so a retried job can't send the alert twice. With the REST API:

```bash
curl -X POST https://reloop.sh/api/mail/v1/send \
  -H "x-api-key: $RELOOP_API_KEY" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: usage-alert-80-usr_123-2026-05" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "from": "Acme <billing@mail.acme.com>",
    "to": "ada@example.com",
    "subject": "You'\''ve used 80% of your monthly events",
    "template": { "id": "tmpl_usage_alert", "variables": { "used": "80,000", "limit": "100,000" } },
    "tags": [{ "name": "type", "value": "usage_alert" }]
  }'
```

See [idempotency](/docs/api/idempotency) for how long keys are remembered.

### 4. Send digests on a schedule

For a weekly digest, a cron job builds each user's summary and sends it with the same pattern: one template, variables for the numbers. Use `scheduled_at` if you want every digest to land at the same local time, for example Monday 9am in the user's timezone.

### 5. Give users control

Digests and milestone emails are optional. Put them in a [channel](/docs/learn/contacts/channels) (Reloop's subscription topics) so users can turn off "Weekly digest" in the preference center without unsubscribing from everything. Keep receipts, invites and security emails out of channels: users should always get those.

<Callout type="tip">
  Send transactional mail from its own subdomain (for example `mail.acme.com`) and marketing from another (`news.acme.com`). Reputation is tracked per domain, so a bad campaign can't drag down your password resets. Each subdomain needs its own [SPF, DKIM and DMARC](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide) records.
</Callout>

---

## A quick audit you can do today

1. List every transactional email your product sends. Most teams find a few they forgot about.
2. For each one, write down its single job and its one possible next step.
3. Read them on your phone. Anything over a screen and a half is too long.
4. Check who they come from. Replace `noreply@` with a real `reply_to` where replies would be useful.
5. Make sure each has a tag, so you can measure clicks per email type.
6. Pick the two with the most volume (usually invites and receipts) and improve those first.

---

## FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Can I put promotional content in a transactional email?">
    A small amount, if the transactional content is clearly the main point.
    In the US the FTC's "primary purpose" test applies; other countries have
    similar rules. Keep it to one relevant line or link, and check with your
    own legal counsel for anything more.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Do transactional emails need an unsubscribe link?">
    Purely transactional emails like receipts and password resets generally
    don't. Optional ones like digests should have one, and are best managed
    through subscription channels so users can opt out of just that type.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Should transactional and marketing email come from the same domain?">
    Use subdomains of the same brand domain, one for each. Recipients still
    recognise you, and reputation problems in one stream don't spill into
    the other.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Templates or HTML in code?">
    Templates. They let someone improve the copy without a deploy, and the
    same template can be sent from your app, an automation or the dashboard.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>
