# Reloop vs ZeptoMail (2026): Pricing, Features and Which to Choose

Path: /blog/reloop-vs-zeptomail
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-zeptomail
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-zeptomail.md

Reloop vs ZeptoMail (now Zoho CPaaS) compared honestly: pay-as-you-go credits vs monthly plans, transactional-only rules, inbound and agent inboxes, campaigns, self-hosting, and how to switch.

**ZeptoMail is one of the cheapest ways to send transactional email, and it's very good at exactly that one job.** Zoho sells it on prepaid credits with no monthly fee, it only allows transactional mail, and it recently became part of **Zoho CPaaS** alongside SMS, WhatsApp and voice. **Reloop costs a little more at high volume, but it also receives mail into real inboxes, runs campaigns and automations, and is open source, so you can host it yourself.**

We build Reloop, so weigh this accordingly. Where ZeptoMail is the better pick, we say so.

---

## The 30-second comparison

| | **Reloop** | **ZeptoMail (Zoho CPaaS)** |
|---|---|---|
| Pricing model | Monthly plans, or prepaid credits | Prepaid credits, no monthly fee |
| Free tier | 6,000 / mo, 200 / day | First credit free (10,000 emails) |
| 50,000 emails | **$10 / mo** | About $12.50 in credits |
| 100,000 emails | $20 / mo | About $25 in credits |
| Credits expire | After 6 months (if you buy credits) | After 6 months |
| Marketing email | Yes (campaigns) | Not allowed |
| Inbound email | Mailboxes with threads, API, MCP, IMAP | Not offered for receiving and storing mail |
| Automations | Yes | No |
| Dedicated IP | Included on Growth ($20) | Paid add-on (US, EU, IN) |
| SMTP relay | Yes | Yes |
| Open source / self-host | Yes (Apache 2.0) | No |

ZeptoMail's model is on [Zoho's pricing page](https://www.zoho.com/zeptomail/pricing.html): one credit sends 10,000 emails, the first credit is free, and credits are valid for 6 months. The per-credit price is widely listed at **$2.50** and varies by region, so check the page for yours. Reloop's prices are on [reloop.sh/pricing](/pricing).

---

## ZeptoMail is now Zoho CPaaS

If you've looked recently, you'll have noticed the change. Zoho's site now says "ZeptoMail is now Zoho CPaaS", built on the same email infrastructure and adding **SMS** (India only, in beta), **WhatsApp** and **voice**. The email product, API and SMTP relay are unchanged, and the API now lives at `cpaas.zoho.com`.

That's a plus if you also want OTPs over WhatsApp or SMS from one vendor. If you only need email, it doesn't change much.

---

## Pricing at real volumes

ZeptoMail is pay-as-you-go: you buy credits of 10,000 emails and spend them down. At the widely listed $2.50 per credit:

| Monthly volume | Reloop | ZeptoMail (approx.) | Cheaper |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3,000 | $0 | $0 (free credit) | Tie |
| 50,000 | $10 | $12.50 | Reloop |
| 100,000 | $20 | $25 | Reloop |
| 250,000 | $20 + $75 overage = $95 | $62.50 | **ZeptoMail** |
| 1,000,000 | $20 + $450 overage = $470 | $250 | **ZeptoMail** |

Being straight about it: **above roughly 150,000 emails a month, ZeptoMail is cheaper per email.** Below that, Reloop's flat plans win, and they include things ZeptoMail doesn't sell at all (inboxes, campaigns, automations, a dedicated IP on Growth).

Two details matter with credits:

- **They expire after 6 months.** Buying in bulk to save time can waste money if your volume drops.
- **The free credit is one-off.** It's 10,000 emails to get started, not a monthly allowance. Reloop's 6,000 free emails reset every month.

Reloop sells prepaid credits too, at $0.50 per 1,000 and also valid for 6 months. That's twice ZeptoMail's rate, so if credits are all you want, ZeptoMail is cheaper. Reloop's credits make sense when you want paid-plan limits without a monthly subscription.

And if you self-host Reloop, there's no per-email fee at all. See [self-hosted email infrastructure](/blog/self-hosted-email-infrastructure) for what that really involves.

---

## Developer experience

Both give you a REST API, an SMTP relay and official SDKs.

**ZeptoMail**

```typescript

const client = new SendMailClient({
  url: "api.zeptomail.com/",
  token: process.env.ZEPTOMAIL_TOKEN!,
});

await client.sendMail({
  from: { address: "hello@acme.com", name: "Acme" },
  to: [{ email_address: { address: "user@example.com", name: "Ada" } }],
  subject: "Welcome",
  htmlbody: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
});
```

**Reloop**

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY! });

const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Welcome",
  html: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
});
```

| | Reloop | ZeptoMail |
|---|---|---|
| Recipient shape | `"user@example.com"` or an array of strings | `[{ email_address: { address, name } }]` |
| Auth | `x-api-key` header | `Authorization: Zoho-enczapikey <token>` |
| Templates | Sent by ID with `{{{variables}}}` | `template_key` or `template_alias` with `merge_info` |
| Grouping sends | Domains and API keys | Mail Agents (per product, environment or team) |
| Error format | `message`, `why` and `fix` | Error code and message |
| SMTP | `smtp.reloop.sh`, API key as user and password | `smtp.zeptomail.com`, user `emailapikey` |

ZeptoMail's **Mail Agents** are a nice touch: each one has its own tokens, domains, webhooks and stats, so you can keep staging and production, or two products, cleanly apart.

Reloop's error shape is our one strong opinion. When a send fails, the error says **why** and **how to fix it**:

```json
{
  "message": "Domain not found",
  "why": "The domain mail.acme.com was not found or is not authorized for your organization",
  "fix": "Ensure the domain is registered and verified in your dashboard"
}
```

---

## Transactional only vs everything in one place

This is the biggest product difference.

**ZeptoMail only allows transactional email.** Its terms say you must not use it for marketing, promotional mail or newsletters, and accounts that keep doing so get blocked. That's a deliberate choice that protects its deliverability, but it means you need a second tool (often Zoho Campaigns) for anything else.

**Reloop covers both** while keeping them separate where it matters:

- **Transactional API and SMTP** for receipts, resets and alerts.
- **Contacts, groups and subscription channels**, with one suppression list across everything.
- **Broadcast campaigns** with scheduling.
- **Event-triggered automations**: call `reloop.automations.start` when a user signs up and run a sequence of delays, conditions and emails. See [welcome sequences that convert](/blog/welcome-email-sequences-that-convert).

If you'll only ever send receipts and OTPs, ZeptoMail's restriction costs you nothing. If you'll want onboarding or product announcements later, it's a second vendor and a second suppression list.

---

## Receiving email and agent inboxes

ZeptoMail is a sending service. Its webhooks report **opens, clicks and bounces**; we didn't find a feature for receiving mail on your domain and storing or threading it.

**Reloop receives mail into mailboxes.** Messages are stored, threaded, spam-scored with Rspamd, and readable over the API, the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) or IMAP. You can reply in-thread with one call, and an `email.received` webhook pushes new mail to you.

That matters for:

- **AI agents that handle email.** Give an agent its own address and let it read and reply. See [build an AI agent that reads and replies to email](/blog/build-ai-agent-sends-emails).
- **Support and reply handling** ("reply to this email to comment").

| | Reloop | ZeptoMail |
|---|---|---|
| Receive on your domain | Yes | No |
| Stored mailboxes with threads | Yes | No |
| Reply in thread via API | Yes | No |
| MCP and IMAP access | Yes | No |
| Delivery webhooks | Yes, signed (`Reloop-Signature`) | Yes (opens, clicks, bounces) |

---

## Deliverability

Both run their own sending infrastructure and handle SPF, DKIM, bounces, complaints and suppression.

- **ZeptoMail** keeps transactional mail on infrastructure that never carries marketing, which is the whole point of its policy. Dedicated IPs are a paid add-on in the US, EU and India regions.
- **Reloop** runs its own MTA (KumoMTA) with per-domain throttling and automatic pauses when bounce or complaint rates spike, and includes a dedicated IP on Growth. Read [how bounce processing works](/blog/email-bounce-processing-automation).

Either way, your own domain setup matters more than the provider. Check yours with our free [auth checker](/tools/auth-checker) and [blocklist checker](/tools/blocklist-checker).

---

## Self-hosting and lock-in

ZeptoMail is hosted-only, on Zoho's data centers. Reloop is Apache 2.0: start on Reloop Cloud, move to your own server later with the [one-command installer](/self-host) or [Coolify](/blog/reloop-coolify-setup), and point the SDK's `baseUrl` at your instance. Nothing else in your code changes.

---

## Where ZeptoMail is the better choice

- **You send a lot of purely transactional mail.** Above about 150k emails a month, credits are cheaper than Reloop's plans.
- **Your volume is spiky or seasonal.** No monthly fee means quiet months cost nothing, as long as you use credits within 6 months. Reloop has credits too, but at twice the per-email rate.
- **You're already on Zoho** (CRM, Desk, Books) and want one vendor and one bill.
- **You want WhatsApp, SMS or voice** from the same platform as email.

If you're comparing more cheap transactional senders, see the [best ZeptoMail alternatives](/blog/best-zeptomail-alternatives).

## Where Reloop is the better choice

- **You're under about 150k emails a month**, where Reloop's flat plans are cheaper.
- **You need to receive email**, especially for AI agents or support.
- **You want campaigns and automations** without a second tool.
- **You need open source or self-hosting** for compliance or data residency.

---

## Switching from ZeptoMail to Reloop

1. **Add your domain in Reloop** and publish the DKIM record (`reloop._domainkey`). Merge `include:reloop.sh` into your existing SPF record; don't add a second one.
2. **Swap the client.** Replace `client.sendMail` with `reloop.mail.send`. Flatten recipients from `{ email_address: { address } }` to plain strings, and rename `htmlbody` → `html`, `textbody` → `text`.
3. **Move templates.** Recreate them in Reloop and change placeholders to triple braces: `{{{user_name}}}`. Values you passed in `merge_info` become template variables.
4. **Map Mail Agents.** Use separate domains or API keys where you had separate agents.
5. **Point webhooks** at a new handler. Reloop events are `email.delivered`, `email.bounced`, `email.complained` and so on, signed with HMAC-SHA256 in the `Reloop-Signature` header.
6. **Ramp traffic** from 10% to 100% over a week or two. Use up remaining credits first if they're close to expiring.

Our [SendGrid migration guide](/blog/migrating-from-sendgrid) covers the traffic-split flag and suppression import in more detail.

# SPF, DKIM, and DMARC: The Complete Setup Guide (2026)

Path: /blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide.md

A thorough, practical guide to configuring SPF, DKIM, and DMARC for your sending domain  with exact DNS records, common mistakes, and a step-by-step verification checklist.

**Email authentication is no longer optionalwithout SPF, DKIM, and DMARC properly configured, your transactional emails will consistently land in spam or be dropped by inbox providers.**

When email protocols were originally designed in the 1970s, there was zero built-in identity verification. Anyone could inject arbitrary sender addresses into the `From:` header. Over subsequent decades, **SPF (Sender Policy Framework)**, **DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail)**, and **DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting & Conformance)** were introduced to close this vulnerability.

In 2024, **Google, Yahoo, and Microsoft made all three protocols strictly mandatory** for senders. If you are sending [transactional emails](/features/transaction-emails) today without valid authentication records, you are battling deliverability with both hands tied behind your back (see our deep dive on [why emails land in spam and how to fix it](/blog/why-emails-land-in-spam-fix)).

This guide walks you through configuring all three authentication layers correctly, in the exact sequence required, and verifying them with real-world tools before sending your first production message.

## Step 1: SPF (Sender Policy Framework)

**SPF is a DNS TXT record that explicitly declares which mail transfer agents and IP addresses are authorized to send email on behalf of your domain.**

When a mailbox provider (like Gmail or Outlook) receives a message claiming to come from `you@yourdomain.com`, it queries the SPF TXT record for `yourdomain.com` and checks whether the originating IP address is authorized. If the sender IP is not on that list, the message fails SPF evaluationand depending on your DMARC policy, it will be marked as spam or rejected outright.

### What an SPF record looks like

```
v=spf1 include:_spf.reloop.sh ~all
```

Breaking down the core components:

- `v=spf1`  **declares this record as an SPF version 1 specification** (must appear at the very beginning).
- `include:_spf.reloop.sh`  **authorizes all IP addresses published in Reloop's sending pool** to dispatch emails for your domain.
- `~all`  **specifies a SoftFail policy for unauthorized IPs**. This signals to receiving servers that unlisted IPs should be treated with suspicion, while allowing legitimate messages through during testing. Once your records are fully validated, you can graduate to `-all` (HardFail).

### How to add your SPF record

1. Log in to your DNS management console ([Cloudflare](https://dash.cloudflare.com), [AWS Route 53](https://aws.amazon.com/route53/), Namecheap, GoDaddy, etc.).
2. Create a new **TXT record** on your sending domain (`@` or `yourdomain.com`).
3. Set the record value to: `v=spf1 include:_spf.reloop.sh ~all`
4. Set the **TTL (Time to Live)** to **300 seconds** (a low TTL ensures quick propagation while debugging; increase to 3600+ after confirming delivery).

### The most common SPF mistake: Multiple TXT records

**Never create two SPF records for the same domain.** DNS RFC specifications strictly permit only **one SPF TXT record per hostname**. If you maintain multiple sending services (such as [Reloop](https://github.com/reloop-labs/reloop) for [transactional emails](/features/transaction-emails) alongside Google Workspace for corporate email), you must combine them into a single consolidated string:

```
v=spf1 include:_spf.reloop.sh include:_spf.google.com ~all
```

> **The 10-DNS-Lookup Limit**: SPF specifications enforce a strict limit of **10 DNS lookups** during recursive evaluation. Each `include:`, `a`, `mx`, `ptr`, and `exists` mechanism counts toward this quota. Exceeding 10 lookups triggers an immediate `PermError` validation failure. If you use numerous external providers, use an SPF flattening utility or consolidate providers.

### Verifying your SPF record

You can verify your DNS publication immediately using standard CLI utilities:

```bash
dig TXT yourdomain.com +short | grep spf
```

Alternatively, use the [MXToolbox SPF Lookup](https://mxtoolbox.com/spf.aspx) web tool. You should see a single TXT entry returned with your authorized `include:` directives.

## Step 2: DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail)

**DKIM adds an asymmetric cryptographic signature to every outgoing email header, guaranteeing that the message was not forged or tampered with in transit.**

When [Reloop's delivery engine](/features/deliverability) transmits an email, it calculates a hash of the headers and body, signs that hash with your private key, and embeds a `DKIM-Signature` header. The receiving mail server queries the corresponding public key published in your DNS, decrypts the signature, and verifies the hash matches. If the cryptographic signature matches, the recipient is assured that the email genuinely originated from your server and arrived intact.

### How Reloop handles DKIM

When you register a sending domain in the [Reloop dashboard](https://reloop.sh/dashboard/signup), Reloop automatically provisions a dedicated **2048-bit RSA cryptographic key pair** unique to your domain:

1. **Private Key**: Kept strictly confidential in Reloop's database and used by [Reloop's KumoMTA sending engine](/features/deliverability) to sign outgoing emails at send-time.
2. **Public Key**: Formatted as a standard DKIM DNS TXT record that you publish to your DNS provider under the `reloop._domainkey` selector.

### What Reloop's DKIM record looks like

You will receive a DNS TXT record structured as follows:

| Record Type | Host / Name | Value / Content |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **TXT** | `reloop._domainkey` | `v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=MIIBIjANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQEFAAOCAQ8AMIIBCgKCAQEA...` |

**Add the record exactly as shown in your Reloop dashboard.** The selector `reloop` tells receiving mail servers which public key record to look up when verifying signatures from your domain.

### Verifying your DKIM record

To confirm that your DKIM TXT record resolves properly in DNS:

```bash
dig TXT reloop._domainkey.yourdomain.com +short
```

You should see the published TXT record returned containing `v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=...`.

You can also send a test email to [mail-tester.com](https://mail-tester.com) or [check your raw message headers](/blog/why-emails-land-in-spam-fix) to inspect the evaluated `DKIM: PASS (selector=reloop)` status.

### Why DKIM sometimes fails after setup

- **DNS propagation delay**: DNS record updates can take anywhere from 15 minutes to 24 hours to propagate globally across resolver caches.
- **Accidental quote wrapping or truncation**: Some DNS providers (like Namecheap or GoDaddy) limit TXT record lengths or wrap strings in double quotes. Ensure the entire `p=` public key string is pasted without truncation or extra quotes.
- **Hostname duplication**: A frequent mistake is entering the full domain twice (e.g. `reloop._domainkey.yourdomain.com.yourdomain.com`). If your DNS provider automatically appends your domain, enter only `reloop._domainkey`.

## Step 3: DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting & Conformance)

**DMARC is the overarching policy and reporting framework that instructs receiving mail servers on how to handle messages that fail SPF or DKIM validation.**

Without DMARC, receiving servers must guess whether an unauthenticated email is malicious spoofing or simply a misconfigured server. DMARC gives you explicit control over enforcement, while instructing receiving servers to send XML telemetry reports regarding all messages delivered under your domain identity.

### The three DMARC policy modes

| Policy | Level | Effect on Delivery | Purpose |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `p=none` | **Monitoring** | **Zero impact on delivery**. Failing emails are still delivered to the inbox. Daily aggregate reports are generated. | **Always start here** to audit legitimate email traffic before enforcing rules. |
| `p=quarantine` | **Protection** | Emails that fail authentication are routed directly to the **Spam / Junk folder**. | Protects recipients from phishing while catching edge-case false positives. |
| `p=reject` | **Enforcement** | Emails failing authentication are **blocked and dropped outright at the SMTP handshake**. | The gold standard for complete brand protection and prerequisite for [BIMI logo verification](/blog/bimi-email-setup-guide). |

**Always begin your DMARC rollout at `p=none`. Never jump straight to `p=reject` on day one.** You need a minimum observation period (typically 2 to 4 weeks) to confirm that all legitimate outbound mail streams (transactional alerts, invoices, support platforms) are passing alignment.

### Your starter DMARC record

```
v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@yourdomain.com; ruf=mailto:dmarc@yourdomain.com; fo=1
```

Deconstructing the DMARC parameters:

- `v=DMARC1`  **identifies this record as DMARC protocol version 1** (must be the first tag).
- `p=none`  **sets the monitoring policy** so no valid messages are blocked during initial testing.
- `rua=mailto:dmarc@yourdomain.com`  **the destination email address for daily aggregate XML reports** (summary metrics across all receivers).
- `ruf=mailto:dmarc@yourdomain.com`  **the destination email address for real-time forensic failure reports** (sample headers of failed messages).
- `fo=1`  **generates forensic failure notifications** if either SPF or DKIM fails alignment.

### How to add your DMARC record

1. In your DNS dashboard, create a new **TXT record**.
2. In the **Host / Name** field, enter: `_dmarc` (or `_dmarc.yourdomain.com` depending on your provider).
3. In the **Value / Content** field, paste the DMARC record string above.
4. Save the record with a **300 second TTL**.

```bash
# Verify DMARC in DNS
dig TXT _dmarc.yourdomain.com +short
```

### Understanding DMARC Identifier Alignment

**DMARC evaluation requires identifier alignment between the header `From:` domain and the authenticated domains.**

An email passes DMARC if **either** of the following conditions is met:

1. **SPF Alignment**: The domain validated in the envelope sender (`Return-Path` / `Mail From`) matches the domain in the user-visible `From:` header.
2. **DKIM Alignment**: The domain specified in the `d=` tag of a valid `DKIM-Signature` header matches the domain in the user-visible `From:` header.

Because third-party email forwarders and mailing lists often break SPF by altering sending IPs, **DKIM alignment is crucial for reliable DMARC compliance**.

### Analyzing DMARC reports

Aggregate DMARC reports arrive as compressed XML files. Rather than reading raw XML, connect your reporting mailbox to free analysis tools such as [DMARC Analyzer](https://www.dmarcanalyzer.com), [Postmark DMARC Monitor](https://dmarc.postmarkapp.com), or [Valimail](https://www.valimail.com).

**Key metrics to monitor in your reports:**

- **Authentication Pass Rate**: Your legitimate sending services should maintain a **99%+ pass rate**.
- **Unrecognized Sending Sources**: Identify rogue marketing tools, unconfigured staging environments, or spoofing attempts sending under your brand.

### Graduating your DMARC policy to full enforcement

Once your reports confirm that 100% of your legitimate outbound mail passes SPF and DKIM:

1. **Step 1  Gradual Quarantine**:
   ```
   v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; pct=10; rua=mailto:dmarc@yourdomain.com
   ```
   The `pct=10` parameter applies quarantine enforcement to only 10% of failing messages.

2. **Step 2  Full Quarantine**:
   After 2 weeks with zero legitimate delivery issues, remove `pct=10` (or set `pct=100`):
   ```
   v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; rua=mailto:dmarc@yourdomain.com
   ```

3. **Step 3  Strict Reject Enforcement**:
   Upgrade your policy to `p=reject` to completely neutralize email spoofing:
   ```
   v=DMARC1; p=reject; rua=mailto:dmarc@yourdomain.com
   ```

At `p=reject`, you are also eligible to configure [BIMI (Brand Indicators for Message Identification)](/blog/bimi-email-setup-guide) to display your official brand logo in user inboxes.

## The complete verification checklist

Run through this pre-flight checklist before routing production traffic:

- [ ] **Single SPF record**: `dig TXT yourdomain.com` returns exactly one consolidated SPF TXT record without duplicate tags.
- [ ] **SPF lookup limit under 10**: The record contains fewer than 10 total DNS lookups.
- [ ] **Reloop SPF included**: The SPF string contains `include:_spf.reloop.sh`.
- [ ] **DKIM TXT record active**: `dig TXT reloop._domainkey.yourdomain.com` resolves with your valid public key.
- [ ] **DMARC TXT record in place**: `_dmarc.yourdomain.com` is published with at least `p=none` and a working `rua` report destination.
- [ ] **Mail-Tester test passed**: Send a message to [mail-tester.com](https://mail-tester.com) and confirm a score of **9+/10** with SPF, DKIM, and DMARC passing.
- [ ] **Google Postmaster Tools configured**: Register your domain with [Google Postmaster Tools](https://postmaster.google.com) to track domain and IP reputation.
- [ ] **Automated bounce tracking**: Verify that hard and soft bounces are captured via [signed webhooks](/features/webhooks) (see our guide on [email bounce processing automation](/blog/email-bounce-processing-automation)).

## What Reloop's dashboard does for you

When you add a sending domain in the [Reloop dashboard](https://reloop.sh/dashboard/signup), the platform simplifies the entire authentication lifecycle:

1. **Automated Key Generation**: Reloop automatically provisions dedicated RSA-2048 DKIM key pairs for your domain.
2. **One-Click DNS Directives**: Copy ready-to-paste SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records tailored to your specific domain structure.
3. **Live DNS Status Probing**: Reloop periodically queries your DNS records and provides real-time verification indicators in the dashboard.
4. **Deliverability & Bounce Management**: Built-in [bounce classification](/blog/email-bounce-processing-automation), [real-time email analytics](/features/email-analytics), and suppression lists keep your sender reputation safe.
5. **Developer APIs & Drop-in SDKs**: Send authenticated mail via [Node.js, Python, or Go SDKs](/sdk) or drop-in [SMTP relay](/features/smtp).

Whether you choose [Reloop Cloud pricing](/pricing) for managed deliverability or [self-host Reloop on your own infrastructure](/self-host) (for under $5/mo with our [self-host tutorial](/blog/self-host-email-5-dollars)), the authentication requirements remain identical.

## Common gotchas & deliverability pitfalls

### 1. Subdomain vs. root domain sending
If you send notifications from `notifications.yourdomain.com`, your SPF and DKIM records must be added directly to the `notifications` subdomain DNS zone. While DMARC policies on the root domain (`yourdomain.com`) automatically protect subdomains by default, SPF and DKIM do not inherit down.

### 2. IP warming for high-volume senders
Email authentication establishes your domain identity, but **it does not replace IP and domain reputation**. If you plan to send more than 10,000 emails per day, follow our structured [IP warming sequence guide](/blog/ip-warming-guide) to avoid triggering algorithmic spam filters at Gmail and Microsoft.

### 3. Separating transactional and marketing streams
**Never mix transactional receipts with marketing newsletters on the same sending domain or IP.** Protect your mission-critical password resets and auth tokens by isolating them on a dedicated transactional subdomain (see [transactional email best practices](/blog/transactional-email-best-practices)).

# Reloop vs Amazon SES (2026): Pricing, Features and Which to Choose

Path: /blog/reloop-vs-aws-ses
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-aws-ses
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-aws-ses.md

Reloop vs Amazon SES compared honestly: per-email cost vs total cost, the sandbox, bounce and complaint handling, templates, logs, inbound mail, self-hosting, and how to switch.

**Amazon SES is the cheapest way to push an email out of a server.** At $0.10 per 1,000 messages, nothing hosted beats it on the per-email line item, and we won't pretend otherwise. **Reloop is a complete email product**: API, SMTP, templates, logs, webhooks, campaigns, automations and inboxes in one place, open source, and self-hostable. The real question isn't which is cheaper per email. It's how much of the product around SES you want to build and run yourself.

We build Reloop, so weigh this accordingly. SES prices below are from the [Amazon SES pricing page](https://aws.amazon.com/ses/pricing/), and where SES is the better pick, we say so.

---

## The 30-second comparison

| | **Reloop** | **Amazon SES** |
|---|---|---|
| Free | 6,000 / mo, 200 / day | $200 AWS Free Tier credits (first 6 months) |
| List price | $10 / mo for 50,000 | $0.10 per 1,000 |
| 100,000 emails / mo | $20 | **~$10 + data transfer** |
| Extra emails | $0.50 per 1,000 | **$0.10 per 1,000** + $0.12 / GB outbound |
| What you get | Full platform | Sending pipe |
| Bounce and complaint events | Signed webhooks | SNS / EventBridge, you wire it up |
| Delivery logs and dashboard | Built in | CloudWatch / DIY |
| Template management | Yes, with editor | Limited (API-managed) |
| Inbound email | Mailboxes with threads, API, MCP, IMAP | Receipt rules to S3, SNS or Lambda |
| Agent inbox | Yes | No |
| Campaigns and automations | Yes | No (DIY) |
| Open source | Yes (Apache 2.0) | No |
| Self-host | Yes | AWS-managed only |

---

## Pricing: SES wins the line item

Let's get this out of the way. If you compare only the send price, SES is cheaper at every paid volume:

| Monthly volume | Reloop | Amazon SES (send only) |
|---|---|---|
| 3,000 | $0 | ~$0.30 (or covered by credits) |
| 50,000 | $10 | ~$5 |
| 100,000 | $20 | ~$10 |
| 1,000,000 | $20 + $450 overage = $470 | ~$100 |

SES also charges $0.12 per GB of outbound data, which adds up with large HTML or attachments, and $0.16 per 1,000 on the Essentials tier if you want its extra features. At a million emails a month, though, SES is clearly cheaper on paper.

What that table leaves out is everything you build around SES:

- **Event handling.** A configuration set, an SNS topic or EventBridge rule, and a Lambda or queue consumer to process bounces, complaints and deliveries.
- **Suppression and logs.** Somewhere to store every message's status so support can answer "did the reset email arrive?"
- **Templates.** A way for non-engineers to edit email content without a deploy.
- **A dashboard.** CloudWatch metrics, or an internal admin UI.
- **Campaigns.** A separate tool for newsletters and lifecycle mail.

None of that is hard on its own. Together it's weeks of engineering plus ongoing maintenance, and engineering time costs far more than the $10 difference at 100k emails. That's the trade: **SES is cheaper to send with; Reloop is cheaper to own** until you reach the volume where the per-email savings pay for a team to maintain the glue.

And if you self-host Reloop, there's no per-email fee at all. You pay for the server, the same way you would around SES.

<Callout type="tip">
  Price your whole stack, not the send call. Add up the SNS, Lambda, storage and CloudWatch pieces, plus the hours to build and maintain them, before deciding SES is cheaper for you.
</Callout>

---

## Getting started

### The SES sandbox

Every new SES account starts in the **sandbox**: you can only send to addresses and domains you've verified, with low sending limits. To email real users you request production access from AWS, describe your use case and how you handle bounces and complaints, and wait for approval. It's a sensible anti-abuse step, but it's a step, and requests are sometimes denied or need a second round.

On Reloop, you verify your domain and send. The free tier's 200-a-day cap is the only limit on day one.

### Sending code

**Amazon SES (AWS SDK v3)**

```typescript

const ses = new SESv2Client({ region: "us-east-1" });

await ses.send(
  new SendEmailCommand({
    FromEmailAddress: "Acme <hello@acme.com>",
    Destination: { ToAddresses: ["user@example.com"] },
    Content: {
      Simple: {
        Subject: { Data: "Welcome" },
        Body: { Html: { Data: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>" } },
      },
    },
    ConfigurationSetName: "transactional",
  }),
);
```

**Reloop**

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY! });

const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Welcome",
  html: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
});
```

The SES call needs IAM credentials with `ses:SendEmail` permission and a region. Reloop needs an API key. SES throws exceptions such as `MessageRejected`; Reloop returns errors as values, with a `message`, a `why` and a `fix`:

```json
{
  "message": "Domain not found",
  "why": "The domain mail.acme.com was not found or is not authorized for your organization",
  "fix": "Ensure the domain is registered and verified in your dashboard"
}
```

---

## Bounces, complaints and suppression

This is where most of the SES glue code lives.

**On SES**, delivery events are published through a configuration set to SNS, EventBridge, Kinesis Firehose or CloudWatch. You then:

1. Create the topic or rule and subscribe a Lambda, queue or HTTPS endpoint.
2. Parse each event and store it against the message.
3. Decide which bounces are permanent and add those addresses to a suppression list (SES has an account-level list, but your app usually needs its own view too).
4. Alert someone when bounce or complaint rates climb, because AWS reviews and can pause accounts that stay too high.

**On Reloop**, the same events arrive as webhooks (`email.delivered`, `email.bounced`, `email.complained` and so on), signed with HMAC-SHA256 in the `Reloop-Signature` header. Hard bounces and complaints are suppressed automatically, every message has a searchable log, and sending pauses itself when bounce or complaint rates spike. See [how bounce processing works](/blog/email-bounce-processing-automation).

| | Reloop | Amazon SES |
|---|---|---|
| Delivery events | Signed webhooks | SNS / EventBridge / Firehose |
| Per-message log | Built in, searchable | Build it (e.g. events to S3 or a database) |
| Automatic suppression | Yes | Account-level list; app view is DIY |
| Dashboard | Built in | CloudWatch |
| Templates | Editor, sent by ID with `{{{variables}}}` | API-managed templates |

---

## Receiving email and agent inboxes

**SES** can receive mail on your domain. Receipt rules hand each message to S3, SNS or Lambda, and from there storage, threading, spam handling and replies are yours to build.

**Reloop** receives mail into **mailboxes**. Messages are stored, threaded, spam-scored with Rspamd, and readable over the API, the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) or IMAP. You can reply in-thread with one call, and there's an `email.received` webhook for push notifications.

That's the difference between "a raw MIME file landed in a bucket" and "an AI agent can read the conversation and answer it." If you're building agents, support inboxes or reply-by-email features, see [build an AI agent that reads and replies to email](/blog/build-ai-agent-sends-emails).

---

## Campaigns and automations

SES is a sending service. Newsletters, contact lists, unsubscribe handling and lifecycle sequences need another tool or your own code.

Reloop includes contacts with custom properties, groups, subscription channels, scheduled broadcasts, and **event-triggered automations** with delays, conditions and email steps. Transactional and marketing mail share one suppression list, so an address that bounced on a receipt doesn't get your next newsletter. See [welcome sequences that convert](/blog/welcome-email-sequences-that-convert) for an example.

---

## Deliverability

Both handle the fundamentals: SPF, DKIM, DMARC, bounce and complaint processing. Deliverability mostly depends on your domain setup and list hygiene, not the provider's logo.

- **Sending path.** SES uses AWS's shared pools, with dedicated IPs as an add-on. Reloop runs its own MTA (KumoMTA) with per-domain throttling, and includes a dedicated IP on Growth ($20/mo).
- **Reputation guardrails.** AWS watches your bounce and complaint rates and can put your account under review. Reloop pauses sending automatically when rates spike, before a mailbox provider has to.
- **Tools.** Reloop ships free [domain reputation](/tools/domain-reputation-checker), [blocklist](/tools/blocklist-checker) and [auth](/tools/auth-checker) checkers you can run before you send.

---

## Self-hosting and lock-in

SES is AWS-managed only, and the glue you build around it (SNS topics, Lambdas, IAM policies) is AWS-specific too.

Reloop is Apache 2.0. You can start on Reloop Cloud, then move to your own server, including inside your AWS account, with the [one-command installer](/self-host). Point the SDK's `baseUrl` at your instance and nothing else in your code changes. That keeps data in your VPC without assembling the product yourself. Read [self-hosted email infrastructure](/blog/self-hosted-email-infrastructure) for what running it really involves.

---

## Where Amazon SES is the better choice

Being honest about it:

- **You send millions of emails a month** and already have a platform team. At that scale the per-email savings can pay for the glue code.
- **You only need a pipe.** Password resets from one service, no dashboard, no campaigns, no inbound, and an engineer who's happy to own the SNS wiring.
- **You're all-in on AWS** and your compliance setup requires everything to be an AWS-managed service.

If neither fits, our list of the [best Amazon SES alternatives](/blog/best-aws-ses-alternatives) compares more options at a similar price.

## Where Reloop is the better choice

- **You want logs, webhooks, suppression and templates on day one** instead of building them.
- **You need inbound mail as real inboxes**, especially for AI agents.
- **You want transactional mail, campaigns and automations** in one product with one suppression list.
- **You want open source or self-hosting** without being tied to one cloud.

---

## Switching from SES to Reloop

1. **Add your domain in Reloop** and publish the DKIM record (`reloop._domainkey`). Merge `include:reloop.sh` into your existing SPF record. Don't add a second SPF record.
2. **Swap the client.** Replace `SendEmailCommand` calls with `reloop.mail.send`. If you send through SES's SMTP interface, point it at `smtp.reloop.sh` and use your Reloop API key as both username and password.
3. **Move templates.** Change SES's `{{variable}}` placeholders to triple braces: `{{{variable}}}`.
4. **Replace the event pipeline.** Point a webhook at a new handler, verify the `Reloop-Signature` header, and retire the SNS topics and Lambdas once traffic has moved.
5. **Import suppressions** from SES's account-level suppression list so you don't re-mail addresses that already bounced.
6. **Ramp traffic** from 10% to 100% over a week or two, then remove SES's DNS records.

Our [SendGrid migration guide](/blog/migrating-from-sendgrid) covers the traffic-split flag and suppression import in more detail; the same approach works when coming from SES.

---

## FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Is Reloop cheaper than Amazon SES?">
    Not per email. SES lists $0.10 per 1,000 messages, and Reloop's overage is
    $0.50 per 1,000. Reloop competes on total cost: the logs, webhooks,
    suppression, templates, campaigns and inboxes you'd otherwise build and
    maintain around SES.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Does Reloop use SES to send?">
    No. Reloop runs its own MTA (KumoMTA). Self-hosted Reloop includes outbound
    delivery, so you don't need SES alongside it.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can I run Reloop inside my AWS account?">
    Yes. Reloop is Apache 2.0 and runs anywhere Docker runs, including EC2,
    ECS or EKS, so your data stays in your VPC.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Is there a sandbox on Reloop like on SES?">
    No production-access review. Verify your domain and you can send to any
    recipient, within the free tier's 6,000 a month and 200 a day.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can I migrate my SES SMTP integration without code changes?">
    Mostly. Change the SMTP host to `smtp.reloop.sh` and use your Reloop API
    key as the username and password. You'll still need new DNS records and a
    webhook handler in place of SNS.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# How to Send Email in C#: MailKit, ASP.NET Core and API

Path: /blog/send-email-csharp
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/send-email-csharp
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/send-email-csharp.md

Send email from C# and .NET with MailKit over SMTP or with an email API. Copy-paste examples for ASP.NET Core minimal APIs, HTML email, attachments, background sending and retries without duplicates.

**C# sends email over SMTP with [MailKit](https://github.com/jstedfast/MailKit), or over HTTPS with an email API SDK.** Skip the built-in `System.Net.Mail.SmtpClient`: Microsoft's own documentation says it is not recommended for new development because it does not support many modern protocols, and points you to MailKit instead.

This guide covers MailKit, the Reloop .NET SDK and ASP.NET Core minimal APIs, then the production details: attachments, background sending with `BackgroundService` and `Channel<T>`, and safe retries.

Writing another language? See [how to send email in Python](/blog/send-email-python), [Node.js](/blog/send-email-nodejs) or [Java](/blog/send-email-java).

---

## Which approach should you use?

| | MailKit (SMTP) | Email API SDK |
|---|----------------|---------------|
| **Install** | `dotnet add package MailKit` | `dotnet add package Reloop` |
| **Transport** | SMTP on port 587 (STARTTLS) | HTTPS on port 443 |
| **Building the message** | `MimeMessage` and `BodyBuilder` | A `SendMailParams` object with `Html`, `Text`, `Attachments` |
| **Errors** | `SmtpCommandException`, `AuthenticationException` | `ReloopApiException` with a `Status` |
| **Safe retries** | No, a retry can send twice | Yes, with an idempotency key |
| **Works with libraries that expect SMTP** | Yes, natively | Through SMTP settings |

If a library or an existing system only speaks SMTP, use MailKit. If you are writing the send call yourself, use the API.

---

## Prerequisites

1. **.NET 8 or later**
2. A **verified sending domain** with [SPF, DKIM and DMARC](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide)
3. An **API key** from the [Reloop dashboard](https://reloop.sh/dashboard). Keys start with `rl_`, and the same key works for the API and SMTP.

```bash
```

Keep the key in the environment, user secrets or a secrets manager, never in your code, `appsettings.json` or git.

---

## Method 1: Send email with MailKit

```bash
dotnet add package MailKit
```

MailKit builds messages with MimeKit, which it installs for you. `BodyBuilder` creates the multipart body with the plain-text and HTML versions:

```csharp
using MailKit.Net.Smtp;
using MailKit.Security;
using MimeKit;

var apiKey = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("RELOOP_API_KEY")
    ?? throw new InvalidOperationException("RELOOP_API_KEY is not set");

var message = new MimeMessage();
message.From.Add(new MailboxAddress("Acme", "hello@mail.acme.com"));
message.To.Add(MailboxAddress.Parse("user@example.com"));
message.Subject = "Welcome to Acme";

var body = new BodyBuilder
{
    TextBody = "Welcome! Thanks for signing up.",
    HtmlBody = "<h1>Welcome!</h1><p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
};
message.Body = body.ToMessageBody();

using var smtp = new SmtpClient { Timeout = 30_000 };
await smtp.ConnectAsync("smtp.reloop.sh", 587, SecureSocketOptions.StartTls);
await smtp.AuthenticateAsync("reloop", apiKey);
await smtp.SendAsync(message);
await smtp.DisconnectAsync(true);
```

The username can be any string. The password is your API key. `Timeout` is in milliseconds; the default is two minutes.

`SmtpClient` here is `MailKit.Net.Smtp.SmtpClient`. If a file also imports `System.Net.Mail`, the names clash, so leave that namespace out or use an alias.

### When port 587 is blocked

Some hosts block outbound 587. Reloop also accepts STARTTLS on port **2587** (and 2025), so only the port number changes:

```csharp
await smtp.ConnectAsync("smtp.reloop.sh", 2587, SecureSocketOptions.StartTls);
```

Reloop does not offer implicit TLS on port 465, so do not use `SecureSocketOptions.SslOnConnect`. Prefer `StartTls` over `Auto` or `StartTlsWhenAvailable`: it fails the connection if the server does not offer STARTTLS, instead of carrying on without encryption. If the connection hangs or times out, see [SMTP ports explained](/blog/smtp-ports-explained).

### Handle SMTP errors

```csharp
try
{
    using var smtp = new SmtpClient { Timeout = 30_000 };
    await smtp.ConnectAsync("smtp.reloop.sh", 587, SecureSocketOptions.StartTls);
    await smtp.AuthenticateAsync("reloop", apiKey);
    await smtp.SendAsync(message);
    await smtp.DisconnectAsync(true);
}
catch (AuthenticationException)
{
    Console.Error.WriteLine("Wrong API key");
}
catch (SmtpCommandException ex) when (ex.ErrorCode == SmtpErrorCode.RecipientNotAccepted)
{
    Console.Error.WriteLine($"Rejected recipient: {ex.Mailbox}");
}
catch (SmtpCommandException ex)
{
    Console.Error.WriteLine($"SMTP error {(int)ex.StatusCode}: {ex.Message}");
}
catch (Exception ex) when (ex is SmtpProtocolException or IOException
    or System.Net.Sockets.SocketException or TimeoutException)
{
    Console.Error.WriteLine($"Connection failed: {ex.Message}");
}
```

`AuthenticationException` here is `MailKit.Security.AuthenticationException`, not the one in `System.Security.Authentication`. A refused connection throws `SocketException`, and a connection that hits `Timeout` throws `TimeoutException`.

### Can I send with Gmail from C#?

For a personal script, yes: use `smtp.gmail.com` on port 587 with an [App Password](https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/185833). For an app, no. Gmail limits personal accounts to about 500 recipients a day, every message comes from your `@gmail.com` address, and bulk sending gets the account suspended.

## Method 2: Send email with the .NET SDK

### Install

```bash
dotnet add package Reloop
```

The package targets .NET Standard 2.0, so .NET Framework projects can reference it too.

### Send an email

```csharp
using Reloop;
using Reloop.Exceptions;
using static Reloop.Models.MailModels;

using var reloop = new ReloopClient(
    Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("RELOOP_API_KEY")
        ?? throw new InvalidOperationException("RELOOP_API_KEY is not set"));

try
{
    var result = await reloop.Mail.SendAsync(new SendMailParams
    {
        From = "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
        To = "user@example.com",
        Subject = "Welcome to Acme",
        Html = "<h1>Welcome!</h1><p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
        Text = "Welcome! Thanks for signing up.",
    });
    Console.WriteLine($"Sent: {result?.Id}");
}
catch (ReloopValidationException ex)
{
    Console.Error.WriteLine($"Invalid {ex.Field}: {ex.Message}");
}
catch (ReloopApiException ex)
{
    Console.Error.WriteLine($"Failed: {ex.Status} {ex.Message} {ex.Body.Fix}");
}
```

The SDK **throws** on failure:

- `ReloopValidationException` means a required field (`From`, `To` or `Subject`) is missing. No request is made.
- `ReloopApiException` means the API returned a non-2xx status, or the request never got a response. Network failures come back with `Status` `0`. `Body` holds the API's `Message`, `Why`, `Fix` and `Link`.
- A request that runs past the `HttpClient` timeout throws `TaskCanceledException`, not `ReloopApiException`. Treat it as a network error.

The model classes (`SendMailParams`, `SendMailTag`, `SendMailAttachment`, `SendMailTemplate`) are nested in `Reloop.Models.MailModels`, which is why the example uses `using static`.

Create the client **once** and reuse it. It wraps an `HttpClient`, and `ReloopClient` is `IDisposable`. In ASP.NET Core, register it as a singleton (shown below).

### Send to several recipients

```csharp
await reloop.Mail.SendAsync(new SendMailParams
{
    From = "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
    To = new[] { "ada@example.com", "grace@example.com" },
    Cc = "team@acme.com",
    ReplyTo = "support@acme.com",
    Subject = "Your weekly report",
    Text = "Here is your report.",
    Tags = new List<SendMailTag> { new("type", "weekly_report") },
});
```

`To` takes a single string or a collection of strings. Every address in `To` sees the others. For personalized mail, send one message per recipient.

### Send a stored template

Keep copy out of your code so non-developers can edit it. Create the template in Reloop, then send it by ID with variables:

```csharp
await reloop.Mail.SendAsync(new SendMailParams
{
    From = "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
    To = "user@example.com",
    Subject = "Welcome to Acme",
    Template = new SendMailTemplate
    {
        Id = "tmpl_welcome",
        Variables = new Dictionary<string, object>
        {
            ["first_name"] = "Ada",
            ["plan"] = "Pro",
        },
    },
});
```

See [templates](/docs/learn/templates) for variables and defaults.

## ASP.NET Core

Put the settings in configuration and bind them to an options class. The sender address can live in `appsettings.json`:

```json
{
  "Reloop": {
    "From": "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>"
  }
}
```

The API key does not belong there. In development, store it with user secrets:

```bash
dotnet user-secrets init
dotnet user-secrets set "Reloop:ApiKey" "rl_your_api_key"
```

In production, set the environment variable `Reloop__ApiKey`. The double underscore maps to the `Reloop:ApiKey` configuration key.

```csharp
// ReloopOptions.cs
using System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations;

public sealed class ReloopOptions
{
    public const string Section = "Reloop";

    [Required]
    public string ApiKey { get; set; } = "";

    [Required]
    public string From { get; set; } = "";
}
```

Register the client as a singleton so the whole app shares one connection pool:

```csharp
// Program.cs
using System.Net.Mail;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Options;
using Reloop;
using Reloop.Exceptions;
using static Reloop.Models.MailModels;

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services
    .AddOptions<ReloopOptions>()
    .Bind(builder.Configuration.GetSection(ReloopOptions.Section))
    .ValidateDataAnnotations()
    .ValidateOnStart();

builder.Services.AddSingleton(sp =>
{
    var options = sp.GetRequiredService<IOptions<ReloopOptions>>().Value;
    var http = new HttpClient(new SocketsHttpHandler
    {
        PooledConnectionLifetime = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5),
    })
    {
        Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30),
    };
    return new ReloopClient(options.ApiKey, httpClient: http);
});

var app = builder.Build();

app.MapPost("/contact", async (
    ContactRequest body,
    ReloopClient reloop,
    IOptions<ReloopOptions> options) =>
{
    if (!MailAddress.TryCreate(body.Email, out _))
    {
        return Results.BadRequest(new { error = "Invalid email address" });
    }

    try
    {
        var result = await reloop.Mail.SendAsync(new SendMailParams
        {
            From = options.Value.From,
            To = "support@acme.com",
            ReplyTo = body.Email,
            Subject = $"New message from {body.Email}",
            Text = body.Message,
        });
        return Results.Ok(new { id = result?.Id });
    }
    catch (ReloopApiException ex)
    {
        app.Logger.LogError(ex, "Send failed with status {Status}", ex.Status);
        return Results.Problem("Could not send message", statusCode: 502);
    }
});

app.Run();

record ContactRequest(string Email, string Message);
```

A few details matter here:

- `ValidateOnStart` makes the app fail at startup if the key or sender is missing, instead of on the first send.
- Passing your own `HttpClient` sets the timeout (the default is 100 seconds) and `PooledConnectionLifetime` lets a long-lived client pick up DNS changes.
- The visitor's address goes in `ReplyTo`, never in `From`. You can only send from your verified domain, and putting someone else's domain in `From` fails [DMARC](/blog/gmail-yahoo-bulk-sender-requirements).

### ASP.NET Core Identity emails

Identity sends confirmation and [password reset emails](/blog/password-reset-email-best-practices) through `IEmailSender<TUser>`. Implement it with the shared client:

```csharp
using System.Net;
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Identity;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Options;
using Reloop;
using static Reloop.Models.MailModels;

public sealed class ReloopIdentityEmailSender(
    ReloopClient reloop,
    IOptions<ReloopOptions> options) : IEmailSender<IdentityUser>
{
    public Task SendConfirmationLinkAsync(IdentityUser user, string email, string confirmationLink) =>
        SendAsync(email, "Confirm your email",
            $"<p><a href=\"{confirmationLink}\">Confirm your email</a></p>",
            $"Confirm your email: {WebUtility.HtmlDecode(confirmationLink)}");

    public Task SendPasswordResetLinkAsync(IdentityUser user, string email, string resetLink) =>
        SendAsync(email, "Reset your password",
            $"<p><a href=\"{resetLink}\">Reset your password</a></p>",
            $"Reset your password: {WebUtility.HtmlDecode(resetLink)}");

    public Task SendPasswordResetCodeAsync(IdentityUser user, string email, string resetCode) =>
        SendAsync(email, "Your password reset code",
            $"<p>Your code is <strong>{resetCode}</strong></p>",
            $"Your code is {resetCode}");

    private Task SendAsync(string to, string subject, string html, string text) =>
        reloop.Mail.SendAsync(new SendMailParams
        {
            From = options.Value.From,
            To = to,
            Subject = subject,
            Html = html,
            Text = text,
        });
}
```

```csharp
builder.Services.AddTransient<IEmailSender<IdentityUser>, ReloopIdentityEmailSender>();
```

Identity passes the links already HTML-encoded, which is right for the `href` but not for the plain-text body, hence `WebUtility.HtmlDecode`. Use your own user type in place of `IdentityUser` if you have one.

---

## Attachments

With the SDK, pass base64 content:

```csharp
var pdf = await File.ReadAllBytesAsync("invoice-1042.pdf");

await reloop.Mail.SendAsync(new SendMailParams
{
    From = "Acme Billing <billing@mail.acme.com>",
    To = "user@example.com",
    Subject = "Your invoice #1042",
    Text = "Your invoice is attached.",
    Attachments = new List<SendMailAttachment>
    {
        new()
        {
            Filename = "invoice-1042.pdf",
            Content = Convert.ToBase64String(pdf),
            ContentType = "application/pdf",
        },
    },
});
```

With MailKit, add the file to the `BodyBuilder` before you call `ToMessageBody()`:

```csharp
var builder = new BodyBuilder { TextBody = "Your invoice is attached." };
builder.Attachments.Add("invoice-1042.pdf", pdf, ContentType.Parse("application/pdf"));
message.Body = builder.ToMessageBody();
```

Keep attachments small. Reloop caps attachment size by plan, many inboxes reject large messages, and large files hurt deliverability. For big files, send a signed download link.

---

## Send in the background with `BackgroundService` and `Channel<T>`

Sending inside a request adds latency and fails the request when the provider is slow. A hosted service that reads from an in-memory `Channel<T>` moves the send off the request path with no extra infrastructure:

```csharp
using System.Threading.Channels;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Options;
using Reloop;
using Reloop.Exceptions;
using static Reloop.Models.MailModels;

public sealed record EmailJob(string To, string Subject, string Text);

public sealed class EmailQueue
{
    private readonly Channel<EmailJob> _channel =
        Channel.CreateBounded<EmailJob>(new BoundedChannelOptions(1_000)
        {
            FullMode = BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait,
        });

    public ValueTask EnqueueAsync(EmailJob job, CancellationToken ct = default) =>
        _channel.Writer.WriteAsync(job, ct);

    public IAsyncEnumerable<EmailJob> ReadAllAsync(CancellationToken ct) =>
        _channel.Reader.ReadAllAsync(ct);
}

public sealed class EmailWorker(
    EmailQueue queue,
    ReloopClient reloop,
    IOptions<ReloopOptions> options,
    ILogger<EmailWorker> logger) : BackgroundService
{
    private const int MaxAttempts = 5;

    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
    {
        await foreach (var job in queue.ReadAllAsync(stoppingToken))
        {
            try
            {
                await SendWithRetryAsync(job, stoppingToken);
            }
            catch (Exception ex) when (ex is not OperationCanceledException)
            {
                logger.LogError(ex, "Giving up on email to {To}", job.To);
            }
        }
    }

    private async Task SendWithRetryAsync(EmailJob job, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        for (var attempt = 1; ; attempt++)
        {
            try
            {
                await reloop.Mail.SendAsync(new SendMailParams
                {
                    From = options.Value.From,
                    To = job.To,
                    Subject = job.Subject,
                    Text = job.Text,
                });
                return;
            }
            catch (Exception ex) when (attempt < MaxAttempts && IsRetryable(ex, ct))
            {
                var delay = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(Math.Pow(2, attempt));
                logger.LogWarning(ex, "Send failed, retrying in {Delay}", delay);
                await Task.Delay(delay, ct);
            }
        }
    }

    private static bool IsRetryable(Exception ex, CancellationToken ct) => ex switch
    {
        ReloopApiException api => api.Status is 0 or 429 or >= 500,
        TaskCanceledException => !ct.IsCancellationRequested, // HttpClient timeout
        _ => false,
    };
}
```

Register both and enqueue from your endpoint:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddSingleton<EmailQueue>();
builder.Services.AddHostedService<EmailWorker>();

app.MapPost("/signup", async (SignupRequest body, EmailQueue queue) =>
{
    // ... create the user ...
    await queue.EnqueueAsync(new EmailJob(
        To: body.Email,
        Subject: "Welcome to Acme",
        Text: "Thanks for signing up."));
    return Results.Accepted();
});
```

**Retry** network errors (status `0`), timeouts, `429` and `5xx`. **Do not retry** other `4xx` errors: an invalid address or unverified domain fails the same way every time. The worker catches every failure per job because an unhandled exception in `ExecuteAsync` stops the whole host by default (since .NET 6).

Be honest about what this gives you. The channel lives in memory, so a deploy, crash or scale-down loses whatever is still queued, and `SendAsync` does not take a `CancellationToken`, so a send in flight at shutdown runs until it finishes or times out. That is fine for a welcome email. For mail that must arrive, such as receipts and password resets, use a durable queue: [Hangfire](https://www.hangfire.io) with persistent storage, a broker like RabbitMQ, Azure Service Bus or Amazon SQS, or an outbox table written in the same transaction as the order.

---

## Retries without duplicate emails

A request times out and your worker retries. If the first attempt actually went through, the user gets two emails. The API prevents this with an [`Idempotency-Key` header](/docs/api/idempotency): repeat a request with the same key and Reloop returns the original result instead of sending again.

The .NET SDK does not set this header, so call the endpoint with `HttpClient` and `System.Net.Http.Json`:

```csharp
using System.Net.Http.Json;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Options;
using static Reloop.Models.MailModels;

public sealed class ReceiptSender(HttpClient http, IOptions<ReloopOptions> options)
{
    public async Task<string?> SendReceiptAsync(
        string orderId, string to, CancellationToken ct = default)
    {
        using var request = new HttpRequestMessage(
            HttpMethod.Post, "https://reloop.sh/api/mail/v1/send")
        {
            Content = JsonContent.Create(new
            {
                from = "Acme <orders@mail.acme.com>",
                to,
                subject = $"Receipt for order {orderId}",
                text = "Thanks for your order.",
            }),
        };
        request.Headers.Add("x-api-key", options.Value.ApiKey);
        request.Headers.Add("Idempotency-Key", $"receipt-{orderId}");

        using var response = await http.SendAsync(request, ct);
        response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();

        var result = await response.Content.ReadFromJsonAsync<SendMailResponse>(cancellationToken: ct);
        return result?.Id;
    }
}
```

Register it as a typed client. The API rejects requests without a `User-Agent` header, and `HttpClient` does not send one by default, so set it here:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddHttpClient<ReceiptSender>(client =>
{
    client.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30);
    client.DefaultRequestHeaders.UserAgent.ParseAdd("acme-app/1.0");
});
```

Base the key on the business event (`receipt-{orderId}`), not a new `Guid` per attempt, so retries from any worker are safe. If a retry arrives while the first request is still running, the API answers `409` with `Retry-After: 1`; wait and retry with the same key. Reusing a key with a different body returns `422`.

---

## Testing without sending real email

- **Unit tests:** put sending behind your own interface and fake it. `ReloopClient` also accepts an `HttpClient`, so you can pass one backed by a fake `HttpMessageHandler` that returns a canned response.
- **Staging:** send to [test addresses](/docs/guides/testing-email-addresses) so you do not hurt your [sender reputation](/blog/why-emails-land-in-spam-fix) with bounces.
- **Local SMTP:** run [Mailpit](https://mailpit.axllent.org) with `docker run -p 1025:1025 -p 8025:8025 axllent/mailpit` and connect MailKit to it with `ConnectAsync("localhost", 1025, SecureSocketOptions.None)`, without `AuthenticateAsync`. Open `http://localhost:8025` to see the messages.

---

## Production checklist

- [ ] API key in user secrets, an environment variable or a secrets manager
- [ ] Sending domain verified with SPF, DKIM and DMARC
- [ ] `From` on your verified domain; user addresses in `ReplyTo`
- [ ] Both HTML and plain-text bodies
- [ ] One `ReloopClient` registered as a singleton
- [ ] Options validated at startup with `ValidateOnStart`
- [ ] Sending in a background worker, and a durable queue for mail that must arrive
- [ ] Retries only on network errors, timeouts, `429` and `5xx`
- [ ] Idempotency keys on anything that retries
- [ ] [Webhooks](/features/webhooks) for bounces and complaints
- [ ] Disposable addresses blocked at signup ([how](/blog/block-disposable-emails-at-signup))

---

## FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Should I use System.Net.Mail.SmtpClient or MailKit?">
    Use MailKit. Microsoft's documentation marks System.Net.Mail.SmtpClient as
    not recommended for new development because it does not support many
    modern protocols, and suggests MailKit instead. MailKit is actively
    maintained and has async methods throughout.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="How do I send an HTML email in C#?">
    With MailKit, create a BodyBuilder, set HtmlBody and TextBody, and assign
    builder.ToMessageBody() to the message body. With the Reloop SDK, set Html
    and Text on SendMailParams.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Which SecureSocketOptions should I use?">
    Use StartTls for port 587, and for 2587 when 587 is blocked. Use
    SslOnConnect only for servers that offer implicit TLS on port 465, which
    Reloop does not. Picking the wrong one for the port makes the connection
    hang or fail with a TLS error.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Why do my C# emails go to spam?">
    Usually the sending domain is not authenticated, or the From domain does
    not match the domain that signed the message. Set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC,
    send from your own domain, and always include a plain-text body.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Does the Reloop .NET SDK work with .NET Framework?">
    Yes. The package targets .NET Standard 2.0, so .NET Framework projects can
    reference it as well as .NET 8 and newer. Microsoft recommends .NET
    Framework 4.7.2 or later for .NET Standard 2.0 libraries.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# Reloop vs useSend (2026): Open-Source Resend Alternatives Compared

Path: /blog/reloop-vs-usesend
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-usesend
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-usesend.md

Reloop vs useSend compared honestly: license, hosted pricing at 3k to 1M emails, self-hosting with and without AWS SES, API and webhooks, inbound mail, and how to switch.

**Reloop and useSend are both open-source alternatives to Resend.** Both give you a clean REST API, SMTP, webhooks, contacts and marketing campaigns, plus a hosted cloud if you don't want to run anything. The big difference is underneath: **useSend is a layer on top of Amazon SES, while Reloop runs its own mail server, so self-hosting Reloop needs no AWS account.** Reloop also receives mail into real inboxes your agents can reply from, which useSend lists as not yet built.

We build Reloop, so weigh this accordingly. useSend (formerly Unsend) is a well-made project we respect, and where it's the better pick, we say so. Every useSend fact below comes from its [website](https://usesend.com), [docs](https://docs.usesend.com) or [GitHub repo](https://github.com/usesend/useSend).

---

## The 30-second comparison

| | **Reloop** | **useSend** |
|---|---|---|
| License | Apache 2.0 | AGPL-3.0 |
| Free tier (hosted) | 6,000 / mo, 200 / day | 3,000 / mo, 100 / day |
| Paid pricing | Plans: $10 for 50k, $20 for 100k | Usage: $0.40 per 1k transactional, $1.00 per 1k marketing, $10 minimum |
| Sending path | Own MTA (KumoMTA) | Amazon SES |
| Self-host needs AWS | No | Yes (SES and SNS) |
| Dedicated IP | Included on Growth ($20) | Not listed |
| REST API and SMTP | Yes | Yes |
| Webhooks | Yes, HMAC signed | Yes, HMAC signed |
| Contacts and campaigns | Yes | Yes |
| Event-triggered automations | Yes | Not listed |
| Inbound email | Mailboxes with threads, API, MCP, IMAP | On the roadmap |
| Status | Generally available | Beta, per the README |

useSend's prices are from the pricing section on [usesend.com](https://usesend.com). Reloop's are on [reloop.sh/pricing](/pricing). Both change; check before you commit.

---

## Pricing at real volumes

Reloop's free tier is double useSend's: 6,000 emails a month capped at 200 a day, vs 3,000 and 100.

After that, the models differ. **Reloop sells plans** with a fixed amount of email. **useSend charges per email**, with a $10 monthly minimum in usage credits, and transactional mail ($0.0004 each) costs less than marketing mail ($0.001 each).

For transactional mail only:

| Monthly volume | Reloop | useSend |
|---|---|---|
| 3,000 | $0 | $0 |
| 25,000 | $10 | $10 |
| 50,000 | **$10** | $20 |
| 100,000 | **$20** | $40 |
| 250,000 | $20 + $75 overage = $95 | $100 |
| 1,000,000 | $20 + $450 overage = $470 | **$400** |

The useSend column is our math from its published per-email rates. The shape is clear, though:

- **Below about 250k a month, Reloop is cheaper.** Its plans include a lot of email for a flat fee.
- **Around 250k, they're roughly even.**
- **Well above that, useSend's $0.40 per 1,000 beats Reloop's $0.50 overage.** If you send millions of transactional emails, useSend's hosted pricing wins.

Marketing mail flips this further in Reloop's favor: useSend charges $1.00 per 1,000 for it, while Reloop counts every email the same.

<Callout type="tip">
  Self-hosting changes the math for both. With Reloop you pay only for the server. With useSend you pay for the server plus Amazon SES, which is $0.10 per 1,000 emails.
</Callout>

---

## Developer experience

Both APIs are shaped after Resend's, so the code looks almost the same.

**useSend**

```typescript

const usesend = new UseSend(process.env.USESEND_API_KEY!);

await usesend.emails.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@acme.com>",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Welcome",
  html: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
});
```

**Reloop**

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY! });

const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Welcome",
  html: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
});
```

The details:

| | Reloop | useSend |
|---|---|---|
| Endpoint | `POST /api/mail/v1/send` | `POST /api/v1/emails` |
| Field style | `reply_to`, `scheduled_at` (snake_case) | `replyTo`, `scheduledAt` (camelCase) |
| Idempotent retries | `Idempotency-Key` header | `Idempotency-Key` header |
| Scheduling | Yes | Yes, plus update and cancel endpoints |
| Stored templates | Yes, `{{{variables}}}` | Yes, by `templateId` with `variables` |
| Error format | `message`, `why` and `fix` | Not documented |
| Official SDKs | Node, Python, Go, PHP, Ruby, Rust, Java, .NET, Elixir | Node, Python, Go |

useSend has two nice touches worth calling out: endpoints to **update or cancel a scheduled email**, and a visual **email editor** for campaigns, built on Tiptap and jsx-email.

Reloop's strong opinion is its error shape. A failed send tells you **why** it failed and **how to fix it**:

```json
{
  "message": "Domain not found",
  "why": "The domain mail.acme.com was not found or is not authorized for your organization",
  "fix": "Ensure the domain is registered and verified in your dashboard"
}
```

### Webhooks

Both sign webhooks with HMAC-SHA256.

- **useSend** sends `X-UseSend-Signature` and `X-UseSend-Timestamp`, retries up to six times with exponential backoff, and turns a webhook off after 30 failures in a row. Events cover emails, contacts and domains. [Docs](https://docs.usesend.com/guides/webhooks).
- **Reloop** sends a `Reloop-Signature` header, with events like `email.delivered`, `email.bounced`, `email.complained` and `email.received`.

---

## Self-hosting: the real difference

This is where the two projects split.

**useSend is a layer on top of Amazon SES.** Its [self-hosting guide](https://docs.usesend.com/self-hosting/overview) asks you to:

1. Run PostgreSQL and Redis (docker-compose does it for you).
2. Create an AWS IAM user with SES and SNS access.
3. Get your SES account **out of the sandbox**, which needs an AWS review.
4. Expose a public callback URL so SNS can report delivery events back.
5. Set up GitHub OAuth for logins.

That's a good trade if you already live in AWS. SES is cheap, Amazon handles IP reputation, and you skip running a mail server.

**Reloop ships its own mail server** (KumoMTA). You need a server with [2 vCPUs and 4 GB of RAM](/docs/self-host/requirements) at minimum, port 25 open, and DNS. There's no AWS account, no sandbox review, and no per-email fee to anyone. Install it with [one command](/self-host) or on [Coolify](/blog/reloop-coolify-setup).

The flip side: **with Reloop you own your IP reputation.** Warming new IPs and watching blocklists is your job. Our free [blocklist checker](/tools/blocklist-checker) and [domain reputation checker](/tools/domain-reputation-checker) help, and the [self-hosting guide](/blog/self-hosted-email-infrastructure) covers what that really involves.

| | Reloop | useSend |
|---|---|---|
| Sends through | Its own MTA | Amazon SES |
| AWS account needed | No | Yes |
| Approval before sending | No | SES sandbox exit |
| Per-email cost when self-hosted | None | SES fee |
| IP reputation | Yours to manage | Managed by AWS |
| One-click deploy | Installer script, Coolify | Docker, Railway |

---

## Licensing

Both are open source, under different licenses.

- **useSend is AGPL-3.0.** You can self-host freely, but if you modify it and offer it to others over a network, you must publish your changes.
- **Reloop is Apache 2.0.** It's a permissive license: you can modify it, embed it in your product, and keep your changes private.

For most teams that just run it internally, both are fine. If you plan to build a product on top, Apache 2.0 gives you more room.

---

## Receiving email and agent inboxes

**useSend** lists inbound email as a roadmap item in its README, so today it's a sending platform.

**Reloop** receives mail into **mailboxes**. Messages are stored, threaded, spam-scored with Rspamd, and readable over the API, the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) or IMAP. You can reply in-thread with one call.

That matters if you're building:

- **AI agents that handle email.** Give an agent its own address and let it read and reply. See [build an AI agent that reads and replies to email](/blog/build-ai-agent-sends-emails).
- **Support or shared inboxes** where humans and agents work the same threads.
- **Reply handling** for transactional mail.

---

## Marketing and automations

Both handle more than transactional mail.

- **useSend** has contact books, campaigns with scheduling, double opt-in, and the visual editor. It manages unsubscribes for you.
- **Reloop** has contacts with custom properties, groups, subscription channels, scheduled campaigns, and **event-triggered automations**. Call `reloop.automations.start` when a user signs up and a sequence of delays, conditions and emails runs. See [welcome sequences that convert](/blog/welcome-email-sequences-that-convert).

---

## Where useSend is the better choice

- **You send millions of transactional emails a month** on the hosted plan. Its $0.40 per 1,000 beats our overage.
- **You're already deep in AWS** and want SES's managed reputation without running a mail server.
- **You want a visual editor** for marketing emails out of the box.
- **You're happy with AGPL** and like how small and focused the codebase is.

For more open-source options, with or without AWS, see the [best useSend alternatives](/blog/best-usesend-alternatives).

## Where Reloop is the better choice

- **You send under about 250k emails a month.** Plans are cheaper.
- **You want to self-host without AWS**, with no sandbox review and no per-email fee.
- **You need inbound mail as real inboxes**, especially for AI agents.
- **You need event-triggered automations** or a dedicated IP on a $20 plan.
- **You want a permissive license** to build on.

---

## Switching from useSend to Reloop

1. **Add your domain in Reloop** and publish the DKIM record (`reloop._domainkey`). Merge `include:reloop.sh` into your SPF record; don't add a second SPF record. Remove the SES records once you've fully moved.
2. **Swap the client.** Replace `usesend.emails.send` with `reloop.mail.send`, and rename `replyTo` → `reply_to` and `scheduledAt` → `scheduled_at`.
3. **Move templates.** Recreate them in Reloop with triple-brace placeholders: `{{{first_name}}}`.
4. **Export contacts** and import them into Reloop, keeping unsubscribed contacts marked as unsubscribed.
5. **Point webhooks** at a handler that verifies `Reloop-Signature`.
6. **Ramp traffic** from 10% to 100% over a week or two.

If you use SMTP instead, change the host to `smtp.reloop.sh` and use your Reloop API key as both username and password. Our [SendGrid migration guide](/blog/migrating-from-sendgrid) covers the traffic split in more detail.

---

  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Do I need AWS to self-host Reloop?">

  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Which is cheaper?">
    On the hosted plans, Reloop is cheaper below about 250k emails a month and
    useSend is cheaper well above that for transactional mail. Self-hosted,
    Reloop has no per-email cost, while useSend passes through SES fees.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can useSend receive email?">

    threaded mailboxes you can read over the API, MCP or IMAP.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Which license is more permissive?">

  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>
