# Migrating from SendGrid to Reloop

Path: /blog/migrating-from-sendgrid
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/migrating-from-sendgrid
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/migrating-from-sendgrid.md

A step-by-step SendGrid to Reloop migration: map the v3 Mail Send API, switch SMTP, move templates and suppressions, rewire webhooks, update DNS, and cut over without hurting deliverability.

**Migrating from SendGrid to Reloop takes most teams an afternoon of code changes and a week of careful cutover.** The code is the easy part: Reloop's send call is simpler than SendGrid's v3 payload, and if you use SMTP you only change four settings. The part that deserves care is moving your suppression list and ramping traffic so your sender reputation comes with you.

This guide walks through the whole thing in the order we'd do it. If you're still deciding, start with [Reloop vs SendGrid](/blog/reloop-vs-sendgrid).

---

## The migration at a glance

| Step | What changes | Effort |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Verify your domain | Add Reloop's DKIM and SPF next to SendGrid's | 15 min + DNS propagation |
| 2. Export suppressions | Bounces, spam reports, unsubscribes into Reloop | 30 min |
| 3. Swap the send code | v3 Mail Send → `reloop.mail.send` (or SMTP settings) | 1–3 hours |
| 4. Move templates | Dynamic templates → Reloop templates (`{{x}}` → `{{{x}}}`) | Depends on count |
| 5. Rewire webhooks | Event Webhook → Reloop webhooks | 1 hour |
| 6. Ramp traffic | 10% → 50% → 100% over 1–2 weeks | Calendar time |
| 7. Clean up | Remove SendGrid DNS records and keys | 15 min |

Keep SendGrid running until step 7. Running both in parallel is what makes this safe.

---

## 1. Verify your sending domain in Reloop

Add your domain in the [Reloop dashboard](/dashboard) under **Domains**. Reloop shows the exact records to add. They don't conflict with SendGrid's, so you can publish both at once.

| Record | SendGrid (today) | Reloop (add) |
|---|---|---|
| DKIM | `s1._domainkey`, `s2._domainkey` CNAMEs | `reloop._domainkey` TXT |
| Return path / tracking | `em1234` and `url1234` CNAMEs | `link` CNAME → `link.reloop.sh` |
| SPF | `include:sendgrid.net` | `include:reloop.sh` |
| DMARC | Unchanged | Unchanged |

Because DKIM selectors are different, both providers can sign mail for the same domain at the same time. That's what lets you ramp gradually instead of flipping a switch.

<Callout type="warning">
  You can only have **one** SPF record per host. Merge Reloop into your existing one rather than adding a second: `v=spf1 include:sendgrid.net include:reloop.sh -all`. Two SPF records is a permanent fail.
</Callout>

If you haven't set up DMARC yet, now is a good time. See the [SPF, DKIM and DMARC guide](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide).

---

## 2. Move your suppression list first

This is the step people skip, and it's the one that hurts. Your SendGrid suppression list holds every address that hard-bounced, marked you as spam, or unsubscribed. If you don't bring it over, your first sends from Reloop will hit those addresses again, and mailbox providers will notice.

Export each list from SendGrid's API:

```bash
for list in bounces spam_reports unsubscribes invalid_emails; do
  curl -s "https://api.sendgrid.com/v3/suppression/$list?limit=500" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $SENDGRID_API_KEY" > "sg-$list.json"
done
```

Each endpoint is paginated with `limit` and `offset`, so loop until you get an empty page if you have more than 500 entries.

Then add them to Reloop's suppression list:

```typescript

const lists = ["bounces", "spam_reports", "unsubscribes", "invalid_emails"];

for (const list of lists) {
  const rows = JSON.parse(readFileSync(`sg-${list}.json`, "utf8")) as {
    email: string;
  }[];

  for (const { email } of rows) {
    await fetch("https://reloop.sh/api/contacts/v1/suppressions", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        "x-api-key": process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY!,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({ email, reason: `Imported from SendGrid: ${list}` }),
    });
  }
}
```

Suppressed addresses are rejected before they're sent, for both transactional and marketing mail. From here on, Reloop adds [hard bounces and complaints](/blog/email-bounce-processing-automation) to the list automatically.

---

## 3. Swap the send code

### Option A: you use SMTP

If your app sends through `smtp.sendgrid.net`, this is a settings change.

| Setting | SendGrid | Reloop |
|---|---|---|
| Host | `smtp.sendgrid.net` | `smtp.reloop.sh` |
| Port | `587` | `587` (STARTTLS) |
| Username | `apikey` | Your Reloop API key |
| Password | Your SendGrid API key | Your Reloop API key |

With Nodemailer, for example:

```typescript

  host: "smtp.reloop.sh",
  port: 587,
  secure: false,
  auth: {
    user: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY,
    pass: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY,
  },
});
```

That's it. Everything else in your code stays the same. More examples for PHP, Python, Go, Ruby and Rust are in the [SMTP docs](/docs/examples/smtp/introduction).

### Option B: you use the v3 Mail Send API

SendGrid's v3 payload nests recipients inside `personalizations`. Reloop's is flat.

**Before (SendGrid):**

```typescript

sgMail.setApiKey(process.env.SENDGRID_API_KEY!);

await sgMail.send({
  from: { email: "hello@acme.com", name: "Acme" },
  to: "user@example.com",
  replyTo: "support@acme.com",
  subject: "Your receipt",
  html: "<p>Thanks for your order.</p>",
  text: "Thanks for your order.",
  categories: ["receipt"],
});
```

**After (Reloop):**

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY! });

const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@acme.com>",
  to: "user@example.com",
  reply_to: "support@acme.com",
  subject: "Your receipt",
  html: "<p>Thanks for your order.</p>",
  text: "Thanks for your order.",
  tags: [{ name: "category", value: "receipt" }],
});

if (emailError) {
  // emailError has message, why, fix and a docs link
  console.error(emailError);
}
```

Install the SDK with `npm install reloop-email` (the [Node.js guide](/blog/send-email-nodejs) covers setup). There are official SDKs for [Python, Go, PHP, Ruby, Rust and more](/sdk) too.

### Field mapping

| SendGrid v3 | Reloop |
|---|---|
| `from: { email, name }` | `from: "Name <email>"` |
| `personalizations[].to` | `to` (string or array, up to 50) |
| `personalizations[].cc` / `bcc` | `cc` / `bcc` |
| `reply_to` | `reply_to` |
| `content[]` (`text/plain`, `text/html`) | `text`, `html` |
| `template_id` + `dynamic_template_data` | `template: { id, variables }` |
| `categories` | `tags: [{ name, value }]` |
| `custom_args` | `tags` (for filtering) or `headers` |
| `send_at` (Unix seconds) | `scheduled_at` (ISO 8601) |
| `attachments[]` (`content`, `filename`, `type`) | `attachments[]` (`content`, `filename`, `content_type`) |
| `headers` | `headers` |
| `asm.group_id` | Contact channels (subscription topics) |

Two differences worth knowing:

- **One recipient list per call.** SendGrid lets one request contain many `personalizations`, each with different recipients and data. In Reloop, send one request per message. It's simpler to reason about and you get one email ID per recipient for tracking.
- **Retries are safe.** Add an `Idempotency-Key` header to retry a failed request without risking a duplicate send. See [idempotency](/docs/api/idempotency).

---

## 4. Move your templates

SendGrid dynamic templates use Handlebars, with placeholders like `{{first_name}}`. Reloop placeholders use **triple braces**: `{{{first_name}}}`. The HTML itself carries over unchanged, so the move is a copy, paste and placeholder rename.

1. In SendGrid, open each dynamic template and copy its HTML from the code editor.
2. Convert the placeholders: `{{first_name}}` becomes `{{{first_name}}}`, in the subject as well as the body.
3. In Reloop, create a template and paste the HTML. Or design it in the visual editor.
4. Replace the template ID in your code.

A one-line conversion for simple placeholders:

```bash
sed -E 's/\{\{\s*([a-zA-Z0-9_]+)\s*\}\}/{{{\1}}}/g' sendgrid-template.html > reloop-template.html
```

Handlebars logic such as `{{#if}}` and `{{#each}}` has no Reloop equivalent. Resolve those in your code before sending and pass the result in as a plain variable.

```typescript
await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@acme.com>",
  to: user.email,
  subject: "Reset your password",
  template: {
    id: "tmpl_password_reset",
    variables: { name: user.name, reset_url: resetUrl },
  },
});
```

If you have dozens of templates, list them with SendGrid's `GET /v3/templates?generations=dynamic` endpoint and script the copy.

---

## 5. Rewire webhooks

SendGrid's Event Webhook sends a JSON **array** of events in each request. Reloop sends **one event per request**, wrapped in a consistent envelope and signed with HMAC-SHA256.

### Event mapping

| SendGrid event | Reloop event |
|---|---|
| `processed` | `email.sent` |
| `delivered` | `email.delivered` |
| `deferred` | `email.delivery_delayed` |
| `bounce` | `email.bounced` |
| `dropped` | `email.failed` |
| `spamreport` | `email.complained` |
| `open` | `email.opened` |
| `click` | `email.clicked` |
| Inbound Parse | `email.received` |

### Payload

```json
{
  "id": "whev_01h…",
  "type": "email.bounced",
  "created_at": "2025-09-23T12:00:00.000Z",
  "data": {
    "email_id": "em_…",
    "from": "hello@acme.com",
    "to": ["user@example.com"],
    "subject": "Your receipt",
    "status": "bounced",
    "error": { "code": 550, "message": "User unknown" }
  }
}
```

### Handler

```typescript
// app/api/webhooks/reloop/route.ts

  const rawBody = await request.text();
  const ok = verifyReloopWebhook({
    secret: process.env.RELOOP_WEBHOOK_SECRET!,
    rawBody,
    signatureHeader: request.headers.get("Reloop-Signature") ?? "",
  });
  if (!ok) return new Response("Invalid signature", { status: 401 });

  const event = JSON.parse(rawBody);

  switch (event.type) {
    case "email.bounced":
    case "email.complained":
      await markUndeliverable(event.data.to[0]);
      break;
    case "email.delivered":
      await markDelivered(event.data.email_id);
      break;
  }

  return new Response("ok");
}
```

The `verifyReloopWebhook` helper is a few lines of Node crypto. Copy it from [verifying webhook requests](/docs/webhooks/verify-webhooks-requests). Failed deliveries are retried with backoff, and you can replay events from the dashboard.

<Callout type="tip">
  During the parallel run, keep **both** webhook handlers live. Each provider only reports on the mail it sent.
</Callout>

---

## 6. Ramp traffic gradually

Don't move 100% of your volume on day one. Mailbox providers judge reputation per sending IP and domain, and a sudden jump from a new source looks suspicious.

A simple flag does the job:

```typescript
const RELOOP_SHARE = Number(process.env.RELOOP_SHARE ?? "0.1");

  if (Math.random() < RELOOP_SHARE) {
    return sendWithReloop(message);
  }
  return sendWithSendGrid(message);
}
```

A schedule that works for most senders:

| Days | Share on Reloop | What to watch |
|---|---|---|
| 1–3 | 10% | Delivery rate, bounces, any `email.failed` |
| 4–7 | 50% | Gmail and Outlook inbox placement |
| 8–14 | 100% | Complaint rate under 0.1% |

Start with transactional mail ([password resets](/blog/password-reset-email-best-practices), receipts). Those recipients expect the message and engage with it, which builds reputation quickly. Move marketing campaigns last.

If you're sending high volume on a dedicated IP, follow the longer [IP warming schedule](/blog/ip-warming-guide) instead.

---

## 7. Clean up

Once Reloop has handled 100% of traffic for a week with healthy numbers:

1. Remove `include:sendgrid.net` from your SPF record.
2. Delete the `s1._domainkey`, `s2._domainkey`, `em…` and `url…` CNAMEs.
3. Revoke your SendGrid API keys.
4. Delete the old webhook handler and the `RELOOP_SHARE` flag.
5. Cancel your SendGrid plan.

Keep DMARC reports on for another month. They'll show if anything is still sending through SendGrid that you missed, like a forgotten cron job or a third-party tool.

---

## Migration checklist

- [ ] Domain verified in Reloop, SPF merged, both DKIM selectors live
- [ ] Suppressions exported from SendGrid and imported into Reloop
- [ ] Send code or SMTP settings switched behind a flag
- [ ] Templates copied and template IDs updated
- [ ] Reloop webhook endpoint live and signature verified
- [ ] Traffic ramped 10% → 50% → 100%
- [ ] SendGrid DNS, keys and plan removed

---

## FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Will I lose my sender reputation by switching?">
    Your **domain** reputation comes with you because it's tied to your
    domain, not to SendGrid. IP reputation doesn't transfer, which is why the
    gradual ramp matters. Hosted Reloop sends from warm shared IPs by default.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Do I need to change my DMARC record?">
    No. DMARC checks that SPF or DKIM aligns with your From domain. Once
    Reloop's DKIM record is published, Reloop mail passes DMARC with the
    record you already have.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can I move SendGrid Marketing Campaigns contacts too?">
    Yes. Export contacts as CSV from SendGrid and import them in the Reloop
    dashboard under Contacts. Bring the suppression list across first so
    unsubscribed contacts stay unsubscribed.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="How long does the whole migration take?">
    Code changes usually take a few hours. The traffic ramp takes one to two
    weeks. Most of that is waiting and watching dashboards.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# Reloop vs Sweego (2026): Pricing, Features and Which to Choose

Path: /blog/reloop-vs-sweego
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-sweego
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-sweego.md

Reloop vs Sweego compared honestly: pricing by volume, French hosting and data residency, the send API, SMS, inbound email and agent inboxes, webhooks, marketing sends, self-hosting, and how to switch.

**Sweego is a French transactional email and SMS API, run by a French company on French data centers.** Reloop is open-source email infrastructure: an email API and SMTP relay, plus campaigns, event-triggered automations and inboxes your AI agents can read and reply from. The short version: **if you need SMS, or hosted email that provably stays in France, Sweego is the better pick. If you want more of the email stack in one product, lower prices at volume, or the option to self-host, Reloop fits better.**

We build Reloop, so weigh this accordingly. Every Sweego fact below comes from [sweego.io](https://www.sweego.io/), its [pricing page](https://www.sweego.io/pricing), its [documentation](https://learn.sweego.io/) and its [legal notice](https://www.sweego.io/legal-notice). Where Sweego is the better pick, we say so.

---

## The 30-second comparison

| | **Reloop** | **Sweego** |
|---|---|---|
| Company | Reloop Labs | Mindbaz SAS (Lille, France) |
| Hosting | Reloop Cloud (Hetzner, with EU data centers) or your own server | France (OVHcloud and Scaleway) |
| Free tier | 6,000 / mo, 200 / day | 100 / day |
| Entry paid plan | **$10** for 50,000 emails | From €10 (Individual, 20k to 50k) |
| ~100,000 emails / mo | **$20** | From €79 (Startup, 100k to 200k) |
| Dedicated IP | Included on Growth ($20) | Available on Startup, included on Scaleup |
| SMS | No | Yes, prepaid credits |
| Inbound email | Mailboxes with threads, API, MCP, IMAP | Webhook per message, paid plans |
| Campaigns and automations | Yes, on every plan | Bulk send API, no lists or automations |
| Log retention | 45 days | 7 to 90 days, by plan |
| Open source | Yes (Apache 2.0) | No |
| Self-host | Yes | No |
| SMTP relay | Yes | Yes |

Prices change. Check [Sweego's pricing page](https://www.sweego.io/pricing) and [ours](/pricing) before you commit.

---

## What each one is

**Sweego** launched in [March 2024](https://www.sweego.io/corporate/sweego-launch) from Mindbaz, a French email sending company whose expertise dates back to 2009. Its pitch is sovereignty: its [cloud sovereignty page](https://www.sweego.io/corporate/understanding-the-cloud-sovereignty-framework-and-sweegos-position-within-this-new-european-benchmark) says it hosts on OVHcloud (Gravelines) and Scaleway (DC5), both French, and that Mindbaz is "100% French-owned". Its docs say "Your data is never sent outside the European Union." You get a REST API and SMTP for email, an SMS API, a drag-and-drop template builder, inbound routing and signed webhooks.

**Reloop** is email infrastructure you can use hosted or run yourself. The same codebase covers transactional sending, an SMTP relay, contacts, broadcast campaigns, automations, webhooks and inbound mailboxes. It runs its own MTA (KumoMTA) and spam scoring (Rspamd), and it's Apache 2.0.

So the overlap is transactional email. Sweego adds SMS; Reloop adds the marketing and inbox side.

---

## Pricing at real volumes

Sweego prices email in bands, and you pick a volume within each plan:

| Monthly volume | Reloop | Sweego |
|---|---|---|
| ~3,000 | $0 (Free) | €0 (Free, 100 / day) |
| 20,000 | $10 | From €10 (Individual) |
| 50,000 | $10 | Individual, top of its range |
| 100,000 | $20 | From €79 (Startup) |
| 500,000 | $20 + $200 overage = $220 | From €270 (Scaleup) |
| 1M+ | $20 + $0.50 per 1,000 above 100k | Unicorn (custom) |

Reloop's overage is $0.50 per 1,000 emails above your plan. Sweego takes 20% off for annual billing and allows bursts of up to 30% above your plan's volume.

What stands out:

- **Reloop's free tier is bigger.** Reloop gives 6,000 a month (200 a day) against Sweego's 100 a day, roughly double. Sweego's free plan has no inbound routing and keeps logs for 7 days.
- **Entry plans are close; the gap opens at 100k.** At 100,000 a month Reloop Growth is $20 with a dedicated IP, while Sweego Startup starts at €79.
- **Sweego includes more with the plan in some places.** Log retention grows with the plan (30, 60 and 90 days on Individual, Startup and Scaleup), and Startup and up get unlimited templates. Reloop keeps 45 days of data on every plan.
- **Dedicated IPs.** Reloop includes one on Growth. Sweego makes one available on Startup and includes one on Scaleup, with extra IPs at €30 a month.

If you self-host Reloop, there's no per-email fee at all, only your server.

<Callout type="tip">
  Prices are in different currencies: Sweego bills in euros, Reloop in US dollars. Compare at today's exchange rate.
</Callout>

---

## Data residency and jurisdiction

This is where Sweego is strongest, and it's probably why you're reading this.

**Sweego** answers both questions a security review asks. *Where is the data?* In France, on OVHcloud and Scaleway. *Who runs it?* A French company with French capital. Its sovereignty page also lists its sub-processors, which are European too: CM.com (Netherlands) for SMS, Mollie (Netherlands) for payments, Hyperline (France) for billing and Chamaileon (Hungary) for the template builder. One honest note from that same page: Sweego says it is "GDPR compliant, no formal security certification yet."

**Reloop Cloud** runs on Hetzner, the German hosting company, with EU data centers. We publish a [Data Processing Addendum](/dpa) that relies on the EU Standard Contractual Clauses for transfers outside the EEA, and a [sub-processor list](/dpa/subprocessors).

If you want to control exactly where everything lives, Reloop also offers **self-hosting**: run the same code on an EU server (Hetzner, OVHcloud, Scaleway or your own hardware) and you decide where everything lives. That's more control than any hosted provider gives you, but it's also more work. If you specifically want French hosting by a French-owned company, pick Sweego. Our [EU email API roundup](/blog/eu-email-api-providers-2026) covers this choice in more depth.

---

## Developer experience

Sweego doesn't publish an official Node SDK; its docs show plain HTTP calls. You send to `/send` with an `Api-Key` header:

**Sweego**

```typescript
await fetch("https://api.sweego.io/send", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
    "Api-Key": process.env.SWEEGO_API_KEY!,
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    channel: "email",
    provider: "sweego",
    recipients: [{ email: "user@example.com" }],
    from: { name: "Acme", email: "hello@mail.acme.com" },
    subject: "Welcome",
    "message-html": "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
  }),
});
```

**Reloop**

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY! });

const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Welcome",
  html: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
});
```

| | Reloop | Sweego |
|---|---|---|
| Auth | API key (`x-api-key`) | API key (`Api-Key`) or OAuth2 bearer |
| Field style | `from`, `to`, `html` | `recipients`, `from`, `message-html`, plus `channel` and `provider` |
| Template variables | `{{{first_name}}}` | `{{ name }}` with `template-id` and `variables` |
| Many recipients | Up to 50 per send; campaigns for audiences | `/send/bulk/email`, up to 500 per request with per-recipient variables |
| Official SDKs | Node, Python, Go, PHP, Ruby, Rust, Java, .NET, Elixir | Symfony Mailer and Notifier; community packages for Convex, Payload, Odoo, Gleam, Terraform and WordPress |
| AI tooling | [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) that sends, reads inboxes and manages resources | Docs-only MCP server (read-only, cannot send) |

A few Sweego details we like: a `dry-run` flag that runs a send without actually delivering it, an expiration-date header so old messages can be deleted, and daily log exports over SFTP.

Reloop's errors tell you **why** a send failed and **how to fix it**:

```json
{
  "message": "Domain not found",
  "why": "The domain mail.acme.com was not found or is not authorized for your organization",
  "fix": "Ensure the domain is registered and verified in your dashboard"
}
```

---

## SMS

Sweego sends SMS from the same account and API as email. You buy prepaid credits, from €20 (about 500 SMS at €0.040 each in its example), valid for 12 months, with prices that vary by country. It supports custom sender IDs, SMS templates, SMS webhooks and, for the US and Canada, toll-free numbers.

**Reloop does not send SMS.** It's email only. If you need SMS alongside email from one European provider, that's a clear point for Sweego. You can also mix them: send email through Reloop and keep Sweego for SMS.

---

## Receiving email and agent inboxes

**Sweego** offers inbound routing on paid plans. You point a subdomain's MX at Sweego, and each incoming message is posted to your webhook as JSON. Attachments arrive as metadata, and you fetch their content from the API. Failed deliveries are retried every 5 minutes, up to 20 times. To match replies to the email you sent, [Sweego's docs](https://learn.sweego.io/docs/inbound/conversational_flow) recommend a unique Reply-To address per message. Storing, threading and replying is up to you.

**Reloop** receives mail into **mailboxes**. Messages are stored, threaded, spam-scored with Rspamd, and readable over the API, the MCP server or IMAP. Replying in-thread is one call, and an `email.received` webhook is there if you also want push.

| | Reloop | Sweego |
|---|---|---|
| Receive on your domain | Yes, every plan | Yes, paid plans |
| Stored mailboxes with threads | Yes | No |
| Reply in thread via API | Yes | Build it yourself |
| MCP access for agents | Yes | No |
| IMAP access | Yes | No |

If you're building an AI agent that handles email, or a support inbox where humans and agents work the same threads, this is the biggest difference. See [build an AI agent that reads and replies to email](/blog/build-ai-agent-sends-emails).

---

## Webhooks and deliverability

Both sign webhooks with HMAC-SHA256. Sweego sends `webhook-id`, `webhook-timestamp` and `webhook-signature` headers; Reloop sends `Reloop-Signature`. Sweego's email events cover sent, delivered, soft and hard bounces, list-unsubscribe, spam complaints, opens (split into proxy and human opens) and clicks. Tracking events can arrive up to 10 minutes late. Multiple webhooks need Startup or above; Reloop allows 3, 5 or 10 depending on plan.

On suppression, Sweego automatically blocks an address for 90 days after a "user unknown" hard bounce. Its docs say viewing the suppression list from the dashboard or API is "not yet available". Reloop handles bounces, complaints and suppression in its MTA, with one list across transactional mail, campaigns and automations. See [how bounce processing works](/blog/email-bounce-processing-automation).

Both handle SPF, DKIM and DMARC setup. Reloop also ships free [domain reputation](/tools/domain-reputation-checker) and [blocklist](/tools/blocklist-checker) checkers.

---

## Marketing, contacts and automations

Sweego is built for transactional mail and SMS, but it does accept marketing sends: set `campaign-type` to `newsletter` or `market` and Sweego adds a `List-Unsubscribe` header and collects the unsubscribes for you. What we didn't find in its docs is the rest of a marketing tool: no contact lists, no campaign scheduler, no automations. You'd manage audiences in your own app and loop through the bulk endpoint.

Reloop covers that layer: contacts with custom properties, groups, subscription channels, scheduled broadcast campaigns, and **event-triggered automations** that start when your app tracks an event like `user.signed_up`. Automations are on every plan, including Free.

---

## Self-hosting and lock-in

Sweego is hosted only. Reloop is Apache 2.0, so you can:

1. Start on Reloop Cloud.
2. Move to your own server later with the [one-command installer](/self-host).
3. Keep the same API. Point the SDK's `baseUrl` at your instance and nothing else changes.

Self-hosting isn't free in effort: you own IP reputation, warm-up, backups and uptime. The [requirements](/docs/self-host/requirements) start at 2 vCPUs and 4 GB of RAM.

---

## Where Sweego is the better choice

- **You need hosted email that stays in France**, run by a French company on French infrastructure, without running servers yourself.
- **You need SMS** next to email in one account and one API.
- **You want longer log retention** on higher plans (60 or 90 days) or daily log exports over SFTP.
- **You work in Symfony**, where Sweego has official Mailer and Notifier components.

Looking at more EU email APIs? See our roundup of the [best Sweego alternatives](/blog/best-sweego-alternatives).

## Where Reloop is the better choice

- **You send 100k or more a month.** $20 with a dedicated IP vs from €79.
- **You need inbound mail as real inboxes**, especially for AI agents.
- **You want campaigns and automations** in the same product as your transactional mail.
- **You need open source or self-hosting**, including running it on your own EU server.

---

## Switching from Sweego to Reloop

1. **Add your domain in Reloop** and publish the DKIM record (`reloop._domainkey`). Merge `include:reloop.sh` into your existing SPF record rather than adding a second one.
2. **Swap the client.** Replace calls to `/send` with `reloop.mail.send`, and map `recipients`/`from`/`subject`/`message-html`/`message-txt` to `to`/`from`/`subject`/`html`/`text`. If you use SMTP, change the host and credentials.
3. **Move templates.** Export the HTML and change placeholders to triple braces: `{{ name }}` becomes `{{{name}}}`.
4. **Carry over suppressions.** Export hard bounces and unsubscribes from your Sweego logs or webhook history and import them, so you never mail someone who opted out.
5. **Point webhooks** at a new handler. Reloop events are named `email.delivered`, `email.bounced`, `email.complained` and so on.
6. **Move inbound.** Point the inbound subdomain's MX at Reloop and read replies from the mailbox instead of a webhook.
7. **Ramp traffic** from 10% to 100% over a week or two, then remove Sweego's DNS records. Keep your Sweego account if you still send SMS.

Our [SendGrid migration guide](/blog/migrating-from-sendgrid) walks through the same steps in more detail.

# The Hidden Costs of Disposable Emails (And How Blocking Them Saves You Thousands)

Path: /blog/how-temp-email-checker-saves-you-money
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/how-temp-email-checker-saves-you-money
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/how-temp-email-checker-saves-you-money.md

From CRM contact-tier inflation to free-trial credit farming and burned domain reputation, here is the real cost of disposable emails and how a free temp email checker saves thousands.

When builders think about temporary or disposable email addresses, they usually view them as a minor product annoyance: *"A few anonymous users testing the app or downloading a guide. No big deal, right?"*

In reality, disposable emails are a silent drain on your company's balance sheet. 

Every throwaway inbox that slips past your signup form creates a ripple effect of recurring SaaS fees, stolen compute credits, degraded sender reputation, and wasted engineering hours. If you run a SaaS, an e-commerce platform, or a newsletter, unvetted signups can quietly cost you hundreds to thousands of dollars every month.

Here is a financial breakdown of the true costs of disposable emails, and how putting a [free temp email checker](/tools/temp-email-checker) at the front door protects both your margins and your domain.

---

## 1. The "Zombie Contact Tax" on Marketing & CRM Platforms

Most marketing automation platforms and CRMs (including HubSpot, Mailchimp, Klaviyo, ActiveCampaign, and Loops) price their tiers based on **audience size or total stored contacts**.

Here is how the economics work against you:

- A visitor signs up with a 10-minute temporary inbox (`@mailinator.com`, `@guerrillamail.com`, or `@yopmail.com`).
- Your backend creates the contact record and syncs it to your CRM or marketing tool.
- Fifteen minutes later, the temporary mailbox ceases to exist.
- That contact sits in your CRM forever unless you manually audit and purge it.

When your contact list grows from 9,500 to 10,500 contacts because of 1,000 burner emails, you are automatically bumped to the next pricing tier:

| Platform | Tier A (10,000 contacts) | Tier B (15,000+ contacts) | The "Zombie Contact" Cost |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **HubSpot Marketing Hub** | ~$800 / month | ~$1,250 / month | **+$450 / month** |
| **Klaviyo** | ~$150 / month | ~$245 / month | **+$95 / month** |
| **Mailchimp Standard** | ~$135 / month | ~$210 / month | **+$75 / month** |

You are literally paying a monthly subscription fee to store dead, unreachable inboxes. Filtering disposable domains at the registration step stops dead records from ever entering your CRM sync pipeline.

---

## 2. Preventing Free Trial and AI Credit Farming Abuse

If your product offers free trial credits, sign-up perks, or API allowances (such as $5 in free LLM tokens, 20 AI generations, or a $10 coupon code), disposable emails are an open invitation for exploit scripts.

Script-kiddies and bot operators use automated disposable email generators to cycle through thousands of accounts:
1. They script automated signups using disposable domains.
2. They consume the sign-up compute, AI tokens, or cloud bandwidth for free.
3. Once credits run dry, they discard the email and trigger another signup.

```
Without Validation:
Bot Script ──> Temp Email ──> Free Sign-Up ──> Burns $5 in AI API Credits ──> Discards Inbox
(Repeated 500x = $2,500 unrecoverable cloud/LLM bill)
```

If 200 bot signups each consume $3 worth of OpenAI API tokens or GPU inference, that is **$600 per month charged directly to your infrastructure credit card**, with zero conversion chance.

[Gating signups with a disposable detector](/blog/block-disposable-emails-at-signup) immediately kills 95%+ of low-effort multi-accounting scripts without requiring heavy, high-friction CAPTCHAs for legitimate users.

---

## 3. The $15,000 Deliverability Death Spiral

The most catastrophic cost of disposable emails is not the storage. It is **sender domain reputation**.

Major mailbox providers (Google Workspace, Gmail, Microsoft 365, Yahoo) evaluate how recipients treat your mail. One of their most strictly enforced signals is **hard bounce rate**. 
- Industry standard delivery targets keep hard bounces **under 2%**. 
- Exceeding **5%** triggers immediate scrutiny, spam foldering, or rate-limiting.

Because disposable inboxes are deleted minutes after creation, every automated email you send after signup (your [welcome email](/blog/welcome-email-sequences-that-convert), onboarding sequence, email verification link, or day-3 check-in) will **hard bounce**.

```
High Disposable Signups
        │
        ▼
Elevated Hard Bounce Rate (>3-5%)
        │
        ▼
Domain Reputation Downgraded by Gmail & Microsoft
        │
        ▼
Legitimate Customer Emails Land in Spam Folder
        │
        ▼
Real Customers Miss Password Resets, Invoices & Onboarding
        │
        ▼
Direct Churn, Lost Revenue, & Costly Remediation
```

### What does recovering a burned domain cost?
When your transactional emails [start landing in spam](/blog/why-emails-land-in-spam-fix):
* Legitimate paying customers can't log in (missing 2FA and [password reset](/blog/password-reset-email-best-practices) tokens), driving up customer support tickets.
* Trial activation rates plummet because users never see the onboarding steps.
* Restoring a burned IP and domain requires hiring deliverability consultants, purchasing dedicated IPs, and executing a multi-month [IP warming schedule](/blog/ip-warming-guide), often costing **$5,000 to $15,000+** in lost revenue and tooling.

Checking for disposable providers on signup keeps your [hard bounce rate](/blog/email-bounce-processing-automation) near zero, protecting the inbox placement of your revenue-generating emails.

## How to Implement in Your App in 60 Seconds

You don't need a bulky SDK or a paid subscription to protect your registration endpoints. Here is how you can gate user signups in a standard Next.js, Node.js, or Express backend:

```typescript
// app/api/signup/route.ts or similar backend registration handler
  const { email, password } = await req.json();

  // 1. Call Reloop's public checker endpoint
  const checkRes = await fetch("https://reloop.sh/api/tools/v1/temp-email-checker", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify({ email }),
  });

  const check = await checkRes.json();

  // 2. Reject disposable providers before writing to your database
  if (check.isDisposable) {
    return Response.json(
      { error: "Please use a permanent work or personal email address to sign up." },
      { status: 400 }
    );
  }

  // 3. Proceed with normal account creation & CRM sync
  // await db.user.create({ data: { email, ... } });

  return Response.json({ success: true });
}
```

Notice what happens:
1. Malformed emails and disposable providers are rejected before any row is written to PostgreSQL.
2. No welcome email is queued in BullMQ or your MTA, so no hard bounce ever happens.
3. No ghost user is synced to HubSpot or Loops.
4. No free compute or AI trial tokens are issued.

Protect your signup pipeline today by testing a domain on the [Free Temp Email Checker](/tools/temp-email-checker) or integrating the endpoint directly into your auth flow.

## First: what "GDPR-friendly" actually means

This isn't legal advice. Talk to your DPO or counsel for your own situation. But a few points clear up most of the confusion.

1. **GDPR doesn't require EU hosting.** It requires a lawful basis for processing, a data processing agreement (DPA) with your email provider, and a valid transfer mechanism whenever personal data leaves the EEA.
2. **Email providers process personal data.** Recipient addresses, names in templates and event logs are all personal data, so your provider is a processor and you need a signed DPA and a list of its sub-processors.
3. **Transfers outside the EEA need a mechanism.** The usual ones are an adequacy decision (such as the EU-US Data Privacy Framework for certified US companies) or Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) plus a transfer risk assessment.
4. **Schrems II is why teams still care.** In 2020 the EU's top court struck down Privacy Shield and said SCCs alone aren't enough if the destination country's surveillance laws undermine them. The Data Privacy Framework replaced Privacy Shield, but it has faced legal challenges, and many teams prefer not to depend on it.
5. **Location and jurisdiction are different questions.** Data in a Frankfurt data center run by a US company can still be subject to US law (the CLOUD Act). If that's your concern, look at who owns the provider and its hosting, not only where the servers are.

That gives you three levels to choose from:

- **EU-hosted:** servers are in the EU.
- **EU-hosted and EU-owned:** the provider and its hosting are European companies.
- **Self-hosted:** you run it, so you decide both.

## 1. Lettermint: best EU-owned, EU-hosted API

[Lettermint](https://lettermint.co/) is a Dutch company (Lettermint B.V.) whose site says it is "built in the Netherlands" and "hosted in Europe". It covers transactional email, broadcasts and inbound in one product, with a REST API and SMTP relay.

**Pricing:** free for 300 emails a month. Paid plans come in Starter, Growth and Pro, each priced by volume: 10,000 emails is €10, €13 or €15 a month, and 50,000 is €40, €45 or €55. A dedicated IP is €50 a month on Pro at 300,000 emails and up. Paid plans share one monthly volume across transactional, broadcast and inbound mail.

**Strengths**

- **European company, European hosting.** The simplest answer if your security review asks both "where" and "who".
- **ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certified**, which shortens vendor questionnaires.
- Transactional, broadcast and inbound on one plan.
- SDKs and integrations for Node, PHP, Python, Go and Laravel, among others.

**Weaknesses**

- More expensive than Reloop Cloud per email: €40 vs $10 at 50k.
- Inbound mail is delivered by webhook, not stored as mailboxes.
- Hosted-only.

**Best for:** EU companies that want a modern hosted API and a clean answer on data sovereignty. Already on Lettermint? See the [best Lettermint alternatives](/blog/best-lettermint-alternatives).

## 2. Sweego: best French-hosted option with SMS

[Sweego](https://sweego.io/) is a French email and SMS platform from the team behind Mindbaz, a long-running French bulk-email company. Sweego says its infrastructure runs on OVHcloud and Scaleway across several data centers in France.

**Pricing:** free for 100 emails a day, with webhooks and 7 days of logs. Individual starts at €10 a month for 20,000 to 50,000 emails. Startup starts at €79 for 100,000 to 200,000, with a dedicated IP available. Scaleup starts at €270 for 500,000 to 1 million and includes a dedicated IP. Extra IPs are €30 a month, and annual billing saves 20%. SMS is sold as credits, from €20.

**Strengths**

- **Hosted in France on French cloud providers**, a strong answer for French public-sector and regulated buyers.
- Email and SMS in one account.
- Log retention grows with the plan: 30 days on Individual, 60 on Startup, 90 on Scaleup.
- API and SMTP on every paid plan.

**Weaknesses**

- Focused on transactional email and SMS; no marketing campaigns or automations.
- Its documentation and community are smaller than the bigger names'.
- Hosted-only.

**Best for:** French and EU teams that want transactional email and SMS from one French provider. Already on Sweego? See the [best Sweego alternatives](/blog/best-sweego-alternatives).

## 3. MailPace: best privacy-first transactional

[MailPace](https://mailpace.com/) is made in the UK and, in its own words, "100% European Union hosted". Its stance is the most opinionated here: **"We never track email opens or clicks."** Instead of tracking pixels, it only reports whether the receiving server accepted the message.

**Pricing:** from $10 a month for the first 10,000 emails, scaling with a volume slider. Every feature is on every plan. There's an unadvertised free plan of up to 100 emails a month; you request it from support.

**Strengths**

- **No tracking pixels at all.** If your privacy policy or works council objects to open tracking, this removes the question.
- Inbound email turned into JSON webhooks.
- Idempotent requests and a simple HTTP API or SMTP.
- SDKs for Ruby, JavaScript, PHP, Go, Rust and Erlang.

**Weaknesses**

- **Transactional only.** MailPace prohibits marketing and newsletters.
- Shared IPs only; no dedicated or static IPs.
- At most 50 recipients per send.
- No open or click data, which some product teams do want.

**Best for:** privacy-focused products that send only transactional mail. Already on MailPace? See the [best MailPace alternatives](/blog/best-mailpace-alternatives).

## 4. Reloop: open source, hosted on Hetzner or self-hosted

[Reloop](/self-host) is open-source email infrastructure under Apache 2.0: a transactional API, SMTP relay, inbound mailboxes, contacts, campaigns, automations and webhooks. You can use it hosted, or run the same code on your own server.

**Where Reloop Cloud is hosted:** on [Hetzner](https://www.hetzner.com/), a German hosting company, across multiple regions including its EU data centers. The infrastructure provider is European, which also helps if your review asks about US jurisdiction over the hosting. We also publish:

- A [Data Processing Addendum](/dpa) that relies on the EU Standard Contractual Clauses (including the UK Addendum) for any transfer outside the EEA.
- A [sub-processor list](/dpa/subprocessors). Reloop Cloud runs on infrastructure Reloop Labs operates itself, so the systems that touch customer data (PostgreSQL, Redis, NATS, MinIO, ClickHouse, KumoMTA, Rspamd and so on) are our own deployments, not third-party SaaS.

If you want every byte on servers you control, **self-host** instead:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://reloop.sh/install.sh | sudo bash
```

Run that on an EU VPS (Hetzner, OVHcloud, Scaleway or your own hardware). Point attachments and template images at EU object storage, such as Hetzner Object Storage or a MinIO box you run. Then you decide where everything lives, and no third party processes your mail.

Your application code doesn't change. Point the SDK at your own server:

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({
  apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY!,
  baseUrl: "https://mail.example.eu",
});
```

**Pricing:** Reloop Cloud is Free (6,000 a month), Pro $10 for 50,000, and Growth $20 for 100,000 with a dedicated IP, the lowest of any provider here at those volumes. Self-hosting is free; you pay for the server. The [VPS guide](/docs/self-host/vps) lists a minimum of 2 vCPUs and 4 GB of RAM.

**Strengths**

- **Hosted on European infrastructure** (Hetzner), or on your own server if you self-host.
- Cheapest hosted option here: $10 for 50k and $20 for 100k with a dedicated IP.
- Full platform: transactional, campaigns, event automations and inbound mailboxes with API, MCP and IMAP access.
- No per-email fee when self-hosted.
- Open source, so security reviewers can read the code that handles your users' mail.

**Weaknesses**

- If your policy requires the provider company itself to be registered in the EU (not just EU hosting), check that in each provider's DPA. Lettermint and Sweego state it on their sites.
- Self-hosting means you own IP reputation, warm-up, backups and uptime.

**Best for:** EU teams that want the lowest price with European hosting, inbound mailboxes for support or AI agents, or the option to move to their own servers later. See [self-hosted email infrastructure](/blog/self-hosted-email-infrastructure) for what running it really involves.

[Mailjet](https://www.mailjet.com/) started in France and is now owned by Sinch (Sweden). Its [security and privacy page](https://www.mailjet.com/security-privacy/) says customer data is stored in Google Cloud data centers in Frankfurt (Germany) and Saint-Ghislain (Belgium).

## How to choose

- **"Our security review asks where the data is *and* who can be compelled to hand it over."** Lettermint or Sweego, or self-hosted Reloop on EU hardware you control.
- **"We can't use tracking pixels."** MailPace. In Reloop you can switch open and click tracking off per domain.
- **"We need marketing campaigns too."** Brevo or Mailjet hosted, Lettermint for broadcasts, or Reloop for campaigns plus automations.
- **"We need inbound mail as real mailboxes, for support or AI agents."** Reloop, hosted or self-hosted.
- **"We want the lowest cost with EU hosting."** Reloop Cloud at $10 for 50k, on Hetzner, with a DPA.

Whichever you choose, ask for three documents before signing: the **DPA**, the **sub-processor list**, and a statement of **where data is stored and backed up**. A provider that can't produce all three quickly is telling you something.

---

## Switching to an EU provider

The mechanics are the same for every provider here:

1. **Sign the DPA** and record the provider in your records of processing.
2. **Verify your domain.** Add the new DKIM record, merge the provider's include into your existing SPF record (never publish a second SPF record), and keep DMARC in place. Our [SPF, DKIM and DMARC guide](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide) covers it.
3. **Export your suppression list** from the old provider and import it, so you don't email people who bounced or unsubscribed.
4. **Swap the client and templates**, then move webhooks to the new event names.
5. **Ramp traffic** over one to two weeks and watch bounce and complaint rates.
6. **Delete data at the old provider** once you're done, and ask for written confirmation.

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Do I need an EU-hosted email provider to comply with GDPR?">
    Not strictly. GDPR allows transfers outside the EEA with a valid
    mechanism, such as an adequacy decision or Standard Contractual Clauses
    with a transfer assessment. Many teams still choose EU hosting because it
    removes the transfer question and makes security reviews shorter. This
    isn't legal advice; check with your DPO.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Is data in an EU data center safe from US law?">
    Not necessarily. If the provider or its hosting company is a US company,
    US law such as the CLOUD Act may still reach that data wherever it's
    stored. If that matters to you, choose an EU-owned provider on EU-owned
    hosting, or self-host.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Does Reloop have an EU region?">
    Yes. Reloop Cloud runs on Hetzner, a German hosting company, across
    multiple regions including its EU data centers, and comes with a DPA and
    a public sub-processor list. If you'd rather keep everything on your own
    hardware, self-host Reloop on an EU server; it's the same open-source code
    under Apache 2.0.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Which EU email API is cheapest?">
    At 50,000 emails a month, Reloop Cloud is $10, while Mailjet Essential is
    $40 and Lettermint Starter is €40. Self-hosted Reloop has no per-email fee
    at all, only the server cost.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can I turn off open and click tracking?">
    MailPace never tracks them at all. In Reloop, open and click tracking are
    per-domain settings. They're on for new domains, and you can switch either
    off in the domain's settings, so no tracking pixel or rewritten links are
    added. Check each other provider's settings for the equivalent.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# Why We Open-Sourced Our Email Infrastructure

Path: /blog/why-we-open-sourced-email-infrastructure
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/why-we-open-sourced-email-infrastructure
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/why-we-open-sourced-email-infrastructure.md

The story behind Reloop: why we built an open-source alternative to SendGrid, Resend, and Mailgun, why email infrastructure is too critical to rent forever, and what we're changing.

**Email is the most critical communication backbone of modern software, yet it has quietly become one of the most expensive and locked-down tools in SaaS.**

When your auth tokens, receipts, password resets, and user notifications fail, your business is effectively down. Yet for over a decade, developers have been forced to accept a frustrating tradeoff: **either pay skyrocketing bills to closed email vendors**, or **spend months wrestling with fragile mail servers** that lack modern APIs, webhooks, and analytics.

We built [Reloop](https://github.com/reloop-labs/reloop) because we believe **email infrastructure belongs in the open**. Here is the story behind why we started, the structural problems we kept running into, and why we made Reloop [Apache 2.0](/license).

---

## The problem: Email became a hostage situation

Every growing startup and engineering team we spoke with was hitting the same predictable wall: **monthly email bills exploding from $20 to $2,000+ as user volume scaled**, without any corresponding increase in value or underlying infrastructure costs.

Beyond pricing, closed-source email providers introduce compounding technical risks:

- **Vendor lock-in by design**: Proprietary APIs, custom template formats, and vendor-specific webhook payloads ensure that **leaving a provider requires a painful, multi-week engineering rewrite**.
- **Opaque black-box delivery**: When emails silently fail or get flagged as spam, closed vendors offer vague deliverability scores rather than raw [SMTP](/features/smtp) transcripts and transparent queue visibility.
- **Zero data sovereignty**: Every user interaction, email address, password reset token, and payload metadata passes through third-party servers, **creating compliance headaches for HIPAA, GDPR, and enterprise audits**.
- **Single point of failure**: If your closed email SaaS suffers an outage, **your entire authentication and notification loop goes dark with zero fallback**.

To see how these tradeoffs compare across the ecosystem, check our [2026 email provider comparison](/blog/email-provider-comparison-2026) or explore side-by-side breakdowns against [SendGrid](/compare/sendgrid), [Resend](/compare/resend), [Mailgun](/compare/mailgun), and [AWS SES](/compare/aws-ses).

---

## Why "just use Postfix" isn't the answer

The traditional counterargument from senior engineers has always been: *"Why not just run your own Postfix, KumoMTA or Haraka instance?"*

**The harsh reality is that raw Postfix provides a mail transfer agent, not modern developer infrastructure.** 

Running bare SMTP solves packet transmission, but it leaves you with months of grueling undifferentiated engineering work:

1. **Reputation & protocol engineering**: Configuring [SPF, DKIM, and DMARC](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide), handling [IP warming sequences](/blog/ip-warming-guide), and managing suppression lists.
2. **Bounce classification**: Distinguishing between temporary soft bounces and permanent hard bounces automatically to protect domain reputation (see our guide on [email bounce processing automation](/blog/email-bounce-processing-automation)).
3. **Developer ergonomics**: Building ergonomic REST APIs, multi-language [SDKs](/sdk), and template render engines.
4. **Visibility & observability**: Parsing real-time delivery events into signed [webhooks](/features/webhooks) and actionable [email analytics](/features/email-analytics).

Building all of this in-house takes **6 to 9 months of full-time platform engineering** before sending your first production receipt. Most teams cannot afford that distraction, so they reluctantly pay the SaaS.

---

## What we built with Reloop

Reloop bridges this gap: **a production-grade, fully open-source email engine with the developer experience of modern email SaaS, built to run anywhere.**

<SendEmailCodeSamples />

Reloop gives you the complete lifecycle out of the box:

- **Unified REST API & Drop-in SDKs**: Ergonomic endpoints and official [SDKs for Node.js, Python, and Go](/sdk) designed for seamless migration from existing providers (see our [SendGrid migration guide](/blog/migrating-from-sendgrid)).
- **[SMTP relay](/features/smtp) & Drop-in replacement**: Instantly plug Reloop into Nodemailer, Next.js, Django, Laravel, Rails, or Supabase.
- **Automated deliverability loop**: Built-in [SPF/DKIM validation](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide), feedback loops, and intelligent retry queues powered by BullMQ (detailed in [how we built our queue engine](/blog/how-we-built-email-delivery-queue-bullmq)).
- **Real-time [email analytics](/features/email-analytics)**: Full visibility into deliveries, opens, click tracking, bounces, and complaint rates with zero third-party tracking scripts.
- **Signed [webhook delivery](/features/webhooks)**: Guaranteed event delivery with automatic backoff, replay capabilities, and secret signing.
- **[AI Agent inboxes & MCP support](/features/ai-agents)**: Two-way inbound parsing and Model Context Protocol tooling so autonomous agents can send, receive, and reason over email safely (explore our [AI agent inbox use case](/use-cases/ai-agent-inbox) and [email infrastructure for AI agents](/blog/email-infrastructure-for-ai-agents)).

---

## The open-source bet: Boring infrastructure must be open

Think about the foundational software that powers modern computing: **Linux, PostgreSQL, Redis, Kubernetes, and Nginx**. 

Nobody rents their primary database or operating system behind a closed, proprietary paywall where the underlying code cannot be inspected, self-hosted, or audited. **Email sits squarely in that foundational tier.**

By releasing Reloop under the **[Apache 2.0 license](/license)**, we guarantee:

1. **Complete Stack Ownership**: The cloud platform and the open-source release run the **exact same codebase**. You can `docker compose up` locally, host on [Fly.io](/blog/reloop-flyio-deployment) or [Coolify](/blog/reloop-coolify-setup), or run on bare metal for under $5/mo (see [how to self-host email for $5/month](/blog/self-host-email-5-dollars)).
2. **Auditability & Security**: Security teams can inspect every line of delivery logic and keep sensitive communication strictly within their own VPC boundary.
3. **No Ransom Pricing**: If your business grows 100x, your outbound communication channel doesn't become your most expensive utility. You can choose managed [Reloop Cloud pricing](/pricing) for zero ops, or [self-host](/self-host) with complete independence.

For a deeper dive into our architectural philosophy, read our [product beliefs](/about) and [why open source matters](/why-open-source).

---

## Where we go from here

We are building Reloop in the open with a public roadmap driven by real developer feedback, not arbitrary pricing metrics.

Whether you are an indie hacker shipping your first app, a high-growth startup outgrowing vendor limits, or an enterprise demanding strict compliance: **you should never have to compromise between world-class developer experience and complete infrastructure ownership.**

# Best Mailgun Alternatives in 2026: Lower Prices and a Real Free Tier

Path: /blog/best-mailgun-alternatives
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-mailgun-alternatives
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-mailgun-alternatives.md

The best Mailgun alternatives in 2026 compared: Reloop, Resend, Postmark, Amazon SES, SendGrid, MailerSend, SMTP2GO and Elastic Email on price at 50k and 100k emails, free tiers, inbound routing, overage and migration.

**The short version:** if you're leaving Mailgun because of price, **Reloop** is the closest like-for-like replacement: the same REST and SMTP sending, stored templates, webhooks and inbound mail, for **$10 at 50,000 emails instead of $35**, with a permanent free tier and open source. **Postmark** is the pick for pure transactional deliverability, and **Amazon SES** is the cheapest pipe if you'll build the tooling yourself.

We build Reloop, so weigh that. Every price below comes from the providers' public pricing pages, linked in our head-to-head posts, and each section says where that provider beats us.

---

## Why teams leave Mailgun

Mailgun, now part of Sinch, still does the basics well. People usually leave for the same handful of reasons:

- **No real free tier.** The free option is a trial at 100 emails a day.
- **Small entry plan.** Basic is $15 for only 10,000 emails. 50,000 needs Foundation at $35.
- **Expensive overage.** Extra mail costs from $1.30 per 1,000 ($1.80 on Basic), so 100,000 a month lands around $100.
- **Paid extras.** Dedicated IPs and email validation are add-ons.
- **Marketing lives elsewhere.** Campaigns are a separate Sinch product.
- **Hosted only.** No source and no self-hosting.

If Mailgun's routes, log search and validation are central to your stack, it may still be worth the price. Otherwise, here are the alternatives.

## 1. Reloop: best overall Mailgun alternative

Reloop is open-source email infrastructure: a transactional API, SMTP relay, inbound mailboxes, contacts, campaigns, automations and webhooks in one product, hosted or on your own server.

**Pricing:** Free is 6,000 emails a month (200 a day) with no end date. Pro is $10 for 50,000. Growth is $20 for 100,000 and includes a dedicated IP. Extra mail costs $0.50 per 1,000. Or prepay credits at $0.50 per 1,000, valid for 6 months. Self-hosting is free under Apache 2.0.

**Why it fits Mailgun users**

- **A fraction of the price.** $10 vs $35 at 50k, and $20 vs about $100 at 100k. Overage is $0.50 per 1,000 instead of $1.30 or more.
- **Inbound that goes further than routes.** Mailgun matches and forwards messages. Reloop stores them in threaded mailboxes, scores spam, and lets you read and reply over the API, the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) or IMAP, with an `email.received` webhook when you want push.
- **A JSON API with readable errors.** No `multipart/form-data` and no domain argument: Reloop reads the domain from `from`, returns errors as values with `message`, `why` and `fix`, and supports `Idempotency-Key` for safe retries.
- **Campaigns and automations on the same plan**, sharing one suppression list with your transactional mail.
- **Open source and self-hostable.** Reloop Cloud runs on Hetzner, a German hosting company, with EU data centers.

**Where Mailgun is still ahead**

- **Template logic.** Mailgun templates use Handlebars. Reloop substitutes variables like `{{{first_name}}}`; logic stays in your code.
- **Years of history.** More Stack Overflow answers, client libraries and edge cases already solved.

**Best for:** teams that want Mailgun's sending surface at a much lower price, plus real inboxes.

Full breakdown: [Reloop vs Mailgun](/blog/reloop-vs-mailgun) · [Mailgun alternative overview](/alternatives/mailgun) · [Feature comparison](/compare/mailgun)

**Strengths:** excellent docs, a JSON API with a small SDK, first-class React Email, and Broadcasts for simple marketing.

**Weaknesses:** $35 at 100k vs $20 on Reloop, a dedicated IP needs the $90 Scale plan plus a $30/mo add-on, inbound is a webhook per message, and it's hosted only.

**Strengths:** a long transactional-only track record, message streams that keep bulk mail away from password resets, and excellent support.

**Weaknesses:** priced like Mailgun or higher once you pass 10,000, a tiny free tier, and hosted only.

**Best for:** teams leaving Mailgun for reliability, not price.

## 4. Amazon SES: cheapest raw sending

**Pricing:** $0.10 per 1,000 emails plus $0.12 per GB of outbound data. Receiving costs $0.10 per 1,000. Dedicated IPs are $24.95 a month. New AWS accounts get up to $200 in Free Tier credits for six months.

**Strengths:** the lowest list price by far, deep AWS integration, and huge scale.

**Weaknesses:** a sandbox to escape, and no logs dashboard, templates editor, bounce processing or inbound mailboxes unless you build them. Inbound is receipt rules into S3 or Lambda, a step down from Mailgun's routes.

**Best for:** AWS-native teams with engineering time.

**Strengths:** proven at huge volume, Twilio procurement, subusers and IP pools, and Handlebars logic in templates.

**Weaknesses:** no permanent free plan, separate plans for marketing, an older API, and hosted only.

**Strengths:** a drag-and-drop builder, SMS in the US and Canada, and inbound forwarding.

**Weaknesses:** the same $35 at 50k as Mailgun, a small free tier, and marketing in a separate product (MailerLite).

## How to choose

- **"We want the same features for much less."** Reloop: $10 at 50k and $0.50 per 1,000 overage.
- **"We rely on inbound routes."** Reloop if you want stored, threaded mailboxes; stay on Mailgun if pattern-based forwarding is all you need.
- **"Deliverability is everything."** Postmark.
- **"We're on AWS and price per email is all that matters."** Amazon SES, or SES behind Reloop.
- **"We just need a dependable SMTP relay."** SMTP2GO or Reloop.
- **"We need to self-host or audit the code."** Reloop, the only open-source option here.

---

## Migrating off Mailgun

1. **Verify your domain** with the new provider. For Reloop, publish the `reloop._domainkey` DKIM record and merge `include:reloop.sh` into your existing SPF record. Never publish a second SPF record.
2. **Export suppressions** (bounces, unsubscribes, complaints) from Mailgun and import them.
3. **Swap the client.** Replace `mg.messages.create(domain, {...})` with a JSON send. In Reloop that's `reloop.mail.send`, with the domain taken from `from`.
4. **Move templates.** Handlebars `{{first_name}}` becomes `{{{first_name}}}` in Reloop, and values are passed as template variables instead of `h:X-Mailgun-Variables`.
5. **Replace routes.** If you forward inbound mail, point MX records at the new provider and read from its mailboxes or inbound webhook.
6. **Point webhooks** at a new handler. Reloop events like `email.delivered` and `email.bounced` are signed in the `Reloop-Signature` header.
7. **Ramp traffic** from 10% to 100% over one to two weeks.

The [SendGrid migration guide](/blog/migrating-from-sendgrid) covers the same steps in detail, including a traffic-split flag and a suppression import script that work just as well from Mailgun.

# Reloop vs MailPace (2026): Pricing, Privacy and Which to Choose

Path: /blog/reloop-vs-mailpace
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-mailpace
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-mailpace.md

Reloop vs MailPace compared honestly: pricing by volume, EU hosting and the DPA, MailPace's no-tracking stance, the send API, inbound email and agent inboxes, campaigns, self-hosting, and how to switch.

**MailPace is a small, opinionated transactional email API: EU-hosted, run by a UK company, and built around one rule, that it never tracks opens or clicks.** Reloop is a broader platform. **It sends transactional mail and campaigns, runs event-triggered automations, receives mail into inboxes your AI agents can reply from, and it's open source, so you can host it yourself.** MailPace is the cleaner answer if you want a hosted EU provider with no tracking at all. Reloop is cheaper per email once you pass 10,000 a month, and does more.

We build Reloop, so weigh this accordingly. MailPace facts below come from its own [pricing page](https://mailpace.com/pricing), [documentation](https://docs.mailpace.com/), [DPA](https://mailpace.com/dpa), [privacy policy](https://mailpace.com/privacy) and [terms](https://mailpace.com/terms). Where MailPace is the better pick, we say so.

---

## The 30-second comparison

| | **Reloop** | **MailPace** |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | Email infrastructure: API, SMTP, campaigns, automations, inboxes | Transactional email API and SMTP |
| Company | Reloop Labs | OhMySMTP Ltd, England and Wales |
| Hosted data location | Hetzner, with EU data centers (or self-host to choose) | France (per its DPA) |
| Free tier | 6,000 / mo, 200 / day | Up to 100 / mo, on request |
| 10,000 emails / mo | $10 (Pro) | $10 |
| 50,000 emails / mo | **$10** | $50 |
| 100,000 emails / mo | **$20** | $100 |
| Open / click tracking | Per domain, can be turned off | **Never** |
| Marketing / campaigns | Yes | Prohibited |
| Automations | Every plan | No |
| Inbound email | Mailboxes with threads, API, MCP, IMAP | JSON webhook per message |
| Dedicated IP | Included on Growth ($20) | No, shared IPs only |
| Idempotent sends | Yes | Yes |
| Open source | Yes (Apache 2.0) | No (SDKs and templates are MIT) |
| Self-host | Yes | No |

Prices change. Check [MailPace's pricing page](https://mailpace.com/pricing) and [ours](/pricing) before you commit.

---

## Pricing at real volumes

MailPace has one plan. It's $10 a month for the first 10,000 emails, and its pricing calculator adds $1 for every 1,000 after that. Every feature is on that plan. Two details matter:

- **It counts mail you send and receive.** The pricing page asks "How many emails do you send and receive each month?", so inbound volume is billed too.
- **The free plan is unadvertised.** The pricing FAQ calls it a "secret free plan" of up to 100 emails a month, which you request by email.

Reloop has Free (6,000 a month, 200 a day), Pro at $10 for 50,000, and Growth at $20 for 100,000 with a dedicated IP. Above your plan, it's $0.50 per 1,000.

| Monthly volume | Reloop | MailPace |
|---|---|---|
| 3,000 | $0 | $10 (free only up to 100) |
| 10,000 | $10 | $10 |
| 50,000 | $10 | $50 |
| 100,000 | $20 | $100 |
| 250,000 | $20 + $75 overage = $95 | $250 |

MailPace prices are in US dollars from its calculator; it shows local currencies too, so your exact figure depends on where you are billed.

At 10,000 emails the two cost the same. Past that, MailPace grows at $1 per 1,000 and Reloop at $0.50 per 1,000 beyond a much larger included volume.

If you self-host Reloop, there's no per-email fee at all. See [self-hosted email infrastructure](/blog/self-hosted-email-infrastructure) for what that really takes.

<Callout type="tip">
  If you receive a lot of mail through MailPace's inbound webhooks, add that volume to your estimate. MailPace bills sent and received mail together.
</Callout>

---

## Privacy, hosting and jurisdiction

This is why most people look at MailPace, and it's well documented.

**Who runs it.** MailPace's terms and privacy policy name the company as OhMySMTP Ltd, incorporated in England and Wales (company number 13200428). The service was called OhMySMTP until January 2022. Its terms are governed by UK law.

**Where data lives.** The homepage says MailPace is "100% European Union hosted". The [DPA](https://mailpace.com/dpa) is more specific: stored data is "encrypted and hosted in France", and it "never leaves the EU and EU-owned cloud infrastructure, except for actually sending each email, which is sent via SMTP servers based in the UK". Its [sub-processor list](https://mailpace.com/privacy) names Clever Cloud for EU-hosted servers and databases, Freethought (a UK hosting company) for infrastructure hosting, and Hetzner for off-site backups in Germany. If your review needs every hop inside the EU, ask MailPace about the UK sending servers.

**How long it keeps mail.** Emails are visible in the dashboard for 30 days and removed from backups 7 days later, so 37 days at most, per the DPA.

**Tracking.** MailPace says: "We never track email opens or clicks." It only reports whether the receiving server accepted the message. If you want an open pixel anyway, its FAQ says you can add one yourself, with user opt-in.

**Reloop's side.** Reloop Cloud runs on Hetzner, the German hosting company, with EU data centers. It comes with a [Data Processing Addendum](/dpa) based on the EU Standard Contractual Clauses and a public [sub-processor list](/dpa/subprocessors). If you want to decide both location and jurisdiction yourself, [self-host Reloop](/self-host) on your own EU server. Open and click tracking in Reloop are per-domain settings. New domains start with them on, and you can switch either off on the domain's Configuration tab.

<Callout type="info">
  For a hosted service with no tracking pixels anywhere, MailPace is the more direct answer. Reloop can match it only if you turn tracking off on each domain, or self-host.
</Callout>

---

## Developer experience

Both APIs are small and easy to call. MailPace authenticates with a per-domain token in a `MailPace-Server-Token` header.

**MailPace**

```typescript
await fetch("https://app.mailpace.com/api/v1/send", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    Accept: "application/json",
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
    "MailPace-Server-Token": process.env.MAILPACE_TOKEN!,
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    from: "hello@acme.com",
    to: "user@example.com",
    subject: "Welcome",
    htmlbody: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
  }),
});
```

**Reloop**

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY! });

const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Welcome",
  html: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
});
```

| | Reloop | MailPace |
|---|---|---|
| Send endpoint | `POST /api/mail/v1/send` | `POST /api/v1/send` |
| Auth | Account API key (`x-api-key`) | One token per domain (`MailPace-Server-Token`) |
| Body fields | `from`, `to`, `html`, `text` | `from`, `to`, `htmlbody`, `textbody` |
| Recipients per send | Up to 50 in `to` | Up to 50 in `to` |
| Idempotency | `Idempotency-Key` header | `Idempotency-Key` header |
| Stored templates | Yes, with variables | No; send rendered HTML |
| Attachments | Up to 1 MB (Free) or 5 MB (paid) | Allow-listed file extensions only |
| Webhook signing | HMAC-SHA256 (`Reloop-Signature`) | Ed25519 (`X-MailPace-Signature`) |
| SMTP | `smtp.reloop.sh` | `smtp.mailpace.com` |

A few things worth knowing:

- **Idempotency is a tie.** MailPace highlights it as a differentiator, and it's a good feature. Reloop supports the same `Idempotency-Key` header on sends.
- **Libraries.** MailPace's docs cover Rails, JavaScript, PHP, Erlang, Go and Rust. Reloop has [official SDKs](/docs/resources/sdks) for Node, Python, Go, PHP, Ruby, Rust, Java, .NET and Elixir.
- **Errors.** Reloop's errors include `message`, `why` and `fix`, so the response tells you what to change. MailPace returns a short `error` string or per-field `errors`.
- **MCP.** MailPace publishes an MIT-licensed [MCP server](https://github.com/mailpace/mailpace-mcp) with one tool, `send-email`. Reloop's [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) covers sending plus inboxes, contacts, templates, automations and domains.

---

## Receiving email and agent inboxes

**MailPace** catches all mail sent to a subdomain you choose (for example `*@inbound.acme.com`) once you add a CNAME to `inbound.mailpace.com`. Each message is POSTed to your HTTPS endpoint as JSON, with the raw message, parsed fields and attachments. It retries five times, then marks the message failed and bounces it to the sender. Storing, threading and replying is up to you.

**Reloop** receives mail into **mailboxes**. Messages are stored, threaded, spam-scored with Rspamd, and readable over the API, the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) or IMAP. Replying in-thread is one call, and an `email.received` webhook is there if you also want push.

| | Reloop | MailPace |
|---|---|---|
| Receive on your domain | Yes | Yes, on a subdomain |
| Webhook per message | Yes (`email.received`) | Yes |
| Stored mailboxes with threads | Yes | No |
| Reply in thread via API | Yes | Build it yourself |
| MCP access for agents | Yes | No |
| IMAP access | Yes | No |

If you're building an AI agent or a support inbox that has to read a thread and answer it, Reloop saves you the storage and threading work. See [build an AI agent that reads and replies to email](/blog/build-ai-agent-sends-emails).

---

## Campaigns, contacts and automations

MailPace doesn't do this, on purpose. Its terms allow "sending transactional email only", and its docs say marketing emails and newsletters are "strictly prohibited". There are no contact lists, campaigns or automations.

Reloop has contacts with custom properties, groups, subscription channels, scheduled broadcast campaigns, and **event-triggered automations** that start when your app tracks an event like `user.signed_up`. Automations are on every plan, including Free.

If you only send password resets, receipts and alerts, MailPace's focus is a feature: a provider that only carries transactional mail keeps its shared IPs clean of newsletter traffic. If you also send onboarding sequences or product updates, you'd need a second provider next to MailPace, and Reloop covers both.

---

## Deliverability

Both handle the basics: DKIM signing, bounce handling and a block list of addresses that bounced.

- **IPs.** MailPace's docs say "Static IP addresses are not available"; every customer shares its IPs. Reloop includes a dedicated IP on Growth at $20 a month, and shared IPs on the other plans.
- **Spam filtering.** MailPace runs an internal spam filter on outgoing mail and refuses to send what it flags. Reloop runs its own MTA (KumoMTA) with per-domain throttling and automatic pauses when bounce or complaint rates spike. Read [how bounce processing works](/blog/email-bounce-processing-automation).
- **Signals.** Without opens and clicks, MailPace tells you whether mail was accepted, deferred or bounced. Reloop reports the same delivery events, plus opens and clicks if you leave tracking on.
- **Free tools.** Reloop ships a [domain reputation checker](/tools/domain-reputation-checker), [blocklist checker](/tools/blocklist-checker) and [temp email checker](/tools/temp-email-checker).

---

## Self-hosting and lock-in

MailPace is hosted only. It publishes its client libraries, an [HTML email template set](https://github.com/mailpace/templates) and its MCP server under MIT, but not the service itself.

Reloop is Apache 2.0. You can:

1. Start on Reloop Cloud.
2. Move to your own server later with the [one-command installer](/self-host) or [Coolify](/blog/reloop-coolify-setup).
3. Keep the same API. Point the SDK's `baseUrl` at your instance and nothing else in your code changes.

Self-hosting isn't free in effort: you own IP reputation, warm-up, backups and uptime. The [requirements](/docs/self-host/requirements) start at 2 vCPUs and 4 GB of RAM.

---

## Where MailPace is the better choice

- **You want a hosted EU provider and no tracking, full stop.** MailPace stores data in France and never adds open or click tracking. Reloop Cloud is EU-hosted too, but it offers tracking (on by default for new domains).
- **You send only transactional mail** and like a provider that refuses marketing traffic on its IPs.
- **You send around 10,000 emails a month** and value a tiny, focused product. At that volume the price is the same.

For other privacy-friendly options, see our roundup of the [best MailPace alternatives](/blog/best-mailpace-alternatives).

## Where Reloop is the better choice

- **You send more than 10,000 emails a month.** $10 vs $50 at 50k and $20 vs $100 at 100k.
- **You also send campaigns or onboarding sequences**, and want one provider and one suppression list for both.
- **You need inbound mail as real inboxes**, especially for AI agents.
- **You need a dedicated IP**, or open source and self-hosting for compliance or control.

---

## Switching from MailPace to Reloop

1. **Add your domain in Reloop** and publish the DKIM record (`reloop._domainkey`). Merge `include:reloop.sh` into your existing SPF record rather than adding a second one.
2. **Decide on tracking.** If you chose MailPace for its no-tracking stance, turn click and open tracking off on the domain before you send.
3. **Swap the client.** Replace the `/api/v1/send` call with `reloop.mail.send`, and map `htmlbody`/`textbody`/`replyto` to `html`/`text`/`reply_to`. Keep sending your `Idempotency-Key`.
4. **Or swap SMTP settings.** Point your app at `smtp.reloop.sh` on port 587 with STARTTLS, using your Reloop API key as username and password.
5. **Carry over your block list.** Copy the bounced addresses from your domain's Block List page in MailPace and suppress them in Reloop, so you don't mail them again.
6. **Point webhooks** at a new handler. `email.delivered` and `email.bounced` keep their names; MailPace's `email.deferred` becomes `email.delivery_delayed`. Verify Reloop's HMAC-SHA256 `Reloop-Signature` instead of the Ed25519 signature.
7. **Move inbound.** Add a receiving address in Reloop and change the subdomain's DNS once you're ready, then read mail from the mailbox or the `email.received` webhook.
8. **Ramp traffic** over a week or two, then remove MailPace's DNS records and delete your MailPace account, which deletes its stored emails.

Our [SendGrid migration guide](/blog/migrating-from-sendgrid) walks through the same steps in more detail, including a traffic-split flag and a suppression import script.

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Is Reloop cheaper than MailPace?">
    Above 10,000 emails a month, yes. At 50,000 Reloop is $10 and MailPace
    is $50; at 100,000 it's $20 vs $100. At exactly 10,000 both are $10.
    Below 6,000 a month, Reloop's free tier costs nothing, while MailPace's
    free plan covers up to 100 emails on request.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Where does MailPace host data?">
    Its DPA says stored data is hosted in France and stays in the EU, except
    that outgoing mail is sent through SMTP servers in the UK. MailPace
    itself is a UK company, OhMySMTP Ltd.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can I send marketing email with MailPace?">
    No. MailPace's terms allow transactional email only, and its docs say
    newsletters and other marketing mail are strictly prohibited. Reloop
    sends both transactional mail and campaigns.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Does Reloop track opens and clicks?">
    Only if the domain has tracking turned on. Open and click tracking are
    per-domain settings; new domains start with them on, and you can turn
    either off. MailPace never tracks them.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can I self-host MailPace?">
    No. MailPace is a hosted service, though its SDKs, templates and MCP
    server are MIT-licensed. Reloop is open source under Apache 2.0 and runs
    on your own server with the same API.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>
