## How to choose

- **"We chose SES for the price but spend too much time on glue code."** Reloop. Same idea of cheap sending, with logs, suppression and webhooks built in.
- **"We send millions of emails a month and have a platform team."** Stay on SES, or self-host Reloop to keep zero per-email fees with a product on top.
- **"Our whole app runs on Cloudflare Workers."** Cloudflare Email Service.
- **"We only send transactional mail and want the lowest bill."** ZeptoMail, or Reloop below about 150k a month.
- **"Deliverability is the only thing that matters."** Postmark.
- **"We need inbound mail as real inboxes, for support or AI agents."** Reloop.
- **"We want to run our own mail server."** Postal for a pure MTA, Reloop for the full platform.

---

## Migrating off Amazon SES

The steps are the same whichever provider you pick:

1. **Verify your domain** with the new provider. Add its DKIM record and merge its include into your existing SPF record; never publish a second SPF record. Keep DMARC in place. Our [SPF, DKIM and DMARC guide](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide) covers it.
2. **Export your suppression list** from SES's account-level list and your own store, and import it so you don't email addresses that bounced or complained.
3. **Swap the send call.** Replace `SendEmailCommand` with the new SDK. On Reloop, change `{{variable}}` placeholders to `{{{variable}}}`.
4. **Replace the SNS or EventBridge consumer** with a webhook handler. On Reloop, verify the `Reloop-Signature` header.
5. **Ramp traffic** from 10% to 100% over one to two weeks, watching bounce and complaint rates.
6. **Tear down** the configuration sets, SNS topics and Lambda functions you no longer need.

# Reloop vs SparkPost (2026): Pricing, Features and Which to Choose

Path: /blog/reloop-vs-sparkpost
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-sparkpost
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-sparkpost.md

Reloop vs SparkPost (now Bird Email) compared honestly: pricing from 3k to 500k emails a month, what changed after the Bird move, inbound mail, analytics, self-hosting and how to switch.

**SparkPost isn't really SparkPost anymore.** sparkpost.com now redirects to Bird, and the product is sold as **Bird Email**, built on what Bird calls "the SparkPost engine, now one API." If you're comparing the two today, you're comparing Reloop with Bird's email product, and with a migration you'd have to plan either way.

The short version: **Reloop is cheaper up to about 300k emails a month, has a real free tier, and is open source, so you can run it yourself.** Bird gets cheaper per email at very high volume and comes with the analytics and deliverability tooling SparkPost was known for.

We build Reloop, so weigh this accordingly. Bird's numbers below are from [bird.com/pricing/email](https://bird.com/pricing/email) as of October 2026, and where Bird is the better pick, we say so.

---

## What happened to SparkPost

- MessageBird [agreed to acquire SparkPost](https://bird.com/blog/sparkpost-joins-bird) and later rebranded as Bird.
- [sparkpost.com](https://www.sparkpost.com) now redirects to Bird's email product page, and the old pricing page redirects to Bird's email pricing.
- Bird's own [SparkPost page](https://bird.com/email-api/features/sparkpost) says Bird Email "has its own API and SDKs" and advises you to review sending, templates, domains and webhooks "rather than assuming that a SparkPost request can be sent unchanged."

So if you're on SparkPost today, **you're facing a migration whichever way you go**. The real question is where to land.

## Pricing at real volumes

Bird's model is different from a classic plan. Each paid plan adds a **monthly deposit** to your Bird balance, and every email is charged against that balance at the plan's rate. Bird is clear that "a paid deposit adds spendable balance, not a fixed number of included emails," and unused funds carry forward.

| Plan | Monthly deposit | Transactional rate per 1,000 |
|---|---|---|
| Free | $0 | 1,000 emails / mo, 50 / day |
| Startup | $15 | $0.40 |
| Growth | $250 | $0.45 |
| Scale 1,000 | $1,000 | $0.35 |
| Scale 2,500 | $2,500 | $0.30 |
| Scale 5,000 | $5,000 | $0.25 |
| Scale 10,000 | $10,000 | $0.20 |

Here's what that looks like next to Reloop. Bird figures are usage at the Startup rate, rounded:

| Monthly volume | Reloop | Bird Email | Cheaper |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3,000 | $0 | $15 deposit (free plan stops at 1,000) | Reloop |
| 50,000 | $10 | ~$20 | Reloop |
| 100,000 | $20 | ~$40 | Reloop |
| 300,000 | $20 + $100 overage = $120 | ~$120 | Even |
| 500,000 | $20 + $200 overage = $220 | ~$200 | Bird |

The pattern:

- **Under 300k a month, Reloop costs less**, and the gap is widest for small teams. Bird's free plan is 1,000 emails, so most real apps start paying sooner.
- **Above 300k, Bird's per-email rate wins**, and at Scale volumes ($0.20 – $0.35 per 1k) it pulls clearly ahead on list price.
- **Dedicated IPs:** on Reloop one is included on Growth ($20/mo). On Bird they're a paid add-on, and only on Growth ($250 deposit) and up.

And if you self-host Reloop, there's no per-email fee at all. You pay for the server. See [self-hosted email infrastructure](/blog/self-hosted-email-infrastructure) for what that really involves.

<Callout type="tip">
  Price the volume you expect in a year, not today's. If you're heading past a few hundred thousand emails a month, run both numbers at that volume, including dedicated IPs.
</Callout>

---

## Developer experience

SparkPost's classic API was built around **transmissions**: a content block plus a list of recipients.

**SparkPost (legacy client)**

```typescript

const client = new SparkPost(process.env.SPARKPOST_API_KEY);

await client.transmissions.send({
  content: {
    from: "hello@mail.acme.com",
    subject: "Welcome",
    html: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
  },
  recipients: [{ address: "user@example.com" }],
});
```

Bird Email has its own API and SDKs, so existing SparkPost code is not guaranteed to work unchanged. Plan for a rewrite of the sending layer either way.

**Reloop**

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY! });

const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Welcome",
  html: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
});
```

Reloop returns errors as values with a **why** and a **fix**, so a failed send tells you what to change:

```json
{
  "message": "Domain not found",
  "why": "The domain mail.acme.com was not found or is not authorized for your organization",
  "fix": "Ensure the domain is registered and verified in your dashboard"
}
```

| | Reloop | Bird Email |
|---|---|---|
| Send shape | One message: `from`, `to`, `subject`, `html` | Bird's own API (SparkPost used transmissions) |
| Stored templates | Yes, sent by ID with `{{{variables}}}` | Yes, including React Email |
| SMTP relay | Yes | Yes |
| Webhooks | Signed with HMAC-SHA256 in `Reloop-Signature` | Yes |
| Official SDKs | Node, Python, Go, PHP, Ruby, Rust, Java, .NET, Elixir | Bird SDKs |

---

## Analytics and deliverability

This is where SparkPost earned its reputation, and Bird keeps that focus.

**Bird Email** lists real-time delivery tracking, opens, clicks and bounce reasons, IP warming, suppression lists, email validation and **Inbox Insights** for inbox placement monitoring. Bird also publishes customer results like Binance holding 99.01% inbox placement while scaling marketing email.

**Reloop** covers the fundamentals: SPF, DKIM and DMARC setup, bounce and complaint events, open and click tracking, and automatic suppression. It sends through its own MTA (KumoMTA), with per-domain throttling and automatic pauses when bounce or complaint rates spike. Read [how bounce processing works](/blog/email-bounce-processing-automation). Free [domain reputation](/tools/domain-reputation-checker), [blocklist](/tools/blocklist-checker) and [auth](/tools/auth-checker) checkers help before you send.

If inbox placement testing and deep deliverability analytics are a daily job for your team, Bird has more of that built in.

---

## Receiving email and agent inboxes

Both handle inbound. Bird includes inbound email and a number of mailboxes on every plan (5 on Free up to 100 on Scale), and routes replies and attachments into your app.

**Reloop** receives mail into **mailboxes** that are stored, threaded, spam-scored with Rspamd, and readable over the API, the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) or IMAP. You can reply in-thread with one call, and the `email.received` webhook gives you push notifications too.

That matters most if you're building:

- **AI agents that handle email.** Give an agent its own address and let it read and reply over MCP. See [build an AI agent that reads and replies to email](/blog/build-ai-agent-sends-emails).
- **Support or shared inboxes** where humans (over IMAP) and agents work the same threads.

---

## Self-hosting and lock-in

SparkPost and Bird are hosted-only, and the move to Bird is a good reminder of what that means: **when the vendor changes, your integration changes with it.**

Reloop is Apache 2.0. You can:

1. Start on Reloop Cloud.
2. Move to your own server later with the [one-command installer](/self-host) or [Coolify](/blog/reloop-coolify-setup).
3. Keep the same API. Point the SDK's `baseUrl` at your instance and nothing else in your code changes.

Self-hosting isn't free in effort. You own IP reputation, warm-up and uptime. Most teams should start hosted and keep self-hosting as an option.

---

## Where SparkPost (Bird) is the better choice

- **You send hundreds of thousands to millions of emails a month.** Above about 300k, Bird's per-email rate beats Reloop's overage, and at Scale it's as low as $0.20 per 1,000.
- **Deliverability analytics are a core need.** Inbox placement monitoring and SparkPost-grade analytics are built in.
- **You want email, SMS and WhatsApp on one balance.** Bird is an omnichannel platform; Reloop is email only.
- **You already work with SparkPost's account team** and want their help through the migration.

If you're leaving SparkPost and comparing more providers, see the [best SparkPost alternatives](/blog/best-sparkpost-alternatives).

## Where Reloop is the better choice

- **You send under 300k emails a month**, where Reloop is cheaper, often by half.
- **You want a usable free tier**: 6,000 a month vs 1,000.
- **You want a dedicated IP without a $250 monthly deposit.**
- **You need inbound mail your agents can use** over MCP and IMAP.
- **You want open source or self-hosting**, so a vendor change can't force a rewrite again.

---

## Switching from SparkPost to Reloop

You'll need to touch the sending layer whether you move to Bird or to us, so plan it the same way.

1. **Add your domain in Reloop** and publish the DKIM record (`reloop._domainkey`). Merge `include:reloop.sh` into your existing SPF record. Don't add a second SPF record.
2. **Export suppressions** from SparkPost and import them into Reloop, so you never mail an address that bounced or complained.
3. **Swap the client.** Replace `transmissions.send` with `reloop.mail.send`. Each recipient becomes `to`, and `content.from`, `content.subject` and `content.html` move to the top level.
4. **Move templates.** SparkPost templates use `{{variable}}`. Change placeholders to triple braces: `{{{first_name}}}`.
5. **Point webhooks** at a new handler. Reloop events are named `email.delivered`, `email.bounced`, `email.complained` and so on, and are signed with HMAC-SHA256 in the `Reloop-Signature` header.
6. **Ramp traffic** from 10% to 100% over a week or two, then remove the old DNS records.

Our [SendGrid migration guide](/blog/migrating-from-sendgrid) covers these steps in more detail, including a traffic-split flag and a suppression import script.

# I Let an AI Agent Read and Reply to My Emails. Here's How the Infrastructure Works.

Path: /blog/email-infrastructure-for-ai-agents
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/email-infrastructure-for-ai-agents
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/email-infrastructure-for-ai-agents.md

Building an AI agent that reads and replies to email is easy in LangChain. Owning the send-and-receive layer is the hard part, and why open-source email infrastructure matters.

Right now, everyone's building AI agents that do everything: book flights, negotiate contracts, run support, chase down leads. They all hit the exact same wall.

An AI can write the perfect reply in two seconds. But if it can't receive what the customer writes back, it's not having a conversation. It's just sending one message into the void.

Building the reply logic in something like LangChain is maybe an hour of work. Getting it to actually send and receive real email is where things get complicated, often taking far longer than the AI part itself.

## The default move: a third-party API key

The obvious first move: grab a Resend or SendGrid key, wire it to the agent, ship it.

It doesn't take much to go wrong this way. An agent that occasionally sends a slightly repetitive or oddly-formatted reply is normal LLM behavior, not a bug. Managed providers run abuse and compliance systems for a reason. Unexpected send patterns can get an account restricted, sometimes quickly.

That's the trap: when you send through someone else's platform, you don't own your sending reputation. They do. An autonomous agent is, by definition, going to occasionally do something a little weird. Building on infrastructure where a third-party compliance decision can take your whole send path offline is a real product risk.

[Self-hosting](/blog/self-hosted-email-infrastructure) doesn't mean Gmail and Outlook stop filtering mail. What changes is who controls your domain, your keys, and your operational rules, and whether a vendor's compliance queue can shut you down overnight.

## Sending is only half the job

For an agent to be useful, it also has to **read replies**.

If your agent offers a calendar slot and the customer writes back *"Actually, can we do Saturday at 2 PM?"*, that reply has to land somewhere your code can process, as structured fields, not a raw MIME blob sitting in someone's personal Gmail.

Many teams still treat email as send-only. Some providers do offer inbound parsing, and a few, like AgentMail, are built only for agent inboxes ([how the two compare](/blog/reloop-vs-agentmail)). The harder part is usually the whole loop in one place:

- receive at your domain
- parse MIME into text, HTML, headers, and attachments
- keep thread context
- send authenticated replies from the same identity
- keep data and ops under your control when you need to

That loop is the product surface agents actually need. The model is the brain. Email is the mouth and the ears.

## Reloop is the plumbing, not the AI

To be clear: **Reloop is not an AI calendar bot.** Reloop is open-source email infrastructure.

Your agent (LangChain, Autogen, a custom Python service, whatever you build) is the brain. Reloop is the send-and-receive layer: APIs, SMTP, inbound mailboxes, parsing, DKIM, and the option to self-host.

Think of it this way: you bring the LLM. Reloop gives that LLM a real mailbox.

Here's how that wiring looks in practice. For the setup steps, see [how to give an AI agent its own email address](/blog/give-ai-agent-email-address).

### 1. Inbound (the ears)

Point your domain's MX records at your Reloop instance (or use Reloop hosted). When mail hits `support@yourcompany.com`, Reloop accepts it, runs spam checks, and parses the MIME message into plain text, HTML, headers, and attachments.

### 2. Handoff

Reloop stores the message against a mailbox and correlates it into a thread. Your agent reads that clean payload through the inbox APIs, or you work from the agent inbox when you want a human in the loop.

### 3. Your LLM brain

Your code, not Reloop, decides what the message means. Check a calendar. Look up an order. Draft a reply. Apply your own allowlists, rate limits, and approval rules.

### 4. Outbound (the mouth)

Your app sends the reply through Reloop's REST API (or SMTP). Reloop signs the message with DKIM and delivers it. Same domain identity on the way out as on the way in.

When you self-host, that path runs on infrastructure you operate. You own the data plane. You make the operational rules.

## What you get that agents actually need

For agent workflows, the useful Reloop surface looks like this:

- **Inbound + outbound in one stack**: receive at your domain and reply from the same platform
- **MIME parsing**: plain text, HTML, headers, and attachments ready for your agent context
- **Thread correlation**: replies stay attached to the conversation
- **Agent inbox**: a mailbox UI and APIs built for programmatic and human-assisted workflows
- **DKIM-signed sending**: REST and SMTP with authentication you configure on your domain
- **Delivery events**: opens, clicks, bounces, and complaints via [webhooks](/blog/building-webhook-delivery-system) so your agent can react to what happened after send
- **Hosted or self-hosted**: same product idea either way; self-host when ownership and data residency matter

Reloop also covers the rest of a modern email platform (templates, campaigns, contacts, analytics), but for agents, the core loop is inbound, parse, decide, send.

<Callout type="info">
  **Coming next: inbound notify.** Today your agent pulls new mail from the inbox APIs (or the agent inbox UI). We're building inbound webhooks so Reloop can push a notification to your app the moment a message arrives, using the same event-driven pattern as delivery webhooks, for the receive side. Not shipped yet; watch the repo for it.
</Callout>

## Your agent. Your rules.

Owning the email layer doesn't make an unsupervised agent safe. Self-hosting means you own the reputation, and the responsibility.

Allowlist recipients. Rate-limit sends. Keep a human in the loop when it matters.

Reloop moves mail. You decide what the model is allowed to say.

## The takeaway

AI agents are becoming real participants in businesses: negotiating, following up, handling support. But an agent that can't reliably talk to a human, both ways, is just a very good draft generator.

If you're building agents that need to hold a real conversation, you need infrastructure that receives, not just sends, and you need to own it, not rent it. For a full walkthrough with code, see [build an AI agent that reads and replies to email](/blog/build-ai-agent-sends-emails).

[Check out Reloop on GitHub](https://github.com/reloop-labs/reloop) and see the inbound flow yourself. Build the brain. Let Reloop be the ears and the mouth.

  href="/features/ai-agents"
  label="Explore AI agent email"

# Transactional Email Best Practices: The Complete Developer Guide

Path: /blog/transactional-email-best-practices
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/transactional-email-best-practices
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/transactional-email-best-practices.md

Everything you need to send fast, reliable, inbox-landing transactional email, from domain setup and template design to delivery patterns and monitoring.

## What makes transactional email different

Transactional emails (password resets, receipts, order confirmations, notifications, onboarding sequences) are different from marketing email in one critical way: **the recipient expects them.** That expectation drives open rates of 45–65%, compared to 20–25% for marketing campaigns.

But that expectation also creates an obligation. When someone clicks "Forgot password?" and your reset email takes 4 minutes to arrive, or [lands in spam](/blog/why-emails-land-in-spam-fix), it's not an inconvenience. It's a product failure. Your transactional email infrastructure is part of your product.

This guide covers everything you need to get transactional email right: from domain architecture to template patterns, delivery behaviour, and what to monitor.

---

## 1. Domain and subdomain architecture

### Use a dedicated sending subdomain

Never send transactional email from your root domain (`yourdomain.com`). Use a dedicated subdomain:

- `mail.yourdomain.com`: clean, generic
- `notifications.yourdomain.com`: descriptive
- `noreply.yourdomain.com`: avoid this (more on why below)
- `tx.yourdomain.com`: short, unambiguous

Why it matters: if your marketing emails damage your sender reputation (high unsubscribes, spam complaints from cold outreach), a dedicated transactional subdomain insulates your password resets and receipts from that reputation hit.

### Separate transactional from marketing at the subdomain level

| Email type | Subdomain |
|------------|-----------|
| Password resets, 2FA | `mail.yourdomain.com` |
| Receipts, order confirmations | `mail.yourdomain.com` |
| Product notifications | `notifications.yourdomain.com` |
| Newsletter, campaigns | `marketing.yourdomain.com` |

### Never send from `noreply@`

`noreply@` is a red flag for spam filters and a poor experience for recipients. Spam filters correlate `noreply` addresses with bulk, impersonal sending. And when a recipient wants to reply to a receipt or reset email and they can't, it damages trust.

Use a monitored address like `hello@` or `support@` with a reply-to if you don't want replies going to your engineering inbox. The deliverability improvement alone is worth the setup cost.

---

## 2. Authentication: table stakes, not optional

Before your first production send, your sending domain must have:

- **SPF**: authorizes your sending servers
- **DKIM**: signs each message cryptographically
- **DMARC**: sets policy and sends you reports on failures

[Gmail and Yahoo have required all three](/blog/gmail-yahoo-bulk-sender-requirements) since February 2024. Skipping any one of them will result in your email being rejected or spam-foldered by major ISPs.

See the [complete SPF, DKIM, DMARC setup guide](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide) for step-by-step configuration.

---

## 3. Sending patterns that affect deliverability

### Send immediately, never batch transactional mail

Transactional email must be sent with near-zero latency. A user who triggers a [password reset](/blog/password-reset-email-best-practices) expects that email within 30 seconds. If you're batching emails or running them through a slow queue, you're creating support tickets.

The correct pattern:
1. User action triggers email send
2. API call to Reloop is made inline or in an immediate background job
3. Email departs within seconds

Never schedule transactional emails for "later" or include them in a batch job that runs every few minutes.

### Use dedicated queues for different priority tiers

If you have a job queue, separate email types into priority lanes:

```typescript
// High priority: password resets, 2FA codes
await queue.add("send-email", payload, { priority: 1 });

// Standard: receipts, welcome emails
await queue.add("send-email", payload, { priority: 5 });

// Low: digest emails, weekly summaries
await queue.add("send-email", payload, { priority: 10 });
```

This prevents a surge of digest emails from delaying password resets.

### Implement retry logic, but not for hard bounces

If a send fails due to a temporary issue (rate limit, provider timeout), retry with exponential backoff:

- Attempt 1: immediate
- Attempt 2: 30 seconds
- Attempt 3: 5 minutes
- Attempt 4: give up and alert

But never retry a hard bounce (invalid address, domain doesn't exist). Hard bounces are permanent. Re-sending damages your reputation. Reloop's [bounce processing](/blog/email-bounce-processing-automation) handles this automatically: addresses that hard bounce are suppressed and never re-sent to. To reduce hard bounces upstream, verify addresses at collection with a [free email validator](/tools/email-validator) (syntax, disposable domains, and MX checks) before they hit your transactional send queue.

---

## 4. Template design for transactional email

### Keep HTML minimal

Heavy, image-rich email templates built for marketing campaigns perform poorly as transactional email. Spam filters treat complex HTML with many images, heavy CSS, and tracking pixels with more suspicion.

For transactional email, aim for:
- Simple one-column layout
- System fonts or Google Fonts (not embedded fonts)
- Inline CSS (email clients ignore `<style>` blocks)
- Single, clear CTA button
- No background images

### Always include a plain text version

Every transactional email must have both `html` and `text` parts. Some email clients prefer plain text. Others use the presence of a text part as a positive signal.

```typescript
await reloop.emails.send({
  from: "mail@yourdomain.com",
  to: user.email,
  subject: "Reset your password",
  html: `<p>Click <a href="${resetUrl}">here</a> to reset your password. This link expires in 15 minutes.</p>`,
  text: `Reset your password: ${resetUrl}\n\nThis link expires in 15 minutes.`,
});
```

### The right subject lines for transactional email

Transactional subject lines should be **specific and functional**, not clever:

| Type | Bad | Good |
|------|-----|------|
| Password reset | "Action required" | "Reset your Reloop password" |
| Receipt | "Your order" | "Receipt for $49.00 (Order #12345)" |
| Welcome | "Welcome!" | "Your Reloop account is ready" |
| Notification | "New activity" | "5 emails failed delivery in the last hour" |

Specificity reduces support tickets ("I never got my reset email") because users can search their inbox for it by keyword.

### Personalise beyond first name

First-name personalisation is table stakes. Go further:

- Include the specific action the user took that triggered the email
- Reference the specific resource (order number, domain name, project name)
- Show the current state they care about (balance, count, status)

```html
<!-- Weak -->
<p>Hi Sarah, your email was sent.</p>

<!-- Strong -->
<p>Hi Sarah, your email to 3 recipients from <strong>onboarding@acme.com</strong>
was delivered successfully. <a href="/logs/abc123">View delivery details →</a></p>
```

---

## 5. Managing suppression and bounces

### Never send to a bounced address

Sending to an address that has previously hard bounced is one of the fastest ways to damage your sender reputation. Reloop maintains a suppression list automatically: addresses that hard bounce or mark your email as spam are added and never re-sent to.

If you're managing email sends outside of Reloop, implement your own suppression list and check it before every send. For imported or legacy lists, run a [bulk email verifier](/tools/email-validator) first so you suppress (or remove) undeliverable addresses before the first transactional send.

### Handle unsubscribes for every email type

Even transactional emails should have a way for recipients to manage their notification preferences. The legal threshold varies by country (CAN-SPAM, GDPR, etc.), but the practical threshold is simpler: if someone doesn't want an email, give them an easy way to stop receiving it. Frustrated users who can't unsubscribe hit "Report spam" instead.

For truly transactional emails (password resets, receipts), an unsubscribe isn't appropriate, but for notification-style emails, it is.

### Monitor your bounce and complaint rates

Track these metrics per sending domain:

| Metric | Healthy threshold | Action if exceeded |
|--------|------------------|--------------------|
| Hard bounce rate | < 2% | Stop, audit list quality |
| Spam complaint rate | < 0.1% | Audit content + list |
| Soft bounce rate | < 5% | Review and retry strategy |

Google Postmaster Tools provides domain-level reputation data for Gmail. Register your domain there and check it weekly.

---

## 6. What to monitor in production

### Delivery rate per email type

Don't just track aggregate delivery rate. Break it down by email type (password reset, welcome, receipt) and by ISP (Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo). A deliverability problem at one ISP with one email type is invisible in aggregate metrics.

### Time to delivery

Measure how long it takes from the send API call to the delivery event. For critical email types (password resets, 2FA), set an alert if P95 exceeds 30 seconds.

### Open rate as a deliverability proxy

A sudden drop in open rate for a specific email type (without a content change) usually means something changed in deliverability. If your password reset open rate drops from 70% to 30%, investigate immediately.

### Use Reloop's webhook events

Reloop emits events for every step of the email lifecycle: `email.sent`, `email.delivered`, `email.opened`, `email.clicked`, `email.bounced`, `email.complained`. Subscribe to these with a [webhook](/blog/building-webhook-delivery-system) and build dashboards, alerts, or automated responses (like removing a complained address from your list in real-time).

```typescript
// Webhook handler: remove complaints from your user preferences
  const event = await req.json();

  if (event.type === "email.complained") {
    await db.userPreferences.update({
      where: { email: event.data.to },
      data: { marketingEmails: false },
    });
  }
}
```

---

## 7. Testing before you ship

### Test in multiple email clients

The same HTML renders very differently in Gmail, Outlook (desktop), Apple Mail, and Gmail on Android. Use a tool like [Litmus](https://litmus.com) or [Email on Acid](https://www.emailonacid.com) to preview across clients before shipping.

### Check your spam score

Send a test email to [mail-tester.com](https://mail-tester.com). It scores your email from 0–10 and shows you exactly what's penalizing you: missing authentication, suspicious content patterns, missing plain text part, and so on.

Target a score of 9 or above before any email type goes to production.

### Load test your send path

If you have a feature that sends email on every user action, test what happens when 1,000 users trigger it simultaneously. Make sure your queue doesn't back up and that rate limiting is in place before you're in that situation in production.

---

## Quick-reference checklist

Before any transactional email goes live:

- [ ] Sending from a dedicated subdomain, not the root domain
- [ ] `From` address is a monitored inbox, not `noreply@`
- [ ] SPF, DKIM, DMARC all configured and verified
- [ ] Both `html` and `text` parts included
- [ ] Subject line is specific and functional
- [ ] Tested at [mail-tester.com](https://mail-tester.com) with a score of 9+
- [ ] Previewed in Gmail, Outlook, and Apple Mail
- [ ] Sending immediately (not batched) for critical types
- [ ] Retry logic implemented with exponential backoff
- [ ] Bounced addresses suppressed and never re-sent to
- [ ] Webhook handler set up for `email.bounced` and `email.complained` events
- [ ] Delivery rate and time-to-delivery monitored in production

---

# How to Send Email in Python: smtplib, Django and API

Path: /blog/send-email-python
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/send-email-python
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/send-email-python.md

Send email from Python with smtplib, Django, FastAPI or Flask, or with an email API. Copy-paste examples for HTML email, attachments, background sending and retries without duplicates.

**Python can send email with the built-in `smtplib` module, no install needed.** For anything in production, send through a provider: either over SMTP with `smtplib` or your framework's mail settings, or over HTTPS with an email API SDK.

This guide covers plain `smtplib`, the Reloop Python SDK, Django, FastAPI and Flask, then the production details: attachments, background sending and safe retries.

Working in JavaScript? See [how to send email in Node.js](/blog/send-email-nodejs).

---

## Which approach should you use?

| | `smtplib` / framework SMTP | Email API SDK |
|---|---------------------------|---------------|
| **Install** | Nothing, it is in the standard library | `pip install reloop-email` |
| **Transport** | SMTP on port 587 (STARTTLS) | HTTPS on port 443 |
| **Building the message** | `EmailMessage`, MIME parts | A dict with `html`, `text`, `attachments` |
| **Errors** | `SMTPException` subclasses | Result object with status and message |
| **Safe retries** | No, a retry can send twice | Yes, with an idempotency key |
| **Works with Django's `send_mail`** | Yes, natively | Through SMTP settings |

If you are wiring up Django's built-in auth emails or a third-party package, use SMTP settings. If you are writing the send call yourself, use the API.

---

## Prerequisites

1. **Python 3.9 or later**
2. A **verified sending domain** with [SPF, DKIM and DMARC](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide)
3. An **API key** from the [Reloop dashboard](https://reloop.sh/dashboard). Keys start with `rl_`, and the same key works for the API and SMTP.

```bash
```

Keep the key in the environment or a secrets manager, never in your code or git.

## Method 1: Send email with smtplib

Use `EmailMessage` from the standard library. It handles encoding, headers and multipart bodies for you, so you do not need the older `MIMEMultipart` and `MIMEText` classes.

```python
from email.message import EmailMessage

msg = EmailMessage()
msg["From"] = "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>"
msg["To"] = "user@example.com"
msg["Subject"] = "Welcome to Acme"

# Plain-text body first, then the HTML alternative
msg.set_content("Welcome! Thanks for signing up.")
msg.add_alternative(
    "<h1>Welcome!</h1><p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
    subtype="html",
)

with smtplib.SMTP("smtp.reloop.sh", 587, timeout=30) as server:
    server.starttls()
    server.login("reloop", os.environ["RELOOP_API_KEY"])
    server.send_message(msg)
```

The username can be any string. The password is your API key.

### When port 587 is blocked

Some hosts block outbound 587. Reloop also accepts STARTTLS on port **2587** (and 2025), so only the port number changes:

```python
with smtplib.SMTP("smtp.reloop.sh", 2587, timeout=30) as server:
    server.starttls()
    server.login("reloop", os.environ["RELOOP_API_KEY"])
    server.send_message(msg)
```

Reloop does not offer implicit TLS on port 465, so do not use `smtplib.SMTP_SSL` with it. If the connection hangs or times out, see [SMTP ports explained](/blog/smtp-ports-explained).

### Handle SMTP errors

```python
try:
    with smtplib.SMTP("smtp.reloop.sh", 587, timeout=30) as server:
        server.starttls()
        server.login("reloop", os.environ["RELOOP_API_KEY"])
        server.send_message(msg)
except smtplib.SMTPAuthenticationError:
    print("Wrong API key")
except smtplib.SMTPRecipientsRefused as e:
    print("Rejected recipients:", e.recipients)
except (smtplib.SMTPException, OSError) as e:
    print("Send failed:", e)
```

### Can I send with Gmail from Python?

For a personal script, yes: use `smtp.gmail.com` on port 587 with an [App Password](https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/185833). For an app, no. Gmail limits personal accounts to about 500 recipients a day, every message comes from your `@gmail.com` address, and bulk sending gets the account suspended.

## Method 2: Send email with the Python SDK

### Install

```bash
pip install reloop-email
```

### Send an email

```python
from reloop_email import Reloop

reloop = Reloop(api_key=os.environ["RELOOP_API_KEY"])

result = reloop.mail.send({
    "from": "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
    "to": "user@example.com",
    "subject": "Welcome to Acme",
    "html": "<h1>Welcome!</h1><p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
    "text": "Welcome! Thanks for signing up.",
})

if result.email_error:
    print("Failed:", result.email_error.status, result.email_error)
else:
    print("Sent:", result.response["id"])
```

The SDK **returns** errors instead of raising them. Every call gives you a result with either `response` or `email_error`. Network failures come back with status `0`. If you prefer exceptions, `raise result.email_error`: it is an `Exception` subclass.

Create the client **once** at startup and reuse it. It keeps an HTTP connection pool open. Call `reloop.close()` on shutdown, or use it as a context manager in scripts:

```python
with Reloop(api_key=os.environ["RELOOP_API_KEY"]) as reloop:
    reloop.mail.send({...})
```

### Send to several recipients

```python
reloop.mail.send({
    "from": "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
    "to": ["ada@example.com", "grace@example.com"],
    "cc": "team@acme.com",
    "reply_to": "support@acme.com",
    "subject": "Your weekly report",
    "text": "Here is your report.",
    "tags": [{"name": "type", "value": "weekly_report"}],
})
```

Every address in `to` sees the others. For personalised mail, send one message per recipient.

### Send a stored template

Keep copy out of your code so non-developers can edit it. Create the template in Reloop, then send it by ID with variables:

```python
reloop.mail.send({
    "from": "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
    "to": "user@example.com",
    "subject": "Welcome to Acme",
    "template": {
        "id": "tmpl_welcome",
        "variables": {"first_name": "Ada", "plan": "Pro"},
    },
})
```

See [templates](/docs/learn/templates) for variables and defaults.

## Django

Django's mail functions work with any SMTP provider. Add these settings and `send_mail`, [password reset emails](/blog/password-reset-email-best-practices) and admin error emails all go through Reloop:

```python
# settings.py

EMAIL_BACKEND = "django.core.mail.backends.smtp.EmailBackend"
EMAIL_HOST = "smtp.reloop.sh"
EMAIL_PORT = 587
EMAIL_USE_TLS = True
EMAIL_HOST_USER = "reloop"
EMAIL_HOST_PASSWORD = os.environ["RELOOP_API_KEY"]
DEFAULT_FROM_EMAIL = "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>"
SERVER_EMAIL = "errors@mail.acme.com"
```

Keep `EMAIL_USE_SSL` off: Reloop uses STARTTLS, not implicit TLS. If 587 is blocked, set `EMAIL_PORT = 2587`.

```python
from django.core.mail import EmailMultiAlternatives

message = EmailMultiAlternatives(
    subject="Welcome to Acme",
    body="Welcome! Thanks for signing up.",
    to=["user@example.com"],
)
message.attach_alternative("<h1>Welcome!</h1>", "text/html")
message.send()
```

In development, set `EMAIL_BACKEND = "django.core.mail.backends.console.EmailBackend"` to print emails to the terminal instead of sending them. Full example: [Django guide](/docs/examples/python/django).

## FastAPI

The SDK is synchronous. Declare the route with `def`, not `async def`, and FastAPI runs it in a thread pool so it does not block the event loop:

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr
from reloop_email import Reloop

app = FastAPI()
reloop = Reloop(api_key=os.environ["RELOOP_API_KEY"])

class Contact(BaseModel):
    email: EmailStr
    message: str

@app.post("/contact")
def contact(body: Contact):
    result = reloop.mail.send({
        "from": "Acme Website <contact@mail.acme.com>",
        "to": "support@acme.com",
        "reply_to": body.email,
        "subject": f"New message from {body.email}",
        "text": body.message,
    })
    if result.email_error:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=502, detail="Could not send message")
    return {"id": result.response["id"]}
```

The visitor's address goes in `reply_to`, never in `from`. You can only send from your verified domain, and putting someone else's domain in `from` fails [DMARC](/blog/gmail-yahoo-bulk-sender-requirements).

To return before the email is sent, use `BackgroundTasks`:

```python
from fastapi import BackgroundTasks

@app.post("/signup")
def signup(email: EmailStr, tasks: BackgroundTasks):
    # ... create the user ...
    tasks.add_task(reloop.mail.send, {
        "from": "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
        "to": email,
        "subject": "Welcome to Acme",
        "text": "Thanks for signing up.",
    })
    return {"ok": True}
```

`BackgroundTasks` is lost if the process restarts. For emails that must arrive, use a real queue (see below). Full example: [FastAPI guide](/docs/examples/python/fastapi).

## Flask

```python
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
from reloop_email import Reloop

app = Flask(__name__)
reloop = Reloop(api_key=os.environ["RELOOP_API_KEY"])

@app.post("/contact")
def contact():
    data = request.get_json()
    result = reloop.mail.send({
        "from": "Acme Website <contact@mail.acme.com>",
        "to": "support@acme.com",
        "reply_to": data["email"],
        "subject": "New contact form message",
        "text": data["message"],
    })
    if result.email_error:
        return jsonify(error="Could not send message"), 502
    return jsonify(id=result.response["id"])
```

Prefer SMTP with Flask-Mail? Use the same host, port and credentials as the Django settings above. Full example: [Flask guide](/docs/examples/python/flask).

## Attachments

With the SDK, pass base64 content:

```python
from pathlib import Path

pdf = Path("invoice-1042.pdf").read_bytes()

reloop.mail.send({
    "from": "Acme Billing <billing@mail.acme.com>",
    "to": "user@example.com",
    "subject": "Your invoice #1042",
    "text": "Your invoice is attached.",
    "attachments": [{
        "filename": "invoice-1042.pdf",
        "content": base64.b64encode(pdf).decode(),
        "content_type": "application/pdf",
    }],
})
```

With `smtplib`, use `add_attachment`:

```python
msg.add_attachment(
    pdf,
    maintype="application",
    subtype="pdf",
    filename="invoice-1042.pdf",
)
```

Keep attachments small. Many inboxes reject messages over 25 MB, and large files hurt deliverability. For big files, send a signed download link.

---

## Send in the background with Celery

Sending inside a web request adds latency and fails the request when the provider is slow. Move it to a worker and let the queue handle retries:

```python
# tasks.py
from celery import Celery
from reloop_email import Reloop

app = Celery("tasks", broker=os.environ["REDIS_URL"])
reloop = Reloop(api_key=os.environ["RELOOP_API_KEY"])

class RetryableSendError(Exception):
    pass

@app.task(
    autoretry_for=(RetryableSendError,),
    retry_backoff=True,
    max_retries=5,
)
def send_welcome(email: str) -> str:
    result = reloop.mail.send({
        "from": "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
        "to": email,
        "subject": "Welcome to Acme",
        "text": "Thanks for signing up.",
    })
    if result.email_error:
        status = result.email_error.status
        if status == 0 or status == 429 or status >= 500:
            raise RetryableSendError(str(result.email_error))
        raise result.email_error  # 4xx: do not retry
    return result.response["id"]
```

**Retry** network errors (status `0`), `429` and `5xx`. **Do not retry** other `4xx` errors: an invalid address or unverified domain fails the same way every time.

---

## Retries without duplicate emails

A request times out and your task retries. If the first attempt actually went through, the user gets two emails. The API prevents this with an [`Idempotency-Key` header](/docs/api/idempotency): repeat a request with the same key and Reloop returns the original result instead of sending again.

The SDK does not set this header yet, so call the endpoint with `httpx` (already installed with the SDK):

```python

def send_receipt(order_id: str, to: str) -> dict:
    res = httpx.post(
        "https://reloop.sh/api/mail/v1/send",
        headers={
            "x-api-key": os.environ["RELOOP_API_KEY"],
            "Idempotency-Key": f"receipt-{order_id}",
        },
        json={
            "from": "Acme <orders@mail.acme.com>",
            "to": to,
            "subject": f"Receipt for order {order_id}",
            "text": "Thanks for your order.",
        },
        timeout=30,
    )
    res.raise_for_status()
    return res.json()
```

Base the key on the business event (`receipt-{order_id}`), not a new UUID per attempt, so retries from any worker are safe.

---

## Testing without sending real email

- **Django:** the test runner swaps in the `locmem` backend automatically. Assert on `django.core.mail.outbox`.
- **Anything else:** mock the client in unit tests, and send to [test addresses](/docs/guides/testing-email-addresses) in staging so you do not hurt your [sender reputation](/blog/why-emails-land-in-spam-fix) with bounces.
- **Local SMTP:** run [Mailpit](https://mailpit.axllent.org) with `docker run -p 1025:1025 -p 8025:8025 axllent/mailpit` and point `smtplib.SMTP("localhost", 1025)` at it, without `starttls()` or `login()`. Open `http://localhost:8025` to see the messages.

---

## Production checklist

- [ ] API key in an environment variable or secrets manager
- [ ] Sending domain verified with SPF, DKIM and DMARC
- [ ] `from` on your verified domain; user addresses in `reply_to`
- [ ] Both HTML and plain-text bodies
- [ ] One shared client, created at startup
- [ ] Sending in a worker (Celery, RQ, Dramatiq), not the request
- [ ] Retries only on network errors, `429` and `5xx`
- [ ] Idempotency keys on anything that retries
- [ ] [Webhooks](/features/webhooks) for bounces and complaints
- [ ] Disposable addresses blocked at signup ([how](/blog/block-disposable-emails-at-signup))

## FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="How do I send an HTML email in Python?">
    Build an EmailMessage, call set_content with the plain-text version, then
    add_alternative with your HTML and subtype="html". With the Reloop SDK,
    pass html and text keys in the send dict.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="What is the difference between smtplib.SMTP and SMTP_SSL?">
    SMTP connects in plain text and you call starttls() to upgrade, which is
    what port 587 expects. SMTP_SSL starts TLS immediately, which is what port
    465 expects. Using the wrong one for the port makes the connection hang or
    fail with an SSL error.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Is there an async Python SDK?">
    The Reloop Python SDK is synchronous. In FastAPI, declare routes with def
    so they run in the thread pool, or call the HTTP API directly with
    httpx.AsyncClient from async code.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Why do my Python emails go to spam?">
    Usually the sending domain is not authenticated, or the From domain does
    not match the domain that signed the message. Set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC,
    send from your own domain, and always include a plain-text body.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can I use Reloop with Django's password reset emails?">
    Yes. Set the SMTP settings shown above and every email Django sends,
    including password resets and admin error reports, goes through Reloop with
    no code changes.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# How to Check if an Email is Disposable (Free Temp Email Checker)

Path: /blog/disposable-email
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/disposable-email
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/disposable-email.md

In this guide, you'll learn what disposable emails are, why they matter, and how you can quickly check if an email is disposable.

Every day, millions of users sign up for websites using temporary email addresses. While these emails help protect privacy, they can also create problems for businesses.

If you run a SaaS product, e-commerce store, newsletter, or online community, disposable email addresses can lead to fake accounts, spam, coupon abuse, and inaccurate analytics.

In this guide, you'll learn what disposable emails are, why they matter, and how you can quickly check if an email is disposable.

## What Is a Disposable Email?

A disposable email (also called a temporary email or temp mail) is an email address that exists for a short time. Users create these addresses to receive emails without using their personal inbox. Most disposable email services delete emails automatically after a few minutes or hours.

People commonly use disposable emails to:

- Protect their personal email address
- Avoid spam and promotional emails
- Test applications
- Access free downloads without sharing their main inbox

While these are valid use cases, disposable emails can also be misused to create fake accounts.

## Why Businesses Should Check Disposable Emails

Not every temporary email is harmful, but many businesses choose to detect them to improve data quality and prevent abuse.

Here are the most common reasons.

### 1. Prevent Fake Registrations

Users can create multiple accounts using different temporary email addresses. This inflates your user numbers without adding real customers.

### 2. Stop Free Trial Abuse

If your product offers a free trial, users can repeatedly sign up with disposable emails to avoid paying for your service. We added up what that costs in [the hidden costs of disposable emails](/blog/how-temp-email-checker-saves-you-money).

### 3. Reduce Coupon Abuse

Many online stores offer discounts for new customers. Disposable emails make it easy to claim the same offer multiple times.

### 4. Improve Email Deliverability

Marketing emails sent to temporary inboxes often bounce or are never opened, affecting your sender reputation. Over time that's one of the reasons [emails land in spam](/blog/why-emails-land-in-spam-fix).

### 5. Keep Analytics Clean

Fake accounts can distort important metrics such as:

- Active users
- Conversion rate
- Customer retention
- Marketing performance

Accurate data leads to better business decisions.

## How to Check if an Email Is Disposable

There are several ways to identify temporary email addresses.

### Method 1: Use a Free Disposable Email Checker (Recommended)

The easiest and fastest method is to use an online disposable email checker.

Simply enter an email address, and the tool checks whether the domain belongs to a known temporary email provider.

If you're looking for a free solution, try the **[Reloop Temp Email Checker](https://reloop.sh/tools/temp-email-checker)**.

It instantly tells you whether an email address is disposable, making it easy to detect fake signups before they enter your system.

Example:

- `john@gmail.com` ✅ Personal email
- `user@mailinator.com` ❌ Disposable email
- `demo@tempmail.com` ❌ Disposable email

### Method 2: Check the Email Domain

Many temporary email services use publicly known domains.

Examples include:

- mailinator.com
- guerrillamail.com
- yopmail.com
- 10minutemail.com
- tempmail.com

If an email belongs to one of these domains, it is likely disposable.

However, this method requires maintaining an updated list because new temporary email providers appear regularly.

### Method 3: Detect Disposable Emails Programmatically (API / Code)

If your website accepts user registrations, checking every email manually isn't practical.

Instead, integrate disposable email detection into your signup process to automatically flag temporary email addresses before accounts are created. Our step-by-step guide to [blocking disposable emails at signup](/blog/block-disposable-emails-at-signup) shows the full form and server code.

The [Reloop Temp Email Checker](https://reloop.sh/tools/temp-email-checker) is a thin wrapper over one public endpoint. `POST` an address to `https://reloop.sh/api/tools/v1/temp-email-checker` with no API key and no account.

<TempEmailCheckerCodeSamples />

A throwaway mailbox comes back with `"verdict": "disposable"` and `"isDisposable": true`:

```json
{
  "input": "you@mailinator.com",
  "kind": "email",
  "domain": "mailinator.com",
  "verdict": "disposable",
  "isValidSyntax": true,
  "isDisposable": true,
  "disposableMatch": {
    "kind": "exact",
    "domain": "mailinator.com"
  },
  "isAllowlisted": false,
  "isRoleAddress": false,
  "isFreeProvider": false,
  "signals": {
    "syntax": "pass",
    "disposable": "fail",
    "role": "pass",
    "freeProvider": "pass"
  }
}
```

Reject or flag the signup when `isDisposable` is `true`. The endpoint is rate limited per IP, so keep it to signup-time checks rather than bulk list scrubbing.

This saves time and helps prevent abuse from the start.

Need more than disposable detection? Use Reloop's free [email validator](/tools/email-validator) to check syntax, role addresses, live MX records, and clean CSV lists (up to 1,000) in one pass.

## When Should You Block Disposable Emails?

Blocking temporary emails isn't always necessary.

### Consider Blocking Them If:

- You offer free trials
- You run a paid SaaS product
- You provide welcome discounts
- You want high-quality customer data
- You need verified users

### Consider Allowing Them If:

- Privacy is important for your audience
- Users submit anonymous feedback
- Registration isn't required
- Your service is completely free

Choose the approach that best matches your product and users.

## Best Practices for Email Validation

Checking for disposable emails works best when combined with other validation methods.

We recommend:

- Validate email format.
- Detect disposable email domains.
- Verify ownership with email confirmation.
- Add CAPTCHA to signup forms.
- Monitor suspicious signup activity.
- Limit repeated registrations from the same IP address.

Using multiple layers of protection significantly reduces fake registrations.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Are Disposable Emails Legal?

Yes. Temporary email services are legal and are widely used to protect personal privacy.

### Can Disposable Emails Receive Verification Emails?

Yes. Most temporary email providers can receive verification emails immediately after the address is created.

### Should Every Website Block Disposable Emails?

Not necessarily.

Some websites benefit from anonymous access, while others require verified users. The decision depends on your business goals.

### Can Disposable Email Lists Become Outdated?

Yes. New temporary email domains are created frequently, which is why regularly updated detection tools are much more reliable than static blocklists.

## Final Thoughts

Disposable email addresses are useful for protecting user privacy, but they can also be used to create fake accounts, abuse free trials, and reduce the quality of your customer data.

By checking email addresses during registration, you can improve security, keep your database clean, and make better business decisions.

If you need a quick and free way to verify an email address, try the **[Reloop Temp Email Checker](https://reloop.sh/tools/temp-email-checker)**.

For full list cleaning (syntax + disposable + MX), use the free **[Email Validator](/tools/email-validator)**.

Looking for more developer tools?

Visit **[Reloop](https://reloop.sh)**

# Best AgentMail Alternatives in 2026: Email Inboxes for AI Agents Compared

Path: /blog/best-agentmail-alternatives
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-agentmail-alternatives
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-agentmail-alternatives.md

The best AgentMail alternatives for giving AI agents their own email: Reloop, Nylas Agent Accounts, Cloudflare Email Routing, Postmark, Mailgun, Resend and Amazon SES, compared on inboxes, pricing, MCP, IMAP and self-hosting.

**The short version:** if you want an AgentMail alternative that still gives each agent a **real inbox** with threads, replies, IMAP and an MCP server, the two closest options are **Reloop** (open source, much cheaper per email, plus transactional mail and campaigns) and **Nylas Agent Accounts** (hosted mailboxes from a company that already connects to Gmail and Outlook). If you only need to **receive** mail and hand it to your code, an inbound webhook from **Cloudflare**, **Postmark**, **Mailgun**, **Resend** or **Amazon SES** can be enough, as long as you're willing to build storage and threading yourself.

We build Reloop, so factor that in. Each section says plainly where another option beats us.

---

## Why teams look for an AgentMail alternative

AgentMail is a good product. It gives an agent a working `@agentmail.to` address in one API call, with no DNS, and it adds agent-specific helpers like extracted reply text, drafts and WebSockets. Teams usually look elsewhere for one of these reasons (all figures from [AgentMail's pricing page](https://www.agentmail.to/pricing)):

- **Email volume gets expensive.** The $20 Developer plan includes 10,000 emails a month, and extra sends are $2 per 1,000. Agents that do outreach or notifications burn through that fast.
- **It's only inboxes.** If your product also needs password resets, receipts, newsletters or onboarding sequences, that's a second provider with a second set of DNS records and a second suppression list.
- **It's hosted only.** The SDKs are open source, but the inbox service isn't something you can run yourself. That's a problem for agents that read contracts, invoices or medical mail.
- **Dedicated IPs are Enterprise only.**

---

## Top picks at a glance

| Category | Pick | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Best overall AgentMail alternative** | Reloop | Real agent inboxes plus a full email platform, open source, $10 for 50k emails |
| **Best for many hosted agent mailboxes** | Nylas Agent Accounts | 50 agent accounts on the $49 Pro plan, plus calendar |
| **Best free inbound forwarding** | Cloudflare Email Routing | Unlimited inbound, handled in a Worker |
| **Best inbound webhook on a deliverability-first provider** | Postmark | Parsed JSON per message, strong sending reputation |
| **Best regex routing of inbound mail** | Mailgun | Inbound routes match on recipient and headers |
| **Best for AWS-native agents** | Amazon SES | Receipt rules to S3, SNS or Lambda |
| **Best self-hosted** | Reloop | Apache 2.0, no inbox limits when you run it yourself |

---

## Mailboxes vs webhooks: the distinction that matters

There are two very different things sold as "inbound email":

1. **A mailbox.** Mail is stored, threaded and searchable. Your agent can list conversations, read a thread and reply in it, and a human can open the same inbox over IMAP. AgentMail, Reloop and Nylas Agent Accounts work this way.
2. **A webhook.** Each incoming message is parsed and posted to your URL once. Storage, threading, spam handling and reply headers are yours to build. Cloudflare, Postmark, Mailgun, Resend and SES work this way.

If your agent needs memory of a conversation, pick from the first group. If it only needs to react to individual messages (a "reply to this email to comment" feature, a support ticket intake), the second group is cheaper and simpler.

---

## The comparison table

| | Reloop | AgentMail | Nylas Agent Accounts | Cloudflare | Postmark | Mailgun | Resend | Amazon SES |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Inbound model** | Mailboxes with threads | Mailboxes with threads | Hosted mailboxes | Routing to address or Worker | Webhook (JSON) | Inbound routes | Webhook per message | Receipt rules |
| **Reply in thread via API** | Yes | Yes | Yes | From a Worker | Build it | Build it | Build it | Build it |
| **IMAP** | Yes | Yes | Yes (app password) | No | No | No | No | No |
| **Hosted MCP server** | Yes | Yes | Yes | No | No | No | No | No |
| **Free tier** | 6,000 emails / mo, 3 inboxes | 3,000 emails / mo, 3 inboxes | 3,000 emails / mo, 3 agent accounts | Inbound free; sending needs Workers Paid | 100 emails / mo | 100 / day trial | 3,000 / mo | $200 AWS credits |
| **First paid plan** | **$10**: 50k emails, 5 inboxes | $20: 10k emails, 10 inboxes | $15: 10k emails, 10 agent accounts | $5 Workers Paid | $15 for 10k (inbound on Pro and up) | $15 for 10k | $20 for 50k | Pay as you go |
| **Transactional + campaigns** | Yes | No | No | Transactional only | Transactional + broadcast streams | Yes | Yes | Sending only |
| **Open source / self-host** | Yes (Apache 2.0) | SDKs only | No | No | No | No | No | No |

Sources: [agentmail.to/pricing](https://www.agentmail.to/pricing), [nylas.com/pricing](https://www.nylas.com/pricing/), [Cloudflare Email Service pricing](https://developers.cloudflare.com/email-service/platform/pricing/), [postmarkapp.com/pricing](https://postmarkapp.com/pricing), [mailgun.com/pricing](https://www.mailgun.com/pricing/), [resend.com/pricing](https://resend.com/pricing), [aws.amazon.com/ses/pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/ses/pricing/), [reloop.sh/pricing](/pricing). Prices change; check before you commit.

---

## 1. Reloop: best overall AgentMail alternative

[Reloop](/) is open-source email infrastructure. Agent inboxes are one part of it: you create a mailbox on your verified domain, and your agent can list threads, read them and reply in thread over the API, the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) or IMAP. The same account sends transactional mail, campaigns and event-triggered automations. Reloop Cloud runs on Hetzner, a German hosting company, with EU data centers.

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY! });

const { threads } = await reloop.inbox.threads.list({ mailboxId: "mbx_123" });

await reloop.inbox.messages.reply("msg_123", {
  html: "<p>Thanks, I've booked that for you.</p>",
});
```

**Pricing:** Free is 6,000 emails a month (200 a day) with 3 inboxes. Pro is $10 for 50,000 emails with 5 inboxes. Growth is $20 for 100,000 emails with 10 inboxes and a dedicated IP. Extra mail is $0.50 per 1,000. Self-hosting is free under Apache 2.0, with no limits on inboxes, emails or domains.

**Strengths**

- **Much cheaper when agents send a lot.** 50,000 emails is $10, vs AgentMail's $20 plan for 10,000 plus $2 per extra 1,000.
- Real mailboxes: threads, reply in thread, IMAP with IDLE, Rspamd spam scoring, and an `email.received` webhook signed with `Reloop-Signature`.
- Hosted MCP server whose inbox tools (`list_inbox_threads`, `reply_to_inbox_message`, `send_mailbox_email` and more) sit next to sending, contacts, templates and automations.
- One suppression list across agent mail, transactional mail and campaigns.
- Open source and self-hostable, so sensitive mail never has to leave your infrastructure.

**Weaknesses**

- Hosted inboxes are capped at 3, 5 and 10 on Free, Pro and Growth. For hundreds of hosted agent addresses, AgentMail or Nylas fit better, or self-host Reloop.
- Mailboxes need a verified domain. There's no instant shared-domain address like `@agentmail.to`.
- No WebSockets; new mail arrives by webhook, IMAP IDLE or polling.

**Best for:** products where agents send real volume, or where agent mail should share an account with transactional mail and campaigns. Full breakdown: [Reloop vs AgentMail](/blog/reloop-vs-agentmail).

---

## 2. Nylas Agent Accounts: best for many hosted agent mailboxes

[Nylas](https://www.nylas.com/) is best known for APIs that connect to users' existing Gmail, Microsoft and IMAP mailboxes. Its newer [Agent Accounts](https://developer.nylas.com/docs/v3/agent-accounts/) are Nylas-hosted mailboxes that an agent owns outright: it sends from its own address, replies land in its own inbox, and it can host and respond to calendar events. Nylas also runs a hosted MCP server and ships a CLI for coding agents. Agent Accounts are labeled beta.

**Pricing** ([nylas.com/pricing](https://www.nylas.com/pricing/)): Free includes 3 Agent Accounts and 3,000 emails a month. Essentials is $15 a month for 10 Agent Accounts and 10,000 emails. Pro is $49 a month ($43 billed annually) for 50 Agent Accounts and 50,000 emails, with extra agent emails at $0.80 per 1,000. Enterprise adds a HIPAA BAA and an uptime SLA.

**Strengths**

- More hosted agent mailboxes per dollar than Reloop's hosted plans: 50 on Pro.
- Calendar built in, useful for scheduling agents.
- Optional IMAP and SMTP access with an app password, so a person can open the mailbox in Outlook or Apple Mail.
- Trial addresses on a Nylas-provided `*.nylas.email` domain, or your own verified domain.
- The same vendor can also connect to your users' own Gmail and Outlook accounts, if your agent needs to act on a human's mailbox too.
- Enterprise compliance options (HIPAA BAA).

**Weaknesses**

- Agent Accounts are still in beta.
- 50,000 emails is $49, vs $10 on Reloop.
- Hosted only; no transactional or campaign platform around the mailboxes.

**Best for:** teams that need dozens of hosted agent mailboxes with calendar support, or that also integrate with users' existing inboxes.

---

## 3. Cloudflare Email Routing: best free inbound forwarding

Cloudflare's [Email Routing](https://developers.cloudflare.com/email-service/get-started/route-emails/) is free and unlimited. Incoming mail is forwarded to a verified address or handed to a Worker's `email()` handler, which can parse it, call your model and reply in thread. Cloudflare's newer Email Service adds outbound sending from Workers.

**Pricing:** inbound routing is free. Sending to arbitrary recipients needs the Workers Paid plan ($5 a month minimum), which includes 3,000 emails a month, then $0.35 per 1,000. Sending is still labeled beta, and your domain must use Cloudflare DNS.

**Strengths**

- Free, unlimited inbound.
- Runs at the edge next to the rest of your Workers code.
- Cheap sending at high volume.

**Weaknesses**

- No stored mailbox, no thread history, no IMAP and no MCP server. Your Worker sees each message once.
- Requires Cloudflare DNS.
- Transactional only.

**Best for:** agents that react to single messages and already live on Cloudflare Workers. Full breakdown: [Reloop vs Cloudflare Email Service](/blog/reloop-vs-cloudflare-email).

---

## 4. Postmark: best inbound webhook on a deliverability-first provider

[Postmark](https://postmarkapp.com/) parses inbound email and posts each message to your webhook as JSON, including a spam score. Its sending side has a long reputation for fast transactional delivery, with message streams that keep transactional and broadcast traffic apart.

**Pricing:** a free developer plan with 100 emails a month. Basic is $15 for 10,000 emails with $1.80 per extra 1,000, but **inbound processing needs Pro or above**.

**Strengths**

- Clean parsed JSON for each inbound message.
- Strong transactional deliverability for your agent's outbound mail.

**Weaknesses**

- Inbound is a webhook, so storage, threading and replies are yours to build.
- Inbound needs a higher plan.
- Expensive per email: 50,000 emails on Basic is $15 plus $72 overage.

**Best for:** teams that care most about outbound deliverability and only need a parsed copy of inbound mail. Full breakdown: [Reloop vs Postmark](/blog/reloop-vs-postmark).

---

## 5. Mailgun: best regex routing of inbound mail

[Mailgun](https://www.mailgun.com/) uses **inbound routes**: you write an expression that matches the recipient or headers, and Mailgun forwards the parsed message to a URL or another address, or stores it briefly for you to fetch.

**Pricing:** a trial at 100 emails a day. Basic is $15 for 10,000 emails and Foundation is $35 for 50,000.

**Strengths**

- Flexible routing: send `support+*@` to one endpoint and `invoices@` to another without code.
- Mature sending API, templates and email validation.

**Weaknesses**

- Routes forward messages; threading, history and replies are yours to build.
- 50,000 emails costs $35, vs $10 on Reloop.

**Best for:** teams that need rule-based fan-out of inbound mail to several services. Full breakdown: [Reloop vs Mailgun](/blog/reloop-vs-mailgun).

More options: [Mailgun alternatives](/blog/best-mailgun-alternatives)

---

## 6. Resend: simplest inbound webhook on a modern API

[Resend](https://resend.com/) can receive mail on your domain and deliver each message to your webhook. It's the same developer experience as its sending API.

**Pricing:** Free is 3,000 emails a month (100 a day). Pro is $20 for 50,000.

**Strengths**

- Clean API and docs; React Email for your agent's outbound templates.
- Generous free tier.

**Weaknesses**

- A webhook per message, not a mailbox: no threads, no IMAP, no MCP inbox tools.
- $35 at 100,000 emails, vs $20 on Reloop.

**Best for:** teams already on Resend that need light inbound handling. Full breakdown: [Reloop vs Resend](/blog/reloop-vs-resend).

More options: [Resend alternatives](/blog/best-resend-alternatives)

---

## 7. Amazon SES: best for AWS-native agents

[Amazon SES](https://aws.amazon.com/ses/) can receive mail on your domain. Receipt rules hand each message to S3, SNS or Lambda, which fits agents already running on AWS.

**Pricing:** $0.10 per 1,000 emails sent, with AWS Free Tier credits for new accounts. See the [SES pricing page](https://aws.amazon.com/ses/pricing/) for receiving charges.

**Strengths**

- Lowest list price for sending.
- Native IAM, Lambda and S3 integration.

**Weaknesses**

- Everything above the pipe is yours to build: storage, threading, spam handling, replies, an inbox UI.
- New accounts start in the sandbox and need production access before mailing real users.

**Best for:** AWS-heavy teams with engineers who are happy to own the plumbing. Full breakdown: [Reloop vs Amazon SES](/blog/reloop-vs-aws-ses).

---

## How to choose

- **"Our agents send a lot of email."** Reloop. 50,000 emails is $10.
- **"We need hundreds of hosted agent addresses."** AgentMail or Nylas Agent Accounts, or self-hosted Reloop with no inbox limits.
- **"We need an address in seconds, with no DNS."** Stay on AgentMail.
- **"Our agent also schedules meetings."** Nylas, for its calendar support.
- **"We only need to react to inbound messages."** Cloudflare Email Routing if you're on Workers, otherwise Postmark, Mailgun or Resend webhooks.
- **"Agent mail can't leave our infrastructure."** Self-hosted Reloop.
- **"We also send password resets and newsletters."** Reloop, so agent mail and product mail share one account and one suppression list.

---

## Switching from AgentMail

1. **Verify a domain** with your new provider. Merge its SPF include into your existing record and publish its DKIM key.
2. **Point MX records** for the agent addresses at the new provider, or use a subdomain such as `agents.example.com` so human mail is untouched.
3. **Recreate inboxes** (on Reloop, `reloop.inbox.mailboxes.create`).
4. **Swap the client calls** for sending, listing threads and replying.
5. **Move event handling** to the new webhook, and verify its signature. On Reloop, that's `email.received` with the `Reloop-Signature` header.
6. **Update MCP clients** to the new server URL.
7. **Run both in parallel** until no new mail reaches the old addresses. Mail to `@agentmail.to` addresses won't follow you, so tell contacts about the new address.

Our [Reloop vs AgentMail guide](/blog/reloop-vs-agentmail) has the code for each step.

---

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="What is the best open-source AgentMail alternative?">
    Reloop. It's Apache 2.0 and includes agent mailboxes with threads,
    reply in thread, IMAP and a hosted MCP server, plus transactional email,
    campaigns and automations. Self-hosted, it has no inbox limits.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Do I need a mailbox, or is an inbound webhook enough?">
    If your agent needs conversation history (support, sales follow-ups,
    scheduling), use a mailbox: Reloop, AgentMail or Nylas Agent Accounts. If
    it only reacts to individual messages, a webhook from Cloudflare,
    Postmark, Mailgun, Resend or SES is enough, and you build any storage
    you need.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Which AgentMail alternative is cheapest?">
    For agents that send a lot, Reloop: $10 for 50,000 emails and $20 for
    100,000. For inbound only, Cloudflare Email Routing is free. For many
    hosted mailboxes that send little, Nylas Pro gives 50 agent accounts for
    $49.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can a human and an agent share the same inbox?">
    On Reloop, yes: the agent works over the API or MCP, and a person can
    open the same mailbox in Apple Mail, Outlook or Thunderbird over IMAP.
    AgentMail and Nylas Agent Accounts also offer IMAP access.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can my agent use my own domain?">
    Yes on every option here. Reloop requires one; AgentMail and Nylas
    support custom domains alongside their own shared addresses
    (`@agentmail.to` and `*.nylas.email`).
  </Accordion>
