# Reloop vs AgentMail (2026): Email Inboxes for AI Agents Compared

Path: /blog/reloop-vs-agentmail
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-agentmail
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-agentmail.md

Reloop vs AgentMail for AI agent inboxes: pricing, inbox limits, threads and replies, IMAP, MCP, webhooks, custom domains, self-hosting, and which one fits your agent.

**AgentMail and Reloop both give your AI agent a real inbox: an address it can receive mail at, read threads from and reply in.** The difference is scope. **AgentMail is built only for agent inboxes, and it's very good at spinning up lots of them fast.** **Reloop is a full email platform (transactional API, SMTP relay, campaigns, automations) where agent inboxes are one part, and it's open source, so you can self-host it with no inbox limits.**

We build Reloop, so weigh this accordingly. AgentMail facts below come from [agentmail.to/pricing](https://www.agentmail.to/pricing) and [docs.agentmail.to](https://docs.agentmail.to). Where AgentMail is the better pick, we say so.

---

## The 30-second comparison

| | **Reloop** | **AgentMail** |
|---|---|---|
| Focus | Full email platform with agent inboxes | Inboxes for AI agents |
| Free tier | 6,000 emails / mo, 200 / day, 3 inboxes | 3,000 emails / mo, 100 / day, 3 inboxes |
| First paid plan | **$10 / mo**: 50,000 emails, 5 inboxes | $20 / mo: 10,000 emails, 10 inboxes |
| Next plan | $20 / mo: 100,000 emails, 10 inboxes, dedicated IP | $200 / mo: 150 inboxes, 15,000 emails / day |
| Instant address without a domain | No (needs a verified domain) | Yes (`@agentmail.to`) |
| Threads and reply in thread | Yes | Yes |
| IMAP access | Yes | Yes |
| Hosted MCP server | Yes | Yes |
| Real-time events | Webhooks | Webhooks and WebSockets |
| Transactional sending API | Yes | Sends from inboxes |
| Campaigns and automations | Yes | No |
| Open source | Yes (Apache 2.0) | SDKs only (MIT) |
| Self-host | Yes, unlimited inboxes | No |

Prices change; check [Reloop pricing](/pricing) and [AgentMail pricing](https://www.agentmail.to/pricing) before you commit.

---

## Pricing: emails vs inboxes

The two products meter different things, so the right choice depends on whether your agent needs **many inboxes** or **lots of email**.

**AgentMail** ([pricing](https://www.agentmail.to/pricing)):

| Plan | Price | Inboxes | Emails | Custom domains |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Free | $0 | 3 | 3,000 / mo, 100 / day | 0 |
| Developer | $20 / mo | 10 | 10,000 / mo, 1,000 / day | 10 |
| Startup | $200 / mo | 150 | 15,000 / day | 150 |
| Enterprise | Custom | Unlimited | Custom | Custom |

Add-ons are $2 / month per extra inbox, $2 / month per extra domain, and $2 / month per extra 1,000 sends. Dedicated IPs are Enterprise only.

**Reloop** ([pricing](/pricing)):

| Plan | Price | Inboxes | Emails | Custom domains |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Free | $0 | 3 | 6,000 / mo, 200 / day | 3 |
| Pro | $10 / mo | 5 | 50,000 / mo | 5 |
| Growth | $20 / mo | 10 | 100,000 / mo, 1 dedicated IP | 10 |
| Self-hosted | $0 | Unlimited | Unlimited | Unlimited |

Overage on Reloop is $0.50 per 1,000 emails.

What that means in practice:

- **A few agents sending a lot.** Reloop is much cheaper. 50,000 emails is $10 on Reloop. On AgentMail it's the $20 Developer plan plus 40 extra blocks of 1,000 sends.
- **Many agents sending a little.** AgentMail fits better. 150 inboxes on the Startup plan is a straightforward deal, and hosted Reloop tops out at 10 inboxes on Growth. If you need more inboxes on Reloop today, self-host it or talk to us about Enterprise.

<Callout type="tip">
  Count how many separate addresses your agents really need. Many products need one support inbox and one outbound address, not one per user. If it's one per user or per customer, AgentMail's inbox pricing or self-hosted Reloop will fit better than a hosted inbox cap.
</Callout>

---

## Creating an inbox and replying

Both APIs are small and feel similar.

**AgentMail** (from the [quickstart](https://docs.agentmail.to/quickstart) and [messages docs](https://docs.agentmail.to/messages))

```typescript

const client = new AgentMailClient({ apiKey: process.env.AGENTMAIL_API_KEY });

// Without a domain, the inbox gets an @agentmail.to address
const inbox = await client.inboxes.create();

await client.inboxes.messages.send(inbox.inboxId, {
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Hello from my agent",
  text: "Hi! I'm your assistant.",
});

// Later: reply in thread
await client.inboxes.messages.reply(inbox.inboxId, messageId, {
  text: "Thanks, I've booked that for you.",
});
```

**Reloop**

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY! });

// Mailboxes live on a domain you've verified in Reloop
const { mailbox, mailboxError } = await reloop.inbox.mailboxes.create({
  domainId: "dom_123",
  email: "assistant@mail.acme.com",
  displayName: "Acme Assistant",
});
if (mailboxError) throw mailboxError;

// Read conversations
const { threads } = await reloop.inbox.threads.list({ mailboxId: mailbox.id });

// Reply in thread; Reloop keeps the In-Reply-To and References headers
const { message, messageError } = await reloop.inbox.messages.reply("msg_123", {
  html: "<p>Thanks, I've booked that for you.</p>",
});
```

The practical difference: **AgentMail gives you a working address in one call, with no DNS.** Reloop mailboxes need a domain you've verified first. That's a few minutes of DNS once, and afterwards your agent sends from your own brand rather than a shared domain. AgentMail supports custom domains too, from the Developer plan up.

AgentMail also has a few agent-specific extras worth knowing about:

- **`extractedText` / `extractedHtml`** on incoming messages, with quoted history and signatures stripped, so your model reads only the new reply.
- **Drafts**, for human-in-the-loop review before a send.
- **Labels**, for tracking state on messages.
- **Pods**, for multi-tenant setups.
- **Allow and block lists**, to limit who an agent can email or hear from.

---

## Receiving: webhooks, WebSockets, IMAP and MCP

Both products give an agent several ways to learn about new mail.

| | Reloop | AgentMail |
|---|---|---|
| Webhook on new mail | `email.received` | `message.received` |
| WebSockets | No | Yes |
| IMAP | `imap.reloop.sh`, API key as password | `imap.agentmail.to`, API key as password |
| SMTP | `smtp.reloop.sh` | `smtp.agentmail.to` |
| Hosted MCP server | `https://reloop.sh/mcp` (OAuth) | `https://mcp.agentmail.to/mcp` (OAuth or API key) |
| Spam handling | Rspamd scores inbound mail; spam goes to Junk | Spam stored but hidden from API results by default |

**Webhooks.** Reloop's `email.received` event includes the mailbox, sender, subject, thread ID and an `isSpam` flag, and is signed with HMAC-SHA256 in the `Reloop-Signature` header. AgentMail has a broader set of message events, including `message.received.spam` and security-review events.

**IMAP.** Both let humans open the same inbox in Apple Mail, Outlook or Thunderbird. Reloop's IMAP server supports IDLE for push, and gives each account INBOX, Sent, Drafts, Archive, Junk and Trash folders. AgentMail exposes INBOX, Sent, Trash and Spam. Either way, agents and humans can work the same threads.

**MCP.** Both host an MCP server, so Claude, Cursor or ChatGPT can use the inbox directly. Reloop's inbox tools include `list_inbox_threads`, `get_inbox_thread`, `reply_to_inbox_message`, `forward_inbox_message` and `send_mailbox_email`. The same server also covers sending, contacts, templates, automations and domains. AgentMail's server has 47 tools, including calendar events and drafts.

---

## Beyond inboxes

This is where the products diverge most.

**AgentMail** is focused on agent mailboxes. It adds things around them, like calendar events and app connections, but it isn't a platform for transactional or marketing email.

**Reloop** is a full email platform, and the agent inbox shares everything else with it:

- **Transactional API and SMTP relay** for password resets, receipts and alerts, with templates (`{{{variables}}}`), scheduling and idempotency keys.
- **Contacts, campaigns and event-triggered automations**, for example a welcome sequence that starts on `user.signed_up`.
- **One suppression list** across agent mail, transactional mail and campaigns, so a bounce or complaint anywhere protects your domain everywhere.
- **Its own sending infrastructure** (KumoMTA) with per-domain throttling and bounce handling. See [how bounce processing works](/blog/email-bounce-processing-automation).

If your app already needs a transactional provider, Reloop lets your agents and your product share one account, one set of DNS records and one sender reputation.

---

## Self-hosting and lock-in

AgentMail is a hosted service. Its SDKs and toolkit are open source under MIT, but the inbox service itself isn't something you can run yourself.

Reloop is Apache 2.0. The self-hosted edition has every feature and **no limits on inboxes, emails or domains**. You can:

1. Start on Reloop Cloud.
2. Move to your own server with the [one-command installer](/self-host) or [Coolify](/blog/reloop-coolify-setup).
3. Keep the same code. Point the SDK's `baseUrl` at your instance.

That matters for agents that read sensitive mail: contracts, invoices, medical or legal correspondence. With self-hosting, the messages never leave your infrastructure, and your security team can read the code that handles them. The trade-off is that you run the server and own IP reputation and warm-up.

---

## Where AgentMail is the better choice

- **You need many inboxes on a hosted service.** 150 inboxes for $200, or $2 per extra inbox, is hard to beat if each user or customer gets their own agent address.
- **You want an address in seconds with no DNS.** `client.inboxes.create()` gives you a working `@agentmail.to` address immediately, which is great for prototypes and demos.
- **You want agent-specific helpers** like extracted reply text, drafts for approval, WebSockets, pods for multi-tenancy, and calendar tools.

Still comparing agent inbox providers? Our roundup of the [best AgentMail alternatives](/blog/best-agentmail-alternatives) covers the rest of the field.

## Where Reloop is the better choice

- **Your agents send a lot of email.** 50,000 emails is $10 and 100,000 is $20, including a dedicated IP.
- **You also need transactional mail, campaigns or automations,** and want them in the same account as your agent inboxes.
- **You need open source or self-hosting** for data residency, security review, or unlimited inboxes without per-inbox fees.
- **You want agents to send from your own domain** with your own deliverability, rather than a shared one.

---

## Switching from AgentMail to Reloop

1. **Verify your domain in Reloop.** Publish the DKIM record (`reloop._domainkey`), merge `include:reloop.sh` into your SPF, then turn on receiving and add the MX record the dashboard shows.
2. **Create a mailbox for each agent address** with `reloop.inbox.mailboxes.create`.
3. **Swap the client calls.** `inboxes.messages.send` becomes `reloop.inbox.messages.send({ mailboxId, ... })`, and `inboxes.messages.reply` becomes `reloop.inbox.messages.reply(messageId, ...)`.
4. **Move event handling.** Subscribe to `email.received` and verify the `Reloop-Signature` header. If you used WebSockets, switch that listener to a webhook endpoint.
5. **Update MCP clients** to `https://reloop.sh/mcp` and sign in with your Reloop account.
6. **Run both in parallel** until no new mail arrives at the old addresses, then retire them.

If your agents use `@agentmail.to` addresses, tell your contacts about the new address, since mail to the old one won't follow you.

# Reloop vs Lettermint (2026): Pricing, EU Hosting and Which to Choose

Path: /blog/reloop-vs-lettermint
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-lettermint
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-lettermint.md

Reloop vs Lettermint compared honestly: pricing at real volumes, EU hosting and jurisdiction, the send API, broadcasts, inbound mail and agent inboxes, deliverability, self-hosting, and how to switch.

**Lettermint is a Dutch email API that keeps your email data in the EU, run by an EU company.** Reloop is open-source email infrastructure you can use hosted or run yourself. The differences: **Reloop costs $10 for 50k emails where Lettermint's cheapest 50k plan is €40, it receives mail into real inboxes your agents can reply from, it has contacts, campaigns and automations built in, and you can self-host it.** Lettermint has the cleaner answer if you need EU hosting without running servers, plus ISO 27001 certification and compliance features Reloop Cloud doesn't publish.

We build Reloop, so weigh this accordingly. Every Lettermint fact below comes from its own site: [pricing](https://lettermint.co/pricing), [docs](https://lettermint.co/docs/introduction), [sub-processors](https://lettermint.co/subprocessors), [privacy policy](https://lettermint.co/privacy-policy), [DPA](https://lettermint.co/dpa) and [GitHub](https://github.com/lettermint). Where Lettermint is the better pick, we say so.

---

## The 30-second comparison

| | **Reloop** | **Lettermint** |
|---|---|---|
| Company | Reloop Labs | Lettermint B.V. (Netherlands) |
| Where email data lives | Self-host: your server. Cloud: Hetzner, with EU data centers | EU (UpCloud in the Netherlands, backups on OVHcloud in Germany) |
| Free tier | 6,000 / mo, 200 / day | 300 / mo, no daily limit |
| 50,000 emails / mo | **$10** | €40 (Starter) / €45 (Growth) / €55 (Pro) |
| Overage | $0.50 per 1,000 | €1.10 to €1.50 per 1,000 at the 10k–50k tiers |
| Dedicated IP | Included on Growth ($20) | €50 / mo add-on, Pro at 300k+ |
| Inbound email | Mailboxes with threads, API, MCP, IMAP | Parsed and posted to a signed webhook (Starter and up) |
| Contacts, campaigns, automations | Yes, every plan | Broadcast sending route; no contacts or automations in its docs |
| Open source | Yes (Apache 2.0) | SDKs only; the platform is proprietary |
| Self-host | Yes | No |
| ISO 27001 | Not published | ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certified |
| SMTP relay | Yes | Yes |

Lettermint prices in euros and Reloop in dollars. Both change prices from time to time, so check [Lettermint's pricing page](https://lettermint.co/pricing) and [ours](/pricing) before you commit.

---

## EU hosting and jurisdiction

This is the main reason people look at Lettermint, so it comes first.

**Lettermint** is Lettermint B.V., registered with the Dutch Chamber of Commerce and based in Zwolle. Its [privacy policy](https://lettermint.co/privacy-policy) says email data "hosted, stored, routed, or processed as part of Lettermint's core European email delivery infrastructure remains within the European Union". Its [sub-processor list](https://lettermint.co/subprocessors) is specific: the private cloud runs on UpCloud (a Finnish company) in the Netherlands, encrypted backups sit on OVHcloud in Germany, and deliverability monitoring is done by Postmastery in the Netherlands. Business tools like Stripe and Slack process billing and internal data in the US, which the privacy policy discloses.

The [DPA](https://lettermint.co/dpa) applies automatically to every customer, is governed by Dutch law, and Lettermint countersigns it on request. Lettermint is also ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certified, with the certificate in its [Trust Center](https://trust.lettermint.co/).

**Reloop Cloud** runs on Hetzner, the German hosting company, with EU data centers. We publish a [Data Processing Addendum](/dpa) based on the EU Standard Contractual Clauses and a [sub-processor list](/dpa/subprocessors). The systems that touch your mail (PostgreSQL, KumoMTA, Rspamd and so on) are deployments we run ourselves, not third-party SaaS.

If you'd rather control the servers and the jurisdiction yourself, **self-host Reloop** on an EU server:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://reloop.sh/install.sh | sudo bash
```

Then you choose both the location and the company that runs it. The trade-off is that you run it.

<Callout type="tip">
  If your security review needs "EU-hosted, EU-owned, certified" and you don't want to operate servers, Lettermint is the simpler answer today. Our [EU email API roundup](/blog/eu-email-api-providers-2026) covers the other options.
</Callout>

---

## Pricing at real volumes

Lettermint has Free, Starter, Growth and Pro plans, each priced by monthly volume. Reloop has Free, Pro ($10) and Growth ($20), with overage above that.

| Monthly volume | Reloop | Lettermint Starter | Lettermint Growth | Lettermint Pro |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 300 | $0 | €0 (Free) | €0 (Free) | €0 (Free) |
| 3,000 | $0 | €10 (10k tier) | €13 | €15 |
| 10,000 | $10 | €10 | €13 | €15 |
| 50,000 | $10 | €40 | €45 | €55 |
| 100,000 | $20 | €85 (125k tier) | €100 | €110 |
| 300,000 | $20 + $100 overage = $120 | €175 | €200 | €215 |
| 1,000,000 | $20 + $450 overage = $470 | €500 | €600 | €620 |

What stands out:

- **Reloop's free tier is twenty times bigger.** 6,000 a month vs 300, though Lettermint has no daily cap and Reloop's free plan allows 200 a day.
- **The gap is widest between 10k and 300k.** At 50k you'd pay €40 or more on Lettermint and $10 on Reloop.
- **At a million emails it gets close.** Reloop's flat $0.50 per 1,000 overage adds up, and Lettermint's per-email price falls with volume. At very high volume, compare a real quote, not just list prices.
- **Lettermint counts inbound mail in your volume.** Its pricing page says the monthly allowance is "Transactional, Broadcast and Inbound emails combined".
- **Some Lettermint features depend on the plan.** Inbound mail, open and click tracking, and sandbox mode start on Starter; email scheduling on Growth; custom tracking domains, spam insights and dedicated IPs on Pro. On Reloop, every plan gets the same features; plans differ by volume, limits on inboxes, webhooks and domains, and a dedicated IP on Growth.

Lettermint also has **spend limits** that pause sending at a monthly cap instead of billing overage, which is a nice touch if you worry about runaway costs.

If you self-host Reloop, there's no per-email fee at all. See [self-hosted email infrastructure](/blog/self-hosted-email-infrastructure) for what that really takes.

---

## Developer experience

Both are developer-first APIs, and the send calls look almost the same.

**Lettermint**

```typescript

const lettermint = new Lettermint({
  sendingToken: process.env.LETTERMINT_PROJECT_TOKEN,
});

const result = await lettermint.emails.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@acme.com>",
  to: ["user@example.com"],
  subject: "Welcome",
  html: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
});
```

**Reloop**

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY! });

const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Welcome",
  html: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
});
```

The Lettermint SDK throws typed errors (`ValidationError`, `RateLimitError` and so on), so you wrap calls in `try`/`catch`. Reloop returns errors as values. Lettermint's SDK is well built: it runs on Node, Bun, Deno and edge runtimes with no dependencies, and supports batch sends with per-email idempotency keys.

| | Reloop | Lettermint |
|---|---|---|
| Auth | One API key (`x-api-key`) | Project sending token (`x-lettermint-token`), separate team token for management |
| Organizing mail | Domains | Projects and routes (transactional, broadcast, inbound) |
| Idempotency | Yes | Yes |
| Error format | `message`, `why` and `fix` | `code`, `message` and field errors |
| MCP server | Yes | Yes |
| Official SDKs | Node, Python, Go, PHP, Ruby, Rust, Java, .NET, Elixir | Node, Python, Go, PHP, Java, .NET, Elixir, Rust, plus Laravel, Symfony and Nuxt packages |

Lettermint also ships a CLI and a Terraform provider. Its SMTP relay is `smtp.lettermint.co`, with the username `lettermint` and your project token as the password. Reloop's is `smtp.reloop.sh` on port 587, with your API key as username and password.

Reloop's errors tell you **why** a send failed and **how to fix it**:

```json
{
  "message": "Domain not found",
  "why": "The domain mail.acme.com was not found or is not authorized for your organization",
  "fix": "Ensure the domain is registered and verified in your dashboard"
}
```

---

## Receiving email and agent inboxes

**Lettermint** handles inbound with [inbound routes](https://lettermint.co/docs/platform/inbound-mail/introduction), on Starter and up. Each route gets a catch-all address domain (`<route-id>.lettermint.app`), or you point your own domain's MX at it. Lettermint parses each message and sends a signed `message.inbound` webhook to your endpoint. Messages above the route's spam threshold are quarantined for review. Storing, threading and replying are up to you.

**Reloop** receives mail into **mailboxes**. Messages are stored, threaded, spam-scored with Rspamd, and readable over the API, the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) or IMAP. Replying in-thread is one call, and an `email.received` webhook is there if you also want push. Inbound is on every plan, including Free (three inboxes).

| | Reloop | Lettermint |
|---|---|---|
| Receive on your domain | Yes | Yes (Starter and up) |
| Stored mailboxes with threads | Yes | No, webhook delivery |
| Reply in thread via API | Yes | Build it yourself |
| MCP access to inboxes | Yes | No |
| IMAP access | Yes | No |

That matters if you're building [AI agents that read and reply to email](/blog/build-ai-agent-sends-emails), support inboxes, or reply handling for transactional mail. If you only need "parse this email and hit my webhook", Lettermint's approach is simpler.

---

## Broadcasts, contacts and automations

**Lettermint** supports broadcast email as its own sending route. Its [broadcast changelog](https://lettermint.co/changelog/marketing-campaigns-newsletters-lettermint-broadcast) says broadcasts go through "a segregated infrastructure", so a big newsletter doesn't slow your password resets, and its [broadcast page](https://lettermint.co/features/broadcast-emails) says every broadcast gets mandatory unsubscribe links and headers. We didn't find contact lists, a campaign editor or automations in its docs: you build the list and the email in your own app or tool, then send through the broadcast route.

**Reloop** has the marketing layer built in: contacts with custom properties, groups, subscription channels, scheduled broadcast campaigns, and **event-triggered automations** with delays, conditions and email steps. Your app reports an event, and every automation listening for it starts for that contact:

```typescript
const { automationError } = await reloop.automations.start({
  event: "user.signed_up",
  email: user.email,
  firstName: user.name,
  properties: { plan: user.plan },
});
```

If you already manage lists and campaigns somewhere else, Lettermint's broadcast route is enough. If you want onboarding sequences and newsletters on the same API and suppression list as your transactional mail, Reloop does that without a second tool. See [welcome sequences that convert](/blog/welcome-email-sequences-that-convert) for a worked example.

---

## Deliverability

Both cover the basics: SPF, DKIM and DMARC, bounce and complaint handling, a suppression list, and per-domain or per-route open and click tracking. The defaults differ: Lettermint's tracking is off until you turn it on per route, while Reloop turns it on for new domains and lets you switch it off per domain.

The differences:

- **Dedicated IPs.** Lettermint sells one for €50 a month on Pro at 300,000 emails and up, and offers bring-your-own-IP for enterprise Pro customers. Reloop includes one on Growth at $20 a month.
- **Sending path.** Reloop runs its own MTA (KumoMTA) with per-domain throttling and automatic pauses when bounce or complaint rates spike. Read [how bounce processing works](/blog/email-bounce-processing-automation). Lettermint separates broadcast and transactional infrastructure, and works with Postmastery on deliverability monitoring.
- **Tracking quality.** Lettermint filters bot opens and clicks (security scanners, link previews) out of its engagement data, which makes open rates more honest.
- **Managed DKIM.** Lettermint hosts the DKIM key behind CNAME records and rotates it every six months.
- **Tools.** Reloop ships free [domain reputation](/tools/domain-reputation-checker), [blocklist](/tools/blocklist-checker) and [auth](/tools/auth-checker) checkers.

---

## Self-hosting and lock-in

Lettermint is hosted only. Its SDKs are open source on [GitHub](https://github.com/lettermint) (MIT, with the Rust SDK under Apache 2.0), but the platform isn't.

Reloop is Apache 2.0. You can:

1. Start on Reloop Cloud.
2. Move to your own server later with the [one-command installer](/self-host) or [Coolify](/blog/reloop-coolify-setup).
3. Keep the same API. Point the SDK's `baseUrl` at your instance and nothing else in your code changes.

That helps with data residency, with security reviews that want to read the code handling your users' mail, and as insurance against price changes.

Self-hosting isn't free in effort: you own IP reputation, warm-up, backups and uptime. The [VPS guide](/docs/self-host/vps) lists a minimum of 2 vCPUs and 4 GB of RAM.

---

## Where Lettermint is the better choice

- **You need an EU company as well as EU hosting, without running servers.** Lettermint answers both "where" and "who" in one line: a Dutch company on EU infrastructure. Reloop Cloud covers the "where" with Hetzner's EU data centers.
- **Your buyers ask for ISO 27001.** Lettermint is certified; that shortens vendor questionnaires.
- **You want enterprise controls on a small plan.** SSO with SCIM from Starter, an API token IP allowlist, enforced TLS, sandbox mode and spend limits.
- **You send around a million emails a month** and its volume pricing comes out close to or below Reloop's overage.

Looking at other EU providers too? See the [best Lettermint alternatives](/blog/best-lettermint-alternatives).

## Where Reloop is the better choice

- **You send between 3,000 and a few hundred thousand emails a month.** $10 vs €40 at 50k and $20 vs €85 at 100k–125k adds up.
- **You need inbound mail as real inboxes**, especially for AI agents, and on the free plan.
- **You want contacts, campaigns and automations** in the same product as your transactional mail.
- **You need open source or self-hosting**, including EU hosting on servers you control.

---

## Switching from Lettermint to Reloop

1. **Add your domain in Reloop** and publish the DKIM record (`reloop._domainkey`). Merge `include:reloop.sh` into your existing SPF record rather than adding a second one.
2. **Swap the client.** Replace `lettermint.emails.send` with `reloop.mail.send`. The fields map closely: `from`, `to`, `subject`, `html`, `text`, `reply_to` and `scheduled_at`.
3. **Move tracking settings.** Lettermint sets open and click tracking per route; in Reloop it's per domain.
4. **Import suppressions.** Export unsubscribed, bounced and complained addresses from Lettermint and import them, so you never mail someone who opted out.
5. **Move broadcasts.** Import your list as Reloop contacts and send newsletters as campaigns, or keep sending them from your own tool through Reloop's API or SMTP.
6. **Move inbound.** Create a mailbox in Reloop and point the domain's MX record at Reloop instead of Lettermint. Replace your `message.inbound` handler with Reloop's `email.received` webhook, or read the mailbox over the API.
7. **Point webhooks** at a new handler. Reloop events are named `email.delivered`, `email.bounced`, `email.complained` and so on, and are signed with HMAC-SHA256 in the `Reloop-Signature` header.
8. **Ramp traffic** from 10% to 100% over a week or two, then remove Lettermint's DNS records.

If you want the servers under your own control, do step 1 on a self-hosted Reloop instead of Reloop Cloud. Our [SendGrid migration guide](/blog/migrating-from-sendgrid) walks through the same steps in more detail.

## FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Is Reloop cheaper than Lettermint?">
    For most volumes, yes. At 50,000 emails a month Reloop is $10 and
    Lettermint is €40 on Starter. Reloop's free tier is also bigger: 6,000 a
    month vs 300. Around a million emails a month the two get close, so price
    your real volume.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Where does Lettermint store data?">
    In the EU. Its sub-processor list names UpCloud in the Netherlands for
    hosting and OVHcloud in Germany for encrypted backups. Lettermint B.V. is a
    Dutch company, and its DPA is governed by Dutch law.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Does Reloop have an EU region?">
    Yes. Reloop Cloud runs on Hetzner, with EU data centers. It comes with a
    DPA based on the EU Standard Contractual Clauses and a public sub-processor
    list. If you want full control over where data lives, you can also
    self-host Reloop on your own EU server; it's the same open-source code.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Does Lettermint support inbound email?">
    Yes, on Starter and up. It parses incoming mail and posts it to your
    endpoint as a signed webhook. Reloop stores incoming mail in threaded
    mailboxes you can read and reply to over the API, MCP or IMAP.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can Lettermint send newsletters?">
    Yes, through a separate broadcast route with its own sending
    infrastructure and automatic unsubscribe handling. You manage the list and
    content yourself. Reloop also has contacts, campaigns and automations.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can I self-host Lettermint?">
    No. Lettermint is a hosted service; only its SDKs are open source. Reloop
    is open source under Apache 2.0 and runs on your own server with the same
    API.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# Best SparkPost Alternatives in 2026: Where to Go Now SparkPost Is Bird

Path: /blog/best-sparkpost-alternatives
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-sparkpost-alternatives
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-sparkpost-alternatives.md

SparkPost is now Bird Email, so a migration is coming either way. The best SparkPost alternatives in 2026 compared: Reloop, Amazon SES, SendGrid, Mailgun, Postmark, Elastic Email and ZeptoMail on price, volume, inbound and migration.

**The short version:** SparkPost is now sold as **Bird Email**, and Bird says SparkPost requests may not work unchanged, so you're planning a migration whichever way you go. Under about 300,000 emails a month, **Reloop** is the cheapest complete platform: $10 for 50,000, a permanent free tier, inbound mailboxes and open source. At millions a month, **Amazon SES** (or Bird itself) wins on price per email.

We build Reloop, so weigh that. Every price below comes from the providers' public pricing pages, linked in our head-to-head posts, and each section says where that provider beats us.

---

## What happened to SparkPost

- MessageBird [agreed to acquire SparkPost](https://bird.com/blog/sparkpost-joins-bird) and later rebranded as Bird.
- [sparkpost.com](https://www.sparkpost.com) now redirects to Bird's email product, and the old pricing page redirects to [Bird's email pricing](https://bird.com/pricing/email).
- Bird's own [SparkPost page](https://bird.com/email-api/features/sparkpost) says Bird Email "has its own API and SDKs" and advises reviewing sending, templates, domains and webhooks "rather than assuming that a SparkPost request can be sent unchanged."

Bird Email is a real option, and we include it below. But since your sending layer needs work anyway, it's the right moment to compare.

---

## 1. Reloop: best overall SparkPost alternative

Reloop is open-source email infrastructure: a transactional API, SMTP relay, inbound mailboxes, contacts, campaigns, automations and webhooks in one product, hosted or on your own server.

**Pricing:** Free is 6,000 emails a month (200 a day). Pro is $10 for 50,000. Growth is $20 for 100,000 and includes a dedicated IP. Extra mail costs $0.50 per 1,000, and pay-as-you-go credits cost the same $0.50 per 1,000 and stay valid for 6 months. Self-hosting is free under Apache 2.0.

**Why it fits SparkPost users**

- **Cheaper below about 300,000 a month.** $10 vs about $20 on Bird at 50k, $20 vs about $40 at 100k. The two meet around 300k, and Bird gets cheaper above that.
- **A dedicated IP for $20.** On Bird it's a paid add-on from the Growth plan ($250 deposit).
- **A simple send model.** SparkPost's transmissions wrap content and a recipients list; Reloop is one flat request per message, with errors that return `message`, `why` and `fix`.
- **Inbound as real mailboxes** you can read and reply to over the API, the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) or IMAP.
- **No more forced migrations.** It's open source, so if the vendor ever changes, you can run the same code yourself. Reloop Cloud runs on Hetzner, a German hosting company, with EU data centers.

**Where SparkPost (Bird) is still ahead**

- **Price at high volume.** Above 300k a month, Bird's $0.20–$0.45 per 1,000 beats Reloop's $0.50 overage.
- **Analytics heritage** and 30 days of message retention on every plan.
- **SMS and WhatsApp** in the same account. Reloop is email only.

**Best for:** SparkPost users sending under a few hundred thousand emails a month who want one platform for transactional, marketing and inbound mail.

Full breakdown: [Reloop vs SparkPost](/blog/reloop-vs-sparkpost)

## 2. Amazon SES: cheapest at millions per month

**Pricing:** $0.10 per 1,000 emails plus $0.12 per GB of outbound data. Receiving costs $0.10 per 1,000. Dedicated IPs are $24.95 a month.

**Strengths:** the lowest list price by far, deep AWS integration, and huge scale. At 1,000,000 emails a month SES is about $100, against $470 on Reloop.

**Weaknesses:** no logs dashboard, template editor, bounce processing or campaigns. You build those with SNS, Lambda and storage, and new accounts start in a sandbox.

**Best for:** very high-volume senders, often former SparkPost customers, with engineers to build the tooling SparkPost gave them.

</Callout>

**Pricing:** each paid plan adds a monthly deposit to a prepaid balance, charged per email. Free covers 1,000 emails a month (50 a day). Startup is a $15 deposit at $0.40 per 1,000, Growth a $250 deposit at $0.45, and Scale plans run from $0.35 down to $0.20 per 1,000.

**Strengths:** the SparkPost engine and analytics, 30-day retention on every plan, inbound included, and SMS and WhatsApp from the same vendor.

**Weaknesses:** a small free tier, a new API to migrate to anyway, and dedicated IPs only from Growth.

**Best for:** high-volume senders who want to keep the SparkPost engine and also need other channels.

**Pricing:** a 60-day trial at 100 emails a day. Essentials is $19.95 for 50,000 and $34.95 for 100,000. Pro, with a dedicated IP, subusers and SSO, starts at $89.95.

**Strengths:** proven at enormous volume, subusers and IP pools, Twilio procurement, and Handlebars logic in templates.

**Weaknesses:** no permanent free plan, marketing on a separate plan, an older API, and hosted only.

## How to choose

- **"We send under 300,000 a month and want one platform."** Reloop.
- **"We send millions a month and have engineers."** Amazon SES, or SES behind Reloop.
- **"We want the SparkPost engine and other channels."** Bird Email.
- **"Enterprise procurement decides."** SendGrid.
- **"We only send transactional mail and want pay-as-you-go."** ZeptoMail.
- **"We never want a forced migration again."** Reloop, the only open-source option here.

---

## Migrating off SparkPost

1. **Verify your domain** with the new provider. For Reloop, publish the `reloop._domainkey` DKIM record and merge `include:reloop.sh` into your existing SPF record. Never publish a second SPF record.
2. **Export your suppression list** from SparkPost and import it before your first send.
3. **Rewrite the sending layer.** Replace `transmissions.send` calls with the new provider's client. In Reloop that's one `reloop.mail.send` per message.
4. **Move templates.** SparkPost uses double-brace placeholders like `{{first_name}}`; in Reloop they become `{{{first_name}}}`.
5. **Point webhooks** at a new handler. Reloop events like `email.delivered` and `email.bounced` are signed in the `Reloop-Signature` header.
6. **Ramp traffic** from 10% to 100% over one to two weeks. If you send at high volume, warm a new dedicated IP gradually.

The [SendGrid migration guide](/blog/migrating-from-sendgrid) covers the same steps in detail, including a traffic-split flag and a suppression import script.

# Send Email from Fly.io Apps with Reloop

Path: /blog/reloop-flyio-deployment
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-flyio-deployment
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-flyio-deployment.md

How to send transactional email from apps on Fly.io: why direct SMTP from Fly machines lands in spam, setting RELOOP_API_KEY with fly secrets, the HTTP API and SMTP relay, background workers, and where to self-host Reloop instead.

**Run your app on Fly.io, and send its email through Reloop.** Fly is a great place for web apps and workers, but it's a poor place to run a mail server: you can't set reverse DNS (PTR) on Fly IPs, and most large mailbox providers penalize or reject mail from IPs without it. So set `RELOOP_API_KEY` with `fly secrets`, send over HTTPS or Reloop's SMTP relay, and let Reloop handle delivery. If you want to self-host Reloop itself, put it on a VPS next to your Fly apps.

This guide covers why, how to wire it up in a few minutes, and how to keep email off your request path with a Fly worker process.

---

## Why not send directly from a Fly machine?

It's tempting to run Postfix, or point Nodemailer straight at recipients' MX servers. Here's what Fly's own staff say about that on the [Fly community forum](https://community.fly.io/t/outbound-port-25-direct-to-mx-smtp-blocked-by-default-on-new-accounts/28537):

- There's no per-account block on outbound port 25.
- But direct-to-MX delivery needs reverse DNS on the sending IP, and Fly doesn't offer customer-configurable PTR records.
- A dedicated egress IP (`fly ips allocate-egress`) gives you a stable address, but still no PTR, which "most large receivers will penalize or outright reject."
- Their recommendation: relay outbound mail through a transactional email service.

Shared egress IPs make it worse. Anyone else's bad mail from the same IP range affects you, and users regularly report connections to Gmail and other providers timing out or being dropped.

| Approach | Reverse DNS | Reputation | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Direct SMTP from a Fly machine | Not configurable | Shared or brand new | [Spam folder](/blog/why-emails-land-in-spam-fix) or rejected |
| Dedicated Fly egress IP | Not configurable | Yours, but cold | Still penalized by large providers |
| Relay through Reloop | Handled | Warm, monitored | Inbox |

---

## What you need

1. An app running on Fly.io (`fly launch` in any project).
2. A Reloop API key from the [dashboard](https://reloop.sh/dashboard/api-keys). Keys start with `rl_`.
3. A verified sending domain in Reloop. See [connect a domain](/docs/guides/connect-domain). DNS for your domain lives wherever it does today; it doesn't need to move to Fly.

---

## 1. Store the API key as a Fly secret

```bash
fly secrets set RELOOP_API_KEY=rl_your_api_key_here
```

Fly encrypts the value and injects it as an environment variable into every machine in the app. Setting a secret triggers a rolling restart, so the new value is live as soon as the command finishes.

Never put the key in `fly.toml` under `[env]`. That section is plain text, committed to your repo.

---

## 2. Send over HTTPS (recommended)

The HTTP API is the simplest and most reliable option from a container: one HTTPS request on port 443, a JSON response with the email ID, and structured errors.

### Node.js

<InstallSdkCode />

```typescript
// src/lib/reloop.ts

```

```typescript
// anywhere on the server

const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Your login link",
  html: '<p><a href="https://app.acme.com/login?token=…">Sign in</a></p>',
  text: "Sign in: https://app.acme.com/login?token=…",
  tags: [{ name: "type", value: "magic-link" }],
});

if (emailError) {
  console.error(emailError.status, emailError.message);
}
```

The SDK returns `{ response, emailError }` instead of throwing, so a failed send never crashes a request handler. More patterns are in the [Node.js email guide](/blog/send-email-nodejs).

### Any language

It's one `POST`, so it works from Elixir, Go, [Python](/blog/send-email-python), Rails or anything else you deploy on Fly:

```bash
curl -X POST https://reloop.sh/api/mail/v1/send \
  -H "x-api-key: $RELOOP_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "from": "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
    "to": "user@example.com",
    "subject": "Hello from Fly.io",
    "text": "Sent from a Fly machine through Reloop."
  }'
```

There are official SDKs for [Python, Go, Ruby, PHP, Rust, Elixir and Java](/sdk) as well.

---

## 3. Or use the SMTP relay

If your framework already sends through SMTP (Rails Action Mailer, Phoenix Swoosh, Django, Laravel), you don't need to change any code. Just change the settings:

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Host | `smtp.reloop.sh` |
| Port | `587` (STARTTLS) |
| Username | Your Reloop API key |
| Password | Your Reloop API key |

Store them as secrets too:

```bash
fly secrets set SMTP_HOST=smtp.reloop.sh SMTP_PORT=587 \
  SMTP_USERNAME=rl_your_api_key_here SMTP_PASSWORD=rl_your_api_key_here
```

For example, in Rails:

```ruby
# config/environments/production.rb
config.action_mailer.delivery_method = :smtp
config.action_mailer.smtp_settings = {
  address: ENV.fetch("SMTP_HOST"),
  port: ENV.fetch("SMTP_PORT").to_i,
  user_name: ENV.fetch("SMTP_USERNAME"),
  password: ENV.fetch("SMTP_PASSWORD"),
  authentication: :plain,
  enable_starttls_auto: true,
}
```

You're connecting to a [relay on 587](/blog/smtp-ports-explained) with authentication, not delivering to recipients' MX on port 25, so the PTR problem above doesn't apply. Examples for other languages are in the [SMTP docs](/docs/examples/smtp/introduction).

---

## 4. Keep email off the request path with a worker process

Fly apps can run several process groups from one image. Use one for your web server and one for background jobs, and send email from the worker. A slow send never slows a page, and failed sends can be retried.

```toml
# fly.toml
app = "acme"

[processes]
  web = "node dist/server.js"
  worker = "node dist/worker.js"

[http_service]
  internal_port = 3000
  processes = ["web"]
```

```typescript
// src/worker.ts (sketch using any queue you already run, e.g. BullMQ on Redis)

new Worker(
  "emails",
  async (job) => {
    const { emailError } = await reloop.mail.send(job.data);
    if (emailError && (emailError.status >= 500 || emailError.status === 429)) {
      throw emailError; // let the queue retry
    }
  },
  { connection: { url: process.env.REDIS_URL! } },
);
```

Then scale each group on its own:

```bash
fly scale count web=2 worker=1
```

If you can't use a queue but want retries to be safe, call the HTTP API with an [`Idempotency-Key`](/docs/api/idempotency) header. Reloop replays the original response for 24 hours instead of sending twice.

---

## 5. Receiving email

Fly apps can't receive mail on port 25 for the same reasons they can't send it well. Use Reloop's inbound instead:

1. Turn on receiving for your domain in Reloop and add the MX record it shows.
2. Create a webhook for the `email.received` event pointing at your Fly app, for example `https://acme.fly.dev/webhooks/reloop`.
3. Verify the `Reloop-Signature` header on each request. See [verifying webhooks](/docs/webhooks/verify-webhooks-requests).

Your Fly app gets a signed JSON event with the sender, subject, thread ID and more. The full message, including attachments, is available through the inbox API.

---

## Should I self-host Reloop on Fly.io?

We don't recommend it, and we don't ship a Fly configuration for it. Reloop's MTA needs to deliver directly to recipients on port 25 and receive on port 25, which runs straight into the PTR limitation. The stack is also a multi-service Docker Compose deployment (around 20 containers and about 22 GB of images), which doesn't map neatly onto Fly Machines.

If you want to run Reloop yourself, use a VPS from a provider that lets you set reverse DNS and open port 25:

| Option | Guide |
|---|---|
| One command on Ubuntu or Debian | [Deploy on VPS](/docs/self-host/vps) |
| Coolify | [Reloop on Coolify](/blog/reloop-coolify-setup) |
| Overview and trade-offs | [Self-hosted email infrastructure](/blog/self-hosted-email-infrastructure) |

Your apps can stay on Fly and point at your instance by setting the SDK's `baseUrl`, or `SMTP_HOST`, to your Reloop server.

---

## Checklist

- [ ] `RELOOP_API_KEY` set with `fly secrets set`, not in `fly.toml`
- [ ] Sending domain verified in Reloop (SPF, DKIM, DMARC)
- [ ] App sends through the HTTP API or `smtp.reloop.sh:587`, never direct-to-MX
- [ ] User-facing sends happen in a worker process or queue
- [ ] Inbound handled by Reloop with a signed `email.received` webhook

---

## FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Does Fly.io block port 25?">
    Fly staff say there's no per-account block on outbound port 25. The
    problem is deliverability: Fly IPs have no customer-configurable reverse
    DNS, so large mailbox providers penalize or reject direct mail from them.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Is port 587 to smtp.reloop.sh fine from Fly?">
    Yes. That's an authenticated connection to a relay, not direct delivery.
    If a network ever blocks SMTP ports, the HTTP API on 443 always works.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Which region should my Fly app run in?">
    Wherever your users are. Sending is a single HTTPS request, so region
    has little effect on email; Reloop queues and delivers it from there.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can I use the free tier while testing?">
    Yes. Reloop's free tier includes 6,000 emails a month with up to 200 a
    day, which is plenty for staging apps on Fly.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# Best ZeptoMail Alternatives in 2026: Cheap Transactional Email, Plus What ZeptoMail Won't Do

Path: /blog/best-zeptomail-alternatives
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-zeptomail-alternatives
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-zeptomail-alternatives.md

The best ZeptoMail alternatives of 2026 compared: Reloop, Amazon SES, Elastic Email, SMTP2GO, Cloudflare Email Service, Postmark, MailerSend and Mailgun on price at 50k and 100k emails, marketing rules, inbound and self-hosting.

**ZeptoMail is one of the cheapest ways to send transactional email, and it's deliberately narrow.** Zoho sells it on prepaid credits, allows only transactional mail, and has folded it into **Zoho CPaaS** alongside SMS, WhatsApp and voice. That's ideal if receipts and OTPs are all you'll ever send. Teams look for alternatives when they need marketing mail, inbound inboxes, predictable monthly pricing, or the option to self-host.

**The short version:** **Reloop** is the closest all-round alternative: cheaper than ZeptoMail below about 150k emails a month, with campaigns, automations and inboxes included, and open source. For the lowest raw price, **Amazon SES**. For a simple SMTP relay, **SMTP2GO**. For a budget API with an optional marketing product, **Elastic Email**.

We build Reloop, so weigh our entry accordingly. Facts about each provider come from our researched head-to-head posts, linked in each section, and each section says where that provider wins.

---

## Why teams look for a ZeptoMail alternative

- **Marketing mail isn't allowed.** ZeptoMail's terms prohibit marketing, promotional mail and newsletters, and accounts that keep sending them get blocked. Onboarding sequences and product announcements need a second tool.
- **No inbound mailboxes.** You can't receive and store replies, which rules out support inboxes and AI agents that answer email.
- **Credits expire.** Each credit is valid for 6 months, so buying in bulk can waste money if volume drops.
- **The free credit is one-off.** 10,000 emails to start, not a monthly allowance.
- **Prices vary by region.** The per-credit price is widely listed at $2.50 but differs by region, which makes budgeting less predictable.
- **The product is changing.** ZeptoMail is now Zoho CPaaS, with the API at `cpaas.zoho.com`. Useful if you want SMS or WhatsApp, a distraction if you only want email.

Full breakdown: [Reloop vs ZeptoMail](/blog/reloop-vs-zeptomail).

## 1. Reloop: best overall ZeptoMail alternative

[Reloop](/) is open-source email infrastructure: a transactional API, SMTP relay, templates, signed webhooks, inbound mailboxes, contacts, campaigns and event automations in one product. It runs its own MTA (KumoMTA), and **Reloop Cloud runs on Hetzner, a German hosting company, with EU data centers**.

**Pricing:** Free for 6,000 emails a month (200 a day), every month. Pro is $10 for 50,000, Growth is $20 for 100,000 with a dedicated IP, and extra mail is $0.50 per 1,000. If you prefer ZeptoMail-style prepaid credits, Reloop sells those too: $0.50 per 1,000, valid for 6 months. Self-hosting under Apache 2.0 has no per-email fee.

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY! });

const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Your code is 481920",
  html: "<p>Your sign-in code is <strong>481920</strong>.</p>",
});
```

**Strengths**

- **Transactional and marketing in one place**, kept apart by domain while sharing one suppression list. Campaigns and event automations (`reloop.automations.start`) cover onboarding and dunning.
- Inbound mail lands in real mailboxes with threads, readable over the API, the MCP server or IMAP (3, 5 and 10 hosted inboxes on Free, Pro and Growth).
- A monthly free tier and flat plans, plus optional prepaid credits.
- Errors return a `message`, a `why` and a `fix`; webhooks are signed with `Reloop-Signature`.
- Open source, so you can move to your own servers later with the same API.

**Weaknesses**

- **Above roughly 150,000 emails a month, ZeptoMail is cheaper per email.** At a million emails, ZeptoMail is about $250 and Reloop is $470 hosted.
- No SMS or WhatsApp. If you want OTPs over several channels from one vendor, Zoho CPaaS covers that.

**Best for:** teams that need more than transactional sending without adding a second tool. Full comparison: [Reloop vs ZeptoMail](/blog/reloop-vs-zeptomail).

---

## 2. Amazon SES: cheapest per email

SES is the lowest-cost hosted sending pipe: $0.10 per 1,000 emails, plus $0.12 per GB of outbound data.

**Strengths:** cheaper than ZeptoMail at every paid volume; deep AWS integration; inbound via receipt rules to S3, SNS or Lambda.

**Weaknesses:** a sandbox you must request to leave; bounce and complaint handling through SNS or EventBridge that you build; no dashboard beyond CloudWatch; no campaigns.

**Best for:** AWS-native teams with engineers to build the pieces around it. Full comparison: [Reloop vs Amazon SES](/blog/reloop-vs-aws-ses), or our [Amazon SES alternatives](/blog/best-aws-ses-alternatives) roundup.

---

## 3. Elastic Email: best budget API with a marketing option

Elastic Email sells an Email API and a separate Email Marketing product.

**Pricing:** the Email API's free plan is 3,000 a month (100 a day). Starter is $19 and Pro is $49 for 50,000; larger volumes are priced on a slider. Dedicated IPs are a $40 add-on on Starter and $50 on Pro.

**Strengths:** a generous free tier; a marketing product from the same vendor; inbound processing on Pro.

**Weaknesses:** webhooks and inbound are Pro-only; logs are kept 3 days on Free and Starter and 7 on Pro; marketing is a separate subscription.

**Best for:** small teams that want low prices and may add marketing later. Full comparison: [Reloop vs Elastic Email](/blog/reloop-vs-elastic-email).

---

## 4. SMTP2GO: best simple SMTP relay

SMTP2GO is a long-standing SMTP relay with an HTTP API, popular with WordPress sites, agencies and devices.

**Pricing:** free for 1,000 a month. Starter is $10 for 10,000 ($1 per extra 1,000). Professional is $75 for 100,000 ($0.85 per extra 1,000), with a dedicated IP included.

**Strengths:** many SMTP ports, including 2525, 8025 and 80 for restrictive networks; SMS; phone and chat support on every plan.

**Weaknesses:** a small free tier; no campaigns; inbound isn't a focus.

**Best for:** plugging a reliable relay into apps and devices. Full comparison: [Reloop vs SMTP2GO](/blog/reloop-vs-smtp2go).

More options: [SMTP2GO alternatives](/blog/best-smtp2go-alternatives)

---

## 5. Cloudflare Email Service: best for Workers apps

Cloudflare's sending entered public beta in April 2026. From a Worker it's one binding and one `send()` call.

**Pricing:** Workers Paid ($5 a month minimum) includes 3,000 emails, then $0.35 per 1,000.

**Strengths:** native Workers binding, no API key; Email Routing for inbound.

**Weaknesses:** still in beta; requires Cloudflare DNS; transactional only, like ZeptoMail; events go to Cloudflare Queues.

**Best for:** apps already on Workers. Full comparison: [Reloop vs Cloudflare Email Service](/blog/reloop-vs-cloudflare-email).

More options: [Cloudflare Email Service alternatives](/blog/best-cloudflare-email-alternatives)

---

## 6. Postmark: best for deliverability focus

Postmark is transactional-first, with separate message streams for transactional and broadcast mail.

**Pricing:** free for 100 a month. Basic starts at $15 for 10,000, with overage at $1.80 per 1,000 ($1.30 on Pro): about $87 at 50,000 and $177 at 100,000 on Basic list price.

**Strengths:** strong transactional reputation, message streams, excellent docs.

**Weaknesses:** several times ZeptoMail's price at volume; dedicated IPs are $50 a month from 300k.

**Best for:** teams that care more about delivery speed than cost. Full comparison: [Reloop vs Postmark](/blog/reloop-vs-postmark).

---

## 7. MailerSend: best with a visual builder

MailerSend pairs a transactional API with a drag-and-drop template builder.

**Pricing:** free for 500 a month. Starter is $35 for 50,000 and $68 for 100,000, with overage at $1.30 per 1,000 (monthly billing).

**Strengths:** visual builder, SMS in the US and Canada, inbound parsing.

**Weaknesses:** small free tier; marketing lives in the separate MailerLite product.

**Best for:** teams where non-developers design templates. Full comparison: [Reloop vs MailerSend](/blog/reloop-vs-mailersend).

More options: [MailerSend alternatives](/blog/best-mailersend-alternatives)

---

## 8. Mailgun: best for inbound routing and validation

Mailgun offers inbound routes and email validation as a paid add-on.

**Pricing:** 100 a day on a trial. Basic is $15 for 10,000, Foundation is $35 for 50,000, and 100,000 is about $100 with overage from $1.30 per 1,000.

**Strengths:** mature API, Handlebars templates, inbound routes, validation.

**Weaknesses:** expensive compared with ZeptoMail; validation and dedicated IPs cost extra.

**Best for:** teams that need validation and routing from one vendor. Full comparison: [Reloop vs Mailgun](/blog/reloop-vs-mailgun).

---

## How to choose

- **"We only send receipts and OTPs, at high volume."** Stay on ZeptoMail, or move to Amazon SES for an even lower price.
- **"We want onboarding emails and newsletters from the same provider."** Reloop.
- **"We need to receive replies, for support or AI agents."** Reloop.
- **"We want a predictable monthly bill instead of credits."** Reloop, Elastic Email or SMTP2GO.
- **"We need an SMTP relay for WordPress or devices."** SMTP2GO or Reloop (`smtp.reloop.sh`).
- **"We want to self-host."** Reloop, under Apache 2.0.

---

## Switching from ZeptoMail

1. **Verify your domain** with the new provider. Add its DKIM record and merge its include into your existing SPF record; never publish a second SPF record.
2. **Export your suppression list** from ZeptoMail and import it, so you don't email addresses that bounced or complained.
3. **Swap the client.** ZeptoMail's recipients look like `[{ email_address: { address, name } }]`; most alternatives take plain strings. On Reloop, use `reloop.mail.send(...)`.
4. **Move templates.** ZeptoMail sends templates by `template_key` with `merge_info`. On Reloop, store the template and use `{{{variables}}}`.
5. **Update SMTP settings** if you use the relay: ZeptoMail's `smtp.zeptomail.com` with user `emailapikey` becomes, for Reloop, `smtp.reloop.sh` with your API key as both username and password.
6. **Ramp traffic** over one to two weeks, then let your remaining credits run out rather than buying more.

# Send Transactional Email from Remix (React Router v7)

Path: /blog/send-email-remix
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/send-email-remix
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/send-email-remix.md

Send transactional email from Remix and React Router v7 with Reloop: a server-only client, route actions, Form and useFetcher, React Email templates, error handling, webhooks and deployment.

**In Remix, send email from a route `action`.** Actions run only on the server, so your API key never reaches the browser. Create one Reloop client in a `.server.ts` module, call `reloop.mail.send()` inside the action, and return a small result the page can show. That's the whole pattern.

A note on names: Remix v2 and React Router v7 are now the same framework. React Router v7's "framework mode" is what Remix v3 would have been, and the Remix team recommends it for new apps. This guide uses React Router v7 code, and points out the one or two places where Remix v2 differs.

Using a different framework? See the guides for [Next.js](/blog/send-email-nextjs-app-router), [SvelteKit](/blog/send-email-sveltekit) or plain [Node.js](/blog/send-email-nodejs).

---

## What you'll build

| Piece | File | Runs on |
|---|---|---|
| Reloop client | `app/lib/reloop.server.ts` | Server only |
| Signup route with an action | `app/routes/signup.tsx` | Server (action) + browser (form) |
| Resource route for webhooks | `app/routes/api.reloop-webhook.ts` | Server only |
| React Email template | `app/emails/welcome.tsx` | Server only |

---

## Prerequisites

1. A React Router v7 app (`npx create-react-router@latest`) or a Remix v2 app.
2. A Reloop API key from the [dashboard](https://reloop.sh/dashboard/api-keys). Keys start with `rl_`.
3. A verified sending domain. See [connect a domain](/docs/guides/connect-domain).

---

## 1. Install the SDK

<InstallSdkCode />

The package is [`reloop-email`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/reloop-email). It has no runtime dependencies besides `fetch`, which every supported Node version has.

---

## 2. Add your API key

In `.env` at the project root:

```env
RELOOP_API_KEY=rl_your_api_key_here
```

Don't rely on the framework to load `.env` into `process.env` for you. Load it explicitly in development, either with `dotenv` (`import "dotenv/config"` at the top of your server entry) or Node's built-in `--env-file=.env` flag. In production, set `RELOOP_API_KEY` in your host's environment settings (Fly, Render, Railway, a VPS's systemd unit, and so on).

<Callout type="warning">
  Don't prefix the variable with `VITE_`. Vite exposes `VITE_` variables to client code, which would put your API key in the browser bundle.
</Callout>

---

## 3. Create a server-only client

The `.server.ts` suffix tells the bundler this module must never end up in client code. If you import it from a component by mistake, the build fails instead of leaking your key.

```typescript
// app/lib/reloop.server.ts

const apiKey = process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY;

if (!apiKey) {
  throw new Error("Missing RELOOP_API_KEY");
}

```

If you self-host Reloop, pass `baseUrl: "https://reloop.example.com"` as well.

---

## 4. Send from a route action

Here's a signup route. The action validates the email, creates the user, and sends a [welcome email](/blog/welcome-email-sequences-that-convert).

```tsx
// app/routes/signup.tsx

  const formData = await request.formData();
  const email = String(formData.get("email") ?? "").trim().toLowerCase();
  const name = String(formData.get("name") ?? "").trim();

  if (!email.includes("@")) {
    return data({ ok: false, error: "Enter a valid email address." }, { status: 400 });
  }

  const user = await createUser({ email, name });

  const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
    from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
    to: user.email,
    subject: name ? `Welcome to Acme, ${name}` : "Welcome to Acme",
    html: `<p>Hi ${name || "there"},</p><p>Your account is ready.</p>`,
    text: `Hi ${name || "there"}, your account is ready.`,
    reply_to: "support@acme.com",
    tags: [{ name: "type", value: "welcome" }],
  });

  if (emailError) {
    // The account exists; don't fail signup because of email.
    console.error("Welcome email failed", emailError.status, emailError.message);
  }

  return { ok: true, emailId: response?.id ?? null };
}

  const actionData = useActionData<typeof action>();
  const navigation = useNavigation();
  const submitting = navigation.state === "submitting";

  return (
    <Form method="post" className="space-y-3">
      <input name="name" placeholder="Name" />
      <input name="email" type="email" required placeholder="you@company.com" />
      <button type="submit" disabled={submitting}>
        {submitting ? "Creating account…" : "Create account"}
      </button>
      {actionData && !actionData.ok ? <p>{actionData.error}</p> : null}
      {actionData?.ok ? <p>Check your inbox.</p> : null}
    </Form>
  );
}
```

A few things worth noticing:

- **The SDK doesn't throw on API errors.** It returns `{ response, emailError }`. `emailError` has the HTTP `status`, a `message`, and the full error `body` with Reloop's `code`, `why` and `fix` fields.
- **`data()` sets the status code** while still returning JSON. In Remix v2, use `json()` from `@remix-run/node` instead.
- **The form works without JavaScript.** `<Form method="post">` posts to the action; React Router upgrades it to a fetch when JS is loaded.
- **Types come for free.** `Route.ActionArgs` is generated by React Router's type generation. In Remix v2, use `ActionFunctionArgs` from `@remix-run/node`.

---

## 5. Send without navigating: `useFetcher`

For things like "resend verification email" buttons, you don't want a page transition. `useFetcher` calls the action in the background:

```tsx
// app/routes/settings.tsx

  const user = await requireUser(request);

  const { emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
    from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
    to: user.email,
    subject: "Verify your email",
    html: `<p><a href="${verifyUrl(user)}">Verify your email</a></p>`,
    text: `Verify your email: ${verifyUrl(user)}`,
  });

  return { sent: !emailError };
}

  const fetcher = useFetcher<typeof action>();

  return (
    <fetcher.Form method="post">
      <button type="submit" disabled={fetcher.state !== "idle"}>
        {fetcher.state !== "idle" ? "Sending…" : "Resend verification email"}
      </button>
      {fetcher.data?.sent ? <span>Sent. Check your inbox.</span> : null}
    </fetcher.Form>
  );
}
```

Always authenticate inside the action (`requireUser` here). An action is a public HTTP endpoint, and an unauthenticated send endpoint can be abused to spam people from your domain.

---

## 6. Use React Email templates

Inline HTML strings get messy fast. The Reloop SDK accepts a `react` field and renders it to HTML for you, using `@react-email/render` if it's installed or `react-dom/server` otherwise.

```bash
npm install @react-email/components @react-email/render
```

```tsx
// app/emails/welcome.tsx

  return (
    <Html>
      <Body style={{ fontFamily: "Inter, Arial, sans-serif" }}>
        <Container>
          <Heading>Welcome, {name}</Heading>
          <Text>Your account is ready. Start with your first project.</Text>
          <Button href={url}>Open dashboard</Button>
        </Container>
      </Body>
    </Html>
  );
}
```

```tsx

await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
  to: user.email,
  subject: "Welcome to Acme",
  react: <WelcomeEmail name={user.name} url="https://app.acme.com" />,
});
```

Keep email components in a server-only folder and import them only from actions or `.server.ts` files.

Prefer to edit templates without a deploy? Create the template in the Reloop dashboard and send it by ID with variables:

```typescript
await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
  to: user.email,
  subject: "Reset your password",
  template: {
    id: "tmpl_password_reset",
    variables: { name: user.name, reset_url: resetUrl },
  },
});
```

---

## 7. Receive delivery events with a resource route

A route with an `action` and no default export is a resource route: a plain HTTP endpoint. That's the right place for Reloop webhooks ([bounces](/blog/email-bounce-processing-automation), complaints, deliveries).

```typescript
// app/routes/api.reloop-webhook.ts

function verify(rawBody: string, header: string, secret: string) {
  const parts = Object.fromEntries(
    header.split(",").map((p) => p.trim().split("=") as [string, string]),
  );
  const timestamp = Number(parts.t);
  if (!parts.v1 || Math.abs(Date.now() / 1000 - timestamp) > 300) return false;

  const expected = createHmac("sha256", secret)
    .update(`${timestamp}.${rawBody}`)
    .digest("hex");
  const a = Buffer.from(expected, "hex");
  const b = Buffer.from(parts.v1, "hex");
  return a.length === b.length && timingSafeEqual(a, b);
}

  const rawBody = await request.text();
  const signature = request.headers.get("Reloop-Signature") ?? "";

  if (!verify(rawBody, signature, process.env.RELOOP_WEBHOOK_SECRET!)) {
    return new Response("Invalid signature", { status: 401 });
  }

  const event = JSON.parse(rawBody) as {
    type: string;
    data: { email_id: string; to: string[] };
  };

  if (event.type === "email.bounced" || event.type === "email.complained") {
    await markEmailUndeliverable(event.data.to[0]);
  }

  return new Response("ok");
}
```

Read the body with `request.text()` before parsing: the signature is computed over the raw bytes. The full algorithm and the list of event types are in the docs on [verifying webhooks](/docs/webhooks/verify-webhooks-requests) and [event types](/docs/webhooks/event-types).

---

## 8. Handle errors and retries

| Situation | What to do |
|---|---|
| `emailError.status` is 4xx | Bad input or config (unverified domain, invalid address). Log it, don't retry. |
| `emailError.status` is 429 | You hit a [rate limit](/docs/api/usage-limits). Retry with backoff. |
| `emailError.status` is 5xx or 0 | Network or server issue. Retry with backoff. |
| Email must not be sent twice | Use the HTTP API with an [`Idempotency-Key`](/docs/api/idempotency) header, or a job queue that tracks sends. |

For high-value sends like receipts, don't send inside the request at all. Put a job on a queue (BullMQ, pg-boss, your host's queue) and send from a worker, so a slow or failed send never affects the user's request.

---

## 9. Deploy

React Router v7 apps run anywhere Node runs, and on edge platforms with the right adapter.

| Host | Where to set `RELOOP_API_KEY` |
|---|---|
| Node server (VPS, Docker) | Process environment, for example a `.env` loaded by your process manager |
| Fly.io | `fly secrets set RELOOP_API_KEY=rl_…` |
| Vercel | Project → Settings → Environment Variables |
| Cloudflare Workers | `wrangler secret put RELOOP_API_KEY`, then read it from the request `context` |

On Cloudflare, the SDK needs the `nodejs_compat` flag. See [sending email from Cloudflare Workers](/blog/send-email-cloudflare-workers) for the details and a dependency-free `fetch` version.

---

## FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="Can I send email from a loader?">
    You can, but you shouldn't. Loaders run on GET requests, which can be
    prefetched, retried and cached. Sending email is a side effect, so it
    belongs in an action.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Remix v2 or React Router v7?">
    The Reloop code is identical. The differences are imports: Remix v2 uses
    `@remix-run/node` for `json` and `ActionFunctionArgs`, React Router v7
    uses `data` from `react-router` and generated `Route` types.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can I use SMTP instead of the SDK?">
    Yes. Point Nodemailer at `smtp.reloop.sh` on [port 587](/blog/smtp-ports-explained) with your API key
    as both username and password. See the [SMTP docs](/docs/examples/smtp/introduction).
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="How do I test emails locally?">
    Send to your own address from a verified domain, then inspect the
    message, its headers and delivery status in the Reloop dashboard logs.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# Introducing Monthly Plans: 50,000 Emails for $10

Path: /blog/introducing-monthly-plans
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/introducing-monthly-plans
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/introducing-monthly-plans.md

Reloop's monthly plans give steady senders a flat price: Pro is $10 for 50,000 emails, Growth is $20 for 100,000 with a dedicated IP, and Enterprise is custom. No daily cap, $0.50 per 1,000 past your allowance.

If you send about the same amount of email every month, you want one thing from pricing: a flat number you can budget for.

Today Reloop gets **monthly plans**. Pro is **$10 a month for 50,000 emails**. Growth is **$20 a month for 100,000**, with a dedicated IP. Enterprise is custom. All of them sit on top of the same product as the [free tier](/blog/reloop-free-tier), with higher limits and no daily cap.

## How it works

1. **Your allowance resets every billing period.** Unused emails do not roll over.
2. **No daily cap.** Send your whole month in a day if a launch calls for it.

4. **Change plans any time.** Upgrade from Pro to Growth when you outgrow it. If you cancel, you drop back to the free tier at the end of the period.

## Who it's for

A monthly plan is the right pick when:

- **Your volume is steady.** Password resets, receipts and notifications that scale with your users, not with launches.
- **You send more than about 26,000 emails a month.** Below that, [pay-as-you-go credits](/blog/introducing-pay-as-you-go) are usually cheaper.
- **You want a fixed bill.** The same charge every month is easier to budget and expense.
- **You'd rather not watch a balance.** Plans keep sending past the allowance, so there's nothing to top up.

Not sure which fits? The full math, with a table for every volume from 6,000 to 150,000 emails a month, is in [pay as you go vs monthly: how to choose](/blog/pay-as-you-go-vs-monthly-email-pricing).
