# How to Send Email in PHP: PHPMailer, Laravel and API

Path: /blog/send-email-php
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/send-email-php
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/send-email-php.md

Send email from PHP with PHPMailer, Laravel, Symfony Mailer or WordPress, or with an email API. Copy-paste examples for HTML email, attachments, queued sending and retries without duplicates.

**PHP has a built-in `mail()` function, but you should not use it for real email.** Send through a provider instead: over SMTP with [PHPMailer](https://github.com/PHPMailer/PHPMailer) or your framework's mailer, or over HTTPS with an email API SDK.

This guide covers PHPMailer, the Reloop PHP SDK, Laravel, Symfony and WordPress, then the production details: attachments, queued sending and safe retries.

Working in another language? See how to send email in [Python](/blog/send-email-python) or [Node.js](/blog/send-email-nodejs).

---

## Which approach should you use?

| | PHPMailer / framework SMTP | Email API SDK |
|---|---------------------------|---------------|
| **Install** | `composer require phpmailer/phpmailer` | `composer require reloop/reloop-email` |
| **Transport** | SMTP on port 587 (STARTTLS) | HTTPS on port 443 |
| **Building the message** | `PHPMailer` properties, MIME handled for you | An array with `html`, `text`, `attachments` |
| **Errors** | `PHPMailer\PHPMailer\Exception` with a text message | `ReloopApiException` with status and JSON body |
| **Safe retries** | No, a retry can send twice | Yes, with an idempotency key |
| **Works with Laravel `Mail` and WordPress `wp_mail`** | Yes, natively | Through SMTP settings |

If you are wiring up Laravel's notifications, password resets or a WordPress plugin, use SMTP settings. If you are writing the send call yourself, use the API.

---

## Prerequisites

1. **PHP 8.1 or later** and [Composer](https://getcomposer.org)
2. A **verified sending domain** with [SPF, DKIM and DMARC](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide)
3. An **API key** from the [Reloop dashboard](https://reloop.sh/dashboard). Keys start with `rl_`, and the same key works for the API and SMTP.

```bash
```

Keep the key in the environment or a secrets manager, never in your code or git.

---

## Why not PHP's mail() function?

`mail()` hands the message to the local `sendmail` binary and returns `true` if that worked. It does not tell you whether the email was delivered, accepted or rejected. On most servers it also means:

- **No authentication.** The message is not DKIM-signed for your domain, so Gmail and Outlook treat it as suspicious or reject it under [the 2024 sender rules](/blog/gmail-yahoo-bulk-sender-requirements).
- **Your server's IP sends the mail.** Shared hosting and cloud IPs often have a poor reputation or sit on blocklists.
- **You build headers by hand.** Concatenating user input into headers invites header injection.
- **It is often disabled.** Many hosts and Docker images ship without a working `sendmail`.

Use SMTP with PHPMailer or an API instead. Both authenticate to a provider that signs and delivers the message.

---

## Method 1: Send email with PHPMailer

### Install

```bash
composer require phpmailer/phpmailer
```

### Send an email

```php
<?php

require __DIR__ . '/vendor/autoload.php';

use PHPMailer\PHPMailer\PHPMailer;

$mail = new PHPMailer(true); // true: throw exceptions on errors

$mail->isSMTP();
$mail->Host = 'smtp.reloop.sh';
$mail->Port = 587;
$mail->SMTPSecure = PHPMailer::ENCRYPTION_STARTTLS;
$mail->SMTPAuth = true;
$mail->Username = 'reloop';
$mail->Password = getenv('RELOOP_API_KEY');
$mail->Timeout = 30;
$mail->CharSet = PHPMailer::CHARSET_UTF8;

$mail->setFrom('hello@mail.acme.com', 'Acme');
$mail->addAddress('user@example.com');

$mail->isHTML(true);
$mail->Subject = 'Welcome to Acme';
$mail->Body = '<h1>Welcome!</h1><p>Thanks for signing up.</p>';
$mail->AltBody = 'Welcome! Thanks for signing up.';

$mail->send();
```

The username can be any string. The password is your API key. `AltBody` is the plain-text version, and PHPMailer builds the multipart message for you. Set `CharSet` to UTF-8: PHPMailer defaults to ISO-8859-1, which mangles names and emoji.

### When port 587 is blocked

Some hosts block outbound 587. Reloop also accepts STARTTLS on port **2587** (and 2025), so only the port number changes:

```php
$mail->Port = 2587;
$mail->SMTPSecure = PHPMailer::ENCRYPTION_STARTTLS;
```

Reloop does not offer implicit TLS on port 465, so do not use `PHPMailer::ENCRYPTION_SMTPS` with it. If the connection hangs or times out, see [SMTP ports explained](/blog/smtp-ports-explained).

### Handle SMTP errors

```php
use PHPMailer\PHPMailer\Exception;
use PHPMailer\PHPMailer\SMTP;

try {
    $mail->send();
} catch (Exception $e) {
    error_log('Send failed: ' . $mail->ErrorInfo);
}
```

PHPMailer uses one exception class for everything, so the reason is in the message: `Could not authenticate` means a wrong API key, and `Could not connect to SMTP host` means a blocked port or a TLS mismatch. To see the full SMTP conversation while debugging, set `$mail->SMTPDebug = SMTP::DEBUG_SERVER;` and turn it off again before you deploy.

### Can I send with Gmail from PHP?

For a personal script, yes: use `smtp.gmail.com` on port 587 with an [App Password](https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/185833). For an app, no. Gmail limits personal accounts to about 500 recipients a day, every message comes from your `@gmail.com` address, and bulk sending gets the account suspended.

---

## Method 2: Send email with the PHP SDK

### Install

```bash
composer require reloop/reloop-email
```

The SDK needs PHP 8.1 or later and uses Guzzle 7 for HTTP.

### Send an email

```php
<?php

require __DIR__ . '/vendor/autoload.php';

use Reloop\Exceptions\ReloopApiException;
use Reloop\Exceptions\ReloopValidationException;
use Reloop\Reloop;

$reloop = Reloop::client(getenv('RELOOP_API_KEY'));

try {
    $result = $reloop->mail->send([
        'from' => 'Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>',
        'to' => 'user@example.com',
        'subject' => 'Welcome to Acme',
        'html' => '<h1>Welcome!</h1><p>Thanks for signing up.</p>',
        'text' => 'Welcome! Thanks for signing up.',
    ]);
    echo 'Sent: ' . $result['id'] . PHP_EOL;
} catch (ReloopValidationException $e) {
    // Bad input, caught before any request was made
    error_log("Invalid {$e->field}: {$e->getMessage()}");
} catch (ReloopApiException $e) {
    error_log("Failed: {$e->status} {$e->getMessage()}");
}
```

`send()` returns the decoded JSON response as an array, with the email ID in `id`. The SDK **throws** on failure:

- `ReloopValidationException` when a required field (`from`, `to`, `subject`) is missing. No request is sent.
- `ReloopApiException` for any non-2xx response or network failure. `$e->status` is the HTTP status, or `0` for a network error, and `$e->body` holds the API's JSON error with `message`, `why` and `fix`.

`Reloop::client()` creates a Guzzle client with a 30-second timeout. Create it **once** and reuse it, for example as a singleton in your framework's container.

### Send to several recipients

```php
$reloop->mail->send([
    'from' => 'Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>',
    'to' => ['ada@example.com', 'grace@example.com'],
    'cc' => 'team@acme.com',
    'reply_to' => 'support@acme.com',
    'subject' => 'Your weekly report',
    'text' => 'Here is your report.',
    'tags' => [['name' => 'type', 'value' => 'weekly_report']],
]);
```

Every address in `to` sees the others. For personalized mail, send one message per recipient.

### Send a stored template

Keep copy out of your code so non-developers can edit it. Create the template in Reloop, then send it by ID with variables:

```php
$reloop->mail->send([
    'from' => 'Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>',
    'to' => 'user@example.com',
    'subject' => 'Welcome to Acme',
    'template' => [
        'id' => 'tmpl_welcome',
        'variables' => ['first_name' => 'Ada', 'plan' => 'Pro'],
    ],
]);
```

The SDK checks for `subject` before sending, so pass one even when the template has its own. See [templates](/docs/learn/templates) for variables and defaults.

---

## Laravel

### SMTP settings

Laravel's `Mail` facade works with any SMTP provider. Set these in `.env` and Mailables, notifications and [password reset emails](/blog/password-reset-email-best-practices) all go through Reloop:

```bash
# .env
MAIL_MAILER=smtp
MAIL_SCHEME=smtp
MAIL_HOST=smtp.reloop.sh
MAIL_PORT=587
MAIL_USERNAME=reloop
MAIL_PASSWORD=rl_your_api_key
MAIL_FROM_ADDRESS=hello@mail.acme.com
MAIL_FROM_NAME="Acme"
```

These map to the `smtp` mailer that ships in `config/mail.php`, so you do not need to edit that file:

```php
// config/mail.php (default, shown for reference)
'smtp' => [
    'transport' => 'smtp',
    'scheme' => env('MAIL_SCHEME'),
    'url' => env('MAIL_URL'),
    'host' => env('MAIL_HOST', '127.0.0.1'),
    'port' => env('MAIL_PORT', 2525),
    'username' => env('MAIL_USERNAME'),
    'password' => env('MAIL_PASSWORD'),
    'timeout' => null,
    'local_domain' => env('MAIL_EHLO_DOMAIN', parse_url((string) env('APP_URL', 'http://localhost'), PHP_URL_HOST)),
],
```

Keep the scheme as `smtp`, never `smtps`. The `smtp` scheme connects in plain text and upgrades with STARTTLS, which is what Reloop expects. If 587 is blocked, set `MAIL_PORT=2587`. On Laravel 10 and earlier, the setting is `MAIL_ENCRYPTION=tls` instead of `MAIL_SCHEME`.

### Mailables

Generate a Mailable with `php artisan make:mail WelcomeMail`, then define its subject and views:

```php
<?php

namespace App\Mail;

use App\Models\User;
use Illuminate\Bus\Queueable;
use Illuminate\Mail\Mailable;
use Illuminate\Mail\Mailables\Content;
use Illuminate\Mail\Mailables\Envelope;
use Illuminate\Queue\SerializesModels;

class WelcomeMail extends Mailable
{
    use Queueable, SerializesModels;

    public function __construct(public User $user)
    {
    }

    public function envelope(): Envelope
    {
        return new Envelope(subject: 'Welcome to Acme');
    }

    public function content(): Content
    {
        return new Content(
            view: 'emails.welcome',
            text: 'emails.welcome-text',
        );
    }
}
```

```php
use App\Mail\WelcomeMail;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Mail;

Mail::to($user)->send(new WelcomeMail($user));
```

Public properties like `$user` are available in the Blade views. The `text` view gives you a plain-text part next to the HTML.

### Queue it

Sending inside the request adds a full SMTP round trip to your response time. Queue the Mailable instead:

```php
Mail::to($user)->queue(new WelcomeMail($user));
```

Or add `implements ShouldQueue` to the class so every `send()` is queued. Set `QUEUE_CONNECTION` to `database` or `redis` and run `php artisan queue:work`. With the default `sync` connection, "queued" mail still sends inside the request.

A queued Mailable can set `public $tries = 3;` and a `backoff()` method. Be aware that SMTP has no idempotency key, so a retry after a timeout can send the email twice. For mail that must go out exactly once, use the API with a job (below).

### Using the SDK in Laravel

Add the key to `config/services.php` and bind one client in a service provider:

```php
// config/services.php
'reloop' => [
    'key' => env('RELOOP_API_KEY'),
],
```

```php
// app/Providers/AppServiceProvider.php
use Reloop\Reloop;

public function register(): void
{
    $this->app->singleton(
        Reloop::class,
        fn () => Reloop::client(config('services.reloop.key')),
    );
}
```

Then type-hint `Reloop` anywhere Laravel resolves dependencies, such as a controller:

```php
<?php

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use Illuminate\Http\JsonResponse;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Reloop\Exceptions\ReloopApiException;
use Reloop\Reloop;

class ContactController extends Controller
{
    public function store(Request $request, Reloop $reloop): JsonResponse
    {
        $data = $request->validate([
            'email' => ['required', 'email'],
            'message' => ['required', 'string', 'max:5000'],
        ]);

        try {
            $result = $reloop->mail->send([
                'from' => 'Acme Website <contact@mail.acme.com>',
                'to' => 'support@acme.com',
                'reply_to' => $data['email'],
                'subject' => "New message from {$data['email']}",
                'text' => $data['message'],
            ]);
        } catch (ReloopApiException $e) {
            report($e);

            return response()->json(['error' => 'Could not send message'], 502);
        }

        return response()->json(['id' => $result['id']]);
    }
}
```

The visitor's address goes in `reply_to`, never in `from`. You can only send from your verified domain, and putting someone else's domain in `from` fails [DMARC](/blog/gmail-yahoo-bulk-sender-requirements).

---

## Symfony

Symfony Mailer reads one DSN from the environment:

```bash
# .env.local
MAILER_DSN=smtp://reloop:rl_your_api_key@smtp.reloop.sh:587
```

The `smtp://` scheme upgrades to STARTTLS automatically when the server offers it, which Reloop always does. On Symfony 7.1 or later, add `?require_tls=true` to refuse to send if TLS is not available. Do not use `smtps://`, which means implicit TLS. If 587 is blocked, change the port to 2587.

```php
<?php

namespace App\Controller;

use Symfony\Bundle\FrameworkBundle\Controller\AbstractController;
use Symfony\Component\HttpFoundation\Response;
use Symfony\Component\Mailer\MailerInterface;
use Symfony\Component\Mime\Address;
use Symfony\Component\Mime\Email;
use Symfony\Component\Routing\Attribute\Route;

class WelcomeController extends AbstractController
{
    #[Route('/welcome', methods: ['POST'])]
    public function send(MailerInterface $mailer): Response
    {
        $email = (new Email())
            ->from(new Address('hello@mail.acme.com', 'Acme'))
            ->to('user@example.com')
            ->subject('Welcome to Acme')
            ->text('Welcome! Thanks for signing up.')
            ->html('<h1>Welcome!</h1><p>Thanks for signing up.</p>');

        $mailer->send($email);

        return new Response('Sent');
    }
}
```

`send()` throws `TransportExceptionInterface` when the SMTP server rejects the message. If Symfony Messenger is installed, route `Symfony\Component\Mailer\Messenger\SendEmailMessage` to an async transport in `config/packages/messenger.yaml` and mail is sent by a worker instead of in the request.

---

## WordPress

WordPress sends everything (password resets, new user emails, WooCommerce receipts) through `wp_mail()`, which uses PHP's `mail()` by default. Point it at SMTP and all of those go through Reloop.

The no-code route is an SMTP plugin such as WP Mail SMTP. The [WordPress guide](/docs/integrations/wordpress) has the exact settings. If you prefer code, `wp_mail()` uses PHPMailer internally, so you can configure it with the `phpmailer_init` hook. Put the key in `wp-config.php`:

```php
// wp-config.php
define('RELOOP_API_KEY', 'rl_your_api_key');
```

Then add a must-use plugin:

```php
<?php
// wp-content/mu-plugins/reloop-smtp.php

add_action('phpmailer_init', function ($phpmailer) {
    $phpmailer->isSMTP();
    $phpmailer->Host = 'smtp.reloop.sh';
    $phpmailer->Port = 587;
    $phpmailer->SMTPSecure = 'tls'; // STARTTLS
    $phpmailer->SMTPAuth = true;
    $phpmailer->Username = 'reloop';
    $phpmailer->Password = RELOOP_API_KEY;
});

add_filter('wp_mail_from', fn () => 'hello@mail.acme.com');
add_filter('wp_mail_from_name', fn () => 'Acme');
```

The `wp_mail_from` filter matters: WordPress defaults to `wordpress@yourdomain.com`, which must be on your verified domain to send.

---

## Attachments

With PHPMailer, attach a file from disk or from memory:

```php
$mail->addAttachment('/path/to/invoice-1042.pdf', 'invoice-1042.pdf');

// Or from a string you generated
$mail->addStringAttachment($pdfBytes, 'invoice-1042.pdf', PHPMailer::ENCODING_BASE64, 'application/pdf');
```

Laravel Mailables return attachments from an `attachments()` method, for example `Attachment::fromPath(storage_path('invoices/1042.pdf'))`. Symfony's `Email` has `attachFromPath()` and `attach()`.

With the SDK, pass a `path` that Reloop fetches when it builds the message, such as a short-lived signed URL to the file in your storage bucket:

```php
$reloop->mail->send([
    'from' => 'Acme Billing <billing@mail.acme.com>',
    'to' => 'user@example.com',
    'subject' => 'Your invoice #1042',
    'text' => 'Your invoice is attached.',
    'attachments' => [[
        'filename' => 'invoice-1042.pdf',
        'path' => 'https://files.acme.com/invoices/1042.pdf?signature=...',
        'content_type' => 'application/pdf',
    ]],
]);
```

The URL must be reachable from the internet. Keep attachments small: Reloop caps them by plan (1 MB on the free plan, 5 MB on paid plans, see [pricing](/pricing)), and large files hurt deliverability. For big files, send a download link instead.

---

## Send in the background with a Laravel job

Sending inside a web request adds latency and fails the request when the provider is slow. Move it to a queued job and let the queue handle retries:

```php
<?php

namespace App\Jobs;

use Illuminate\Bus\Queueable;
use Illuminate\Contracts\Queue\ShouldQueue;
use Illuminate\Foundation\Bus\Dispatchable;
use Illuminate\Queue\InteractsWithQueue;
use Reloop\Exceptions\ReloopApiException;
use Reloop\Exceptions\ReloopValidationException;
use Reloop\Reloop;

class SendWelcomeEmail implements ShouldQueue
{
    use Dispatchable, InteractsWithQueue, Queueable;

    public int $tries = 5;

    public function __construct(public string $email)
    {
    }

    /** @return array<int, int> seconds to wait before each retry */
    public function backoff(): array
    {
        return [10, 30, 60, 120];
    }

    public function handle(Reloop $reloop): void
    {
        try {
            $reloop->mail->send([
                'from' => 'Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>',
                'to' => $this->email,
                'subject' => 'Welcome to Acme',
                'text' => 'Thanks for signing up.',
            ]);
        } catch (ReloopApiException $e) {
            if ($e->status === 0 || $e->status === 429 || $e->status >= 500) {
                throw $e; // the queue retries with backoff
            }
            $this->fail($e); // 4xx: do not retry
        } catch (ReloopValidationException $e) {
            $this->fail($e);
        }
    }
}
```

```php
SendWelcomeEmail::dispatch($user->email);
```

**Retry** network errors (status `0`), `429` and `5xx`. **Do not retry** other `4xx` errors: an invalid address or unverified domain fails the same way every time. Outside Laravel, Symfony Messenger and plain worker scripts follow the same rule.

---

## Retries without duplicate emails

A request times out and your job retries. If the first attempt actually went through, the user gets two emails. The API prevents this with an [`Idempotency-Key` header](/docs/api/idempotency): repeat a request with the same key and Reloop returns the original result instead of sending again.

The PHP SDK does not set this header, so call the endpoint with Guzzle (already installed with the SDK):

```php
<?php

use GuzzleHttp\Client;

function sendReceipt(Client $http, string $orderId, string $to): array
{
    $response = $http->post('https://reloop.sh/api/mail/v1/send', [
        'headers' => [
            'x-api-key' => getenv('RELOOP_API_KEY'),
            'Idempotency-Key' => "receipt-{$orderId}",
        ],
        'json' => [
            'from' => 'Acme <orders@mail.acme.com>',
            'to' => $to,
            'subject' => "Receipt for order {$orderId}",
            'text' => 'Thanks for your order.',
        ],
        'timeout' => 30,
    ]);

    return json_decode((string) $response->getBody(), true, 512, JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
}
```

Guzzle throws `ConnectException` on network errors and `ClientException` or `ServerException` on `4xx` and `5xx`, so the same retry rules apply. In Laravel, the HTTP client does the same in a few lines:

```php
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Http;

$response = Http::withHeaders([
    'x-api-key' => config('services.reloop.key'),
    'Idempotency-Key' => "receipt-{$order->id}",
])->timeout(30)->post('https://reloop.sh/api/mail/v1/send', [
    'from' => 'Acme <orders@mail.acme.com>',
    'to' => $order->email,
    'subject' => "Receipt for order {$order->id}",
    'text' => 'Thanks for your order.',
])->throw();
```

Base the key on the business event (`receipt-{$orderId}`), not a new UUID per attempt, so retries from any worker are safe. If a retry arrives while the first request is still running, Reloop returns `409`; retry that too, with the same key.

---

## Testing without sending real email

- **Laravel:** call `Mail::fake()` in the test, then `Mail::assertSent(WelcomeMail::class)` or `Mail::assertQueued(...)`. For jobs that call the API through `Http`, use `Http::fake()` and `Http::assertSent()`.
- **Symfony:** set `MAILER_DSN=null://null` in `.env.test` to discard mail, and use the mailer assertions in `KernelTestCase`.
- **SDK unit tests:** `Reloop::client()` accepts a Guzzle client as its third argument, so you can pass one built on a Guzzle `MockHandler` (with `base_uri` set to `https://reloop.sh/`) and assert on the request without network access.
- **Local SMTP:** run [Mailpit](https://mailpit.axllent.org) with `docker run -p 1025:1025 -p 8025:8025 axllent/mailpit`, then point PHPMailer at `localhost` port `1025` with `SMTPAuth = false` and `SMTPAutoTLS = false` (or set `MAIL_HOST=127.0.0.1` and `MAIL_PORT=1025` in Laravel). Open `http://localhost:8025` to see the messages.
- **Staging:** send to [test addresses](/docs/guides/testing-email-addresses) so you do not hurt your [sender reputation](/blog/why-emails-land-in-spam-fix) with bounces.

---

## Production checklist

- [ ] API key in an environment variable or secrets manager, not in `config/` or git
- [ ] Sending domain verified with SPF, DKIM and DMARC
- [ ] `from` on your verified domain; user addresses in `reply_to`
- [ ] Both HTML and plain-text bodies, UTF-8 charset
- [ ] No calls to `mail()` anywhere, including old plugins
- [ ] One shared SDK client, bound as a singleton
- [ ] Sending in a queue worker, not the request
- [ ] Retries only on network errors, `429` and `5xx`
- [ ] Idempotency keys on anything that retries
- [ ] [Webhooks](/features/webhooks) for bounces and complaints
- [ ] Disposable addresses blocked at signup ([how](/blog/block-disposable-emails-at-signup))

## FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="How do I send an HTML email in PHP?">
    With PHPMailer, call isHTML(true), put the HTML in Body and the plain-text
    version in AltBody. With the Reloop SDK, pass html and text keys in the
    send array. In Laravel, give the Mailable both a view and a text view.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Why shouldn't I use PHP's mail() function?">
    mail() passes the message to the local sendmail binary without
    authentication or DKIM signing, so it often lands in spam or is rejected.
    It only tells you whether sendmail accepted the message, not whether it
    was delivered. Use PHPMailer over SMTP or an email API instead.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Should PHPMailer use STARTTLS or SMTPS?">
    STARTTLS connects in plain text and upgrades to TLS, which is what port
    587 expects. SMTPS starts TLS immediately, which is what port 465
    expects. Using the wrong one for the port makes the connection hang or
    fail. Reloop uses STARTTLS on every port, so set SMTPSecure to the
    STARTTLS constant.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Why do my PHP emails go to spam?">
    Usually the sending domain is not authenticated, the mail comes from
    mail() on a shared server, or the From domain does not match the domain
    that signed the message. Send through a provider from your own verified
    domain with SPF, DKIM and DMARC, and always include a plain-text body.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can I use Reloop with Laravel notifications and WordPress?">
    Yes. Set the SMTP values shown above in Laravel's .env file, or point
    WordPress at Reloop with an SMTP plugin or a small must-use plugin, and
    every email the framework sends goes through Reloop with no other code
    changes.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# Reloop vs Mailjet (2026): Pricing, Features and Which to Choose

Path: /blog/reloop-vs-mailjet
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-mailjet
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/reloop-vs-mailjet.md

Reloop vs Mailjet compared honestly: pricing after Mailjet's September 2026 update, the send API, templates, inbound email and agent inboxes, automations, deliverability, self-hosting, and how to switch.

**Mailjet is a mature email platform that does both marketing and transactional mail, with a drag-and-drop editor that non-developers can use.** Reloop does the same two jobs from a developer-first angle. The differences: **Reloop costs $10 for 50k emails where Mailjet's cheapest 50k plan is $40, it receives mail into real inboxes your agents can reply from, and it's open source, so you can run it yourself.** Mailjet has a more polished visual editor, and the two free tiers are the same size.

We build Reloop, so weigh this accordingly. Mailjet prices below are from [mailjet.com/pricing](https://www.mailjet.com/pricing/) and its [September 9, 2026 pricing update](https://documentation.mailjet.com/hc/en-us/articles/25750983876763-Mailjet-Subscription-Pricing-Update-September-9-2026). Where Mailjet is the better pick, we say so.

---

## The 30-second comparison

| | **Reloop** | **Mailjet** |
|---|---|---|
| Free tier | 6,000 / mo, 200 / day | 6,000 / mo, 200 / day |
| 50,000 emails / mo | **$10** | $40 (Essential) / $59 (Premium) |
| 100,000 emails / mo | **$20** | $112 (Premium) |
| Automations | Every plan | Premium plan |
| Dedicated IP | Included on Growth ($20) | Premium, 100k+ plans, on request |
| Open source | Yes (Apache 2.0) | No |
| Self-host | Yes | No |
| Inbound email | Mailboxes with threads, API, MCP, IMAP | Parse API posts each message to your webhook |
| Agent inbox | Yes | No |
| Drag-and-drop editor | Templates in code or HTML | Yes, a strong one |
| SMTP relay | Yes | Yes |

Both change prices from time to time. Check the pricing pages before you commit.

---

## Pricing at real volumes

Mailjet has five tiers: Free, Starter ($9), Essential, Premium and Custom. The September 2026 update raised Essential and Premium. Monthly prices now look like this:

| Monthly volume | Reloop | Mailjet Essential | Mailjet Premium |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3,000 | $0 | $0 (Free) | $0 (Free) |
| 15,000 | $10 | $19 | $29 |
| 50,000 | $10 | $40 | $59 |
| 100,000 | $20 | See calculator | $112 |
| 250,000 | $20 + $75 overage = $95 | See calculator | $265 |

Mailjet takes 10% off for annual billing. Reloop's overage is $0.50 per 1,000 emails above your plan.

What stands out:

- **The free tiers match.** Both give you 6,000 emails a month and 200 a day, so under 6,000 a month neither costs anything.
- **Above the free tier, the gap is wide.** At 50k a month you'd pay $40 or $59 on Mailjet and $10 on Reloop. At 100k, it's $112 on Premium vs $20.
- **Features are gated by plan on Mailjet.** Segmentation starts on Essential; automations, team management and the dedicated IP are Premium. On Reloop, every plan gets the same product. Plans differ only by volume, plus a dedicated IP on Growth.

If you self-host Reloop, there's no per-email fee at all. See [self-hosted email infrastructure](/blog/self-hosted-email-infrastructure) for what that really takes.

<Callout type="tip">
  Price the plan you'll need, not just the volume. On Mailjet, needing automations means Premium, even at 15k emails a month.
</Callout>

---

## Developer experience

Mailjet's v3.1 Send API takes a `Messages` array with PascalCase fields and authenticates with an API key and a secret key.

**Mailjet**

```typescript

const mailjet = Mailjet.apiConnect(
  process.env.MJ_APIKEY_PUBLIC!,
  process.env.MJ_APIKEY_PRIVATE!,
);

await mailjet.post("send", { version: "v3.1" }).request({
  Messages: [
    {
      From: { Email: "hello@acme.com", Name: "Acme" },
      To: [{ Email: "user@example.com" }],
      Subject: "Welcome",
      HTMLPart: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
    },
  ],
});
```

**Reloop**

```typescript

const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: process.env.RELOOP_API_KEY! });

const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
  from: "Acme <hello@mail.acme.com>",
  to: "user@example.com",
  subject: "Welcome",
  html: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
});
```

The Mailjet SDK throws on failure, so you wrap calls in `try`/`catch`. Reloop returns errors as values. A few more differences:

| | Reloop | Mailjet |
|---|---|---|
| Auth | One API key (`x-api-key`) | API key + secret key (basic auth) |
| Field style | `from`, `to`, `html` | `From`, `To`, `HTMLPart` |
| Error format | `message`, `why` and `fix` | Status code plus per-message errors |
| Template variables | `{{{first_name}}}` | `{{var:first_name}}` with `TemplateLanguage: true` |
| React Email | Pass a component or rendered HTML | Pass rendered HTML |
| Official SDKs | Node, Python, Go, PHP, Ruby, Rust, Java, .NET, Elixir | Node, Python, PHP, Ruby, Java, Go, C# |

Reloop's errors tell you **why** a send failed and **how to fix it**:

```json
{
  "message": "Domain not found",
  "why": "The domain mail.acme.com was not found or is not authorized for your organization",
  "fix": "Ensure the domain is registered and verified in your dashboard"
}
```

---

## Receiving email and agent inboxes

**Mailjet** handles inbound with its Parse API: you point a domain's MX at Mailjet, and each incoming message is posted to your webhook as JSON. Storing, threading and replying is up to you.

**Reloop** receives mail into **mailboxes**. Messages are stored, threaded, spam-scored with Rspamd, and readable over the API, the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) or IMAP. Replying in-thread is one call, and an `email.received` webhook is there if you also want push.

That matters if you're building:

- **AI agents that handle email.** Give an agent an address, let it read the thread and reply. See [build an AI agent that reads and replies to email](/blog/build-ai-agent-sends-emails).
- **Support or shared inboxes** where humans and agents work the same threads.
- **Reply handling** for transactional mail.

| | Reloop | Mailjet |
|---|---|---|
| Receive on your domain | Yes | Yes (Parse API) |
| Stored mailboxes with threads | Yes | No |
| Reply in thread via API | Yes | Build it yourself |
| MCP access for agents | Yes | No |
| IMAP access | Yes | No |

---

## Marketing, contacts and automations

This is Mailjet's home ground. It started as a marketing tool, and it shows:

- A **drag-and-drop email editor** that marketers can use without touching HTML, plus a brand kit and form builder.
- **Segmentation** on Essential, and **automations** and **landing pages** on Premium.
- **Subaccounts** to separate brands or clients.

Reloop covers the same ground with a developer slant: contacts with custom properties, groups, subscription channels, scheduled broadcast campaigns, and **event-triggered automations** that start when your app tracks an event like `user.signed_up`. Automations are on every plan, including Free. See [welcome sequences that convert](/blog/welcome-email-sequences-that-convert) for a worked example.

If the people building your emails are marketers who want a visual editor, Mailjet is the friendlier tool. If they're developers who want templates in code and automations triggered from the app, Reloop fits better.

---

## Deliverability

Deliverability mostly comes down to your domain setup and list hygiene. Both cover the basics: SPF and DKIM, bounce and spam-complaint events, open and click tracking, and suppression of bad addresses.

The differences:

- **Dedicated IPs.** Mailjet offers one on Premium plans of 100k and above, on request. Reloop includes one on Growth at $20 a month.
- **Sending path.** Reloop runs its own MTA (KumoMTA) with per-domain throttling and automatic pauses when bounce or complaint rates spike. Read [how bounce processing works](/blog/email-bounce-processing-automation).
- **Validation.** Mailjet bundles email validation credits on Essential and Premium. Reloop ships a free [temp email checker](/tools/temp-email-checker) and [domain reputation](/tools/domain-reputation-checker) and [blocklist](/tools/blocklist-checker) checkers.

---

## Self-hosting and lock-in

Mailjet is hosted only. Your templates, contacts, logs and suppression lists live in Mailjet's account.

Reloop is Apache 2.0. You can:

1. Start on Reloop Cloud.
2. Move to your own server later with the [one-command installer](/self-host) or [Coolify](/blog/reloop-coolify-setup).
3. Keep the same API. Point the SDK's `baseUrl` at your instance and nothing else in your code changes.

That helps with data residency, with security reviews that need to read the code handling your users' mail, and as insurance against price changes like September's.

Self-hosting isn't free in effort: you own IP reputation, warm-up and uptime. Most teams should start hosted and keep self-hosting as an option.

---

## Where Mailjet is the better choice

- **Marketers build your emails.** The drag-and-drop editor, brand kit, forms and landing pages are built for people who don't write HTML.
- **You manage many brands or clients** and want subaccounts in one billing account.

Shopping around after the price change? See the [best Mailjet alternatives](/blog/best-mailjet-alternatives).

## Where Reloop is the better choice

- **You send more than the free tier.** $10 vs $40 at 50k and $20 vs $112 at 100k adds up quickly.
- **You want automations without a Premium plan.**
- **You need inbound mail as real inboxes**, especially for AI agents.
- **You need open source or self-hosting** for compliance, residency or peace of mind.

---

## Switching from Mailjet to Reloop

1. **Add your domain in Reloop** and publish the DKIM record (`reloop._domainkey`). Merge `include:reloop.sh` into your existing SPF record rather than adding a second one.
2. **Swap the client.** Replace `mailjet.post("send", { version: "v3.1" })` with `reloop.mail.send`, and map `From`/`To`/`Subject`/`HTMLPart`/`TextPart` to `from`/`to`/`subject`/`html`/`text`.
3. **Move templates.** Export the HTML from Mailjet and change placeholders to triple braces: `{{var:first_name}}` becomes `{{{first_name}}}`.
4. **Import contacts and suppressions.** Export contacts, unsubscribes and bounced addresses from Mailjet and import them, so you never mail someone who opted out.
5. **Point webhooks** at a new handler. Reloop events are named `email.delivered`, `email.bounced`, `email.complained` and so on, and are signed with HMAC-SHA256 in the `Reloop-Signature` header.
6. **Rebuild automations** as event-triggered automations, and call `reloop.automations.start` from your app where the trigger happens.
7. **Ramp traffic** from 10% to 100% over a week or two, then remove Mailjet's DNS records.

Our [SendGrid migration guide](/blog/migrating-from-sendgrid) walks through the same steps in more detail, including a traffic-split flag and a suppression import script.

# Best Cloudflare Email Service Alternatives in 2026: Send From Workers Without the Limits

Path: /blog/best-cloudflare-email-alternatives
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-cloudflare-email-alternatives
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-cloudflare-email-alternatives.md

The best Cloudflare Email Service alternatives of 2026 compared: Reloop, Resend, Amazon SES, Postmark, ZeptoMail, MailerSend and Mailgun on price, DNS requirements, templates, webhooks, inbound and marketing mail.

**Cloudflare Email Service is the most convenient way to send email from a Worker**: one binding, one `send()` call, no API key. It's also new, narrow by design, and tied to Cloudflare. Sending entered public beta in April 2026, your domain has to use Cloudflare DNS, and it only allows transactional mail.

**The short version:** if you want the same easy sending from Workers plus templates, webhooks, campaigns and real inboxes, **Reloop** is the closest alternative, and it's cheaper than Cloudflare below about 200k emails a month. If you want the most polished hosted API, **Resend**. If raw price per email is everything, **Amazon SES**. For prepaid, transactional-only sending, **ZeptoMail**.

We build Reloop, so weigh our entry accordingly. Facts about each provider come from our researched head-to-head posts, linked in each section, and each section says where that provider wins.

---

## Why teams look for a Cloudflare Email Service alternative

Cloudflare's email sending is a strong option for Workers-only apps. The reasons people look elsewhere are specific:

- **It's in beta.** Sending is still labeled public beta, which matters if you need a vendor SLA for password resets.
- **Cloudflare DNS is required.** Cloudflare's own guide says you must use Cloudflare DNS to use Email Service. If your domain lives at Route 53 or your registrar, that's a migration.
- **Transactional only.** No newsletters, product announcements or lifecycle campaigns.
- **No real free tier for users.** The free plan only sends to addresses you've verified in your own account. Sending to customers needs Workers Paid.
- **Events go to Queues, not webhooks.** Delivery events land in Cloudflare Queues, so you consume them inside Cloudflare.
- **Missing pieces.** Stored templates, idempotency keys, dedicated IPs and open and click tracking aren't documented.
- **Limits.** 50 recipients and 5 MiB per email, and new accounts start on a conservative daily quota.

Full breakdown: [Reloop vs Cloudflare Email Service](/blog/reloop-vs-cloudflare-email).

## 1. Reloop: best overall Cloudflare Email Service alternative

[Reloop](/) is open-source email infrastructure: a transactional API, SMTP relay, templates, signed webhooks, inbound mailboxes, contacts, campaigns and event automations. It runs its own MTA (KumoMTA), and **Reloop Cloud runs on Hetzner, a German hosting company, with EU data centers**.

From a Worker, it's the SDK with the `nodejs_compat` flag, or one `fetch` call. Our [Cloudflare Workers guide](/blog/send-email-cloudflare-workers) covers both:

```typescript

  async fetch(request: Request, env: { RELOOP_API_KEY: string }) {
    const reloop = new Reloop({ apiKey: env.RELOOP_API_KEY });

    const { response, emailError } = await reloop.mail.send({
      from: "Acme <welcome@mail.acme.com>",
      to: "user@example.com",
      subject: "Welcome",
      html: "<p>Thanks for signing up.</p>",
    });

    return Response.json(emailError ?? response);
  },
};
```

**Pricing:** Free for 6,000 emails a month (200 a day). Pro is $10 for 50,000, Growth is $20 for 100,000 with a dedicated IP, and extra mail is $0.50 per 1,000. Or skip the plan and buy prepaid credits at $0.50 per 1,000, valid for 6 months. Self-hosting under Apache 2.0 has no per-email fee.

**Strengths**

- **Any DNS provider.** Keep your domain where it is.
- A real free tier you can use with customers.
- Stored templates with `{{{variables}}}`, `Idempotency-Key` retries, and errors returned as values with `message`, `why` and `fix`.
- Signed HTTP webhooks (`Reloop-Signature`) that you can consume from a Worker or anywhere else.
- Inbound mailboxes with threads, readable over the API, the MCP server or IMAP (3, 5 and 10 hosted inboxes on Free, Pro and Growth).
- Campaigns and event automations on the same suppression list.
- The same code runs on Workers, Vercel, Fly.io or a Node server.

**Weaknesses**

- **You store one secret** (`wrangler secret put RELOOP_API_KEY`) instead of using a binding.
- **Above roughly 200k emails a month, Cloudflare's $0.35 rate is cheaper** than our $0.50 overage.

**Best for:** Workers apps that need more than transactional sending, or a domain that isn't on Cloudflare DNS. Full comparison: [Reloop vs Cloudflare Email Service](/blog/reloop-vs-cloudflare-email).

## 2. Resend: best hosted developer experience

Resend set the bar for a modern email API and created React Email. It sends through Amazon SES under the hood.

**Pricing:** free for 3,000 a month (100 a day), $20 for 50,000, $35 for 100,000, overage $0.90 per 1,000.

**Strengths:** clean API and SDKs, React Email, a big ecosystem of examples, broadcasts and contacts.

**Weaknesses:** $35 at 100k; a dedicated IP needs the $90 Scale plan plus a $30/mo add-on; inbound is a webhook per message; hosted-only.

**Best for:** teams under 50k emails a month that want the most polished hosted API. Full comparison: [Reloop vs Resend](/blog/reloop-vs-resend), or our [Resend alternative](/alternatives/resend) page.

More options: [Resend alternatives](/blog/best-resend-alternatives)

## 3. Amazon SES: cheapest per email

If Cloudflare's appeal for you was price, SES is cheaper still: $0.10 per 1,000 emails, plus $0.12 per GB of outbound data.

**Strengths:** the lowest per-email price of any hosted option; deep AWS integration.

**Weaknesses:** a sandbox you must request to leave; bounce and complaint handling through SNS or EventBridge that you build; no dashboard beyond CloudWatch; no marketing. Calling it from a Worker means signing AWS requests.

**Best for:** AWS-native teams sending at very high volume. Full comparison: [Reloop vs Amazon SES](/blog/reloop-vs-aws-ses).

ZeptoMail from Zoho, now part of Zoho CPaaS, sells email on prepaid credits: one credit sends 10,000 emails, the first is free, and credits last 6 months.

**Pricing:** about $2.50 per credit (varies by region): roughly $12.50 for 50,000 and $25 for 100,000.

**Strengths:** no monthly fee; cheaper than Reloop above about 150,000 a month; Mail Agents separate products and environments; any DNS provider.

**Weaknesses:** like Cloudflare, marketing mail isn't allowed. No inbound mailboxes, and credits expire.

## How to choose

- **"Our app is all-in on Workers and only sends receipts and resets."** Stay on Cloudflare Email Service. It's a good fit.
- **"Our domain isn't on Cloudflare DNS."** Reloop, Resend or ZeptoMail.
- **"We need onboarding emails, newsletters or automations too."** Reloop.
- **"We need to receive and reply to email, for support or AI agents."** Reloop's mailboxes, readable over API, MCP or IMAP.
- **"We need a GA product with an SLA today."** Any of the established providers here instead of a beta.
- **"We want the lowest price at millions of emails."** Amazon SES, or self-hosted Reloop.

---

## Switching from Cloudflare Email Service

1. **Verify your domain** with the new provider. Cloudflare's onboarding added records on a `cf-bounce` subdomain; leave them until you've fully switched, then remove them. Merge the new provider's include into your existing SPF record rather than adding a second one.
2. **Store an API key** as a Worker secret, for example `wrangler secret put RELOOP_API_KEY`.
3. **Replace `env.EMAIL.send(...)`** with the new SDK call. On Reloop that's `reloop.mail.send(...)`; rename `replyTo` to `reply_to`, and check `emailError` instead of catching exceptions.
4. **Move event handling** from your Queues consumer to an HTTP webhook handler. On Reloop, verify the `Reloop-Signature` header.
5. **Import suppressions** so you don't email addresses that bounced or complained.
6. **Ramp traffic** over one to two weeks and watch bounce and complaint rates.

# Best Mailtrap Alternatives in 2026: For Sending and for Testing

Path: /blog/best-mailtrap-alternatives
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-mailtrap-alternatives
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-mailtrap-alternatives.md

The best Mailtrap alternatives of 2026 compared: Reloop, Resend, Postmark, MailerSend, Mailgun and SendGrid for production sending, plus Mailpit for free local email testing. Prices at 50k and 100k, dedicated IPs, inbound and self-hosting.

**The short version:** Mailtrap is two products, so the right alternative depends on which one you're replacing. **For production sending**, **Reloop** is $10 at 50,000 emails a month (Mailtrap is $20) and includes a dedicated IP at $20 for 100k, where Mailtrap needs its $85 Business plan. **For testing**, **Mailpit** is a free, open-source capture server you run locally or in CI. Many teams use one of each.

We build Reloop, so weigh our pick accordingly. Every competitor price below comes from the provider's public pricing page, linked in each section, and each section says where that provider beats us.

---

## Why teams look for a Mailtrap alternative

Mailtrap started as the place developers send test email so it never reaches real users. It later added a production sending API and a marketing product. It's well built, and its testing sandbox is genuinely good. Teams look elsewhere for a few reasons:

- **Three products, three bills.** Email API/SMTP (sending), Email Sandbox (testing) and Email Marketing are priced separately, each with its own free tier.
- **Dedicated IPs mean Business.** A dedicated IP starts with the Business plan at $85 for 100,000 emails.
- **The sandbox free tier is small.** 50 test emails a month; paid sandbox plans start at $14 a month billed annually.
- **Marketing is contact-priced and separate.** The free tier allows 500 contacts and 1,500 emails a month.
- **Hosted only.** No source and no self-hosting.

If you're happy with both products, stay. If not, here are the options for each job.

## 1. Reloop: best overall for sending

Reloop is open-source email infrastructure: a transactional API, SMTP relay, inbound mailboxes, contacts, campaigns, automations and webhooks in one product. Use it hosted (Reloop Cloud runs on Hetzner, a German hosting company, with EU data centers) or run the same code on your own server.

**Pricing:** Free is 6,000 emails a month (200 a day). Pro is $10 for 50,000. Growth is $20 for 100,000 and includes a dedicated IP. Extra mail is $0.50 per 1,000. Or skip the subscription and buy pay-as-you-go credits at $0.50 per 1,000, valid for 6 months. Self-hosting is free under Apache 2.0.

**Strengths**

- **Half Mailtrap's price at 50k**: $10 vs $20, and $20 vs $30 at 100k.
- **A dedicated IP at $20**, instead of moving to an $85 Business plan.
- **Campaigns and event-triggered automations included**, with one suppression list for transactional and marketing mail. No separate contact-priced marketing product.
- **Inbound as real mailboxes.** Mail is stored, threaded, spam-scored with Rspamd, and readable over the API, the [MCP server](/docs/integrations/ai-tools/mcp-server) or IMAP. Hosted plans include 3, 5 or 10 inboxes on Free, Pro and Growth.
- Errors come back with `message`, `why` and `fix`.

**Weaknesses**

- **No capture-only test sandbox.** For staging, keep Mailtrap's sandbox or run Mailpit (below).
- Open and click tracking are on for new domains; switch them off per domain if you don't want them.

**Best for:** teams sending more than a few thousand emails a month who want sending, inboxes and campaigns in one place.

## 7. Mailpit: best free testing sandbox

If you use Mailtrap for its sandbox, the closest free replacement is [Mailpit](https://github.com/axllent/mailpit), an MIT-licensed email testing tool. It runs an SMTP server that captures everything you send, with a web UI to inspect it. It's the actively maintained successor in spirit to MailHog, which no longer gets updates.

**Pricing:** free and open source.

**Strengths**

- A single static binary or a Docker image; the web UI is on port `8025` and SMTP on `1025` by default.
- A REST API for automated integration tests, so CI can assert that an email was sent and check its contents.
- HTML compatibility scoring across mail clients, link checking and SpamAssassin spam scoring.

**Weaknesses**

- You run it yourself, per developer or per environment. There's no shared hosted inbox for the whole team out of the box.
- It's a testing tool only; it doesn't deliver mail to real inboxes in production.

**Best for:** local development and CI. Point your app's staging SMTP settings at Mailpit, and production at your real sender.

## How to choose

- **"We need to cut the sending bill."** Reloop: $10 at 50k and $20 at 100k with a dedicated IP.
- **"We need a dedicated IP without the Business plan."** Reloop includes one on Growth at $20.
- **"We like Mailtrap's free sending tier and send under 4,000 a month."** Mailtrap is hard to beat there; stay.
- **"We only used Mailtrap for testing."** Mailpit locally and in CI, or keep Mailtrap's sandbox if you want a hosted, shared inbox.
- **"Marketers edit our templates."** MailerSend.
- **"Legal wants source code or self-hosting."** Reloop is the only sender here that's open source.

<Callout type="tip">
  You don't have to replace both products at once. A common setup is a capture tool (Mailtrap's sandbox or Mailpit) for staging and a production sender for real users. Keep the two configured by environment so staging can never email a customer.
</Callout>

## Switching from Mailtrap sending

1. **Add your domain** in the new provider and publish its DKIM record. Merge the new SPF include into your existing record; never publish a second SPF record.
2. **Swap the client.** On Reloop, replace `mailtrap.send` with `reloop.mail.send`, turn `{ name, email }` objects into `"Name <email>"` strings, and check `emailError` instead of catching.
3. **Move templates.** On Reloop, change placeholders to triple braces: `{{{user_name}}}`.
4. **Import your suppression list** so you don't re-mail addresses that bounced or complained.
5. **Point webhooks** at a new handler. Reloop signs events with HMAC-SHA256 in the `Reloop-Signature` header.
6. **Split environments.** Staging SMTP points at your sandbox (Mailtrap or Mailpit); production points at `smtp.reloop.sh` on port 587 with STARTTLS, using your API key as both username and password.
7. **Ramp traffic** from 10% to 100% over a week or two, then remove Mailtrap's sending DNS records.

The [Reloop vs Mailtrap](/blog/reloop-vs-mailtrap) post has the detailed version, and the [SendGrid migration guide](/blog/migrating-from-sendgrid) shows a traffic-split flag that works for any provider.

## FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="What is the cheapest Mailtrap alternative for sending?">
    Among full platforms, Reloop is $10 for 50,000 emails and $20 for 100,000
    with a dedicated IP. Mailtrap itself is $20 and $30 at those volumes, and
    its free tier (4,000 a month) is smaller than Reloop's 6,000.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Is there a free alternative to Mailtrap's sandbox?">
    Yes. Mailpit is an MIT-licensed tool that captures email over SMTP and
    shows it in a web UI, with an API for tests. You run it yourself, locally
    or in CI.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Is there an open-source alternative to Mailtrap?">
    For sending, Reloop is open source under Apache 2.0 and can be self-hosted.
    For testing, Mailpit is open source under MIT.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can I keep Mailtrap's sandbox and send with another provider?">
    Yes. The sandbox works with any sender. Point staging at Mailtrap's
    sandbox and production at your new provider's SMTP or API.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Will my deliverability drop if I leave Mailtrap?">
    Not if your domain is set up properly. Inbox placement depends mostly on
    SPF, DKIM, DMARC, list hygiene and steady sending patterns. Ramp traffic
    over a week or two and check your domain with the free
    [domain reputation checker](/tools/domain-reputation-checker).
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

# Introducing Pay as You Go: Email Credits That Last 6 Months

Path: /blog/introducing-pay-as-you-go
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/introducing-pay-as-you-go
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/introducing-pay-as-you-go.md

Buy Reloop email credits once at $0.50 per 1,000 and use them over 6 months. No subscription, no daily cap, and your free 6,000 emails a month still come first.

Email volume is rarely a straight line. A product launch, a seasonal sale or a viral week can send ten times your usual volume, and then things go quiet again. A subscription makes you pay for the peak every month.

Today Reloop gets **pay as you go**: buy email credits once, use them over 6 months, no subscription. Credits sit on top of the [free tier](/blog/reloop-free-tier), so you only pay for what goes past 6,000 emails a month.

## What you get

## How it works

1. **Your free 6,000 comes first.** Each month the free allowance is used before any credits, so a quiet month costs nothing.
2. **Credits cover the rest.** Anything past 6,000 in a month comes out of your credit balance.
3. **Pro limits while you hold credits.** With an active balance, the 200-a-day cap is gone and you get Pro's limits: 5 inboxes, 5 webhooks, 5 domains and 5 MB attachments.
4. **Top up any time.** A new pack adds to your balance and resets the 6-month clock on all of it.
5. **When credits run out or expire,** your account goes back to the free tier. Your domains, templates and data stay.

<Callout type="tip">

## Who it's for

Pay as you go fits anyone whose sending doesn't look the same every month:

- **Launches and campaigns.** 2,000 emails most months and 40,000 when you ship something big.
- **Seasonal businesses.** Busy in November and December, quiet the rest of the year.
- **New products.** You don't know your volume yet and don't want a subscription before you do.
- **Agencies and side projects.** Many small projects that each send in bursts.
- **One-off sends.** A migration notice or a policy update to your whole user base.

If your volume is steady every month, a [monthly plan](/blog/introducing-monthly-plans) is usually cheaper. Credits and Pro cost the same at about 26,000 emails a month. The full math is in [pay as you go vs monthly: how to choose](/blog/pay-as-you-go-vs-monthly-email-pricing).

- **No surprise bills.** Credits are paid up front. Nothing renews without you.
- **Still open source.** [Self-host](/self-host) with no license fee if you'd rather run it yourself.

# Best Elastic Email Alternatives in 2026: Budget Senders Compared

Path: /blog/best-elastic-email-alternatives
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-elastic-email-alternatives
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/best-elastic-email-alternatives.md

The best Elastic Email alternatives of 2026 compared: Reloop, Amazon SES, ZeptoMail, Brevo, Mailjet, MailerSend and Mailgun on price at 50k and 100k emails, webhooks, inbound, dedicated IPs and self-hosting.

**The short version:** people choose Elastic Email to keep costs down, so the alternatives worth looking at are the ones that stay cheap. **Reloop** is $10 for 50,000 emails with webhooks, inbound mailboxes and campaigns on every plan, and $20 for 100,000 with a dedicated IP. **Amazon SES** and **ZeptoMail** are cheaper per email if you only need a sending pipe and are happy to build the rest.

We build Reloop, so weigh our entry accordingly. Every price below comes from the provider's own pricing page, and each section says where that provider beats us.

---

## Why teams look for an Elastic Email alternative

Elastic Email is one of the longest-running budget providers, and its free API tier (3,000 a month, 100 a day) is one of the more generous ones. The usual reasons people move:

- **Key features sit on the $49 Pro plan.** Webhooks and inbound processing aren't on Free or the $19 Starter plan ([Email API pricing](https://elasticemail.com/email-api-pricing)).
- **Short log retention.** Logs are kept for 3 days on Free and Starter, 7 days on Pro.
- **The dedicated IP is an add-on.** $40 a month on Starter, $50 on Pro.
- **Two separate products.** The Email API and the Email Marketing app are priced and managed separately.

If you send millions of emails a month and only need sending, Elastic Email's volume slider may still be your cheapest option. Price it against the alternatives below at your real volume.

## Switching from Elastic Email

1. **Export your suppression list** (bounces and unsubscribes) and import it into the new provider.
2. **Verify your domain.** Merge the new SPF include into your existing record and add the new DKIM record. See our [SPF, DKIM and DMARC guide](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide).
3. **Rebuild templates.** Elastic Email's `{firstname}` merge fields become the new syntax; on Reloop that's `{{{firstname}}}`.
4. **Swap the client**, or change the SMTP host and credentials. On Reloop: `smtp.reloop.sh`, port 587 with STARTTLS, and your API key as both username and password.
5. **Move webhooks** and ramp traffic over one to two weeks.

# Is My Email Blacklisted? How to Check Your Domain and IP (and Get Removed)

Path: /blog/email-blacklist-check
URL: https://reloop.sh/blog/email-blacklist-check
Markdown: https://reloop.sh/blog/email-blacklist-check.md

Find out if your domain or sending IP is on an email blacklist in two minutes, what a listing actually means, and the exact steps to get delisted from Spamhaus, Barracuda, SpamCop and more.

**To check if your email is blacklisted, enter your domain and your sending IP address into a blocklist checker such as the [free Reloop Blocklist Checker](/tools/blocklist-checker).** It looks both up on 42 public blacklists at once. If either one shows up on Spamhaus, Barracuda or SpamCop, fix whatever caused it first, then request removal on that list's own website.

That is the two-minute version. The rest of this guide explains what a blacklist is, how to find the IP address you actually send from (most people check the wrong one), which listings matter, and how to get removed.

---

## What is an email blacklist?

An email blacklist (also called a blocklist, DNSBL or RBL) is a public list of IP addresses and domain names that have been caught sending spam, hosting malware or behaving like a hacked server.

Mail servers check these lists every time an email arrives. If the sender is on a list the receiving server trusts, the email gets:

- **Rejected outright**, with a bounce message such as `550 5.7.1 Service unavailable; client host blocked using zen.spamhaus.org`
- **Sent to spam**, with no error at all
- **Delayed**, while the receiving server decides what to do

There are two kinds of listing, and you should check both:

| Type | What is listed | Example lists | What it affects |
|------|----------------|---------------|-----------------|
| **IP blacklist** | The server address your email leaves from | Spamhaus ZEN, Barracuda BRBL, SpamCop | Every email sent from that IP, whatever the domain |
| **Domain blacklist** | Your domain name, wherever it appears | Spamhaus DBL, URIBL, SURBL | Any email that contains your domain, in the From address or in a link |

<Callout type="info">
  A domain listing follows you. Changing email providers fixes an IP listing, but if your domain is listed, every email that mentions it can be blocked until the listing is removed.
</Callout>

---

## Signs you might be blacklisted

You do not need to be technical to spot these:

- Emails to some people bounce back with words like **"blocked"**, **"blacklisted"**, **"listed"**, **"Spamhaus"** or **"poor reputation"** in the error
- Customers say your emails suddenly started landing in spam
- Open rates fell sharply overnight without any change on your side
- A whole company (one domain) stopped receiving your emails, while Gmail users still get them
- Your website or email host sent you a warning about outgoing spam

If one of these is happening, run a check before changing anything else.

---

## Step 1: Find the IP address you actually send from

**This is where most blacklist checks go wrong.** Your website's IP address is usually not the address your email leaves from.

It depends on how you send:

| How you send email | Whose IP is it? |
|--------------------|-----------------|
| Gmail, Google Workspace, Outlook, Microsoft 365 | Google's or Microsoft's shared servers. You rarely need to check these; the provider handles them. |
| An email service such as Reloop, SendGrid or Mailgun | The provider's IP, shared with other customers unless you pay for a dedicated IP |
| Your own server, VPS or WordPress host | Your server's IP. You are fully responsible for it. |

The reliable way to find it is from an email you have already sent:

1. Send an email from your normal address to a Gmail account you own.
2. Open it in Gmail, click the three dots, and choose **Show original**.
3. Look for the SPF line. It names the IP address directly:

```http
Received-SPF: pass (google.com: domain of hello@yourdomain.com
  designates 203.0.113.10 as permitted sender)
```

In this example `203.0.113.10` is your sending IP. Note it down alongside your domain name.

---

## Step 2: Check the domain and IP against blacklists

### The quick way (anyone)

Open the [Reloop Blocklist Checker](/tools/blocklist-checker) and enter your **domain**, then your **sending IP**. It checks:

- **35 IP blacklists**, including Spamhaus ZEN, Barracuda BRBL, SpamCop, UCEPROTECT and Mailspike
- **7 domain blacklists**, including Spamhaus DBL, URIBL and SURBL

It is free and needs no sign-up. If a lookup on a list fails, it shows an error rather than a false "clean" result.

<Callout type="tip">
  Check your domain too, not just your IP. If your domain publishes dedicated `ip4:` addresses in its SPF record, the checker looks those IPs up automatically.
</Callout>

### The command-line way (developers)

Blacklists are DNS zones, so you can query them with `dig`. Reverse the IP's four numbers and add the list's hostname:

```bash
# IP 203.0.113.10 against Spamhaus ZEN (note the reversed octets)
dig +short 10.113.0.203.zen.spamhaus.org

# Domain against Spamhaus DBL
dig +short yourdomain.com.dbl.spamhaus.org
```

- **No answer**: not listed on that list.
- **An answer in `127.0.0.x`**: listed. The last number tells you which sub-list.
- **`127.255.255.254`**: not a listing. Spamhaus refuses queries sent through public DNS resolvers such as `8.8.8.8` or `1.1.1.1`. Run the query from a different resolver, or use a checker.

To automate the check, call the public API (no API key, 60 requests per minute):

```bash
curl -X POST https://reloop.sh/api/tools/v1/blocklist-check \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "target": "203.0.113.10" }'
```

Add it to a daily cron job or uptime monitor so you hear about a listing before your customers do.

---

## Step 3: Decide if the listing actually matters

**Not every listing is an emergency.** There are hundreds of blacklists and most large mailbox providers ignore the majority of them.

| List | How much it matters | Notes |
|------|---------------------|-------|
| **Spamhaus ZEN / DBL** | Critical | Used by a very large share of mail servers. Fix it immediately. |
| **Barracuda BRBL** | High | Common in business email filters. |
| **SpamCop** | Medium to high | Clears itself about 24 hours after spam reports stop. |
| **URIBL / SURBL** | High for links | Blocks emails containing your domain in links. |
| **Spamhaus PBL** | Usually fine | Lists home and dynamic IPs that should not send mail directly. Expected for a home connection; a problem only if it is your mail server. |
| **UCEPROTECT Level 2 / 3** | Low | Lists entire networks for a neighbour's behaviour. Few major providers use it. You don't need to pay for express removal. |

<Callout type="warning">
  Gmail, Outlook and Yahoo mostly rely on their own private reputation data, not public blacklists. A clean blacklist result does not guarantee inbox placement. Check [Google Postmaster Tools](https://postmaster.google.com) and Microsoft [SNDS](https://sendersupport.olc.protection.outlook.com/snds/) as well.
</Callout>

---

## Step 4: Fix the cause before you ask for removal

Blacklists list you for a reason. If you request removal without fixing it, you are relisted, often faster and for longer the second time.

The usual causes, roughly from most to least common:

1. **A hacked account or password.** Someone is sending spam through your email account, SMTP credentials or website contact form. Change passwords, rotate API keys and look for sending you don't recognise.
2. **A bad email list.** Bought lists, old lists and scraped addresses contain **spam traps**: addresses that exist only to catch senders who don't get permission. Remove anyone who has not opted in or engaged recently.
3. **A sudden volume spike.** Going from 50 emails a day to 50,000 on a new IP or domain looks like a spammer. [Warm up gradually](/blog/ip-warming-guide).
4. **Too many bounces and complaints.** Keep hard bounces under 2% and spam complaints under 0.1%. [Automate bounce handling](/blog/email-bounce-processing-automation) so dead addresses are suppressed.
5. **Missing authentication.** Without [SPF, DKIM and DMARC](/blog/spf-dkim-dmarc-setup-guide), anyone can send email pretending to be you, and your domain takes the blame.
6. **A shared IP neighbour.** On a shared IP, another customer's spam can list the IP you share. Your provider should handle this; if it keeps happening, ask them about it or move to a provider that polices its IPs.

---

## Step 5: Request removal (delisting)

Once the cause is fixed, go to the list's own removal page. **Removal is free on every reputable list.** Be careful with anyone who offers to delist you for a fee.

| List | How to get removed |
|------|--------------------|
| **Spamhaus** | Look up your IP or domain at [check.spamhaus.org](https://check.spamhaus.org) and follow the removal instructions for that listing |
| **Barracuda** | Submit the [Barracuda removal request form](https://www.barracudacentral.org/rbl/removal-request); usually processed within 12 to 24 hours |
| **SpamCop** | No form. The listing expires about 24 hours after spam reports stop. |
| **Microsoft (Outlook, Hotmail)** | If Outlook rejects you, request delisting at [sender.office.com](https://sender.office.com) |
| **UCEPROTECT Level 1** | Expires automatically after 7 days without new spam |
| **Others** | The checker links to each list's removal page when it finds a hit |

When you write the removal request, say briefly what went wrong and what you changed. "A contact form was abused by a bot; we added a CAPTCHA and rotated credentials" gets processed much faster than "please remove us".

After removal, run the check again 24 to 48 hours later to confirm the listing is gone.

---

## How to stay off blacklists for good

- **Only email people who asked for it.** Never buy lists.
- **Authenticate your domain** with SPF, DKIM and DMARC. Gmail and Yahoo now [require it for bulk senders](/blog/gmail-yahoo-bulk-sender-requirements).
- **Suppress bounces and complaints automatically**, so you never email the same dead address twice.
- **Use a separate subdomain for marketing**, such as `news.yourdomain.com`, so a campaign problem does not hit your password resets and receipts.
- **Protect your forms** with CAPTCHA and rate limits, and [block disposable emails at signup](/blog/block-disposable-emails-at-signup).
- **Monitor weekly.** A scheduled call to the blocklist API catches listings in hours instead of weeks.

---

## FAQ

<AccordionGroup>
  <Accordion title="How do I check if my email domain is blacklisted for free?">
    Enter your domain into the free [Reloop Blocklist Checker](/tools/blocklist-checker).
    It looks the domain up on 7 domain blacklists, including Spamhaus DBL, URIBL
    and SURBL, and checks any dedicated sending IPs listed in your SPF record. No
    sign-up is needed.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Can a Gmail or Outlook address be blacklisted?">
    Not in the usual sense. When you send from a free Gmail or Outlook address,
    you send from Google's or Microsoft's servers, and those providers manage
    their own IP reputation. Your individual account can still be limited or
    suspended for sending spam, but that is not a public blacklist.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="How long does it take to get off a blacklist?">
    Most reputable lists remove a fixed listing within 24 to 48 hours. SpamCop
    expires on its own about a day after reports stop, and UCEPROTECT Level 1
    after 7 days. Repeat listings take longer each time.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Why am I blacklisted when I never sent spam?">
    The most common reasons are a hacked password or contact form sending spam
    without your knowledge, an old list that contains spam traps, or sharing an
    IP address with another sender who did send spam. Spamhaus PBL also lists
    home and dynamic IP addresses by design, which is not an accusation of
    spam.
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Is a blacklist the same as going to spam?">
    No. A blacklist is one possible cause of spam placement. Missing SPF, DKIM
    or DMARC, poor engagement and spammy content are others. If you are not
    listed but still land in spam, follow our guide on [why emails land in
    spam](/blog/why-emails-land-in-spam-fix).
  </Accordion>

  <Accordion title="Should I pay to be removed from a blacklist?">
    No. Spamhaus, Barracuda, SpamCop and other major lists remove you for free
    once the problem is fixed. Lists that charge for removal are generally not
    ones the big mailbox providers rely on.
  </Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>
